questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with primary myelofibrosis, in which his bone marrow is progressively replaced by fibrosis, is found on exam to have marked hepatosplenomegaly. A biopsy of the enlarged right upper quadrant organ shows clusters of developing erythroid and myeloid precursors. Reactivation of blood cell production in which of the following organs best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Kidney

choices.label: B
choices.text: Liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymph node

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yolk sac

explanation.summary: When the bone marrow fails, blood formation can resume in former fetal sites such as the liver and spleen (extramedullary hematopoiesis).
explanation.whyCorrect: The liver and spleen serve as hematopoietic organs during fetal life and are normally inactive after birth, but they can revert to producing blood cells when the marrow cannot, such as in bone marrow failure or fibrosis. This is termed extramedullary hematopoiesis and produces the hepatosplenomegaly seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The kidney secretes erythropoietin but is not itself a site of blood cell production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid tissue and are not described as sites that revert to hematopoiesis in marrow failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thymus supports T-cell maturation, not erythroid and myeloid precursor production, and is not a reserve hematopoietic organ.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The yolk sac is an embryonic hematopoietic site that ceases and does not persist into postnatal life.

questions.stem: During a study of fetal development, blood cell production is examined at the fourth month of gestation. Which of the following organs is the chief site of hematopoiesis at this stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kidney

choices.label: C
choices.text: Liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yolk sac

explanation.summary: The fetal liver is the main hematopoietic organ from roughly the second to the seventh month of gestation.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the earliest embryonic hematopoiesis, stem cells infiltrate the liver, which functions as the hematopoietic system from the second to the seventh months of gestation. The fourth month therefore falls within the period of dominant hepatic blood formation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bone marrow only takes over as the definitive site beginning around the seventh month of gestation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The kidney produces erythropoietin later in life but is not a hematopoietic organ.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thymus is a site of T-cell maturation, not the primary organ of overall blood cell production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The yolk sac is the earliest embryonic site but its contribution has ended well before the fourth month.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman requires a bone marrow biopsy to evaluate a suspected hematologic disorder. Which of the following is the preferred site for obtaining the marrow sample in this adult patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anteromedial proximal tibia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Body of the sternum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Distal radial metaphysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Midshaft of the femur

choices.label: E
choices.text: Posterior iliac crest

explanation.summary: The posterior iliac crest is the preferred site for bone marrow sampling in adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: The preferred site for bone marrow sampling is the posterior iliac crest (the back of the hip bone), which safely allows both aspiration and biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The tibia is the preferred site in infants and young children, not in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The sternum is used only as a last resort in adults, and only aspiration (not biopsy) is permitted because of the risk of injuring underlying structures.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The distal radius is not a described site for marrow sampling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The femoral shaft is not the preferred sampling location described for adults.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with fatigue and easy bruising has a peripheral blood smear showing numerous immature blast cells that are normally confined to the bone marrow. This finding is most concerning for which of the following conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leukemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polycythemia from high altitude

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactive reticulocytosis

explanation.summary: Blasts are normally restricted to the marrow; their appearance in peripheral blood suggests leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blasts are normally present in the bone marrow but not in the peripheral blood. Their presence in the peripheral blood is concerning for leukemia, a condition in which blasts overgrow due to uncontrolled proliferation of neoplastic blast cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Extramedullary hematopoiesis reflects blood formation resuming in organs such as the liver and spleen, not neoplastic blasts flooding the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deficiency anemia produces small, pale red cells, not circulating blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: High-altitude polycythemia raises mature red cell mass through erythropoietin, without producing circulating blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reticulocytosis is an increase in immature red cells, not nucleated blast cells, and reflects red cell turnover rather than malignancy.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and chronic hypoxemia is found to have an elevated red blood cell count. The increased red cell production is driven by a hormone secreted mainly by cells in which of the following organs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heart

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kidney

choices.label: D
choices.text: Liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spleen

explanation.summary: Erythropoietin, the primary stimulator of red cell production, is secreted mainly by the kidney in response to hypoxia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low systemic oxygen, as in chronic lung disease, causes the kidney to secrete erythropoietin, which can rise up to 1,000-fold during hypoxia. The kidney is the major source of erythropoietin, produced by renal interstitial cells around the peritubular capillaries of the renal cortex.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bone marrow is the target that responds to erythropoietin by making red cells, not the source of the hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The heart is not involved in secreting hormones that stimulate blood cell production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The liver is the primary erythropoietin source in the fetus and can make some in adults, but it is far less important than the kidney postnatally.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen removes aged red cells but does not secrete erythropoietin.

questions.stem: Circulating erythropoietin binds its receptor on red blood cell progenitor cells and stimulates their maturation. Activation of which of the following intracellular signaling pathways mediates this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gq protein with IP3 and diacylglycerol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gs protein and cyclic AMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Guanylate cyclase and cyclic GMP

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intracellular steroid hormone receptor acting on DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: JAK/STAT tyrosine kinase cascade

explanation.summary: Erythropoietin signals through a JAK/STAT tyrosine kinase cascade to drive red cell maturation.
explanation.whyCorrect: When circulating erythropoietin binds erythropoietin receptors on red blood cell progenitor cells at the first stage of differentiation, binding stimulates red cell maturation by activating a JAK/STAT tyrosine kinase signaling cascade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Gq/IP3/DAG pathway is a G-protein-coupled second messenger system, not the JAK/STAT cascade used by erythropoietin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Gs/cAMP pathway is used by many peptide hormones but is not the mechanism described for erythropoietin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Guanylate cyclase/cGMP signaling is used by agents such as nitric oxide, not by erythropoietin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythropoietin is a peptide hormone acting at a cell-surface receptor, not a steroid acting on an intracellular DNA-binding receptor.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing chronic kidney disease has a normocytic anemia with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count. Which of the following best explains the underlying cause of her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody-mediated destruction of circulating red cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dietary iron deficiency from poor intake

choices.label: C
choices.text: Overproduction of erythropoietin causing marrow exhaustion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced erythropoietin production by damaged renal cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency impairing DNA synthesis

explanation.summary: Anemia of chronic kidney disease results largely from failure of damaged renal cells to make enough erythropoietin.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic kidney disease, renal cells are damaged and fail to make sufficient erythropoietin, leading to reduced hematopoiesis and anemia; shortened red cell survival contributes as well. The low reticulocyte count reflects inadequate erythropoietic stimulation, and treatment uses erythropoiesis-stimulating agents such as epoetin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody-mediated hemolysis would raise, not lower, the reticulocyte count as the marrow compensates.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deficiency is a separate cause of anemia and is not the mechanism attributed to kidney disease here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic kidney disease causes a deficiency, not an excess, of erythropoietin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anemia and is not the described renal mechanism.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents with anemia. Laboratory studies show a markedly elevated reticulocyte count. This finding most strongly suggests that his anemia is caused by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aplastic marrow with absent precursors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythropoietin deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of erythropoiesis from bone marrow disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased destruction of red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Iron deficiency limiting red cell production

explanation.summary: A high reticulocyte count in an anemic patient points to increased red cell destruction, such as hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reticulocytes are counted during evaluation of anemia. Increased counts are seen when anemia is caused by increased red blood cell destruction, such as hemolysis, because the marrow responds by releasing more immature red cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An aplastic marrow lacks precursors and cannot mount a reticulocyte response, so the count would be low.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin deficiency reduces erythropoietic drive and lowers the reticulocyte count.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure of erythropoiesis from bone marrow disease produces a reduced, not elevated, reticulocyte count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron deficiency reflects failure of red cell production and is associated with a low reticulocyte response.

questions.stem: A histology student reviews the maturation of red blood cell precursors in the bone marrow. Which of the following changes normally occurs as the red cell matures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cell progressively enlarges

choices.label: B
choices.text: The chromatin becomes progressively less condensed

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cytoplasm changes from deep blue to red

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nucleus enlarges as the cell matures

choices.label: E
choices.text: The nucleus is retained in the mature red blood cell

explanation.summary: During erythropoiesis the cytoplasm shifts from deep blue to red and develops a pale center as hemoglobin accumulates.
explanation.whyCorrect: As the red cell matures, the cytoplasm turns from deep blue to red and then develops a pale center due to peripheral localization of hemoglobin. The cell shrinks, the nucleus shrinks and disappears, and the chromatin evolves from very fine to very condensed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cell shrinks rather than enlarges during maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The chromatin pattern evolves from very fine to very condensed, the opposite of becoming less condensed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nucleus shrinks, becomes darker, and disappears rather than enlarging.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mature red blood cells lack a nucleus, which is why they cannot divide.

questions.stem: A healthy adult donates blood, and the physiology of red cell turnover is discussed. Approximately how long does a normal red blood cell circulate in an adult before it is removed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1 year

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 7 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 30 days

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 60 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 120 days

explanation.summary: Adult red blood cells circulate for roughly 120 days before macrophages remove them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Red blood cells are removed from the circulation when they are around 120 days old in an adult (and 60 to 90 days old in an infant). Old red cells are cleared by macrophages in the spleen and liver.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One year greatly overestimates the roughly 120-day red cell lifespan.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About a week is the approximate lifespan of a platelet, not a red blood cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thirty days is far shorter than the roughly 120-day adult red cell lifespan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sixty days is closer to the lower end of the infant range, not the adult lifespan.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops severe neutropenia after receiving chemotherapy. She is treated with filgrastim, a recombinant colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). Increasing the number of which of the following cells is the intended effect of this therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granulocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocytes only

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cells

explanation.summary: G-CSF (filgrastim) stimulates production of granulocytes and is used for granulocytopenia after chemotherapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor increases granulocytes and can be used therapeutically as filgrastim (Neupogen) for granulocytopenia due to chemotherapy or other causes, or after bone marrow transplantation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B-cell growth is promoted by cytokines such as IL-4, not by G-CSF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G-CSF specifically raises granulocytes; agents such as M-CSF or GM-CSF are the ones tied to monocyte increases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet production is stimulated by thrombopoietin, not by G-CSF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Red blood cell production is driven by erythropoietin, not G-CSF.

questions.stem: A megakaryocyte in the bone marrow is a very large cell, 50 to 100 micrometers in diameter, with a single prominent enlarged nucleus. This large polyploid nucleus develops through which of the following processes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apoptosis, in which the nuclear membrane fragments during programmed cell death

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binary fission, in which the nucleus divides into separate diploid nuclei

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endomitosis, in which chromosomes replicate without nuclear division

choices.label: D
choices.text: Meiosis, in which two successive divisions produce haploid daughter cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ordinary mitosis, in which replicated chromosomes segregate into two identical cells

explanation.summary: Megakaryocytes enlarge through endomitosis, replicating DNA without dividing the nucleus or cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: When megakaryocyte precursors receive growth signals from thrombopoietin, they undergo endomitosis, a unique type of mitosis in which the nuclear and cellular components divide but do not separate. There is chromosomal replication without nuclear division, unlike ordinary mitosis and meiosis where cells split into two.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, not the mechanism by which the megakaryocyte grows and becomes polyploid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The nucleus becomes a single enlarged polyploid nucleus rather than splitting into separate nuclei.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meiosis produces haploid gametes and does not describe megakaryocyte enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ordinary mitosis splits a cell into two identical cells, whereas endomitosis specifically avoids separation.

questions.stem: In an experiment tracing the earliest blood-forming cells of a human embryo, labeled progenitors are found in mesoderm surrounding the main dorsal artery of the trunk before any labeled cells appear in the liver. These cells are arising from which of the following regions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) region

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatic sinusoids of the embryonic liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Periosteal layer of the developing long bones

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymic epithelial primordium of the third pouch

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yolk sac wall adjacent to the vitelline duct

explanation.summary: The stem cells first observed in the embryo derive from mesoderm surrounding the aorta, an area called the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) region.
explanation.whyCorrect: The stem cells that are first observed in the embryo are derived from the mesoderm surrounding the aorta in an area referred to as the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) region. From there these cells infiltrate the liver, which functions as the hematopoietic system from the second to the seventh months of gestation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The liver is colonized by stem cells that come from elsewhere rather than generating the first ones itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The periosteum contributes vascular connective tissue that later invades the forming bone; it is not the source of the first embryonic stem cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thymus supports T-cell maturation and is not where the earliest embryonic hematopoietic stem cells arise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The yolk sac is an early embryonic hematopoietic site, but it is not the mesoderm surrounding the aorta described here.

questions.stem: In a normally developing fetus, hematopoietic stem cells leave the liver, colonize the bone marrow, and set up shop producing mature blood cells there. This shift occurs at approximately which month of gestation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fifth month

choices.label: B
choices.text: First month

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ninth month

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seventh month

choices.label: E
choices.text: Third month

explanation.summary: Stem cells move from the liver to the bone marrow in the seventh month of gestation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The liver functions as the hematopoietic system from the second to the seventh months of gestation. In the seventh month, these stem cells move from the liver, colonize the bone marrow, and begin producing mature blood cells there.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The fifth month is still within the second-to-seventh-month window of hepatic hematopoiesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The first month falls within the earliest embryonic period, when the yolk sac rather than the marrow is producing blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: By the ninth month the marrow has already taken over; the transfer occurs earlier, in the seventh month.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The third month is within the interval when the liver is serving as the hematopoietic system.

questions.stem: During fetal development, hematopoietic stem cells are deposited inside the forming bones and become the progenitors of marrow blood cells. Which of the following events allows the stem cells to gain access to the interior of the bone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cartilage cells within the shaft dedifferentiate and transform directly into hematopoietic stem cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphatic channels arising from the joint capsule carry stem cells inward through the epiphyseal growth plate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stem cells migrate out of the spleen and travel along nerve fibers that enter the bone at the epiphysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymic T-cell progenitors seed the marrow cavity before the cartilage model of the bone is formed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vascular connective tissue arising from the periosteum invades and breaks the cartilage in the forming bone

explanation.summary: Periosteum-derived vascular connective tissue breaks down the cartilage of the forming bone, depositing stem cells that become marrow progenitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stem cells move from the liver to the bone marrow when vascular connective tissue, arising from the surrounding periosteum, invades and breaks the cartilage within the forming bone. This leads to the deposition of invading stem cells that serve as progenitors for hematopoietic cells within the bone, and the process continues toward the ends of the bones, or epiphyses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cartilage is broken down by the invading tissue; cartilage cells do not convert into hematopoietic stem cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Invasion is by vascular connective tissue from the periosteum, not by lymphatic channels entering from the joint.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stem cells arriving at the marrow come from the liver, and they arrive with invading vascular connective tissue rather than along nerves from the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thymus is a site of T-cell maturation and does not seed the marrow with hematopoietic stem cells.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant with persistent pancytopenia requires a bone marrow sample. Which of the following is the preferred sampling site at this age?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calvarium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Distal femur

choices.label: C
choices.text: Posterior iliac crest

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sternum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tibia

explanation.summary: The tibia is the site used for marrow sampling in infants and young children.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sites for bone marrow sampling include the posterior iliac crest, the sternum, and the tibia, with the tibia being the site used for infants and young children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The calvarium is not among the described bone marrow sampling sites.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The distal femur is not among the described bone marrow sampling sites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The posterior iliac crest is the preferred site in adults, not the site used for infants and young children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sternum is reserved for adults as a last resort, and only aspiration rather than biopsy is allowed there because of the risk of injuring underlying structures.

questions.stem: A marrow progenitor is committed to the lymphoid line rather than the myeloid line. Which of the following mature cells is this progenitor capable of producing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basophilic granulocyte

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating platelet

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eosinophilic granulocyte

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mature erythrocyte

choices.label: E
choices.text: Natural killer cell

explanation.summary: The lymphoid line gives rise to the lymphocyte and its derivatives, including natural killer cells, B cells, T cells, and plasma cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: As hematopoietic stem cells differentiate, they develop within two groups. The lymphoid line gives rise to the lymphocyte and its derivatives, such as natural killer cells, B cells, T cells, and plasma cells, while the myeloid line produces the remaining blood cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophils are granulocytes derived from myeloblasts in the myeloid line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelets are produced by the myeloid line through megakaryocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eosinophils are granulocytes produced by the myeloid line from myeloblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythrocytes are myeloid line products arising from the erythroid precursors.

questions.stem: A bone marrow precursor is committed to producing a circulating cell that later migrates into tissues and becomes a macrophage. From which of the following precursors does this circulating cell develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lymphoblast

choices.label: B
choices.text: Megakaryoblast

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monoblast

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myeloblast

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proerythroblast

explanation.summary: Within the myeloid line, monoblasts develop into monocytes, which migrate into tissues to form macrophages.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the myeloid cell line, white blood cells can develop in two directions: monoblasts develop into monocytes, while myeloblasts develop into neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. Cytokines such as IL-13 and interferon-gamma drive migration of monocytes to tissues to form macrophages.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphoblasts lead to B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells within the lymphoid line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Megakaryoblasts differentiate into megakaryocytes, which shed platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myeloblasts give rise to the three granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils), not to monocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Proerythroblasts are the first recognizable stage of red blood cell development.

questions.stem: In a healthy adult, aged red blood cells are cleared by macrophages in the spleen and liver, and the marrow must replace them at a similar rate. This clearance occurs at approximately which of the following daily rates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2 x 10^11 cells per day

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 x 10^15 cells per day

choices.label: C
choices.text: 2 x 10^18 cells per day

choices.label: D
choices.text: 2 x 10^3 cells per day

choices.label: E
choices.text: 2 x 10^6 cells per day

explanation.summary: Macrophages of the spleen and liver remove about 2 x 10^11 red cells per day, and erythropoiesis must match that rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Old red blood cells are removed from the circulation by macrophages in the spleen and liver at a rate of about 2 x 10^11 cells per day, so the body must make new red blood cells at a similar rate. This is why effective erythropoiesis is critical to maintaining health.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This figure greatly exceeds the stated daily turnover of red blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This figure is far larger than the number of red cells cleared each day.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A few thousand cells per day would be far too few to account for normal red cell turnover.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two million cells per day underestimates daily red cell clearance by many orders of magnitude.

questions.stem: Effective erythropoiesis must continue throughout life at a very high rate. Which of the following properties of the mature erythrocyte best explains this requirement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It converts into a leukocyte after several weeks in the circulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It divides only once before being cleared from the blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is retained in the marrow and never reaches the peripheral blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lacks a nucleus and therefore cannot divide to make new cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It undergoes endomitosis and loses the ability to make hemoglobin

explanation.summary: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, so they cannot divide and must be continuously replaced by the marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Effective erythropoiesis is critical to maintain health because mature red blood cells lack nuclei and so cannot divide to make new cells, unlike most other body cells. New cells must therefore be produced continuously to replace those removed from the circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Red cells do not convert into white blood cells; the two arise from separate maturation pathways.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mature red cell does not divide at all, because it has lost its nucleus during maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The erythrocyte is the predominant cell of the peripheral blood, not a marrow-restricted cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endomitosis is the process that enlarges megakaryocytes, not a feature of erythrocytes.

questions.stem: A hematology fellow orders the erythroid precursors on a marrow smear according to their normal developmental sequence. Which of the following cells is the immediate precursor of the reticulocyte?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basophilic erythroblast with blue cytoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Early polychromatophilic erythroblast

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metamyelocyte of the neutrophil series

choices.label: D
choices.text: Orthochromatophilic erythroblast

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proerythroblast, the earliest erythroid cell

explanation.summary: The erythroid sequence runs proerythroblast, basophilic erythroblast, polychromatophilic erythroblast, orthochromatophilic erythroblast, reticulocyte, and erythrocyte.
explanation.whyCorrect: The red blood cell developmental sequence takes place over about a week and proceeds from the proerythroblast through the basophilic and polychromatophilic erythroblasts to the orthochromatophilic erythroblast, which is the stage immediately preceding the reticulocyte and then the mature erythrocyte.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The basophilic erythroblast follows the proerythroblast and still has deeply blue cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The polychromatophilic erythroblast precedes the orthochromatophilic stage rather than the reticulocyte itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The metamyelocyte belongs to the neutrophil maturation sequence, not to erythropoiesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The proerythroblast is the earliest recognizable erythroid cell, several stages before the reticulocyte.

questions.stem: A stained peripheral smear shows a population of cells identified as reticulocytes, whose cytoplasm has a slight lilac tinge compared with the surrounding mature red cells. Which of the following best accounts for this appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A retained fragment of condensed nuclear chromatin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron-laden mitochondria ringing the cell membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peripheral localization of hemoglobin producing a pale center

choices.label: D
choices.text: Purple azurophilic granules with antimicrobial activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residual RNA left behind after nuclear extrusion

explanation.summary: Reticulocytes retain a small amount of RNA, which gives their cytoplasm a slight lilac tinge.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reticulocytes include a bit of RNA, which gives the cytoplasm a slight lilac tinge. In normal blood they constitute about 1% to 2% of the total erythrocyte count, and that percentage rises during increased erythropoiesis such as after acute blood loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The nucleus shrinks, darkens, and disappears before the reticulocyte stage, so no chromatin remains.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lilac tinge is attributed to residual RNA rather than to mitochondria or iron deposits.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peripheral localization of hemoglobin creates the pale center of the mature red cell, not a lilac cytoplasmic tinge.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Azurophilic granules are a feature of leukocytes and are responsible for antimicrobial activity.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is evaluated for anemia. Her reticulocyte count is below the normal 1% to 2% of the total erythrocyte count. Which of the following best explains this combination of findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accelerated clearance of aged red cells by splenic macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute blood loss from a gastrointestinal bleed one week earlier

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis within the spleen and liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency limiting red blood cell production

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ongoing hemolysis of circulating red blood cells

explanation.summary: A low reticulocyte count in an anemic patient indicates failure of erythropoiesis, as occurs with iron deficiency or bone marrow disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reticulocytes are routinely counted during evaluation of anemia. In anemic patients, reduced reticulocyte counts suggest a failure of erythropoiesis, for example from bone marrow disease or iron deficiency, because the marrow cannot increase output of new red cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased clearance of aged red cells is a destructive process, which would be accompanied by a compensatory rise in reticulocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: After acute blood loss, increased erythropoiesis sends more reticulocytes into the blood, raising the percentage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extramedullary hematopoiesis represents blood formation resuming in the liver and spleen, not a failure to release reticulocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysis increases red cell destruction and raises rather than lowers the reticulocyte count.

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old man spends several weeks at high altitude and develops tissue hypoxia. Compared with his baseline, his erythropoietin production may increase by up to approximately which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1,000-fold

choices.label: C
choices.text: 10-fold

choices.label: D
choices.text: 2-fold

choices.label: E
choices.text: No measurable change

explanation.summary: During tissue hypoxia, erythropoietin production can rise up to 1,000-fold.
explanation.whyCorrect: When tissue oxygenation and red blood cell numbers are normal, blood erythropoietin levels are low, but during tissue hypoxia erythropoietin production may increase up to 1,000-fold. Tissue hypoxia can be due to chronic lung disease from poor ventilation or oxygen diffusion, high altitude, and other conditions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A million-fold increase overstates the maximal erythropoietin response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 10-fold rise is far below the described maximal increase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A doubling greatly understates the hypoxia-driven rise in erythropoietin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypoxia is the primary trigger for erythropoietin secretion, so levels rise substantially.

questions.stem: Erythropoietin is produced in the adult kidney. Which of the following cells is the source of this hormone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Brush border epithelial cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule of the cortex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granular juxtaglomerular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interstitial cells around the peritubular capillaries of the renal cortex

choices.label: D
choices.text: Principal cells lining the collecting duct in the renal medulla

choices.label: E
choices.text: Visceral epithelial cells (podocytes) covering the glomerular capillary tuft

explanation.summary: Renal interstitial cells located around the peritubular capillaries of the renal cortex make erythropoietin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The kidney is the major source of erythropoietin production, specifically in renal interstitial cells located around the peritubular capillaries in the renal cortex. Hepatocytes and perisinusoidal cells of the liver are the primary fetal source and can also make the hormone in adults, but they are less important than the kidney.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Proximal tubular cells perform reabsorption; erythropoietin comes from interstitial cells around the peritubular capillaries.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Juxtaglomerular granular cells are associated with renin release rather than erythropoietin production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Collecting duct principal cells handle sodium and water transport, not erythropoietin secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Podocytes form the filtration barrier of the glomerulus and are not described as erythropoietin-producing cells.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old competitive cyclist is found to have an unexplained elevated hematocrit. He admits to injecting a recombinant hormone, banned in most sports, that he obtained illicitly to improve his endurance. Which of the following hormones did he most likely use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macrophage colony-stimulating factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stem cell factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombopoietin

explanation.summary: Erythropoietin, given as epoetin alfa, is taken illicitly by some athletes for endurance and is banned in most sports.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erythropoietin can be given pharmacologically as epoetin alfa and is indicated for patients with reduced erythropoietin levels such as chronic kidney disease, as well as some patients with AIDS and with chemotherapy-induced anemia. It is also taken illicitly by some athletes to improve endurance, and its use is banned in most sports.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor raises granulocyte counts and is used for granulocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrophage colony-stimulating factor increases monocytes and would not raise the hematocrit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stem cell factor maintains hematopoietic stem cells rather than selectively expanding the red cell mass.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No pharmacologic form of thrombopoietin has been developed, and it would raise platelets rather than hematocrit.

questions.stem: Myeloblasts in the bone marrow give rise to neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. Approximately how long does this process take?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 2 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 2 hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 2 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 2 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 2 years

explanation.summary: Granulopoiesis, the production of neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils from myeloblasts, takes about 2 weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myeloblasts give rise to the three types of granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils) in a process termed granulopoiesis, which takes about 2 weeks. For comparison, the red blood cell developmental sequence takes place over about a week.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two days underestimates the roughly 2-week granulopoiesis interval.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A few hours is far too short for the full granulocyte maturation sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Two months substantially overestimates the time required for granulopoiesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two years is far longer than the stated duration of granulocyte development.

questions.stem: A marrow differential is reported using the six stages of neutrophil maturation. Which of the following stages immediately follows the metamyelocyte?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Band

choices.label: B
choices.text: Myeloblast

choices.label: C
choices.text: Myelocyte

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promyelocyte

choices.label: E
choices.text: Segmented neutrophil

explanation.summary: Neutrophil maturation proceeds myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, and segmented neutrophil.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are six stages of neutrophil maturation: myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, and segmented neutrophil. The band therefore directly follows the metamyelocyte, and although they differ in appearance, mature neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils all go through a similar process.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The myeloblast is the first stage of the sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The myelocyte precedes the metamyelocyte in the sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The promyelocyte is the second stage, well before the metamyelocyte.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The segmented neutrophil is the final stage and follows the band, not the metamyelocyte.

questions.stem: A student states that monocytes and lymphocytes are true agranulocytes because they contain no granules at all. Which of the following is the most accurate correction of this statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They acquire granules only after they have migrated out of the blood into tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: They contain granules only during fetal life and lose them at birth

choices.label: C
choices.text: They contain hemoglobin-filled granules that support oxygen transport

choices.label: D
choices.text: They contain large specific granules identical to those of the eosinophil

choices.label: E
choices.text: They contain small purple azurophilic granules responsible for antimicrobial activity

explanation.summary: All leukocytes, including monocytes and lymphocytes, carry small purple azurophilic granules with antimicrobial activity, so the term agranulocyte is not technically correct.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monocytes and lymphocytes are traditionally called agranulocytes based on a lack of visible granules under the microscope, but this is not technically correct: all leukocytes, including monocytes and lymphocytes, do in fact have small purple azurophilic granules, which are responsible for antimicrobial activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The azurophilic granules are present in these circulating cells, not acquired only after tissue migration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These granules are a feature of leukocytes generally and are not limited to fetal life.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin belongs to the erythroid line and is not packaged in leukocyte granules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The granules of monocytes and lymphocytes are small azurophilic granules, not the distinctive specific granules that give eosinophils their characteristic look.

questions.stem: A researcher removes a single signaling molecule from a marrow culture, and the undifferentiated hematopoietic stem cell pool fails to be maintained and stops dividing, although mature cell survival is unaffected. Which of the following molecules was most likely removed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interleukin-5

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macrophage colony-stimulating factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stem cell factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombopoietin

explanation.summary: Stem cell factor induces division of hematopoietic stem cells and maintains the stem cell pool.
explanation.whyCorrect: The division of hematopoietic stem cells is induced by stem cell factor (SCF), and its listed effect is that it maintains hematopoietic stem cells. Loss of this signal would therefore deplete the undifferentiated stem cell pool while leaving lineage-specific effects of other cytokines intact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor increases granulocytes rather than maintaining stem cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interleukin-5 increases eosinophils rather than maintaining the stem cell pool.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrophage colony-stimulating factor increases monocytes, a lineage-specific effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombopoietin drives megakaryocyte growth and development, leading to platelet production.

questions.stem: A patient has a markedly elevated eosinophil count while the neutrophil, basophil, and monocyte counts remain normal. Increased activity of which of the following cytokines best accounts for this selective pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Interleukin-12

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interleukin-3

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interleukin-4

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interleukin-5

choices.label: E
choices.text: Macrophage colony-stimulating factor

explanation.summary: Interleukin-5 specifically increases eosinophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the cytokines that regulate blood cell development, interleukin-5 has the listed effect of increasing eosinophils. A rise limited to eosinophils, with other myeloid lineages unchanged, fits this narrowly targeted cytokine effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Interleukin-12 increases T cells and natural killer cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interleukin-3 increases granulocytes and monocytes broadly, so the monocyte and neutrophil counts would not stay normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-4 promotes growth of B cells, which would not produce an isolated eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Macrophage colony-stimulating factor increases monocytes rather than eosinophils.

questions.stem: A single megakaryocyte in the bone marrow sheds platelets over the course of its lifetime. Approximately how many platelets does one megakaryocyte produce?

explanation.summary: Each megakaryocyte produces roughly 1,000 to 3,000 platelets during its lifetime.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each megakaryocyte can produce 1,000 to 3,000 platelets during its lifetime. To form platelets, the megakaryocyte cell membrane undergoes cavitation and folding and forms an outward projection called a proplatelet, which over time breaks down into individual platelets.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A few dozen platelets per megakaryocyte is far below the stated yield.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A few hundred platelets underestimates the output of a single megakaryocyte.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hundreds of thousands of platelets per megakaryocyte greatly exceeds the stated yield.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Millions of platelets per cell overstates megakaryocyte output by several orders of magnitude.

questions.stem: Platelets break off from megakaryocytes and enter the bloodstream, where they participate in clot formation. Approximately how long does an individual platelet survive in the circulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1 week

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 1 year

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 12 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 30 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 120 days

explanation.summary: Each platelet lives in the blood circulation for about a week.
explanation.whyCorrect: Platelets break off from the megakaryocytes, and each platelet lives in the blood circulation for about a week. Because platelets lack a nucleus, they cannot divide or create additional cellular components, so their numbers must be continuously replenished from megakaryocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A year far exceeds the circulating lifespan of a platelet.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Half a day is much shorter than the roughly one-week platelet lifespan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thirty days overestimates how long a platelet circulates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 120 days is the lifespan of an adult red blood cell, not a platelet.

questions.stem: The hormone also known as megakaryocyte growth and development factor stimulates megakaryocyte growth and development. This hormone is produced mostly by which of the following organs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kidney

choices.label: C
choices.text: Liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymus

explanation.summary: Thrombopoietin, also called megakaryocyte growth and development factor, is produced mostly by the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Megakaryocyte growth and development is stimulated by a hormone called thrombopoietin, which is produced mostly by the liver. Its alternative name, megakaryocyte growth and development factor, describes exactly what it does.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bone marrow houses the megakaryocytes that respond to the hormone rather than producing it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The kidney is the major source of erythropoietin, whereas thrombopoietin comes mostly from the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen removes aged blood cells and can host extramedullary hematopoiesis, but it is not the source of this hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymus supports T-cell maturation and does not secrete thrombopoietin.

questions.stem: A patient's circulating platelet count falls below normal, and the measured thrombopoietin level in the blood rises. Which of the following best explains the increase in circulating hormone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endomitosis within megakaryocytes discharges thrombopoietin into marrow sinusoids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fewer circulating platelets are available to bind and clear thrombopoietin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Megakaryocytes begin secreting thrombopoietin once the platelet count falls

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelets release stored thrombopoietin as they are consumed within clots

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal interstitial cells increase thrombopoietin output in response to hypoxia

explanation.summary: Thrombopoietin is regulated by a negative feedback loop in which circulating platelets bind and clear the hormone.
explanation.whyCorrect: A negative feedback loop regulates the amount of thrombopoietin in the body: thrombopoietin is bound and cleared by circulating platelets, so if the number of platelets dips below normal, the amount of thrombopoietin in the circulation increases and the bone marrow produces more platelets. Conversely, increased platelets clear more thrombopoietin, lowering the hormone level and reducing platelet production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endomitosis is how megakaryocytes become large and polyploid and does not release hormone into the sinusoids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Megakaryocytes respond to thrombopoietin with growth and development; they are not the source of the hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The feedback works through reduced binding and clearance by platelets, not through release of a stored hormone pool.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal interstitial cells around the peritubular capillaries secrete erythropoietin in response to hypoxia, not thrombopoietin.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has chronic thrombocytopenia from suppressed platelet formation. Her physician notes that no pharmacologic form of the hormone that drives megakaryocyte development has been developed, but that an agent stimulating its receptor is available. Which of the following agents is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epoetin alfa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Filgrastim

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recombinant interleukin-3

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recombinant stem cell factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Romiplostim

explanation.summary: Thrombopoietin mimetics such as eltrombopag and romiplostim stimulate the thrombopoietin receptor when platelet formation is suppressed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike erythropoietin, there is no pharmacologic form of thrombopoietin yet developed, which could be useful clinically to stimulate platelet formation in disorders where formation is suppressed (thrombocytopenia). However, pharmacologic thrombopoietin mimetics, or analogues, that stimulate the thrombopoietin receptor are available, and these include eltrombopag and romiplostim.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epoetin alfa is the pharmacologic form of erythropoietin and stimulates red cell maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Filgrastim is granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, used for granulocytopenia rather than thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-3 increases granulocytes and monocytes and does not act at the thrombopoietin receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stem cell factor maintains hematopoietic stem cells and is not a thrombopoietin receptor agonist.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman comes to the clinic with worsening shortness of breath and blue-gray discoloration of her lips and nail beds. She recently started taking a nitrate for angina. Examination shows tachycardia and cyanosis. Pulse oximetry reads 85%, but arterial blood gas analysis shows a normal PaO2, and the cyanosis does not improve with supplemental oxygen. A drawn blood sample appears chocolate brown. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydroxocobalamin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methylene blue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Packed red blood cell transfusion

explanation.summary: Nitrate-induced acquired methemoglobinemia is treated with methylene blue.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitrates/nitrites are oxidants that convert ferrous heme iron (Fe2+) to ferric iron (Fe3+), forming methemoglobin that cannot bind oxygen and produces cyanosis with chocolate-brown blood, a normal PaO2, and cyanosis refractory to oxygen. Methylene blue is the first-line treatment for acquired methemoglobinemia because it activates the NADPH-methemoglobin reductase pathway to reduce metHb back to functional hemoglobin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydroxocobalamin is the antidote for cyanide poisoning, not methemoglobinemia; the vignette describes nitrate exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The cyanosis is refractory to oxygen because the defect is oxidized hemoglobin, so hyperbaric oxygen would not correct it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron corrects iron-deficiency anemia; the problem here is oxidation of existing heme iron, not iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion does not address the oxidized hemoglobin already present and is not the primary therapy for acquired methemoglobinemia.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with jaundice and dark urine two days after starting an antimalarial drug for travel prophylaxis. Laboratory studies show anemia, an elevated reticulocyte count, decreased haptoglobin, and increased serum LDH. A peripheral smear shows bite cells and red cells containing insoluble inclusions of denatured hemoglobin. A deficiency of which of the following enzymes best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythrocyte bisphosphoglycerate mutase

choices.label: B
choices.text: NADH-dependent cytochrome b5 reductase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Erythrocyte lactate dehydrogenase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red cell pyruvate kinase isoenzyme

explanation.summary: Oxidant-triggered hemolysis with Heinz bodies and bite cells indicates G6PD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: G6PD generates NADPH, the sole source of reducing power for glutathione-based antioxidant defense in the mature RBC. When an oxidative trigger (such as an antimalarial drug, infection, or fava beans) overwhelms this defense, hemoglobin is oxidatively denatured into insoluble Heinz bodies; splenic macrophages remove these, creating bite cells and hemolytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase makes 2,3-BPG to modulate hemoglobin affinity and is not linked to oxidant-triggered hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency causes methemoglobinemia (cyanosis, chocolate-brown blood), not oxidative hemolysis with bite cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LDH is elevated as a marker of hemolysis; its deficiency does not produce this oxidant-triggered picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolysis from ATP depletion, not oxidant-triggered episodes with Heinz bodies and bite cells.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is evaluated for an acute hemolytic episode that occurred during a febrile illness. A G6PD activity assay obtained during the acute event returns within the normal range, yet his clinical picture strongly suggests G6PD deficiency. Which of the following best explains the falsely normal enzyme activity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Catalase compensates by directly regenerating G6PD activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated 2,3-BPG interferes with the enzyme assay

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fever denatures the assay reagents, artificially raising measured activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mature RBCs continuously synthesize new G6PD to replace defective enzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reticulocytes contain higher, kinetically normal G6PD activity

explanation.summary: Reticulocytosis during hemolysis raises measured G6PD activity and can mask deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Older RBCs have the lowest G6PD activity and lyse first, while newly released reticulocytes contain recently synthesized, kinetically normal G6PD. Testing during a hemolytic crisis, when the reticulocyte count is high, can yield falsely elevated activity. Guidelines therefore recommend testing about 3 months (roughly the 120-day RBC lifespan) after an episode.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase detoxifies hydrogen peroxide but does not regenerate or substitute for G6PD activity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 2,3-BPG modulates hemoglobin oxygen affinity and does not interfere with the G6PD assay.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The falsely normal result reflects the cell population sampled, not denatured assay reagents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mature RBCs lack a nucleus and cannot synthesize new enzyme, which is precisely why aged cells accumulate defective G6PD.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant has had jaundice and anemia since birth. Studies show chronic hemolysis, splenomegaly, and pigmented gallstones. Genetic testing identifies a deficiency of an erythrocyte enzyme that normally provides about half of the ATP produced by glycolysis. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this deficiency causes hemolysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of oxidized hemoglobin forming Heinz bodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of ATP-dependent ion pumps, producing rigid, dehydrated red cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired NADPH generation with loss of glutathione recycling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased hemoglobin oxygen affinity that traps oxygen in the RBC

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidation of heme iron from the ferrous to the ferric state

explanation.summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency depletes ATP, disabling ion pumps and making RBCs rigid and prone to lysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the final ATP-generating step of glycolysis (about 50% of glycolytic ATP). Without adequate ATP, the Na+/K+ pump fails, cells lose water and shrink, intracellular hemoglobin concentration and cytosolic viscosity rise, and the membrane becomes rigid with erratic protrusions, making the cells vulnerable to shear forces and premature clearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heinz bodies and oxidative denaturation characterize G6PD deficiency, not the ATP-depletion mechanism of pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of NADPH and glutathione recycling is the mechanism of G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is actually associated with elevated 2,3-BPG that decreases affinity and improves oxygen delivery, not increased affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidation of heme iron describes methemoglobin formation, a different disorder.

questions.stem: A researcher studies how mature erythrocytes rapidly adjust the position of the oxygen dissociation curve. She focuses on a molecule synthesized in red cells specifically to lower hemoglobin affinity for oxygen. This molecule is produced from a glycolytic intermediate by a dedicated mutase. Which of the following is this molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbaminohemoglobin (HbCO2)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactate from anaerobic glycolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced NADP (NADPH)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced glutathione (GSH)

explanation.summary: 2,3-BPG is made from 1,3-BPG by bisphosphoglycerate mutase to lower Hb oxygen affinity.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the Rapoport-Luebering shunt, bisphosphoglycerate mutase diverts the glycolytic intermediate 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to form 2,3-BPG. 2,3-BPG stabilizes the deoxygenated state of hemoglobin, lowering oxygen affinity and shifting the curve to the right; RBCs modulate affinity rapidly by favoring its synthesis or degradation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbaminohemoglobin forms from CO2 binding hemoglobin, not from bisphosphoglycerate mutase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactate is produced from pyruvate to regenerate NAD+ for glycolysis; it lowers pH but is not the product of bisphosphoglycerate mutase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NADPH is generated by G6PD in the pentose phosphate pathway for antioxidant defense, not to modulate oxygen affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced glutathione is an antioxidant regenerated using NADPH, unrelated to bisphosphoglycerate mutase.

questions.stem: A physiology instructor explains why mature erythrocytes must produce lactate even when oxygen is abundant. Which of the following features of the mature red blood cell best accounts for this obligatory lactate production?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A high rate of oxidative phosphorylation in abundant mitochondria

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absence of mitochondria, limiting ATP production to glycolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dependence on insulin-stimulated GLUT4 for glucose uptake

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lack of the enzyme glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Presence of abundant enzymes for fatty acid beta-oxidation

explanation.summary: Lacking mitochondria, RBCs rely on glycolysis and regenerate NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mature erythrocytes lack all organelles, including mitochondria, so ATP production is limited to substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis. To keep glycolysis running, NAD+ must be regenerated, which is accomplished by reducing pyruvate to lactate; complete oxidation of glucose is impossible without mitochondria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Without mitochondria, RBCs cannot perform oxidative phosphorylation at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RBCs take up glucose via GLUT1 independent of insulin and lack insulin receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GAPDH is present and functions in glycolysis; its NADH also supports metHb reduction via cytochrome b5 reductase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RBCs lack mitochondria and do not perform fatty acid (beta) oxidation.

questions.stem: During prolonged fasting, most tissues shift their fuel utilization, yet red blood cells continue to rely on the same fuel source regardless of dietary state. Consistent with this behavior, mature erythrocytes lack receptors for both insulin and glucagon. Which of the following best explains the unwavering reliance of RBCs on this single fuel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They depend on glycolysis and use GLUT1 to take up glucose

choices.label: B
choices.text: They oxidize ketone bodies when glucose is scarce

choices.label: C
choices.text: They perform gluconeogenesis to sustain their own glucose supply

choices.label: D
choices.text: They store glycogen for use during fasting

choices.label: E
choices.text: They switch to fatty acids as their primary energy source

explanation.summary: RBCs use glucose exclusively via insulin-independent GLUT1 transport in all dietary states.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because RBCs depend entirely on glycolysis for ATP, they must take in circulating glucose continuously. They use GLUT1 to transport glucose even at low concentrations seen with prolonged fasting, and because their fuel does not change with dietary state, they have no need for insulin or glucagon receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ketone body oxidation requires mitochondria, which RBCs lack.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gluconeogenesis occurs in the liver, not in erythrocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mature RBCs do not store glycogen; they rely on circulating glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fatty acid oxidation requires mitochondria and does not occur in RBCs.

questions.stem: In the mature red blood cell, the pentose phosphate pathway is the only source of a reducing cofactor essential for antioxidant defense. Loss of this cofactor impairs the regeneration of reduced glutathione. Which of the following cofactors is produced by glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase to serve this role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATP

choices.label: B
choices.text: FADH2

choices.label: C
choices.text: NADH

choices.label: D
choices.text: NADPH

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate

explanation.summary: G6PD produces NADPH, the sole reducing power in RBCs for regenerating glutathione.
explanation.whyCorrect: G6PD catalyzes the first reaction of the pentose phosphate pathway and generates NADPH. In mature RBCs the PPP is the sole source of NADPH, which glutathione reductase uses to regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH) from its oxidized dimer; GSH then neutralizes oxidants via glutathione peroxidase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP is the energy currency from glycolysis, not the reducing cofactor for glutathione.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FADH2 is generated in mitochondrial pathways, which RBCs lack.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NADH is produced by GAPDH in glycolysis and feeds cytochrome b5 reductase, not glutathione recycling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a coenzyme for transketolase, not the product of G6PD used to regenerate glutathione.

questions.stem: A newborn is noted to have persistent cyanosis and chocolate-brown blood, but arterial PaO2 is normal and the cyanosis does not respond to oxygen. There is no cardiac or pulmonary disease. The infant is found to have a congenital deficiency of the enzyme that normally keeps methemoglobin levels below about 1%. Which of the following enzymes is deficient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytochrome b5 reductase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glutathione peroxidase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyruvate kinase

explanation.summary: Cytochrome b5 reductase normally reduces metHb, and its deficiency causes congenital methemoglobinemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methemoglobin is maintained at very low levels chiefly by cytochrome b5 reductase, which uses NADH formed by GAPDH in glycolysis to reduce ferric heme back to functional ferrous hemoglobin. A congenital deficiency of this enzyme is a cause of congenital methemoglobinemia, presenting with cyanosis and chocolate-brown blood with a normal PaO2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase produces 2,3-BPG and does not reduce methemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G6PD deficiency causes oxidative hemolytic anemia; the NADPH-metHb reductase pathway contributes minimally to routine metHb reduction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glutathione peroxidase neutralizes oxidants but does not reduce methemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolytic anemia from ATP depletion, not methemoglobinemia.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with known G6PD deficiency develops symptomatic acquired methemoglobinemia after a chemical exposure. The physician notes that the usual first-line treatment is relatively discouraged in this patient. Which of the following best explains why methylene blue is contraindicated in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Methylene blue depletes 2,3-BPG, raising hemoglobin oxygen affinity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methylene blue inhibits cytochrome b5 reductase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methylene blue is only effective for congenital forms of methemoglobinemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methylene blue oxidizes ferrous iron to ferric iron, worsening metHb

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduction of methemoglobin by methylene blue is NADPH-dependent

explanation.summary: Methylene blue works through an NADPH-dependent pathway that G6PD-deficient patients cannot support.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methylene blue reduces methemoglobin by activating NADPH-methemoglobin reductase, which relies on NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway. G6PD-deficient patients already have a diminished NADPH pool, so stimulating an additional NADPH-requiring pathway can potentiate hemolysis, making methylene blue relatively contraindicated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The contraindication relates to NADPH dependence, not to 2,3-BPG depletion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methylene blue does not inhibit cytochrome b5 reductase; it acts through the separate NADPH-dependent enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methylene blue is the typical treatment for acquired forms and is actually less effective for congenital forms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methylene blue reduces, not oxidizes, methemoglobin; it does not worsen metHb by oxidation.

questions.stem: During vigorous exercise, working skeletal muscle becomes warm and acidic and accumulates carbon dioxide. These local conditions alter the oxygen dissociation curve of hemoglobin. Which of the following best describes the effect on hemoglobin and its physiologic benefit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased oxygen affinity, impairing oxygen release to tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased oxygen affinity, promoting oxygen delivery to tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased oxygen affinity, promoting oxygen loading in tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased oxygen affinity, shifting the curve to the left

choices.label: E
choices.text: No change in affinity, since local conditions do not affect hemoglobin

explanation.summary: Low pH, high pCO2, and high temperature shift the curve right, unloading oxygen where it is needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low pH (the Bohr effect), elevated pCO2, and high temperature each decrease hemoglobin oxygen affinity and shift the dissociation curve to the right (higher p50). In active, warm, acidic, CO2-rich muscle, this decreased affinity promotes release of oxygen to the tissues that need it most.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased affinity actually enhances oxygen release to tissues, which is the physiologic benefit, not an impairment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These conditions decrease, not increase, affinity, and a right shift favors unloading rather than loading.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A left shift with increased affinity is the opposite of the Bohr effect produced by these conditions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Local pH, CO2, and temperature clearly do alter hemoglobin affinity.

questions.stem: A patient with confirmed methemoglobinemia has a pulse oximetry reading of approximately 85% that does not change despite escalating supplemental oxygen. Which of the following is the most reliable method to accurately measure this patient's methemoglobin level?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calculated oxygen saturation from PaO2 on arterial blood gas

choices.label: B
choices.text: Co-oximetry

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peripheral blood smear

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum haptoglobin measurement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standard pulse oximetry

explanation.summary: Co-oximetry is required to accurately quantify methemoglobin, which confounds pulse oximetry.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methemoglobin interferes with wavelength-based pulse oximetry, driving the reading toward roughly 85% regardless of true saturation. Because pulse oximetry is unreliable, co-oximetry, which measures multiple hemoglobin species directly, is needed to obtain an accurate methemoglobin level.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PaO2 is typically normal in methemoglobinemia, so a calculated saturation overestimates oxygenation and does not measure metHb.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A blood smear evaluates cell morphology but does not quantify methemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Haptoglobin is a marker of hemolysis and does not measure methemoglobin levels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulse oximetry is exactly what is confounded by methemoglobin and reads about 85% regardless of severity.

questions.stem: An investigator perfuses a purified adult hemoglobin solution that has been stripped of 2,3-BPG and CO2 with buffers of progressively lower pH and records a stepwise rise in p50. Which of the following molecular events best accounts for the fall in oxygen affinity produced by the change in pH?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coordination of protons directly by the porphyrin iron center

choices.label: B
choices.text: Displacement of heme from its binding pocket in the beta chains

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dissociation of the tetramer into four independent globin monomers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidation of the heme iron from the ferrous to the ferric state

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protonation of select histidine residues within the globin chains

explanation.summary: The Bohr effect lowers hemoglobin oxygen affinity through protonation of select histidine residues.
explanation.whyCorrect: A lower pH environment protonates select histidine residues on hemoglobin, which causes the tetramer to adopt a conformation with lower affinity for oxygen. The curve shifts right and p50 rises, which physiologically increases oxygen delivery to tissues. No oxidation of iron or change in quaternary assembly is required.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Protons act on amino acid side chains such as histidine, not by binding the porphyrin iron center.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heme remains within its binding pocket; low pH alters affinity through residue protonation rather than heme loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin remains a tetramer over this pH range; the affinity change is conformational, not a loss of subunit assembly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidation of heme iron to the ferric state produces methemoglobin, a separate phenomenon that is not what protons do to hemoglobin.

questions.stem: Blood flowing through the capillary bed of exercising muscle takes up carbon dioxide. Most of the resulting fall in hemoglobin oxygen affinity is attributed to protons generated through the bicarbonate buffer system, but a second, smaller mechanism also contributes. Which of the following best describes that additional mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbon dioxide activates bisphosphoglycerate mutase to generate additional 2,3-BPG

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbon dioxide binds hemoglobin to form carbaminohemoglobin of lower oxygen affinity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbon dioxide is reduced to carbon monoxide, which competes for the heme iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Carbon dioxide oxidizes the heme iron to the ferric state, producing methemoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Carbon dioxide raises intracellular temperature, which augments dissociation of bound gas

explanation.summary: CO2 enrichment also forms carbaminohemoglobin, which has decreased affinity for oxygen binding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elevated pCO2 shifts the bicarbonate blood buffer toward carbonic acid, raising [H+] and producing the Bohr effect. To a smaller extent, enriching CO2 also augments formation of carbaminohemoglobin (HbCO2), a species with decreased affinity for oxygen binding, which further favors unloading in metabolically active tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2,3-BPG is formed from the glycolytic intermediate 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; carbon dioxide is not the stimulus for bisphosphoglycerate mutase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbon dioxide is not converted to carbon monoxide in the erythrocyte; CO is an exogenous poison, not a CO2 metabolite.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidation of heme iron to the ferric state generates methemoglobin and is driven by oxidant chemicals, not by carbon dioxide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: High temperature does lower affinity, but it is a separate parameter and is not produced by carbon dioxide uptake.

questions.stem: An instructor lists low pH, elevated pCO2, high temperature, and 2,3-BPG as natural modulators of hemoglobin affinity, then notes that carbon monoxide also alters hemoglobin affinity but is classified differently. Which of the following best explains why carbon monoxide is regarded as a poison rather than a modulator?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It changes hemoglobin affinity in an unregulated and detrimental fashion

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is generated within the erythrocyte itself as a byproduct of glycolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is neutralized by glutathione peroxidase before it ever reaches hemoglobin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lowers affinity so profoundly that peripheral tissues become over-oxygenated

choices.label: E
choices.text: It oxidizes the porphyrin iron to the ferric state within a few minutes

explanation.summary: Physiologic modulators adjust Hb affinity dynamically, whereas CO imposes an unregulated, harmful change.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protons, CO2, temperature, and 2,3-BPG are natural mechanisms that modulate hemoglobin affinity so oxygen delivery tracks tissue need. Carbon monoxide also alters affinity, but it does so in an unregulated, decremental manner that the body cannot titrate, which is why it is treated as a poison.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbon monoxide is an exogenous exposure; erythrocyte glycolysis produces lactate and ATP, not CO.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutathione peroxidase neutralizes reactive oxygen species; it does not intercept carbon monoxide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carbon monoxide impairs rather than enhances oxygen delivery; tissues become hypoxic, not over-oxygenated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidation of heme iron to the ferric form describes methemoglobin generation by oxidant chemicals such as nitrites.

questions.stem: A pulmonologist reviews an oxygen dissociation curve obtained from a patient and notes that the entire curve lies to the right of the standard adult curve. Which of the following best characterizes this patient's hemoglobin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A higher p50, indicating decreased affinity for oxygen

choices.label: B
choices.text: A higher p50, indicating increased affinity for oxygen

choices.label: C
choices.text: A lower p50, indicating decreased affinity for oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: A lower p50, indicating increased affinity for oxygen

choices.label: E
choices.text: An unchanged p50, indicating only a change in hemoglobin concentration

explanation.summary: A right-shifted oxygen dissociation curve corresponds to a higher p50 and decreased oxygen affinity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The oxygen dissociation curve plots hemoglobin saturation against oxygen tension, and p50 represents relative affinity. Parameters that decrease affinity, such as low pH, elevated pCO2, high temperature, and increased 2,3-BPG, shift the curve to the right and raise p50, meaning a higher oxygen tension is required for half saturation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A higher p50 means more oxygen tension is needed for half saturation, which is decreased rather than increased affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased affinity raises p50; a lower p50 cannot accompany a right-shifted curve.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A lower p50 with increased affinity describes a left-shifted curve, the opposite of what is shown.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A shift of the curve reflects a change in affinity; hemoglobin concentration does not reposition the curve.

questions.stem: Erythrocytes make up roughly 3% of total body mass yet account for about 10% of whole-body glucose metabolism, and their rate of glucose utilization is approximately four times greater than that of any other tissue. Paradoxically, they also have one of the lowest rates of ATP synthesis in the body. Which of the following best explains this pairing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Being acellular, the red cell cannot fully combust glucose and stops at lactate

choices.label: B
choices.text: GLUT1 imports glucose far more slowly than the insulin-responsive transporters

choices.label: C
