choices.text: Glycolysis is uncoupled at pyruvate kinase, so the high-energy phosphate is wasted

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most ATP generated is exported to adjacent endothelial cells of the vessel wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most glucose taken up is diverted into ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis

explanation.summary: Without mitochondria, RBCs burn enormous amounts of glucose for a very small ATP yield.
explanation.whyCorrect: Red cells are acellular, a feature that permits their biconcave, deformable morphology but eliminates mitochondria. In the absence of mitochondria, complete combustion of glucose is impossible, so glucose is only taken to lactate by substrate level phosphorylation. A very high glycolytic flux is therefore needed to produce comparatively little ATP.

whyWrongByChoice.B: GLUT1 transports glucose efficiently even at low circulating concentrations; slow uptake would not explain a very high utilization rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyruvate kinase is the ATP-generating step and accounts for about half of glycolytic ATP; it is not uncoupled in normal red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythrocytes do not export ATP to endothelium as a route of energy disposal; ATP is consumed internally.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pentose phosphate pathway supplies NADPH for antioxidant defense in the mature RBC; nucleotide synthesis is not the sink for most glucose taken up.

questions.stem: A healthy adult has fasted for 72 hours. Which of the following pairs a tissue with the fuel it predominantly uses at this point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adipocytes and glucose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Brain and ketone bodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cardiac muscle and glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Erythrocytes and ketone bodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Liver and glucose

explanation.summary: In prolonged fasting the brain shifts to ketone bodies, while erythrocytes remain glucose-dependent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fuel utilization changes with dietary state in most tissues. The brain uses glucose when fed and during short-term fasting, but with prolonged fasting it shifts substantially to ketone bodies. Erythrocytes are the notable exception to this adaptability and use glucose in every dietary state.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adipocytes use glucose when well fed but turn to fatty acids with fasting and prolonged fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cardiac muscle relies on fatty acids, with ketone bodies added during fasting, rather than on glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythrocytes cannot oxidize ketone bodies because they lack mitochondria; they continue to use glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The liver shifts to fatty acids during fasting and prolonged fasting; it predominantly uses glucose only in the well-fed state.

questions.stem: The pentose phosphate pathway is a shunt off glycolysis that yields NADPH together with one additional product. Which of the following is that other product?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidized glutathione

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phosphoenolpyruvate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ribose 5-phosphate

explanation.summary: The pentose phosphate pathway generates NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pentose phosphate pathway branches from glycolysis at glucose 6-phosphate and yields NADPH plus ribose 5-phosphate. In the mature erythrocyte, the NADPH arm is the critical output because the pathway is the cell's sole source of reducing power for glutathione-based antioxidant defense.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2,3-BPG is generated from the glycolytic intermediate 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate by bisphosphoglycerate mutase in the Rapoport-Luebering shunt.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactate is the terminal product of erythrocyte glycolysis, formed from pyruvate to regenerate NAD+, not a pentose phosphate pathway product.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxidized glutathione is a product of oxidant neutralization by glutathione peroxidase, not of the pentose phosphate pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphoenolpyruvate is a glycolytic intermediate converted to pyruvate by pyruvate kinase.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a known G6PD variant develops hemolysis during a febrile illness. His hepatocytes and adipocytes, which also depend on NADPH for reductive reactions, show no evidence of oxidative injury. Which of the following best explains why only the erythrocyte is damaged?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythrocytes concentrate the oxidant stimulus far above the level reached in other tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythrocytes lack glutathione peroxidase and must rely on catalase for all oxidant defense

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatocytes and adipocytes are not exposed to the reactive species generated during oxygen exchange

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatocytes and adipocytes express a distinct G6PD isoform that the variant does not affect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hepatocytes and adipocytes generate NADPH through alternate routes such as malic enzyme

explanation.summary: Nucleated tissues have backup NADPH sources; the pentose phosphate pathway is the RBC's only one.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many cells, including adipocytes and hepatocytes, can generate NADPH through pathways apart from the pentose phosphate pathway, such as malic enzyme. In mature erythrocytes the pentose phosphate pathway is the sole source of NADPH, so reduced G6PD activity leaves them uniquely vulnerable to oxidative damage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Red cells do not concentrate the trigger; their susceptibility comes from having no alternative NADPH-generating pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythrocytes do express glutathione peroxidase, and they express catalase as well; the deficit is in NADPH supply.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reactive oxygen species are generated in many tissues; the difference lies in the ability to regenerate NADPH, not in exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The same G6PD gene product is expressed across tissues; there is no protective erythrocyte-sparing isoform in other cells.

questions.stem: Erythrocytes express catalase in addition to glutathione peroxidase, yet loss of NADPH-dependent glutathione recycling by itself is sufficient to produce hemolytic disease. Which of the following best explains why catalase cannot compensate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Catalase acts on hydrogen peroxide alone; glutathione peroxidase also clears lipid peroxides

choices.label: B
choices.text: Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide into hydroxyl radicals rather than into water

choices.label: C
choices.text: Catalase is confined to hepatocytes and is entirely absent from the mature erythrocyte

choices.label: D
choices.text: Catalase is irreversibly inactivated by the same drugs that trigger hemolytic episodes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Catalase requires a supply of NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway for each catalytic cycle

explanation.summary: Glutathione peroxidase covers a broader spectrum of oxidants than catalase, so catalase cannot substitute.
explanation.whyCorrect: Catalase, like glutathione peroxidase, converts hydrogen peroxide into water, and red cells do express it. However, glutathione peroxidase neutralizes a spectrum of oxidative species, including lipid peroxides, not merely hydrogen peroxide. When glutathione recycling fails for want of NADPH, these other reactive species accumulate collectively and produce hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Catalase detoxifies hydrogen peroxide by converting it to water; it does not generate hydroxyl radicals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Catalase is highly enriched in the liver but is also expressed by erythrocytes, so absence is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The oxidant triggers of hemolysis act by overwhelming antioxidant capacity, not by destroying catalase itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Catalase does not depend on NADPH the way glutathione reductase does; its limitation is substrate range.

questions.stem: Within the erythrocyte, oxidized glutathione dimers must be converted back into reduced glutathione so that oxidant neutralization can continue. Which of the following enzymes performs this conversion, and which cofactor does it consume?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Catalase, consuming hydrogen peroxide as its reductant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytochrome b5 reductase, consuming NADH from glycolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase, consuming NADPH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glutathione peroxidase, consuming NADH from glycolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Glutathione reductase, consuming NADPH

explanation.summary: Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione from oxidized glutathione dimers.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the erythrocyte antioxidant circuit, glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione (GSH) to neutralize oxidants and leaves behind oxidized glutathione dimers (GSSG). Glutathione reductase then uses the reducing power of NADPH, supplied by G6PD in the pentose phosphate pathway, to regenerate GSH so the cycle can continue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide into water and plays no role in recycling glutathione.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytochrome b5 reductase uses glycolytic NADH to reduce methemoglobin, a different reductive pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G6PD produces the NADPH used for this step but does not itself act on oxidized glutathione.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glutathione peroxidase consumes reduced glutathione to neutralize oxidants; it does not regenerate it.

questions.stem: Individuals carrying G6PD variants are frequently asymptomatic until an oxidative challenge occurs. Which of the following is the most common trigger of a hemolytic episode in these patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antimalarial drugs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antipyretic drugs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ingestion of fava beans

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sulfonamide antibiotics

explanation.summary: Infection is the most common precipitant of hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with G6PD variants are often asymptomatic until an oxidative stressor overwhelms their limited antioxidant capacity. Although drugs and fava beans are classic precipitants, infection is the most common hemolytic trigger in G6PD deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antimalarials fall within the drug categories that can precipitate hemolysis, but drug exposure is less common than infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Select antipyretics can potentiate hemolysis, but they account for fewer episodes than infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fava beans are a well-known trigger, but favism occurs in only a subset of patients and is not the most common precipitant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sulfonamides are among the implicated antibiotics, yet antibiotic exposure is not the leading trigger.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy develops jaundice, dark urine, and anemia hours after eating a meal containing fava beans. His physician recalls that not all individuals with G6PD deficiency exhibit favism, but all persons with favism have G6PD deficiency. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by this patient's episode?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All persons with G6PD deficiency would hemolyze after eating fava beans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every future exposure to fava beans will cause hemolysis in this boy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fava beans are the most common trigger in G6PD deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: The boy has an underlying G6PD deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: The boy has normal G6PD activity with an unrelated membrane defect

explanation.summary: Favism is sufficient but not necessary evidence of G6PD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The relationship is one-directional: not all individuals with G6PD deficiency will exhibit favism, but all persons with favism have G6PD deficiency. Because this boy hemolyzed after fava bean ingestion, the underlying enzyme deficiency can be inferred.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The converse does not hold, since many G6PD-deficient individuals never exhibit favism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Severity varies with the variant and the magnitude of the oxidative challenge, so hemolysis with every exposure cannot be assumed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infection, not fava bean ingestion, is the most common hemolytic trigger in G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysis triggered by fava beans establishes G6PD deficiency rather than excluding it in favor of a membrane disorder.

questions.stem: A peripheral smear from a patient hemolyzing after an oxidant exposure shows red cells in which the hemoglobin has clustered to one side of the cell, leaving a pale, membrane-bounded clearing on the opposite side. Which of the following best names this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bite cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blister cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heinz body

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reticulocyte

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spiculated cell

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin partitioning to one side leaves a pale, membrane-bound clearing called a blister cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oxidatively damaged hemoglobin can partition or cluster to one side of the erythrocyte, causing a retraction of color on the opposite side. The regional clearing appears as a pale, fluid-filled blister still surrounded by membrane, which is why these are called blister cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A bite cell results when splenic phagocytic macrophages remove a chunk of membrane and cytoplasm, leaving a defect that resembles a bite out of a cookie.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heinz bodies are discrete insoluble aggregates of denatured hemoglobin, typically localized near the plasma membrane, not a broad pale clearing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reticulocytes are immature red cells released in response to hemolysis and are not defined by a pale clearing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spiculated cells with erratic membrane protrusions are described with ATP depletion, as occurs in pyruvate kinase deficiency.

questions.stem: More than 400 distinct point mutations have been described in association with G6PD deficiency, producing variants of widely differing severity. Which of the following best describes how these mutations most commonly disrupt enzyme function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They alter the enzyme's binding affinity for NADP+ or destabilize its structure

choices.label: B
choices.text: They block transcription of the gene during erythroid maturation in the marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: They convert the enzyme into a peroxidase that generates hydrogen peroxide

choices.label: D
choices.text: They prevent import of the enzyme into the erythrocyte mitochondrion

choices.label: E
choices.text: They truncate the transcript so that no enzyme protein is produced at all in the cell

explanation.summary: G6PD variants typically alter NADP+ binding affinity or cause gross structural instability.
explanation.whyCorrect: The many described point mutations largely act through two mechanisms: they change the enzyme's binding affinity for NADP+, or they cause gross structural instability of the protein. Instability matters greatly because mature red cells lack a nucleus and cannot replace degraded enzyme, so activity falls progressively as the cell ages.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Newly released reticulocytes contain recently synthesized enzyme, demonstrating that the gene is transcribed during maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The variants reduce NADPH generation; they do not convert G6PD into a peroxide-producing enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mature erythrocytes have no mitochondria, and G6PD is a cytoplasmic enzyme, so mitochondrial import is not relevant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Point mutations generally yield an expressed but kinetically or structurally abnormal enzyme rather than complete absence of protein.

questions.stem: A patient with G6PD deficiency develops acute hemolysis two days after beginning a sulfonamide antibiotic. The antibiotic is continued because no alternative exists, yet over the following several days the hemolysis abates without specific therapy. Which of the following best explains this self-limited course?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rising 2,3-BPG concentration shields the remaining red cells from oxidation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzyme-poor older cells lyse and are replaced by reticulocytes with normal activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methemoglobin formation consumes the oxidant before it can deplete glutathione

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenic macrophages progressively clear the circulating oxidant drug from the plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surviving mature red cells upregulate transcription of the G6PD gene

explanation.summary: Turnover of enzyme-poor old cells plus a reticulocyte burst makes G6PD hemolytic episodes self-limiting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Older red cells have the lowest G6PD activity and lyse first, while the marrow responds with a burst of reticulocytes that contain recently synthesized, kinetically normal enzyme. The combination of clearing the vulnerable population and replacing it with more resistant cells causes hemolytic episodes to be self-limiting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2,3-BPG modulates hemoglobin oxygen affinity and provides no protection against oxidative damage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methemoglobin formation is itself a consequence of oxidative stress, not a mechanism that spares glutathione.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The drug is being continued, so clearance of the oxidant is not what ends the episode.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mature erythrocytes lack a nucleus and cannot transcribe the gene or replace defective enzyme.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant has had jaundice and anemia since the neonatal period. An erythrocyte enzyme activity assay confirms the second most common red cell-specific enzyme disorder. Which of the following features best distinguishes this disorder from the most common G6PD variants?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diagnosis is characteristically delayed until early adulthood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemolysis is chronic and requires no oxidative trigger to occur

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolysis is restricted to periods of infection or oxidant drug exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemolysis occurs with a normal serum LDH and normal haptoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: The peripheral smear characteristically shows Heinz bodies and bite cells

explanation.summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolysis from birth, unlike trigger-dependent G6PD episodes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is the second most common red cell-specific enzyme disorder and presents with chronic hemolysis at an early age, with average diagnosis before 6 months by enzymatic activity assay or genetic testing. The most common G6PD variants instead cause episodic hemolysis that typically requires an oxidative stress trigger.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is typically diagnosed before 6 months of age, not in adulthood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Trigger-dependent, episodic hemolysis describes G6PD deficiency rather than pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Any ongoing hemolysis raises serum LDH and lowers haptoglobin regardless of the underlying enzyme defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heinz bodies and bite cells reflect oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin and are features of G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: Pyruvate kinase deficiency blocks conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate and is accompanied by an approximately three-fold rise in erythrocyte 2,3-BPG concentration. Which of the following is the physiologic consequence of this rise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It lowers hemoglobin oxygen affinity, improving delivery to tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: It normalizes deformability by rehydrating the red cell cytosol

choices.label: C
choices.text: It raises hemoglobin oxygen affinity, conserving oxygen for the red cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: It restores ATP production within the affected red cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It serves as the confirmatory clinical diagnostic for the disorder

explanation.summary: Elevated 2,3-BPG in PK deficiency lowers oxygen affinity and is an adaptive response that eases severity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blockage at the phosphoenolpyruvate-to-pyruvate step backs up glycolytic intermediates and roughly triples 2,3-BPG. Because 2,3-BPG binding decreases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen, the red cells remaining in circulation release oxygen to tissues very efficiently. This does not correct the disorder but is thought to be an adaptive mechanism that alleviates its severity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cellular dehydration and rigidity stem from failed ATP-dependent ion pumping, which 2,3-BPG does not reverse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 2,3-BPG decreases rather than increases oxygen affinity, and red cells do not consume the oxygen they carry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ATP deficit is the core problem and is not repaired by accumulating 2,3-BPG.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diagnosis rests on enzymatic activity assay or genetic testing; the 2,3-BPG elevation is not used as a clinical diagnostic.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with severe pyruvate kinase deficiency and long-standing hemolysis is scheduled for splenectomy because of progressive splenomegaly. Her surgeon plans to remove a second organ during the same operation because of a complication frequently seen with chronic hemolysis. Which of the following is the most likely indication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal infarction from repeated hemolytic crises

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis within the thymus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatic iron overload requiring partial hepatectomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pigmented gallstones composed of bilirubin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal calculi arising from chronic hemoglobinuria

explanation.summary: Chronic hemolysis produces bilirubin-rich pigmented gallstones, so cholecystectomy often accompanies splenectomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with severe pyruvate kinase deficiency develop complications of chronic hemolysis, including extramedullary hematopoiesis, iron overload, and pigmented gallstones composed of bilirubin. Because splenectomy is often required for splenomegaly and gallstone risk is high, cholecystectomy is frequently performed at the same time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenal infarction is not a complication attributed to chronic hemolytic states of this type.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Extramedullary hematopoiesis is a complication of chronic hemolysis, but it is not treated by removing an organ at splenectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron overload is a recognized complication of chronic hemolysis, but it is managed medically rather than by resecting liver.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal calculi are not among the described complications of the chronic hemolysis seen in this disorder.

questions.stem: ATP generated by erythrocyte glycolysis has several obligatory uses. In addition to maintaining transmembrane ion balance and phosphorylating membrane proteins, ATP is consumed within glycolysis itself. Which of the following best describes this use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is consumed by bisphosphoglycerate mutase when 2,3-BPG is formed

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is consumed by GAPDH when NADH is generated at step 6

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is consumed by GLUT1 to import glucose against its concentration gradient

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is consumed by lactate dehydrogenase when pyruvate is reduced to lactate

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is consumed in the priming reactions of glycolysis, steps 1 and 3

explanation.summary: Glycolysis invests ATP in its priming reactions, steps 1 and 3, before any net ATP is made.
explanation.whyCorrect: Red cells require ATP for maintaining ion balance across the membrane (Na+, K+, and Ca2+), for phosphorylating membrane proteins, and for the priming reactions of glycolysis, specifically steps 1 and 3. This investment phase must be paid before the payoff steps generate net ATP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase rearranges the existing high-energy phosphate of 1,3-BPG and does not consume ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GAPDH generates NADH and incorporates inorganic phosphate rather than consuming ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLUT1 is a facilitative transporter that moves glucose down its gradient without ATP hydrolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate using NADH to regenerate NAD+; it does not hydrolyze ATP.

questions.stem: A patient with acquired methemoglobinemia has a methemoglobin fraction of about 20%. Many of his hemoglobin tetramers contain a mixture of ferric and ferrous heme groups. Beyond the simple loss of oxygen binding at the oxidized sites, which of the following additional effects further impairs tissue oxygen delivery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ferric subunits shift tetramer conformation, raising affinity of remaining ferrous heme

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ferric subunits catalyze peroxidation of the erythrocyte membrane lipids

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ferric subunits consume 2,3-BPG, depleting the red cell's modulator pool

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ferrous subunits are converted to carbaminohemoglobin and can no longer bind oxygen

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ferrous subunits dissociate from the tetramer and are cleared in the urine

explanation.summary: In mixed tetramers, ferric subunits increase the oxygen affinity of the remaining normal ferrous heme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemoglobin with only ferric iron centers cannot bind oxygen at all. In milder forms, however, a single tetramer usually contains a mix of ferric and ferrous states, and the ferric subunits alter the tetrameric conformation so that the remaining normal ferrous heme groups have increased oxygen affinity. That increased affinity impairs unloading in tissue and compounds the hypoxia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipid peroxidation of the membrane is a feature of oxidant-driven hemolysis rather than the delivery defect in methemoglobinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methemoglobin does not consume 2,3-BPG; the impairment of delivery stems from an altered tetramer conformation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carbaminohemoglobin forms when CO2 binds hemoglobin and is unrelated to oxidation of heme iron.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subunits are not shed from the tetramer or excreted; the tetramer remains intact with mixed iron states.

questions.stem: A man is brought to the emergency department after an industrial chemical exposure. He is cyanotic and has a generalized seizure, a new ventricular arrhythmia, and a metabolic acidosis on laboratory studies. Co-oximetry confirms methemoglobinemia. Based on the relationship between methemoglobin fraction and symptoms, which of the following ranges best corresponds to his presentation?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greater than 70%

choices.label: E
choices.text: Less than 15%

explanation.summary: Seizures, arrhythmias, metabolic acidosis, and coma correspond to a methemoglobin fraction of 50 to 70%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Symptom severity in methemoglobinemia is directly proportional to the methemoglobin fraction and the resulting tissue hypoxia. Seizures, arrhythmias, metabolic acidosis, and coma are the manifestations associated with a fraction of roughly 50 to 70%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 15 to 30% range produces cyanosis, anxiety, light-headedness, fatigue, and headache rather than seizures.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The 30 to 50% range is associated with tachypnea, confusion, and syncope.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fractions above 70% are associated with death rather than a survivable constellation of seizure and arrhythmia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fractions below 15% are typically asymptomatic, although chocolate-brown blood may already be evident around 15%.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old infant becomes cyanotic after repeated application of a benzocaine-containing oral gel. PaO2 is normal, the cyanosis does not improve with supplemental oxygen, and methemoglobinemia is confirmed. Which of the following best explains why infants are especially susceptible to this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Infant cytochrome b5 reductase activity is half that of adults, and HbF oxidizes readily

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infant erythrocytes lack GLUT1 and therefore cannot sustain glycolytic NADH production

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infant hemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG more tightly, which strongly favors the oxidized heme state

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infant oral mucosa absorbs topical benzocaine several times faster than adult mucosa tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Infants do not express glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase until roughly six months of age

explanation.summary: Infants have roughly half the cytochrome b5 reductase activity of adults and HbF iron that oxidizes more easily.
explanation.whyCorrect: Two factors make infants particularly vulnerable to acquired methemoglobinemia. They possess only about half the cytochrome b5 reductase activity of adults, blunting the main pathway that reduces methemoglobin, and the iron within fetal hemoglobin is structurally more susceptible to oxidation than that within HbA. Benzocaine applied topically is a recognized cause, which is why it is contraindicated in children under 2 years of age.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Infant erythrocytes use GLUT1 normally; loss of glucose uptake is not the basis of this vulnerability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 2,3-BPG modulates oxygen affinity and does not promote oxidation of heme iron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Susceptibility is attributed to reduced reducing capacity and to fetal hemoglobin, not to a faster rate of mucosal absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: G6PD is expressed in infant red cells, and the NADPH-dependent pathway contributes minimally to routine methemoglobin reduction anyway.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man has had a bluish-gray skin color since infancy without cardiopulmonary disease. Methemoglobin is elevated on co-oximetry, cytochrome b5 reductase activity is normal, and globin gene sequencing identifies a mutation that compromises the structural integrity of the heme binding pocket. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daily long-acting nitrate therapy to stabilize the heme binding pocket

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-dose methylene blue, which is particularly effective in this form

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immediate exchange transfusion at the time of diagnosis for all patients

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenectomy to reduce clearance of the abnormal hemoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supportive care, reserving intervention for advanced cases

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin M causes congenital methemoglobinemia that is managed supportively, as methylene blue works poorly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congenital methemoglobinemia arises either from cytochrome b5 reductase defects or from mutations in globin genes collectively called hemoglobin M. In hemoglobin M, the altered heme binding pocket permits greater auto-oxidation of iron. Unlike acquired forms, congenital disease responds poorly to methylene blue, so management is supportive except in advanced cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nitrates are chemical oxidants that generate methemoglobin and would worsen this patient's condition.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methylene blue is the typical treatment for acquired methemoglobinemia and is notably less effective in congenital forms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Routine exchange transfusion is not the described approach for this chronic, largely tolerated congenital condition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The defect lies in the globin structure itself, and splenectomy does not address heme auto-oxidation.

questions.stem: A patient with cyanide poisoning is treated with sodium nitrite while arrangements are made for definitive care. Which of the following best describes how this agent counteracts the toxin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds cyanide within the plasma to form cobalamin-cyanide complexes

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, blocking any further cyanide binding

choices.label: C
choices.text: It donates sulfur to convert cyanide into thiocyanate for renal excretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: It generates methemoglobin, whose ferric iron sequesters cyanide away from complex IV

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reduces ferric heme iron back to the ferrous state, releasing the bound cyanide ion

explanation.summary: Nitrites deliberately induce methemoglobin so its ferric iron traps cyanide as cyanomethemoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amyl nitrite or sodium nitrite prompts oxidative changes that favor methemoglobin formation. The ferric iron within methemoglobin covalently coordinates cyanide to form cyanomethemoglobin, which promotes excretion and keeps cyanide from binding complex IV of the electron transport chain, restoring ATP production. The tradeoff is iatrogenic methemoglobinemia, which is why hydroxocobalamin is the first-line antidote.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding cyanide as a cobalamin complex describes hydroxocobalamin, the preferred first-line antidote.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cyanide itself poisons cytochrome c oxidase; further inhibition of that enzyme would worsen the poisoning.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sulfur donation to form thiocyanate is a different detoxification strategy and is not how nitrite acts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nitrites oxidize heme iron to the ferric state rather than reducing it; reduction of methemoglobin is what methylene blue does.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with 3 months of fatigue and heavy menstrual bleeding. Her hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL and serum ferritin is low, consistent with iron-deficiency anemia. Which additional red blood cell index finding is most likely on her complete blood count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hematocrit of 52%

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin concentration of 40 g/dL

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean cell volume of 105 fL

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean cell volume of 72 fL

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cell count above the reference range

explanation.summary: Iron-deficiency anemia produces small (microcytic), hemoglobin-poor red cells, so the MCV falls below the normal 80-100 fL range.
explanation.whyCorrect: The MCV measures the average volume (size) of the RBCs, with a reference range of 80-100 fL. Iron deficiency limits hemoglobin synthesis, yielding smaller-than-normal (microcytic) red cells, so an MCV of 72 fL fits the picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anemia lowers the hematocrit; a hematocrit of 52% is at the high end of normal and would not be seen in an anemic patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The MCHC reference range is 32-36 g/dL; iron-deficient cells are hypochromic (low MCHC), not 40 g/dL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An MCV of 105 fL is macrocytic and points to causes such as B12 or folate deficiency, not iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anemia is characterized by a decrease in RBC mass, so the RBC count is typically low, not above the reference range.

questions.stem: A hematology resident is reviewing a complete blood count and wants to know how much the patient's red blood cell sizes vary from one another. Which red blood cell index most directly reflects this variation in cell size?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hematocrit (Hct)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin (Hgb)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin (MCH)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cell distribution width (RDW)

explanation.summary: The RDW quantifies the variability of the MCV, and a wide range of red cell sizes is termed anisocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The red blood cell distribution width (reference range 12-15%) describes the variability of the MCV. When some cells are small and others large, the RDW rises; this variation in RBC size is called anisocytosis and helps distinguish among types of anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume made up of RBCs and says nothing about how uniform the cells are.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin measures the grams of Hgb per volume of blood and does not indicate variation in cell size.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MCH is the average weight of hemoglobin per RBC, not a measure of size variation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MCHC is the average concentration of hemoglobin per RBC and relates to color (chromicity), not size spread.

questions.stem: A medical student is learning why a Wright-Giemsa stain colors different parts of a blood cell differently. On this gold-standard stain, which cellular component takes up eosin and appears red?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA in the nucleus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin in the cytoplasm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Negatively charged nucleic acids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residual cytoplasmic RNA of reticulocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ribosomal RNA

explanation.summary: On Wright-Giemsa staining, positively charged hemoglobin binds eosin and stains red (eosinophilic), while negatively charged nucleic acids bind methylene blue (basophilic).
explanation.whyCorrect: The Wright-Giemsa stain contains eosin, which stains structures red, and methylene blue, which stains structures blue. Positively charged compounds such as hemoglobin are eosinophilic and stain red, whereas negatively charged compounds like DNA and RNA are basophilic and stain blue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nuclear DNA is negatively charged and basophilic, so it takes up methylene blue and stains blue, not red.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Negatively charged nucleic acids bind methylene blue and appear blue (basophilic), the opposite of eosinophilic red.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reticulocyte RNA is basophilic and, moreover, is best seen with supravital stains, not colored red by eosin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ribosomal RNA is negatively charged and basophilic; it also stains blue rather than red.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with chronic myelofibrosis has a peripheral blood smear reviewed. Which red blood cell morphology is most characteristically associated with this marrow disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bite cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Schistocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sickle cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Target cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teardrop cells

explanation.summary: Teardrop cells (dacrocytes) are the classic red cell shape seen in myelofibrosis and other marrow-occupying processes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dacrocytes, or teardrop cells, are associated with chronic myelofibrosis and other space-occupying lesions of the marrow, where red cells are deformed as they squeeze out of a fibrotic marrow. This is the expected finding on this patient's smear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bite cells are seen in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Schistocytes are fragmented cells seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sickle cells are the hallmark of sickle cell anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Target cells (codocytes) are seen in thalassemia, liver disease, and iron deficiency, not myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy underwent splenectomy after traumatic splenic rupture. A follow-up blood smear shows red cells each containing a single round, dark-blue dot representing a residual nuclear DNA remnant. Which inclusion is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basophilic stippling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Howell-Jolly body

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pappenheimer bodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasmodium organisms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rouleaux formation

explanation.summary: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants normally removed by the spleen, so they appear after splenectomy or in functional asplenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Howell-Jolly body is a residual fragment of nuclear DNA that a healthy spleen would ordinarily pit from the red cell. After splenectomy the spleen can no longer remove them, so they persist as a single round dark-blue inclusion, consistent with this post-splenectomy patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophilic stippling is diffuse fine blue granules of aggregated ribosomal RNA seen in lead poisoning and thalassemia, not a single DNA dot.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing granules seen in sideroblastic anemia and cluster at the cell periphery.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasmodium organisms are intracellular parasites (ring forms) diagnostic of malaria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rouleaux formation is stacking of red cells due to increased immunoglobulins, not an intracellular inclusion.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with anemia and abdominal pain is found to have lived in an old home with peeling paint. The blood smear shows red cells with diffuse fine blue granules distributed throughout the cytoplasm. Which inclusion, and its underlying material, best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basophilic stippling composed of ribosomal RNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Howell-Jolly body composed of nuclear DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pappenheimer bodies composed of iron granules

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasmodium ring forms composed of parasites

choices.label: E
choices.text: Target cells composed of excess membrane

explanation.summary: Diffuse fine blue granules of aggregated ribosomal RNA (basophilic stippling) are seen in lead poisoning and thalassemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Basophilic stippling appears as fine blue granules spread throughout the red cell and represents aggregated ribosomal RNA. The classic associations are lead poisoning and thalassemia, fitting this child's lead-exposure history.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A Howell-Jolly body is a single round dot of nuclear DNA seen after splenectomy, not diffuse granules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing granules of sideroblastic anemia that cluster at the cell edge rather than distributing diffusely.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasmodium ring forms indicate malaria and are discrete parasites, not fine RNA granules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Target cells are a shape abnormality, not an inclusion, and are unrelated to lead exposure.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with chronic anemia is being evaluated, and her physician wants to visualize the ribosomal RNA inside her reticulocytes. Which staining method is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) reagent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Periodic acid-Schiff stain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sudan black B stain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supravital stain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wright-Giemsa stain

explanation.summary: Supravital stains such as new methylene blue and brilliant cresyl blue highlight the ribosomal RNA of reticulocytes, which is not well seen on routine smears.
explanation.whyCorrect: Supravital stains are applied to fresh, living cells and reveal structures not visible on dried Wright-Giemsa smears. New methylene blue and brilliant cresyl blue precipitate the residual ribosomal RNA of reticulocytes into a visible blue network, allowing the reticulocyte count.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Coombs reagent detects antibody or complement coating red cells; it does not stain RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Periodic acid-Schiff stains carbohydrates, not ribosomal RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sudan black B stains lipids and is used to characterize leukemias, not reticulocyte RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: On Wright-Giemsa staining reticulocyte RNA is only faintly detectable as a lilac tinge (polychromasia) and is not directly visualized.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with autoimmune hemolytic anemia has a hemoglobin of 8 g/dL and a hematocrit of 27%. Her measured reticulocyte count is 6%. Which interpretation of her bone marrow response is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The elevated reticulocyte count indicates the cells are macrocytic artifacts

choices.label: B
choices.text: The finding indicates the red cells are coated with antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: The marrow is appropriately responding to the anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: The marrow is hypoproliferative and failing to respond

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reticulocyte count is within the normal reference range

explanation.summary: A reticulocyte count above 2%, especially when corrected for the degree of anemia, indicates a hyperproliferative marrow responding to hemolysis or blood loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally 1-2% of circulating RBCs are reticulocytes. A count above 2% signals a hyperproliferative (responding) marrow, typical of hemolysis or hemorrhage. In this hemolytic patient the elevated reticulocyte count shows the marrow is appropriately ramping up red cell production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high reticulocyte count reflects true increased production, not a macrocytic artifact.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody coating of red cells is detected by the direct antiglobulin test, not inferred from the reticulocyte count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A hypoproliferative marrow is reflected by a reticulocyte count below 2%; a value of 6% is the opposite.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The normal reference range is about 1-2%, so 6% is clearly elevated, not normal.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is engaged to a man with sickle cell trait and wants to know whether she carries an abnormal hemoglobin before they have children. Her screening CBC is normal. Which test best identifies and quantifies the different types of hemoglobin in her blood?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin test

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmotic fragility test

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red cell distribution width

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reticulocyte count

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates hemoglobin types by charge and quantifies them, making it the screening test for hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell trait.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemoglobin electrophoresis applies an electric charge to a gel so different hemoglobins migrate to characteristic positions (order A, F, S, C from farthest to closest). It identifies and quantifies hemoglobins, so it can detect hemoglobin S and confirm or exclude sickle cell trait even when the CBC is normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The direct antiglobulin test detects antibody or complement on red cells in immune hemolysis, not hemoglobin variants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osmotic fragility testing measures how readily RBCs lyse in hypotonic saline and is used for hereditary spherocytosis, not for identifying hemoglobin types.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RDW measures variation in red cell size and cannot identify an abnormal hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reticulocyte count assesses marrow production and does not distinguish hemoglobin types.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man with lifelong mild anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly has a smear showing round red cells that lack central pallor. On osmotic fragility testing his red cells lyse at higher-than-normal concentrations of sodium chloride. Which diagnosis best fits these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia from IgG coating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-thalassemia major

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron-deficiency anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sickle cell anemia

explanation.summary: Increased osmotic fragility, with lysis at higher-than-normal NaCl concentrations, is characteristic of hereditary spherocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spherocytes in hereditary spherocytosis have cytoskeleton mutations that make them less deformable and more prone to rupture, so they lyse even in less hypotonic (higher NaCl) solutions, giving increased osmotic fragility. The round cells lacking central pallor further support the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is diagnosed with a positive direct antiglobulin test; the scenario points to a membrane defect rather than antibody coating.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thalassemia is also associated with decreased osmotic fragility because of thin, target-shaped cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron-deficiency anemia produces microcytic hypochromic cells and does not typically cause increased osmotic fragility or spherocytes lacking central pallor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sickle cell anemia is associated with decreased, not increased, osmotic fragility.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman develops worsening anemia. A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is performed: when Coombs reagent is added to her washed red cells, they agglutinate. What does this positive result indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her marrow is producing too many reticulocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her red cells are coated with antibody or complement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her red cells are excessively fragile in hypotonic saline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her red cells are microcytic and hypochromic

choices.label: E
choices.text: Her red cells contain an abnormal hemoglobin

explanation.summary: A positive direct antiglobulin test means the patient's red cells are already coated with immunoglobulin or complement, as in autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the direct antiglobulin test, anti-immunoglobulin/anti-complement (Coombs) reagent is added to the patient's red cells. If the cells are coated with antibody or complement, the reagent cross-links them and they agglutinate, giving a positive result seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, transfusion reactions, hemolytic disease of the newborn, and drug-induced hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reticulocyte production is measured by the reticulocyte count, which the Coombs test does not evaluate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fragility in hypotonic saline is assessed by osmotic fragility testing, a different assay.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cell size and chromicity are read from the MCV and MCHC, not from agglutination with Coombs reagent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abnormal hemoglobins are detected by hemoglobin electrophoresis, not by the antiglobulin test.

questions.stem: An elderly patient's automated CBC returns a very low red blood cell count with a strikingly high MCV. The technologist notes clumping of red cells on the smear consistent with cold agglutinins. Which of the following values is most likely to remain accurate despite the agglutination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin (MCH)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean cell volume (MCV)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cell count

explanation.summary: When red cells agglutinate, clumps are miscounted so the RBC count falls and MCV rises falsely, but hemoglobin stays accurate because it is measured after the cells are lysed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Automated analyzers classify particles by size, so agglutinated clumps are counted as fewer, larger cells: the RBC count is falsely decreased and the MCV falsely increased. Hemoglobin is measured spectrophotometrically after the red cells are lysed, so clumping does not affect it, and it usually remains accurate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MCH is derived from hemoglobin and the falsely low RBC count, so it is falsely increased.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MCHC is likewise falsely increased when agglutination distorts the RBC-derived measurements.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The MCV is falsely increased because clumps are read as abnormally large single cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The RBC count is falsely decreased because clumps are undercounted as single particles.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man has a complete blood count drawn at a routine physical. His hematocrit is reported as 44%. This value represents which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The average volume of a single red blood cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: The average weight of hemoglobin in each red blood cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: The concentration of hemoglobin in the blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: The number of red blood cells present in the blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: The percentage of blood volume composed of red blood cells

explanation.summary: The hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume made up of red blood cells, normally 40%-54% in males and 36%-48% in females.
explanation.whyCorrect: Of the red blood cell indices on the CBC, the hematocrit is defined as the percentage of blood volume composed of RBCs. Together with the hemoglobin and the RBC count, it is used to diagnose anemia, a decrease in RBC mass.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The average volume (size) of the RBCs is the mean cell volume, reported in femtoliters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The average weight of hemoglobin per RBC is the mean cell hemoglobin, reported in pg/cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The concentration of hemoglobin in the blood is the hemoglobin, reported in g/dL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The number of RBCs in the blood is the RBC count, reported as cells x 10^12/L.

questions.stem: A laboratory report lists one of the red blood cell indices as 29 pg/cell. Which index is reported in these units, and what does it measure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin, the concentration of hemoglobin in the blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin concentration, the average concentration of hemoglobin per red blood cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin, the average weight of hemoglobin per red blood cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean cell volume, the average volume of the red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cell distribution width, the variability of the mean cell volume

explanation.summary: The mean cell hemoglobin is the average weight of hemoglobin per red blood cell, with a reference range of 27-31 pg/cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: MCH and MCHC both describe how much hemoglobin is present, on average, in each RBC, in contrast to the hemoglobin, which reports grams of Hgb per volume of blood. The MCH specifically reports the average weight of Hgb per cell and has a reference range of 27-31 pg/cell, so a value of 29 pg/cell is an MCH.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The hemoglobin is reported in g/dL (14-18 in males, 12-16 in females).
whyWrongByChoice.B: The MCHC is reported in g/dL with a reference range of 32-36 g/dL, not in pg/cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The MCV is reported in femtoliters with a reference range of 80-100 fL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The RDW is reported as a percentage with a reference range of 12%-15%.

questions.stem: A hematology attending asks a student about the amount of hemoglobin per red blood cell across the anemias. Which of the following statements is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromicity describes the spread of red cell sizes rather than hemoglobin content

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin content per cell cannot be assessed once a patient is anemic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most anemias are hyperchromic, with an increased amount of hemoglobin per cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most anemias are hypochromic, with a decreased amount of hemoglobin per cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most anemias are normochromic, with a normal amount of hemoglobin per cell

explanation.summary: Although one might expect every anemia to be hypochromic, most types of anemia are in fact normochromic and only a few are hypochromic.
explanation.whyCorrect: RBCs with a normal amount of Hgb are called normochromic, those with a decreased amount hypochromic, and those with an increased amount hyperchromic. Most types of anemia turn out to be normochromic, which is why the MCH and MCHC are often normal even when the hemoglobin and hematocrit are low.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Variation in RBC size is anisocytosis, measured by the RDW; chromicity refers to hemoglobin content.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The MCH and MCHC report hemoglobin per cell regardless of whether the patient is anemic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperchromic describes an increased amount of Hgb per cell and is not the usual pattern in anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only a few types of anemia are hypochromic, even though one might expect all of them to be.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant has a complete blood count performed. Compared with adult reference ranges, which pattern of results is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin and mean cell volume identical to adults, since the ranges do not vary with age

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher hemoglobin and higher mean cell volume, reaching adult values by one year of age

choices.label: C
choices.text: Higher hemoglobin with a lower mean cell volume, reaching adult values by five years of age

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower hemoglobin and lower mean cell volume, reaching adult values after puberty

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lower hemoglobin with a higher mean cell volume, a pattern that persists into adulthood

explanation.summary: Pediatric blood counts differ from adult ones: infants and children tend to have a lower hemoglobin and MCV, and adult levels are achieved after puberty.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normal pediatric blood counts are not the same as adult counts. Newborns often have a higher MCV than adults, but infants and children tend to have a lower hemoglobin and MCV than the adult range. The normal range varies with age and achieves adult levels after puberty.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Normal pediatric blood counts differ from adult counts and vary with age.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It is newborns, not infants and older children, who tend to have a higher MCV, and adult values are not reached at one year.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infants have a lower, not higher, hemoglobin, and adult levels are reached after puberty rather than at age five.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Infants and children tend to have a lower MCV than adults, and the pediatric pattern resolves after puberty.

questions.stem: A student examining a high-power view of a normal Wright-Giemsa-stained smear asks why the center of each red blood cell appears as a pale circle. Which explanation is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bound immunoglobulin at the cell center blocks eosin from staining hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess cell membrane gathers centrally and excludes hemoglobin from that zone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residual ribosomal RNA displaces hemoglobin away from the center of the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: The biconcave-disk shape leaves very little cytoplasm, and thus little hemoglobin, centrally

choices.label: E
choices.text: The spleen pits a fragment from the center of each cell as it circulates

explanation.summary: The zone of central pallor exists because the biconcave-disk shape of the red cell leaves very little cytoplasm, and therefore very little hemoglobin, in the center.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normal RBCs are evenly distributed, round, and roughly the same size, and each shows a zone of central pallor. Because the cell is a biconcave disk, the central region contains very little cytoplasm; with little cytoplasm there is little hemoglobin to take up eosin, so the center appears pale.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immunoglobulin coating is detected by the direct antiglobulin test and does not alter hemoglobin staining.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess membrane relative to volume is a feature of target cells, which show a central spot of hemoglobin rather than normal pallor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Residual ribosomal RNA is the feature of reticulocytes and gives a lilac tinge to the whole cell, not a central pale zone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic pitting removes nuclear remnants such as Howell-Jolly bodies; it does not create central pallor.

questions.stem: A technologist explains that blood smears are prepared with a technique that uses two or more dyes so that some structures take one color and other structures take a different color. This technique is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Differential staining

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin testing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osmotic fragility testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supravital staining

explanation.summary: Differential staining uses two or more dyes to color different structures differently, which is what makes the various blood cell types distinguishable.
explanation.whyCorrect: Differential staining is a process that uses two or more dyes to stain some structures one color and others a different color, making cellular components easier to tell apart. The Wright-Giemsa stain, which combines eosin and methylene blue, is the gold standard differential stain for blood specimens.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Direct antiglobulin testing detects antibody or complement coating the patient's red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates hemoglobin types in a gel using an electrical charge.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osmotic fragility testing measures how readily red cells lyse in saline solutions of varying concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supravital staining is performed on fresh living cells to reveal structures such as reticulocyte ribosomal RNA.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with cirrhosis is evaluated for anemia, and his physician reviews the red blood cell shape abnormalities that accompany liver disease. Which of the following shape abnormalities is caused by liver disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acanthocyte (spur cell)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dacrocyte (teardrop cell)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Echinocyte (burr cell)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schistocyte

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spherocyte

explanation.summary: Acanthocytes, also called spur cells, are the red cell shape abnormality attributed to liver disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the common abnormal RBC shapes, the acanthocyte (spur cell) is listed with liver disease as its cause. Recognizing spur cells on the smear of a patient with cirrhosis therefore fits the expected morphology.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dacrocytes (teardrop cells) point to chronic myelofibrosis or another space-occupying lesion of the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Echinocytes (burr cells) are attributed to blood smear artifact and kidney disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schistocytes are red cell fragments seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spherocytes are seen in warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with end-stage kidney disease has a smear reported as showing echinocytes (burr cells). Besides kidney disease, which of the following is the other common explanation for this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An artifact of blood smear preparation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic myelofibrosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lead poisoning

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prior splenectomy

explanation.summary: Echinocytes (burr cells) are attributed to blood smear artifact as well as to kidney disease, so they must be interpreted with the preparation in mind.
explanation.whyCorrect: The listed causes of the echinocyte, or burr cell, are blood smear artifact and kidney disease. Because the shape can be produced during smear preparation itself, burr cells seen on a smear do not always indicate a true in vivo red cell abnormality.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myelofibrosis is the classic cause of dacrocytes (teardrop cells).
whyWrongByChoice.C: G6PD deficiency is the cause of bite cells, not echinocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lead poisoning produces basophilic stippling, an inclusion of aggregated ribosomal RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy leaves Howell-Jolly bodies, which are nuclear DNA remnants, in the red cells.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia has a blood smear showing numerous red blood cell fragments. These fragmented cells are called which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acanthocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dacrocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Echinocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Schistocytes

explanation.summary: Schistocytes are fragmented red blood cells and are the shape abnormality of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the abnormal RBC shapes, the schistocyte is the fragmented cell, and its listed cause is microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. The fragments are produced as red cells are sheared in the microvasculature.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acanthocytes (spur cells) are attributed to liver disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codocytes (target cells) are seen in thalassemia, liver disease, and iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dacrocytes (teardrop cells) are seen in chronic myelofibrosis and other marrow space-occupying lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Echinocytes (burr cells) are attributed to blood smear artifact and kidney disease.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is diagnosed with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Which red blood cell shape abnormality is most likely to be reported on her peripheral smear?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Codocyte (target cell)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dacrocyte (teardrop cell)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Echinocyte (burr cell)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schistocyte

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spherocyte

explanation.summary: Spherocytes are the shape abnormality of warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (and of hereditary spherocytosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: The listed causes of the spherocyte are warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and hereditary spherocytosis. In warm AIHA, antibody-coated red cells lose membrane to splenic macrophages and become round cells that lack central pallor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Codocytes (target cells) are associated with thalassemia, liver disease, and iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dacrocytes (teardrop cells) are associated with chronic myelofibrosis and marrow space-occupying lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Echinocytes (burr cells) are associated with blood smear artifact and kidney disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schistocytes are fragments seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is found to have markedly increased serum immunoglobulins. Which finding is most likely on his peripheral blood smear?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basophilic stippling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bite cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Howell-Jolly bodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rouleaux formation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teardrop cells

explanation.summary: Increased immunoglobulins cause red cells to stack into rouleaux, one of the two forms of red cell clumping that can also distort analyzer results.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rouleaux formation is listed with increased immunoglobulins as its cause. Like agglutination, rouleaux represents red cell clumping, which is a recognized source of falsely decreased RBC counts and falsely increased MCV values on automated analyzers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophilic stippling, aggregated ribosomal RNA, is seen in lead poisoning and thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bite cells are the shape abnormality of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants found after splenectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Teardrop cells point to chronic myelofibrosis or another marrow space-occupying lesion.

questions.stem: A peripheral smear is reported as showing red blood cell agglutination. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic myelofibrosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

explanation.summary: Red blood cell agglutination on the smear is attributed to cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the abnormal red cell findings, RBC agglutination is listed with cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia as its cause. It is distinguished from rouleaux, the other form of clumping, which is caused by increased immunoglobulins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic myelofibrosis produces dacrocytes (teardrop cells).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hereditary spherocytosis produces spherocytes and increased osmotic fragility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia produces schistocytes, which are fragments rather than clumps.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia produces spherocytes rather than agglutination.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs an abnormal red blood cell shape with its cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bite cell — glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codocyte (target cell) — chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dacrocyte (teardrop cell) — chronic kidney disease with uremia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schistocyte — advanced cirrhotic liver disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spherocyte — homozygous sickle cell anemia (HbSS)

explanation.summary: Bite cells are the red cell shape abnormality caused by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each abnormal shape has a characteristic cause, and the bite cell is paired with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. The remaining pairings in this item all mismatch a shape with the cause of a different one.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Codocytes (target cells) are caused by thalassemia, liver disease, and iron deficiency; chronic myelofibrosis causes dacrocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dacrocytes are caused by chronic myelofibrosis and other marrow lesions; kidney disease is linked to echinocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schistocytes are caused by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia; liver disease causes acanthocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spherocytes are caused by warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and hereditary spherocytosis; sickle cell anemia causes sickle cells.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with sideroblastic anemia has a blood smear showing small dark inclusions within some of his red blood cells. What are these inclusions composed of, and what are they called?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aggregated ribosomal RNA, called basophilic stippling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intracellular parasites, called Plasmodium organisms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron granules, called Pappenheimer bodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nuclear DNA, called a Howell-Jolly body

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polymerized hemoglobin, called sickle hemoglobin

explanation.summary: Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing granules and are the red cell inclusion associated with sideroblastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the common red cell inclusions, Pappenheimer bodies are the iron granules, and the condition in which they appear is sideroblastic anemia. This patient's diagnosis therefore matches Pappenheimer bodies rather than the other inclusions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophilic stippling is aggregated ribosomal RNA seen in lead poisoning and thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasmodium organisms are intracellular parasites seen in malaria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants seen after splenectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin polymerization in sickle cell disease deforms the whole cell rather than producing granular inclusions.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man returns from travel abroad with cyclic fevers and chills. His blood smear shows organisms within the red blood cells. Which condition do these inclusions indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lead poisoning

choices.label: B
choices.text: Malaria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prior splenectomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sideroblastic anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thalassemia

explanation.summary: Plasmodium organisms inside red blood cells are the inclusion of malaria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Of the common red cell inclusions, only Plasmodium organisms are actual organisms residing within the cell, and the condition in which they are seen is malaria. Identifying them on the smear establishes the diagnosis in a febrile traveler.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lead poisoning produces basophilic stippling, fine blue granules of aggregated ribosomal RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Splenectomy leaves Howell-Jolly bodies, which are nuclear DNA remnants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sideroblastic anemia produces Pappenheimer bodies, which are iron granules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thalassemia produces basophilic stippling and target cells rather than intracellular organisms.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with anemia has a hematocrit of 30% and a measured reticulocyte count of 4%. Using a normal hematocrit of 45, what is her corrected reticulocyte count?

explanation.summary: The corrected reticulocyte count equals the reticulocyte count multiplied by the patient's hematocrit divided by a normal hematocrit of about 45.
explanation.whyCorrect: Applying the formula, 4% x 30/45 = 2.7%. Correcting for the degree of anemia is important because the measured percentage is inflated when the total red cell mass is low; the corrected value of 2.7% still exceeds 2%, so the marrow is responding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This value would require a much lower hematocrit ratio than 30/45.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is close to 4% x 20/45 and does not use the patient's hematocrit of 30.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 4.0% is the uncorrected measured reticulocyte count, which overstates marrow output in an anemic patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 6.0% would result from multiplying rather than correcting downward for the low hematocrit.

questions.stem: On hemoglobin electrophoresis, the different hemoglobin types migrate different distances from the point of origin. Which sequence lists them correctly from farthest traveled to closest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A, F, S, C

choices.label: B
choices.text: A, S, F, C

choices.label: C
choices.text: C, S, F, A

choices.label: D
choices.text: F, A, C, S

choices.label: E
choices.text: S, C, A, F

explanation.summary: In hemoglobin electrophoresis the order of travel from farthest to closest is hemoglobin A, F, S, and C.
explanation.whyCorrect: When an electrical charge is applied to the gel, the hemoglobin types migrate away from the negatively charged electrode and land at characteristic distances from the origin. The order from farthest to closest is A, F, S, C, captured by the mnemonic A Fat Santa Claus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: S and F are transposed; hemoglobin F travels farther than hemoglobin S.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the true order; hemoglobin C travels the shortest distance, not the longest.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin A, not F, travels farthest, and C lies closest to the origin rather than between A and S.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin A travels farthest and F is second; this sequence places both incorrectly.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin electrophoresis is performed on an asymptomatic 30-year-old man. The gel shows two bands, one in the hemoglobin A position and one in the hemoglobin S position. Which is the most likely interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin C trait

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin SC disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal adult pattern

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sickle cell disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sickle cell trait

explanation.summary: An AS pattern, with bands at both the A and S positions, indicates sickle cell trait.
explanation.whyCorrect: The electrophoretic patterns map directly onto diagnoses: AA is a normal adult, AF a normal newborn, AS sickle cell trait, SS sickle cell disease, AC hemoglobin C trait, CC hemoglobin C disease, and SC hemoglobin SC disease. Two bands at A and S therefore identify sickle cell trait in this asymptomatic man.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemoglobin C trait gives an AC pattern, with the second band at the C position rather than at S.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin SC disease gives bands at S and C with no hemoglobin A band.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A normal adult shows a single band in the A position (AA).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sickle cell disease shows an SS pattern with a band at S and no hemoglobin A band.

questions.stem: Which hemoglobin normally accounts for about 2% to 3% of adult hemoglobin, and which globin chains compose it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin A, composed of two alpha chains and two beta chains

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin A2, composed of two alpha chains and two delta chains

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin Barts, composed of four gamma chains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemoglobin F, composed of two alpha chains and two gamma chains

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemoglobin S, composed of two alpha chains and two mutated beta chains

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin A2, two alpha chains plus two delta chains, makes up about 2% to 3% of adult hemoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most adult hemoglobin is hemoglobin A (two alpha plus two beta chains). A very small amount, 2%-3%, is hemoglobin A2 (two alpha plus two delta chains), and an even smaller amount, 1%-2%, is fetal hemoglobin F (two alpha plus two gamma chains).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemoglobin A is correctly described but makes up the great majority of adult hemoglobin, not 2%-3%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin Barts is the gamma-chain tetramer of alpha-thalassemia with four gene deletions, not a normal adult fraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin F is correctly described but accounts for only about 1%-2% of adult hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin S arises from a beta-chain mutation and is not a normal adult hemoglobin fraction.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with lifelong anemia is diagnosed with thalassemia, and his parents ask what is wrong with his blood. Which statement best describes the underlying defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A beta-chain mutation lets hemoglobin polymerize when it gives up oxygen

choices.label: B
choices.text: A cytoskeleton mutation makes the red cells less deformable and prone to rupture

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antibody coats the red cells, leading to their destruction in the spleen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inadequate iron supply limits the amount of hemoglobin the cells can make

choices.label: E
choices.text: Production of either the alpha- or the beta-globin chains is decreased

explanation.summary: Thalassemia is caused by decreased production of either the alpha- or the beta-globin chains, with severity varying by mutation and number of genes affected.
