explanation.whyCorrect: In thalassemia the globin chains themselves are underproduced. The degree of impairment and the severity of disease vary according to the specific genetic mutation and the number of genes affected, which is why presentations range from mild anemia to hydrops fetalis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A beta-chain mutation with polymerization on deoxygenation describes sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A cytoskeleton mutation causing less deformable, rupture-prone cells describes hereditary spherocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibody coating of red cells describes autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is detected by a positive direct antiglobulin test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Limited iron supply describes iron-deficiency anemia, not a globin production defect.

questions.stem: Osmotic fragility testing is performed on a patient with chronic anemia. Her curve is shifted so that her red blood cells lyse only at lower-than-normal concentrations of sodium chloride, indicating decreased osmotic fragility. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic myelofibrosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron-deficiency anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thalassemia major

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

explanation.summary: Decreased osmotic fragility, with lysis occurring only in more hypotonic (lower NaCl) solutions, is characteristic of thalassemia and sickle cell anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diseases associated with decreased osmotic fragility include sickle cell anemia and thalassemia. These cells tolerate more water entry before rupturing, so hemolysis requires a lower NaCl concentration than normal, shifting the curve away from the normal range in the direction described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic myelofibrosis is identified by teardrop cells on the smear rather than by an osmotic fragility shift.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hereditary spherocytosis is the classic cause of increased osmotic fragility, with lysis at higher-than-normal NaCl concentrations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron-deficiency anemia is diagnosed from the indices and iron studies and is not among the causes of decreased osmotic fragility.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is evaluated with the direct antiglobulin test, and its spherocytes would not shift the curve toward lower NaCl.

questions.stem: A hematologist notes that osmotic fragility testing is still widely taught for board preparation but is no longer the test used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis. Which test has replaced it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin test

choices.label: B
choices.text: EMA binding test

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reticulocyte count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supravital staining

explanation.summary: Newer EMA binding testing has replaced osmotic fragility testing for the diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although osmotic fragility testing is commonly mentioned for board preparation purposes, it has been replaced by newer testing, the EMA binding test, for diagnosing hereditary spherocytosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The direct antiglobulin test detects antibody or complement on red cells and is used for immune hemolysis, not hereditary spherocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin electrophoresis identifies and quantifies hemoglobin types such as S and C.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The reticulocyte count assesses whether the marrow is responding, not the membrane defect itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supravital staining visualizes reticulocyte ribosomal RNA and does not diagnose a membrane disorder.

questions.stem: A patient with a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia has many schistocytes on her smear. The automated analyzer reports an elevated platelet count, yet very few platelets are seen microscopically. Which explanation is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agglutinated red cells are counted as single large particles, which raises the platelet count

choices.label: B
choices.text: Analyzers classify particles mainly by size, so small red cell fragments are counted as platelets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin is measured spectrophotometrically, which falsely elevates all particle counts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelets are lysed during the hemoglobin measurement, concentrating the particles that remain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reticulocytes retain ribosomal RNA, which the analyzer scores as platelet granules

explanation.summary: Because modern hematology analyzers classify blood cells primarily by size, red cell or white cell fragments of platelet size are counted as platelets, falsely elevating the platelet count.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most modern CBC analyzers sort particles primarily by size. Red or white cell fragments that fall within the size window used for platelets are therefore counted as platelets, producing a falsely elevated platelet count. This is why CBC abnormalities should be investigated to determine whether they represent a true phenomenon in the patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Red cell clumping falsely decreases the RBC count and falsely increases the MCV; it is not the cause of a spuriously high platelet count.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spectrophotometric hemoglobin measurement is unaffected by clumping and does not inflate particle counts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysis is applied to red cells for the hemoglobin measurement; platelet destruction is not the mechanism of a falsely high platelet count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reticulocyte RNA is visualized with supravital stains and is not what the analyzer counts as platelets.

questions.stem: An infant's red blood cells prove resistant to lysis in the hematology analyzer, a problem that can also occur in patients with a hemoglobinopathy. Which pattern of spurious results is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Falsely decreased hematocrit with a falsely decreased mean cell hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Falsely decreased hemoglobin with a falsely increased white blood cell count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Falsely decreased red blood cell count with a falsely increased mean cell volume

choices.label: D
choices.text: Falsely increased hemoglobin with a falsely decreased white blood cell count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Falsely increased platelet count with a falsely increased hemoglobin

explanation.summary: Red cells resistant to lysis, as in a hemoglobinopathy or in infants, give a falsely low hemoglobin and can falsely raise the white blood cell count.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemoglobin is measured after the red cells are lysed, so cells that resist lysis release less hemoglobin and the reported value is falsely low. The intact red cells may then be counted as white blood cells, producing a possible increase in the WBC count.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The problem lies with the hemoglobin measurement and the WBC count; this pairing does not describe the lysis-resistance pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A falsely low RBC count with a falsely high MCV is the pattern produced by red cell clumping from agglutination or rouleaux.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resistance to lysis lowers rather than raises the measured hemoglobin, and the WBC count tends to rise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A falsely elevated platelet count results from cell fragments being sized as platelets, and hemoglobin is decreased rather than increased here.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for fatigue. Her physician explains that a clinical diagnosis of anemia is based on comparing a single laboratory value to an age- and sex-matched reference population. Which of the following laboratory parameters is used to establish this clinical diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin test (DAT)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red cell distribution width (RDW)

explanation.summary: The clinical definition of anemia is a decreased hemoglobin (or hematocrit) relative to a reference population.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anemia is defined clinically as a hemoglobin (or hematocrit) below the reference range for a matched population, which is derived from the mean +/- 2 standard deviations. Hemoglobin is therefore the value used to establish the diagnosis before further indices refine the differential.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The DAT detects antibodies on the red cell surface and is a test for autoimmune hemolysis, not a screen for anemia itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Indirect bilirubin is a marker of hemolysis (increased red cell turnover), not the parameter that defines anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MCV measures red cell size and is used to narrow the differential only after anemia has already been established.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RDW measures variability in red cell size and helps narrow the differential once anemia is diagnosed, but it does not define anemia.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is admitted to the emergency department with a 2-week history of diarrhea, sepsis, hypovolemic shock, and acute kidney injury. His admission hemoglobin is 15.3 g/dL. A repeat complete blood count less than 24 hours later, after large boluses of intravenous fluids, shows a hemoglobin of 9.9 g/dL, along with decreases in his white blood cell count and platelet count. Which of the following best explains the drop in hemoglobin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute intravascular hemolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dilutional anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marrow suppression from sepsis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Occult gastrointestinal hemorrhage

explanation.summary: A hemoglobin that falls acutely after large IV fluid boluses, together with drops in WBC and platelet counts, indicates a dilutional (spurious) anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemoglobin is a ratio of grams of hemoglobin per deciliter of blood. Expanding the plasma volume (denominator) with IV fluids lowers the apparent hemoglobin without true red cell loss. A helpful clue that the drop is dilutional is that the white cell and platelet counts fall in parallel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intravascular hemolysis would not simultaneously lower the white cell and platelet counts, and there is no jaundice or dark urine described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency is a chronic process and cannot account for an acute hemoglobin change over less than a day.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow suppression develops over days to weeks and cannot explain a hemoglobin change within 24 hours tied to fluid administration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GI hemorrhage causes a true drop in red cell mass and would not proportionally lower the WBC and platelet counts.

questions.stem: A 10-week-old, previously healthy, full-term infant is found to have a hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL on routine testing. He is feeding and growing well and is otherwise asymptomatic. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inherited hemolytic anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dilutional anemia from congestive heart failure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate-antagonist medication exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Occult gastrointestinal blood loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physiologic anemia of infancy

explanation.summary: Infants normally experience a physiologic anemia around 8-12 weeks of age with a nadir that can reach 9.5-10 g/dL.
explanation.whyCorrect: After birth, red cell mass declines in response to increased oxygen availability and downregulation of erythropoietin. The count falls until oxygen delivery becomes inadequate and erythropoietin production resumes, producing an expected physiologic nadir at roughly 8-12 weeks. An age-matched reference range must be used because normal hemoglobin varies with age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An inherited hemolytic anemia would typically produce jaundice, dark urine, or a positive family history, none of which are described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dilutional anemia from CHF requires plasma-volume expansion from heart failure, which this healthy infant does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No medication exposure is described, and folate antagonists cause a maturation-defect anemia, not the expected physiologic nadir.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GI blood loss is not suggested in an asymptomatic, well-growing infant and would be an uncommon explanation at this age.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 26 weeks gestation is noted to have a hemoglobin of 10.6 g/dL. She is asymptomatic, and her white cell and platelet counts are normal. Which of the following physiologic changes most likely accounts for the mildly decreased hemoglobin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of red cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow aplasia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase in plasma volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Testosterone-driven erythropoiesis

explanation.summary: Pregnancy causes a physiologic (dilutional) anemia because plasma volume increases relative to red cell mass.
explanation.whyCorrect: In normal pregnancy the plasma volume expands more than the red cell mass, modestly lowering the hemoglobin concentration. Anemia in pregnancy is typically defined as less than 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters and less than 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester, so this value is near the physiologic range.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hemolysis would be accompanied by jaundice or dark urine and is not indicated by an isolated mild hemoglobin drop.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Marrow aplasia typically depresses all cell lines, but this patient's white cell and platelet counts are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic GI blood loss is not suggested here and would cause a true iron deficiency rather than a physiologic dilutional change.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Testosterone raises hemoglobin (an erythropoietic effect) and would not explain a decrease.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue and pallor. She reports heavy periods lasting 7 days, using 5 pads per day with occasional clots, and she has four children ranging from 2 to 6 years of age. She was told she was anemic during a previous pregnancy. She eats a regular diet with meat, has no change in bowel habits or dark stools, and has had no jaundice or dark urine. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia of chronic inflammation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aplastic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dilutional anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual loss combined with several closely spaced pregnancies is a classic history for iron deficiency anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Menstrual blood loss is a very common cause of iron deficiency anemia, and each pregnancy costs roughly 600-750 mg of iron. Several pregnancies at short intervals give the body little time to replenish lost iron, and the absence of hemolysis, GI bleeding, or dilutional features points to iron deficiency from extensive menstrual and pregnancy-related loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No chronic infection, inflammatory disease, or malignancy is described to invoke anemia of chronic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aplastic anemia would typically depress all cell lines and is not suggested by this focused blood-loss history.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no jaundice, dark urine, or other evidence of hemolysis to support an autoimmune hemolytic process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: She is not pregnant now and has no CHF, splenomegaly, or recent IV fluids to cause plasma-volume expansion.

questions.stem: During a history for anemia, a physician emphasizes that each full-term pregnancy represents a large obligate iron loss that predisposes to iron deficiency, particularly with multiple closely spaced pregnancies. Approximately how much iron is lost per pregnancy?

explanation.summary: Each pregnancy represents roughly 600-750 mg of iron loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that each pregnancy represents about 600-750 mg of iron lost, a large amount to replace. Women who have had multiple pregnancies, especially at short intervals, are highly likely to become iron deficient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 20-30 mg is far too small; it is closer to daily dietary iron content, not the cost of a pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 100-150 mg substantially underestimates the obligate iron loss of a pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 200 mg is the iron loss associated with one unit of donated or drawn blood, not a pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 1500-2000 mg overstates the per-pregnancy loss described in the source.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents for follow-up. His mother mentions that he receives red blood cell transfusions once per month for treatment of his anemia, and that his aunt and cousin require similar treatments. Which of the six key history questions is most directly illustrated by this vignette?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Has the patient been exposed to medication or toxins?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Is the anemia inherited or acquired?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Is the patient truly anemic?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Is there evidence of blood loss?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Is there evidence of hemolysis?

explanation.summary: Young age at onset, chronic transfusion dependence, and a positive family history point to the question of whether the anemia is inherited or acquired.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inherited causes of anemia typically present at an earlier age, and a family history of relatives requiring treatment or transfusions suggests a genetic process. Transfusions given at a young age without an obvious acquired cause are a specific clue to an inherited anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No relevant drug or toxin exposure is mentioned that would implicate a medication-induced anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The child clearly has true anemia, since he requires monthly transfusions, so a dilutional cause is not in question.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No source of bleeding such as melena, heavy menses, or hematuria is described in the vignette.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No jaundice, dark urine, or splenomegaly is described to raise the question of hemolysis specifically.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue. On examination he has scleral icterus, and he reports his urine has been dark. His spleen is mildly enlarged. Laboratory studies show an elevated indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin. Which of the following processes best explains this clinical picture?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow aplasia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired DNA synthesis in red cell precursors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasma volume expansion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Premature destruction of red blood cells

explanation.summary: Jaundice with elevated indirect bilirubin, dark urine, and splenomegaly are characteristic signs of hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bilirubin is a breakdown product of heme; unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin rises with the increased red cell turnover of hemolysis, causing jaundice. Dark urine reflects hemoglobinuria when hemolysis is intravascular, and the spleen, a common site of red cell destruction, can enlarge with chronic hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow aplasia reduces cell production and does not generate the increased red cell turnover that raises indirect bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GI blood loss causes iron deficiency and does not elevate indirect bilirubin or cause jaundice and dark urine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A maturation defect from impaired DNA synthesis causes megaloblastic anemia, not the jaundice-and-dark-urine picture of hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma volume expansion causes a dilutional anemia and does not raise bilirubin or produce jaundice.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 25-year-old man develops fatigue, pallor, and jaundice a few days after starting primaquine for malaria prophylaxis. Laboratory studies are consistent with hemolytic anemia. A deficiency of which of the following enzymes best explains his susceptibility to this oxidant drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythrocyte adenosine deaminase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythrocyte pyruvate kinase (PK-R)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysosomal acid glucocerebrosidase

choices.label: E
choices.text: NADPH-dependent dihydrofolate reductase

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency leaves red cells unable to detoxify reactive oxygen species, so oxidant drugs trigger hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with G6PD deficiency lack the enzyme needed to detoxify hydrogen peroxide, making red cells susceptible to oxidant stress. The classic presentation is a previously healthy person who, after an oxidant stressor such as primaquine, dapsone, or sulfa drugs, develops signs of hemolytic anemia (fatigue, pallor, jaundice).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency, not drug-induced hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes a chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia but is not the enzyme defect triggered by oxidant drugs described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disorder, not oxidant-induced hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by folate antagonists such as methotrexate, which cause a maturation-defect anemia, not oxidant hemolysis.

questions.stem: A physician is reviewing a patient's medications while evaluating a new anemia. She notes the patient takes ibuprofen frequently for chronic pain. Through which mechanism is this medication most likely to contribute to anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct suppression of the bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expansion of plasma volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate antagonism impairing red cell maturation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gastrointestinal blood loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidative stress causing hemolysis

explanation.summary: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen classically cause anemia through gastrointestinal blood loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, like ibuprofen) as agents that cause GI blood loss. Chronic GI bleeding depletes iron and produces iron deficiency anemia over time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow suppression is associated with chemotherapy, insecticides, and anticonvulsants such as phenytoin, not NSAIDs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma volume expansion causes dilutional anemia and is unrelated to NSAID use.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate antagonism causing a maturation defect is the mechanism of trimethoprim and methotrexate, not ibuprofen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidant hemolysis is caused by drugs like dapsone, sulfa drugs, and primaquine, not by NSAIDs.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with long-standing chronic kidney disease is found to be anemic. He has no evidence of bleeding, hemolysis, or a dilutional cause, and takes no marrow-toxic medications. Which of the six key history questions best captures the most likely explanation for his anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Is the anemia an inherited disorder or an acquired condition of later life?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Is the patient truly anemic, or is the hemoglobin diluted by plasma volume expansion?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Is there evidence of a systemic illness or non-hematologic organ dysfunction?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Is there evidence of acute or chronic blood loss from the gastrointestinal tract?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Is there evidence of hemolysis, such as jaundice, dark urine, or splenomegaly?

explanation.summary: Renal disease is a non-hematologic organ dysfunction that can cause anemia, captured by the systemic-illness history question.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many underlying conditions, including infection, chronic inflammation, renal disease, liver disease, endocrine disease, and malignancy, can be associated with anemia. Chronic kidney disease is a classic example of a non-hematologic organ dysfunction that produces anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Onset in later adulthood with a clear organ cause argues against an inherited anemia presenting at a young age.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A dilutional cause is excluded by the stem, so the patient is truly anemic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The vignette explicitly states there is no evidence of bleeding, so a blood-loss source is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no jaundice, dark urine, or splenomegaly, and the stem states there is no hemolysis.

questions.stem: A medical student asks how anemia is defined. The attending explains that there are two definitions: a clinical one based on comparison with a reference population, and a physiologic one. Which of the following best states the physiologic definition of anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hematocrit below the mean of the reference population

choices.label: B
choices.text: A red blood cell count below the lower limit of the reference range

choices.label: C
choices.text: A reduction in the average size of the circulating red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxygen-carrying capacity insufficient to meet the oxygen requirement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Premature destruction of circulating red blood cells in the spleen

explanation.summary: The physiologic definition of anemia is insufficient oxygen-carrying capacity in the blood to meet the oxygen requirement.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anemia has two definitions. The physiologic definition is functional: the blood cannot carry enough oxygen to meet the body's oxygen requirement. The clinical definition is the laboratory one, a decreased hemoglobin or hematocrit compared to the reference population.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Comparing the hematocrit to a reference population is the clinical definition of anemia, not the physiologic one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A red cell count below the reference range is a laboratory comparison, which belongs to the clinical rather than the physiologic definition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A reduced average red cell size describes a low MCV, an index used to narrow the differential after anemia is established.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Premature red cell destruction defines hemolysis, which is one cause of anemia rather than a definition of it.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is being evaluated for a newly discovered anemia. When asked about her medications, she replies that she takes none. Which of the following is the most appropriate next question about her drug history?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "Did anyone in your family take medicine for anemia?"

choices.label: B
choices.text: "Did you take any prescription medications as a child?"

choices.label: C
choices.text: "Do you take any over-the-counter medicines or supplements?"

choices.label: D
choices.text: "Have you ever had a reaction during general anesthesia?"

choices.label: E
choices.text: "Have you ever received a blood transfusion?"

explanation.summary: A complete drug history in the evaluation of anemia must include over-the-counter medications and dietary supplements.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many, many medications can be associated with anemia, so a complete drug history is essential. Patients frequently do not count over-the-counter agents or dietary supplements as "medications," yet agents such as NSAIDs are common contributors to anemia, which is why they must be asked about specifically.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A relative's treatment for anemia is part of the family history used to suggest an inherited cause, not part of this patient's drug history.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Remote childhood prescriptions are far less relevant than the agents the patient is taking now.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An anesthetic reaction does not bear on which drugs and supplements the patient is currently exposed to.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion history helps address whether the anemia is inherited or acquired; it does not complete the medication history.

questions.stem: A complete blood count reports several red blood cell indices. Which index reports the percentage of the blood that is composed of red blood cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hematocrit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin concentration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean cell volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cell distribution width

explanation.summary: The hematocrit is the percentage of blood composed of red blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hematocrit is defined as the percentage of the blood volume made up of red cells, with typical reference ranges of 40%-54% in males and 36%-48% in females. Along with hemoglobin, it is the value compared with the reference population to make a clinical diagnosis of anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin is the concentration of hemoglobin in the blood, reported in g/dL rather than as a percentage of blood volume.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mean cell hemoglobin concentration is the average concentration of hemoglobin per red cell, not the fraction of blood made of red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mean cell volume is the average volume, or size, of the red cells, reported in femtoliters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Red cell distribution width reports the variability of the MCV, expressed as a percentage but describing size variation, not blood composition.

questions.stem: A third-year student proposes starting oral iron for a patient whose routine complete blood count showed a hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL, before any further history is taken. The attending cautions against this approach. Which of the following best explains the attending's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A diagnosis of anemia must be confirmed by bone marrow biopsy before any therapy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anemia signals an underlying disease that may be missed if only the anemia is treated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron cannot be started until hemolysis is excluded by a direct antiglobulin test.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral iron alters the red cell indices and invalidates any subsequent complete blood count.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treatment should be deferred until the red cell distribution width returns to normal.

explanation.summary: Anemia is not a diagnosis in itself but an abnormality pointing to an underlying disease, so the cause must be pursued.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anemia is an abnormality that indicates the presence of an underlying disease. Simply chasing the anemia can cause the clinician to miss a significant underlying cause that warrants treatment in its own right, and the most important part of the evaluation is the history.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A marrow biopsy is not a prerequisite for evaluating or treating anemia; the history comes first.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The direct antiglobulin test addresses autoimmune hemolysis specifically and is not a required gateway to treating anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron therapy does not invalidate later complete blood counts; the concern is missing the underlying cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The red cell distribution width is an index that helps narrow the differential; it is not a treatment threshold.

questions.stem: Two red cell indices both describe the hemoglobin content of red blood cells; one is reported in picograms per cell and the other in grams per deciliter. Which index reports the average concentration of hemoglobin per red blood cell, with a typical reference range of 32-36 g/dL?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin concentration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin content per cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean corpuscular volume of red cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red blood cell distribution width (RDW)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole blood hemoglobin concentration

explanation.summary: Mean cell hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) is the average concentration of hemoglobin per red cell, typically 32-36 g/dL.
explanation.whyCorrect: MCHC expresses hemoglobin content relative to cell volume and is reported in g/dL with a reference range of 32-36 g/dL. Its companion index, MCH, expresses the average weight of hemoglobin per cell in picograms.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mean cell hemoglobin is the average weight of hemoglobin per red cell, reported as 27-31 pg/cell rather than as a concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mean cell volume is the average size of the red cells, with a reference range of 80-100 fL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Red cell distribution width reports the variability of the MCV, typically 12% to 15%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin is the concentration of hemoglobin in whole blood, not the concentration within an individual red cell.

questions.stem: A complete blood count on a 45-year-old woman with anemia reports a red blood cell distribution width of 18%. This elevated value indicates an increase in which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Average concentration of hemoglobin per red cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Average weight of hemoglobin per red cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Number of red blood cells per liter of blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Percentage of blood composed of red cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variability of the mean cell volume

explanation.summary: Red cell distribution width measures the variability of the MCV, with a typical reference range of 12% to 15%.
explanation.whyCorrect: RDW is defined as the variability of the mean cell volume, so a value above the typical 12%-15% range means the circulating red cells vary more than normal in size. Like the MCV, it is used to narrow the differential once anemia has been established.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Average hemoglobin concentration per red cell is the MCHC, reported in g/dL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The average weight of hemoglobin per red cell is the MCH, reported in pg/cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The number of red cells per liter of blood is the red blood cell count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The percentage of blood composed of red cells is the hematocrit, a separate index.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old infant born at 29 weeks gestation has a hemoglobin substantially lower than that of a term infant of the same postnatal age. Compared with term infants, the expected postnatal decline in hemoglobin in pre-term infants is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent, because erythropoietin stays elevated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delayed until after 6 months of age

choices.label: C
choices.text: Limited to infants who are formula fed

choices.label: D
choices.text: More abrupt and more profound

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slower in onset and less pronounced

explanation.summary: Pre-term infants experience a more abrupt and profound decline in hemoglobin than term infants.
explanation.whyCorrect: After birth, red cell mass normally declines as oxygen availability rises and erythropoietin is downregulated, producing the physiologic anemia of infancy around 8-12 weeks of age. In pre-term infants this decline is both more abrupt and more profound than the usual nadir seen in term infants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythropoietin is downregulated after birth, which is precisely what allows the red cell mass to fall.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The physiologic decline occurs around 8-12 weeks of age, not after 6 months, and prematurity accelerates rather than delays it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The decline is a physiologic response to increased oxygen availability, not a consequence of feeding method.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A slower, milder decline is the opposite of what prematurity produces.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl has a hemoglobin of 11.5 g/dL on a screening complete blood count. Before concluding that she is anemic, her hemoglobin should be compared with which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An age-matched reference range

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her own hemoglobin measured at birth

choices.label: C
choices.text: The adult female reference range

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mean value for hospitalized children

choices.label: E
choices.text: The range expected after puberty

explanation.summary: Normal hemoglobin varies with age during childhood, so an age-matched reference range must be used.
explanation.whyCorrect: Children have a different "normal" range than adults from birth until puberty, after which hemoglobin approaches the adult range. Because the normal value varies at different ages during childhood, the laboratory should provide an age-matched reference range as part of the complete blood count.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The hemoglobin at birth is far higher than at any later point in infancy or childhood and is not the comparison standard.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adult ranges do not apply to a pre-pubertal child and could misclassify a normal value as anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reference ranges are derived from a normal reference population, not from hospitalized patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin approaches the adult range only after puberty, so that range is inappropriate at age 4.

questions.stem: Laboratory reference ranges for hemoglobin are higher for men (14-18 g/dL) than for women (12-16 g/dL). Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this sex difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A larger circulating plasma volume in men

choices.label: B
choices.text: A lower reference mean cell volume in women

choices.label: C
choices.text: An erythropoietic effect of testosterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greater splenic red cell destruction in women

choices.label: E
choices.text: More rapid clearance of erythropoietin in women

explanation.summary: Men tend to have higher hemoglobin than women, probably because testosterone has an erythropoietic effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sex-based difference in the hemoglobin reference range is attributed to the erythropoietic effect of testosterone, which drives a higher red cell mass in men. Because of this, the laboratory should include sex-appropriate reference ranges in the CBC report.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A larger plasma volume would dilute hemoglobin and lower it, which is the opposite of the observed difference in men.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mean cell volume reference range of 80-100 fL is not sex-specific and does not set the hemoglobin range.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased splenic red cell destruction describes hemolysis, a pathologic process rather than a normal sex difference.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Differences in erythropoietin clearance are not the stated basis for the sex difference in hemoglobin.

questions.stem: A physician evaluating a newly discovered low hemoglobin wonders whether the value reflects expansion of the plasma volume rather than a true decrease in red cell mass. Which of the following elements of the history would best support a dilutional cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A unit of blood donated last month

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congestive heart failure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daily ibuprofen use for knee pain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Long-standing chronic kidney disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several years of untreated heartburn

explanation.summary: Congestive heart failure increases plasma volume and can produce a dilutional anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemoglobin is a ratio of grams of hemoglobin per deciliter of blood, so increasing the plasma volume lowers the ratio without any true loss of red cells. Conditions that expand plasma volume include pregnancy, congestive heart failure, splenomegaly, and recent boluses of IV fluids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Each donated unit represents about 200 mg of iron lost, so donation causes real iron loss rather than dilution.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen cause anemia through gastrointestinal blood loss, a true loss of red cell mass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal disease causes a true anemia as a non-hematologic organ dysfunction, not a dilutional one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heartburn raises the possibility of a gastrointestinal source of bleeding, which again is true blood loss.

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient's hemoglobin falls after aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation. Failure to recognize that this drop is dilutional most directly places the patient at risk for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A falsely elevated white blood cell count

choices.label: B
choices.text: An artificially increased mean cell volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: An unnecessary red blood cell transfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure to detect hemoglobinuria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Overestimation of the distribution width

explanation.summary: Unrecognized dilutional anemia can lead to inappropriate treatment, including unnecessary transfusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: When plasma volume expands, the hemoglobin ratio appears decreased even though red cell mass is unchanged. If this possibility is not recognized, the low value can prompt inappropriate treatment and transfusion, which is why the clinician should step back and ask whether the patient is truly anemic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dilution lowers rather than raises the white blood cell count; a parallel fall in WBC and platelets is in fact the clue that the change is dilutional.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dilution changes the concentration of cells in the sample, not the average size of the individual red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobinuria reflects intravascular hemolysis and is unrelated to plasma-volume expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The red cell distribution width measures variability in cell size and is not driven by plasma volume.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 22 weeks gestation is asymptomatic and has a hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL. Below which of the following hemoglobin values is anemia typically defined at this point in her pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 9.5 g/dL

explanation.summary: Anemia in pregnancy is typically defined as a hemoglobin below 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass in normal pregnancy, modestly lowering the hemoglobin concentration. The thresholds used to define anemia in pregnancy account for this: less than 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, and less than 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 9.5 g/dL approximates the nadir of the physiologic anemia of infancy, not a pregnancy threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 11 g/dL is the threshold used in the first and third trimesters, not the second.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 12 g/dL is the lower end of the non-pregnant female reference range and does not account for the physiologic change of pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 13 g/dL lies within the normal female reference range and is far above any pregnancy threshold.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks gestation has a mildly decreased hemoglobin, which her obstetrician attributes to the expected physiologic change of pregnancy. Which of the following findings would most strongly warrant additional evaluation rather than observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL in the first trimester

choices.label: B
choices.text: A rise in plasma volume exceeding the rise in red cell mass

choices.label: C
choices.text: Absence of jaundice and of dark-colored urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Laboratory evidence of iron deficiency accompanying the anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal white blood cell and platelet counts on the same sample

explanation.summary: Anemia in pregnancy should be evaluated further when it is out of the expected range, symptomatic, or accompanied by evidence of iron deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: A modest hemoglobin decrease in pregnancy is expected from the relative increase in plasma volume. Additional evaluation is warranted when hemoglobin levels are lower or higher than expected, when additional symptoms accompany the anemia, or when there is evidence of iron deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A hemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL in the first trimester is above the 11 g/dL threshold and is therefore within the expected range.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma volume increasing more than red cell mass is the normal physiologic change of pregnancy itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The absence of jaundice and dark urine argues against hemolysis and so reduces, rather than increases, concern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Normal white cell and platelet counts are reassuring and do not by themselves prompt further workup.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue. Over the past 2 months his stools have been black and tarry. This finding most directly suggests which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A folate-related maturation defect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expansion of the plasma volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gastrointestinal blood loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intravascular hemolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of the bone marrow

explanation.summary: Dark, tarry stools (melena) indicate bleeding into the gastrointestinal tract.
explanation.whyCorrect: The gastrointestinal portion of the blood-loss history asks about changes in bowel habits, blood in the stool, and dark tarry stools, called melena. Melena signals gastrointestinal blood loss, a common cause of anemia and of resulting iron deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A maturation defect from folate antagonism impairs red cell production and does not alter the stool.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma-volume expansion causes a dilutional anemia and produces no change in stool appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intravascular hemolysis produces dark urine from hemoglobinuria, not black tarry stools.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marrow suppression reduces cell production and does not cause gastrointestinal bleeding.

questions.stem: While taking a history from a patient with a new anemia, a physician asks specifically about heartburn and symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux. This question is asked primarily to identify which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gastrointestinal source of blood loss

choices.label: B
choices.text: A medication that suppresses the marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: An inherited cause of the anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Expansion of the circulating plasma volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ongoing premature red cell destruction

explanation.summary: Heartburn and reflux symptoms are part of the gastrointestinal history used to uncover a source of blood loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because blood loss is a common cause of anemia, the history asks thorough, specific questions to identify its source. The gastrointestinal portion includes change in bowel habits, blood in the stool or melena, and heartburn or reflux symptoms, all of which point toward a gastrointestinal bleeding source.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Marrow-suppressing drug exposure is identified by taking a complete medication history, not by asking about reflux.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inherited causes are pursued through family history, age at onset, prior treatment, transfusion history, and ethnic background.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A dilutional cause is suggested by pregnancy, heart failure, splenomegaly, or recent IV fluids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysis is suggested by jaundice, dark urine, and splenomegaly rather than by reflux symptoms.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with anemia is asked whether he has ever noticed blood in his urine. Which of the following best characterizes hematuria as a cause of anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A consequence of plasma-volume expansion

choices.label: B
choices.text: A finding specific to inherited causes of anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: A reliable indicator of intravascular hemolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: An uncommon but occasional source of blood loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: The most common source of blood loss in men

explanation.summary: Blood in the urine is an uncommon but occasional source of blood loss that should still be asked about.
explanation.whyCorrect: The urinary portion of the blood-loss history asks whether the patient has seen blood in the urine. Hematuria is described as an uncommon but occasional source of blood loss, which is why it belongs in a thorough history even though gastrointestinal and menstrual losses are far more frequent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Plasma-volume expansion produces a dilutional anemia without any loss of blood.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematuria is a route of blood loss and carries no specific link to inherited anemias.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dark urine from hemoglobinuria suggests intravascular hemolysis; visible blood in the urine is a bleeding source instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gastrointestinal bleeding, not hematuria, is the common source of blood loss to pursue in men.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who donates blood every 8 weeks and takes no supplements is found to be iron deficient. Approximately how much iron is lost with each unit of blood donated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 50 mg

choices.label: B
choices.text: 200 mg

choices.label: C
choices.text: 600 mg

choices.label: D
choices.text: 750 mg

explanation.summary: Each unit of blood represents about 200 mg of iron loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Frequent phlebotomy, whether from blood draws or blood donation, is a recognized source of iron loss. Each unit of blood represents roughly 200 mg of iron, which can cause iron deficiency over time in the absence of supplementation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 50 mg substantially underestimates the iron contained in a unit of blood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 600-750 mg is the iron cost of a pregnancy, which is far greater than a single unit of blood.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 750 mg is the upper end of the per-pregnancy iron loss, not the loss from one donated unit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 1000 mg overstates the iron content of a single unit of blood.

questions.stem: Rather than asking a woman with anemia whether her periods are "heavy," her physician asks how many days each period lasts, how many pads or tampons are used, and whether clots are passed. Which of the following best explains why these specific questions are preferred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heavy menstrual bleeding is an uncommon cause of iron deficiency anemia.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Menstruation is the only source of iron loss in women of child-bearing age.

choices.label: C
choices.text: One person's light period is another's heavy period, so quantities matter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passing clots excludes a gastrointestinal source of bleeding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The length of the period predicts the hemoglobin nadir precisely.

explanation.summary: Perception of menstrual flow is relative, so quantitative questions are needed to assess the risk of iron loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Menstrual blood loss is a very common cause of iron deficiency anemia, but each patient's period is relative to her own experience; one person's light period is another person's heavy period. Asking specific questions about the number of pads and the length of the period allows the clinician to assess the risk of iron loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Menstrual blood loss is in fact a very common cause of iron deficiency anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pregnancy, gastrointestinal bleeding, hematuria, and phlebotomy are all additional sources of iron loss in women.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clot passage describes the menstrual flow and says nothing about whether the gastrointestinal tract is also bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Period length helps estimate risk of iron loss; it does not precisely predict any hemoglobin value.

questions.stem: A physician suspects an inherited cause for a young patient's anemia, but the patient does not know the specific diagnosis of any relative. Which of the following questions is most likely to yield useful information about an inherited cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether any relative has had a change in bowel habits

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether any relative has heartburn or reflux symptoms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether any relative needed iron supplementation or transfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether any relative takes NSAIDs on a regular basis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether any relative was transfused during a major surgery

explanation.summary: Most patients do not know relatives' diagnoses, so ask whether family members required treatment for anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: When taking a family history for anemia, most patients will not know exact diagnoses of family members. Asking instead whether someone in the family had to receive treatment for anemia, such as iron supplementation or blood transfusion, may yield a positive result and point toward an inherited process.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A relative's bowel habits bear on that person's own risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, an acquired cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reflux symptoms in a relative point toward an acquired gastrointestinal source rather than a genetic condition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NSAID use in a relative reflects acquired gastrointestinal blood loss and is not heritable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion with an obvious cause such as surgery or hemorrhage does not suggest an inherited anemia; it is transfusion without such a cause that does.

questions.stem: Certain inherited causes of anemia are far more prevalent among people whose ancestors came from particular regions of the world. This geographic clustering is typically explained by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A survival advantage from resistance to malaria

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher rates of blood donation in those populations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regional differences in laboratory reference ranges

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shared dietary iron deficiency in those regions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Widespread use of oxidant medications in those areas

explanation.summary: Inherited anemias cluster geographically because the responsible traits typically arose as a resistance to malaria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ethnic background is part of the inherited-versus-acquired history because some inherited causes of anemia are more prevalent in certain areas of the world, typically arising as a resistance to malaria. Asking where a patient's family is from can therefore raise or lower suspicion for a genetic cause.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blood donation causes acquired iron loss of about 200 mg per unit and is unrelated to inherited anemias.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reference ranges are derived from normal populations and do not create a true difference in disease prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dietary iron deficiency is an acquired, nutritional problem and would not explain an inherited trait clustering by ancestry.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidant drugs trigger hemolysis in susceptible people but do not account for why the underlying trait is regionally common.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a known hemolytic anemia reports that during flares her urine turns cola-colored. Laboratory studies confirm hemoglobin in the urine. This finding indicates that her red cell destruction is occurring predominantly at which of the following sites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Within the blood vessels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Within the bone marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Within the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Within the lymph nodes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Within the spleen

explanation.summary: Hemoglobinuria, and the dark urine it produces, indicates that hemolysis is intravascular.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dark urine in a hemolytic anemia occurs because of hemoglobinuria, which develops when hemoglobin is released directly into the circulation and filtered into the urine. This happens typically when the hemolysis is intravascular, in contrast to red cell destruction taking place within an organ such as the spleen.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The marrow is the site of red cell production; destruction there would not release hemoglobin into the circulation for urinary filtration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatic involvement in hemolysis relates to processing heme into bilirubin, which causes jaundice rather than dark urine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymph nodes are not a site of red cell destruction in hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen is the site of red cell destruction in many hemolytic disorders, but splenic hemolysis produces splenomegaly rather than free hemoglobin in the urine.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with a chronic hemolytic anemia reports several months of left upper quadrant fullness and abdominal discomfort. Which of the following best explains this symptom?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gastric erosion from long-term NSAID exposure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatic congestion caused by unconjugated bilirubin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marrow expansion within the lower rib cage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal enlargement caused by hemoglobinuria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic enlargement from ongoing red cell destruction

explanation.summary: Abdominal discomfort in chronic hemolysis usually reflects splenomegaly, since the spleen is a major site of red cell destruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen is the site of hemolysis in many disorders, and an enlarged spleen can be a consequence of chronic hemolysis. Abdominal discomfort due to splenomegaly is therefore one of the characteristic symptoms of hemolysis, alongside jaundice and dark urine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NSAID-related gastric injury causes gastrointestinal blood loss, and no NSAID exposure is described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Unconjugated bilirubin rises in hemolysis and causes jaundice; it does not congest the liver and cause left-sided fullness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow expansion is not the mechanism given for the abdominal discomfort that accompanies chronic hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobinuria reflects intravascular hemolysis and does not enlarge the kidneys.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with epilepsy who takes phenytoin develops a new anemia, and her white blood cell and platelet counts are also decreased. This medication belongs to which of the following categories of anemia-associated agents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agents that cause gastrointestinal blood loss

choices.label: B
choices.text: Agents that cause marrow aplasia or suppression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Agents that expand the circulating plasma volume

choices.label: D
choices.text: Folate antagonists that cause maturation defects

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidant drugs that provoke hemolysis

explanation.summary: Anticonvulsants such as phenytoin are classed with agents that cause marrow aplasia or suppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Medications associated with anemia fall into several categories, and agents linked to marrow aplasia or suppression include chemotherapy drugs, insecticides, and anticonvulsants such as phenytoin. Because marrow suppression affects production of all lineages, the white cell and platelet counts fall along with the hemoglobin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastrointestinal blood loss is caused by NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and would not depress the platelet and white cell counts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma-volume expansion is a feature of pregnancy, heart failure, splenomegaly, or IV fluids rather than a drug class here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folate antagonists causing maturation defects are trimethoprim and methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidant drugs that cause hemolysis are dapsone, sulfa drugs, and primaquine, not anticonvulsants.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man treated with trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection develops a new anemia. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this drug impairs erythropoiesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody-mediated destruction of circulating red cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct toxicity to marrow stem cells causing aplasia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erosion of the gastric and duodenal mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Folate antagonism producing a maturation defect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidative injury to hemoglobin within the red cell

explanation.summary: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist and causes anemia through a maturation defect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the drug categories associated with anemia, agents causing maturation defects are the folate antagonists, specifically trimethoprim, an antibiotic, and methotrexate, used as chemotherapy and to treat autoimmune diseases. Interfering with folate impairs maturation of developing red cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody-mediated red cell destruction is detected by the direct antiglobulin test and is not the action of trimethoprim.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Marrow aplasia is associated with chemotherapy drugs, insecticides, and anticonvulsants such as phenytoin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucosal erosion with gastrointestinal blood loss is the mechanism of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidative injury is the mechanism of dapsone, sulfa drugs, and primaquine, which cause hemolytic anemia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency has had normal hemoglobin values throughout his life. Which of the following best explains why the majority of patients with this enzyme deficiency remain asymptomatic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody formation against the red cell surface is suppressed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemolysis requires an oxidant stressor such as a drug or infection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Red cells compensate by producing more hemoglobin per cell.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The enzyme defect is corrected by dietary folate intake.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The spleen clears affected cells before any hemolysis occurs.

explanation.summary: G6PD-deficient red cells hemolyze only when challenged by an oxidant stressor such as a medication or an infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with G6PD deficiency are missing the enzyme needed to detoxify hydrogen peroxide, a reactive oxygen species, which makes their red cells susceptible to oxidant stress. A majority of patients are asymptomatic until they are presented with an oxidant stressor, such as a medication or an infection, and then present with signs of hemolytic anemia including fatigue, pallor, and jaundice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: G6PD deficiency is an enzyme defect, not an antibody-mediated process, so antibody suppression is irrelevant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing hemoglobin per cell does not address the inability to detoxify reactive oxygen species.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folate is relevant to maturation defects caused by folate antagonists and does not replace the missing enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen does not pre-emptively remove the cells; they circulate normally until oxidant stress occurs.

questions.stem: A physician is reviewing a panel of patients to determine who is at lowest risk for developing iron-deficiency anemia. Which of the following patients has the LEAST risk for iron deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 60-year-old man with heme-positive stools

choices.label: B
choices.text: A patient with peptic ulcer disease taking large doses of oral antacids

choices.label: C
choices.text: A pregnant woman who follows a vegan diet

choices.label: D
choices.text: An asymptomatic postmenopausal woman

choices.label: E
choices.text: An asymptomatic premenopausal woman

explanation.summary: Iron-deficiency anemia is driven by blood loss, poor intake/absorption, or increased demand; a postmenopausal woman with no symptoms lacks all of these.
explanation.whyCorrect: Women are at risk for iron deficiency during pregnancy (increased demand) and during their reproductive years (menstrual blood loss). After menopause, menstrual losses stop, so an asymptomatic postmenopausal woman has the lowest risk of the options listed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 60-year-old man with heme-positive stools is losing blood from the GI tract, a classic cause of iron deficiency that should raise concern for malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic high-dose antacids reduce GI iron absorption, promoting iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pregnancy sharply raises iron demand, and a vegan diet supplies only poorly absorbed nonheme iron, compounding the risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A premenopausal woman loses iron through ongoing menstrual bleeding, the most common overall cause of iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman reports several months of fatigue and decreased exercise tolerance. She has four children and a full-time job. Her only notable finding on review of systems is heavy menstrual periods. Vital signs and physical exam are unremarkable. Laboratory studies show a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with low serum ferritin. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia of chronic inflammation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic intravascular hemolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic menstrual blood loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired iron absorption in the duodenum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Occult gastrointestinal malignancy

explanation.summary: Heavy menses is the most common overall cause of iron-deficiency anemia in premenopausal women.
explanation.whyCorrect: Menstrual bleeding causes roughly 1 mg of iron loss per day, and heavy menses in a premenopausal woman is the single most common cause of iron-deficiency anemia. Her low ferritin and microcytic, hypochromic indices fit chronic blood loss from menstruation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anemia of chronic inflammation typically shows normal or elevated ferritin, not the low ferritin seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic intravascular hemolysis (e.g., a malfunctioning heart valve or PNH) is an uncommon cause and is not suggested by her history.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired absorption occurs with malabsorption syndromes or bariatric surgery, none of which are present here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GI malignancy is the leading concern in an older man or postmenopausal woman, not a menstruating 32-year-old with an obvious bleeding source.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis is evaluated for a microcytic anemia thought to be due to iron deficiency. Because of her active inflammatory disease, some iron studies may be misleading. Which of the following laboratory values would be abnormally LOW in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepcidin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Red cell distribution width

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum ferritin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum iron

choices.label: E
choices.text: Total iron-binding capacity

explanation.summary: Serum iron is low in iron deficiency, but is nondiagnostic alone because it is also low in anemia of chronic disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serum iron is decreased in iron-deficiency anemia. Because it is also decreased in anemia of chronic disease/inflammation, it is the low value expected here, though it is nonspecific by itself.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepcidin is increased by inflammatory cytokines, not decreased, and helps drive the anemia of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The red cell distribution width is increased in iron deficiency because red cells vary in size (anisocytosis).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferritin is a positive acute-phase reactant; in a patient with active rheumatoid arthritis it can be normal or elevated, masking iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Total iron-binding capacity rises in iron deficiency as the liver makes more transferrin.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man presents with 3 months of progressive fatigue, shortness of breath, and intermittent lightheadedness. Exam is notable for conjunctival pallor and a positive stool hemoccult test. Complete blood count shows hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL with a low mean corpuscular volume, and serum ferritin is 10 ng/mL. In addition to starting oral iron, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abdominal ultrasound

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blood transfusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Colonoscopy

choices.label: D
choices.text: CT scan of the abdomen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

explanation.summary: Iron-deficiency anemia with occult GI bleeding in an older man requires evaluation for a GI malignancy such as colon cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: This man has microcytic anemia with low ferritin and a positive hemoccult test. Iron deficiency in an older man is due to GI malignancy until proven otherwise, so the appropriate next step is colonoscopy (with upper GI endoscopy if indicated).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abdominal ultrasound is used when hemoperitoneum is suspected in trauma; such patients are acutely symptomatic and unstable.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transfusion is reserved for severe or life-threatening anemia or hemodynamic instability, not this stable patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CT of the abdomen is used to evaluate suspected infection or inflammation of the GI tract and nearby organs, not to localize occult bleeding here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin electrophoresis is used to evaluate suspected thalassemia, which is unlikely given the low ferritin and positive hemoccult.

questions.stem: A researcher is studying how iron deficiency reduces hemoglobin production. Normally, the final step of heme synthesis inserts iron into a ring-shaped precursor molecule. Impairment of which of the following steps best explains the decreased heme production in iron-deficiency anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of iron to transferrin in the plasma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insertion of iron into protoporphyrin by ferrochelatase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidation of ferrous iron to ferric iron by hephaestin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduction of ferric iron to ferrous iron in the gut lumen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Storage of iron within ferritin in the liver

explanation.summary: Heme synthesis ends with ferrochelatase inserting iron into protoporphyrin; iron deficiency starves this step.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heme is the iron-containing component of hemoglobin. Its final synthetic step is the insertion of iron into the protoporphyrin molecule by ferrochelatase. When iron is deficient, this step fails, decreasing heme, then hemoglobin, and eventually the number of red cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transferrin binding is a transport function in blood, not a step of the heme biosynthetic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hephaestin oxidizes iron during absorption/export from enterocytes; it is not the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Luminal reduction of ferric to ferrous iron aids intestinal absorption but is upstream of heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferritin storage sequesters iron; it is not part of assembling the heme molecule.

questions.stem: During infection and inflammation, the body sequesters iron inside cells to keep it away from pathogens. Which of the following molecules causes iron to remain sequestered in cells by degrading ferroportin, thereby preventing iron from entering the bloodstream?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ferritin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ferroportin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepcidin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferrin

explanation.summary: Hepcidin blocks iron export by causing internalization and degradation of ferroportin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin, secreted by hepatocytes and increased by inflammatory cytokines, causes ferroportin to be internalized and degraded. Without functioning ferroportin, iron cannot leave enterocytes, macrophages, or hepatocytes and remains sequestered inside cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythropoietin actually inhibits hepatic hepcidin production, promoting iron release rather than sequestration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferritin is the intracellular storage protein for iron; it packs iron away but does not act on ferroportin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferroportin is the transport protein that is degraded by hepcidin, not the molecule causing sequestration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transferrin transports iron through the bloodstream; it does not regulate ferroportin.

questions.stem: A previously healthy person relocates to a high-altitude region where tissue oxygen levels are chronically low. Over the following weeks, the kidney increases production of a hormone that stimulates red blood cell production and simultaneously enhances delivery of iron to the marrow. Through which of the following mechanisms does this hormone increase circulating iron?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking heme carrier protein 1 in the duodenum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreasing transferrin production in the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing ferritin synthesis to store more iron in cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibiting hepatic hepcidin production

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulating hepcidin release to degrade ferroportin

explanation.summary: Erythropoietin inhibits hepcidin, freeing ferroportin to move more iron into the blood for new red cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: When tissue oxygen is low, the kidney releases erythropoietin, which stimulates the marrow to make red cells and also inhibits hepatic hepcidin production. Less hepcidin means ferroportin is preserved, so more iron is transported into the bloodstream for erythropoiesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking HCP1 would impair intestinal iron absorption, reducing rather than increasing available iron.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin does not work by lowering transferrin; transferrin actually carries the mobilized iron.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing ferritin storage would keep iron inside cells rather than raising circulating iron.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating hepcidin would degrade ferroportin and trap iron in cells, the opposite of what is needed for red cell production.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is brought in by a parent who is worried because the child repeatedly chews on ice cubes and has been caught eating dirt and paint chips. The child appears pale. A complete blood count shows a microcytic, hypochromic anemia. This child's unusual eating behavior is most specifically associated with which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic inflammation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactive thrombocytosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency

explanation.summary: Pica, the craving of nonfood items, is a symptom specifically linked to iron deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Persistent ingestion of nonfood items such as ice, dirt, clay, or paint chips is termed pica and is a symptom specifically related to iron deficiency. This child's microcytic, hypochromic anemia supports iron-deficiency anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic inflammation causes anemia of chronic disease but is not the classic cause of pica.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolysis is not associated with pica and typically does not produce microcytic, hypochromic cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactive thrombocytosis can accompany iron deficiency but is a laboratory finding, not the cause of the behavior.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The microcytic indices point to iron deficiency; B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anemia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a long history of heavy menstrual bleeding is evaluated for chronic fatigue. On examination, her fingernails curve upward into a concave, spoon-like shape, and there are cracks at the corners of her mouth. Which of the following best describes the spoon-shaped nail finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Angular cheilitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atrophic glossitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conjunctival pallor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glossitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Koilonychia

explanation.summary: Koilonychia is the spoon-shaped, upwardly concave nail seen in chronic iron deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Koilonychia describes a condition in which the nails curve upward into a concave, spoon-like shape and is a physical finding suggestive of iron-deficiency anemia. Her heavy menses and fatigue fit chronic iron deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angular cheilitis refers to the cracks and fissures at the corners of the mouth, not the nail change.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atrophic glossitis involves shrinkage of the tongue papillae, producing a shiny, smooth tongue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conjunctival pallor is a nonspecific sign of anemia affecting the mucous membranes, not the nails.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glossitis is inflammation and enlargement of the tongue, unrelated to the nail finding.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old vegetarian woman with fatigue has a complete blood count showing a low hemoglobin and low mean corpuscular volume. A peripheral blood smear is reviewed. Which of the following sets of findings is most consistent with iron-deficiency anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypochromic red cells with increased central pallor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Macrocytic red cells with hypersegmented neutrophils

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normocytic, normochromic red cells with rouleaux formation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schistocytes and helmet cells with thrombocytopenia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spherocytes with no central pallor and polychromasia

explanation.summary: The iron-deficiency smear shows small, pale (hypochromic) cells with increased central pallor and size variation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In iron-deficiency anemia the red cells are hypochromic (abnormally pale) because of decreased hemoglobin content, and the zone of central pallor is increased beyond the normal one-third of cell diameter. Anisocytosis (variation in size) is also seen, matching the elevated RDW.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrocytic cells with hypersegmented neutrophils indicate a megaloblastic anemia (B12 or folate deficiency).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Normocytic, normochromic cells with rouleaux suggest a different process, not the microcytic iron-deficiency picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schistocytes and helmet cells with thrombocytopenia indicate a microangiopathic hemolytic process, not iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spherocytes lacking central pallor with polychromasia point to hemolysis, such as hereditary spherocytosis.
