questions.stem: A patient with iron-deficiency anemia has iron studies drawn. The total iron-binding capacity is elevated. Which of the following best explains why the total iron-binding capacity rises in iron deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ferritin is released from the liver into the plasma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepcidin increases and degrades ferroportin

choices.label: C
choices.text: More binding sites on transferrin become occupied by iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: The kidney decreases erythropoietin production

choices.label: E
choices.text: The liver produces more transferrin

explanation.summary: TIBC measures available transferrin binding sites, which rise as the liver makes more transferrin in iron deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Total iron-binding capacity reflects the number of open iron-binding sites on circulating transferrin. In iron deficiency, the liver produces more transferrin to try to capture the limited iron; because there is little iron and more transferrin, the TIBC goes up.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ferritin is a storage protein, and its level actually falls in iron deficiency; it does not determine TIBC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepcidin degradation of ferroportin controls iron export, not the transferrin binding capacity measured by TIBC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: More occupied binding sites would raise transferrin saturation, which is actually low in iron deficiency; TIBC reflects open sites.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythropoietin from the kidney increases with anemia and does not account for the elevated TIBC.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with severe Crohn disease and documented iron-deficiency anemia cannot tolerate oral iron because it worsens her gastrointestinal symptoms, and her intestinal disease impairs absorption. Which of the following is the most appropriate route of iron replacement for this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single prophylactic blood transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dietary counseling alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral ferrous sulfate at a higher dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral iron combined with an antacid

explanation.summary: Intravenous iron is used for patients who cannot tolerate or absorb oral iron, such as those with inflammatory bowel disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intravenous iron is given to patients who cannot tolerate or receive oral iron and to those who cannot absorb it, such as patients with inflammatory bowel disease, malabsorption syndromes, or prior gastric bypass. This patient meets both criteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transfusion is reserved for severe or life-threatening anemia, not routine iron replacement in a stable patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dietary counseling alone cannot correct an established deficiency in a patient with malabsorption.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Higher-dose oral iron will still cause GI intolerance and will not be absorbed adequately given her intestinal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antacids reduce GI iron absorption, so combining them with oral iron would worsen the problem.

questions.stem: A global health team is reviewing World Health Organization data on the worldwide burden of anemia in order to target a supplementation program. Which of the following groups has the highest worldwide prevalence of anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adult men living in developed countries

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children less than 5 years of age

choices.label: C
choices.text: Postmenopausal women over age 55

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pregnant women of any age worldwide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nonpregnant women of reproductive age

explanation.summary: Worldwide, the highest prevalence of anemia (approximately 42%) is among children younger than 5 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: WHO estimates place the highest prevalence of anemia worldwide, approximately 42%, among children less than 5 years of age. Iron deficiency is also the most common nutritional deficiency in children, especially in developing countries.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adult men in developed countries eat meat and seafood and have no menstrual losses, so deficiency is uncommon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Menstrual iron losses cease after menopause, so this group is not a high-prevalence population.
whyWrongByChoice.D: About 40% of pregnant women worldwide have iron-deficiency anemia, a high figure but below that of young children.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About one-third of all women of reproductive age are affected, less than the prevalence in young children.

questions.stem: A dietitian is explaining to a patient that dietary iron is ingested in two different chemical forms with different food sources. Which of the following correctly describes the iron supplied by meat?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heme-bound ferric iron

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heme-bound ferrous iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron already bound to transferrin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Non-heme-bound ferric iron

choices.label: E
choices.text: Non-heme-bound ferrous iron

explanation.summary: Meat supplies heme-bound ferrous (Fe2+, reduced) iron, whereas vegetables supply non-heme-bound ferric (Fe3+, oxidized) iron.
explanation.whyCorrect: The main dietary source of ferrous iron is meat, which contains a heme-bound form of iron. Ferrous iron is the reduced form, Fe2+, and heme-bound ferrous iron is taken directly into the enterocyte.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ferric iron is the oxidized form found in plant sources and is not heme bound.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transferrin binds iron in the bloodstream for transport; it is not a form of dietary iron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Non-heme-bound ferric iron is the form supplied by vegetables, not by meat.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferrous iron from meat is heme bound; the non-heme forms come from plant sources.

questions.stem: Investigators studying duodenal enterocytes identify the apical membrane protein responsible for taking heme-bound ferrous iron directly out of the intestinal lumen and into the cell. Which of the following proteins did they identify?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT-1)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ferritin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ferroportin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heme carrier protein 1 (HCP1)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hephaestin

explanation.summary: HCP1 on the enterocyte apical membrane absorbs heme-bound ferrous iron from the intestinal lumen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enterocytes in the duodenum directly import heme-bound ferrous iron, and heme carrier protein 1 is the protein responsible for that absorption. Once inside, the surrounding heme structure is degraded to release the ferrous iron.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DMT-1 imports non-heme iron after a brush-border reductase converts ferric iron to ferrous iron.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferritin is the intracellular storage protein that packs iron inside the enterocyte after absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferroportin sits at the basolateral membrane and transports iron out of the cell into the bloodstream.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hephaestin oxidizes ferrous iron to ferric iron as it exits the enterocyte, so transferrin can bind it.

questions.stem: A patient's usual meal consists largely of leafy greens, beans, and whole grains, which supply non-heme-bound ferric iron. Which of the following must occur before this iron can enter the enterocyte?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It must be bound by ferritin within the intestinal lumen

choices.label: B
choices.text: It must be carried into the cell by ferroportin

choices.label: C
choices.text: It must be complexed with transferrin in the lumen

choices.label: D
choices.text: It must be oxidized by hephaestin at the brush border

choices.label: E
choices.text: It must be reduced to ferrous iron by a brush-border reductase

explanation.summary: Non-heme ferric iron cannot enter the enterocyte directly; it must first be reduced to ferrous iron.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike heme-bound ferrous iron, non-heme-bound ferric iron does not enter the enterocyte directly. To be absorbed, ferric iron must first be reduced to ferrous iron by a reductase at the apical surface, after which DMT-1 carries it into the cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ferritin stores iron inside the cell after absorption; it does not act within the intestinal lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferroportin exports iron from the enterocyte into the blood; it does not import luminal iron.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transferrin binds iron only after it has reached the bloodstream, not in the gut lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hephaestin oxidizes iron on the way out of the enterocyte; oxidation at the brush border would block absorption.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman who follows a vegan diet asks how to lower her risk of becoming iron deficient. She already eats leafy greens, beans, legumes, and whole grains daily. Which of the following additional recommendations would best improve her absorption of dietary iron?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pair her iron-rich plant foods with foods high in vitamin C

choices.label: B
choices.text: Replace her plant-based milk with cow's milk at meals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replace legumes and whole grains with refined grains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Take a large dose of oral antacid with each meal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take her doxycycline together with iron-rich meals

explanation.summary: Pairing iron-rich foods with vitamin C-rich foods enhances the body's ability to absorb iron.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plant-based nonheme iron is harder to absorb than the heme iron in meat and seafood, so vegetarians and vegans must both eat iron-rich plant sources and improve absorption. Research has shown that pairing iron-rich foods with foods high in vitamin C enhances the body's ability to absorb iron.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron from cow's milk is not readily absorbed and can cause GI tract irritation and bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leafy greens, beans, legumes, whole grains, nuts, and seeds are the iron-rich plant sources she should keep eating.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antacids are among the medications that reduce GI iron absorption and would worsen her risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tetracyclines such as doxycycline are specifically listed as medications that reduce GI iron absorption.

questions.stem: Most of the ferrous iron taken into an enterocyte is not immediately transported into the blood; instead it is bound to ferritin inside the cell. In addition to serving as a storage reservoir, this protein protects the cell by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Degrading ferroportin so that iron cannot leave the cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutralizing iron's free radicals to avoid cell damage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidizing ferrous iron so that hephaestin can release it

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recycling transferrin molecules back into the bloodstream

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reducing luminal ferric iron so that DMT-1 can import it

explanation.summary: Ferritin both stores iron and neutralizes iron's free radicals, protecting the cell from oxidative damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ferritin is sometimes called storage iron because it serves as a reservoir that packs iron within the cell. Beyond storage, it neutralizes iron's free radicals to avoid cell damage, which is also why ferritin levels rise in inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepcidin is the molecule that causes ferroportin to be internalized and degraded.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hephaestin itself performs the oxidation of ferrous iron as iron exits the cell; ferritin does not.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transferrin is released from iron inside the cell and recycled on its own; ferritin plays no part in that step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A brush-border reductase, not ferritin, reduces luminal ferric iron before DMT-1 imports it.

questions.stem: Hepcidin secretion by hepatocytes is regulated by several competing inputs. Which of the following increases hepcidin secretion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adequate or increased plasma iron levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depleted total body iron stores in macrophages

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erythropoietin released from the kidney

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased erythropoietic activity in the marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low tissue oxygen levels in the kidney

explanation.summary: Hepcidin is secreted by hepatocytes as long as plasma iron levels are adequate; inflammatory cytokines also raise it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin is secreted by liver cells as long as there are adequate plasma iron levels, and increased plasma iron along with inflammatory cytokines drives hepcidin up. High hepcidin then reduces ferroportin so that iron stays sequestered in cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: When body iron stores are depleted, hepcidin falls so that available iron can enter the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythropoietin specifically inhibits hepatic hepcidin production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased erythropoietic activity inhibits hepcidin so that more iron reaches the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Low tissue oxygen triggers renal erythropoietin release, which lowers rather than raises hepcidin.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has a low serum iron level. Her hepcidin level is elevated because of chronic inflammatory cytokine exposure. The iron that cannot enter her bloodstream is retained principally in which of the following forms and locations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: As ferritin in macrophages of the marrow, liver, and spleen

choices.label: B
choices.text: As heme within the hemoglobin of circulating mature erythrocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bound to transferrin in the circulating plasma pool

choices.label: D
choices.text: Within developing erythroblasts in the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Within renal tubular cells awaiting excretion into the urine

explanation.summary: High hepcidin blocks ferroportin, so iron stays sequestered as ferritin in macrophages of the marrow, liver, and spleen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin causes ferroportin to be internalized and degraded, which blocks iron release from enterocytes and from macrophages and hepatocytes. Iron therefore remains sequestered in cells, stored as ferritin in the macrophages of the bone marrow, liver, and spleen.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron trapped by hepcidin has not been incorporated into hemoglobin in circulating red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transferrin carries iron that has already entered the blood; high hepcidin prevents iron from reaching the plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The problem is precisely that the blood does not deliver enough iron to the marrow to make new red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron excretion is minimal and unregulated; the kidney does not serve as an iron storage site.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man admitted with a severe bacterial infection has a serum iron level that falls sharply within 48 hours of admission. Which of the following best explains the purpose of this physiologic response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To accelerate erythropoiesis within the bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: To hide iron from bacteria scavenging the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: To increase absorption of dietary iron in the duodenum

choices.label: D
choices.text: To protect hepatocytes from transferrin-mediated injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: To reduce the amount of iron lost in the urine and sweat

explanation.summary: Inflammation-driven iron sequestration is a protective response that hides iron from scavenging bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Iron is just as valuable to pathogens as it is to humans. During infection and inflammation, cytokines raise hepcidin and the body hijacks its iron storage mechanism to hide iron from scavenging bacteria in the circulation, which is why serum iron falls.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prolonged sequestration starves the marrow of iron and produces the anemia of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: High hepcidin blocks iron release from enterocytes, so less absorbed iron reaches the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transferrin is the normal plasma iron carrier and does not injure hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron excretion is small and not regulated, so this response does nothing to limit urinary or sweat losses.

questions.stem: A serum iron panel is ordered for a patient being evaluated for fatigue. Which of the following values on this panel best reflects whether the body is meeting its iron requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin concentration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serum ferritin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Total iron-binding capacity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferrin saturation

explanation.summary: Transferrin saturation, the percentage of transferrin binding sites occupied by iron, best reflects whether iron requirements are being met.
explanation.whyCorrect: On a serum iron panel, transferrin saturation best reflects the body's ability to meet its iron requirements because it is the percentage of transferrin binding sites actually occupied by iron. When the body is not meeting its iron requirement, as in iron-deficiency anemia, transferrin saturation is low.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemoglobin measures the severity of anemia, not whether iron supply is meeting demand.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferritin reflects total body iron stores but is a positive acute-phase reactant that can be falsely normal or high.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serum iron alone is nondiagnostic because it is also low in anemia of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TIBC measures the number of open binding sites on transferrin rather than how much iron is actually carried.

questions.stem: Iron excretion from the body is not regulated; small amounts are lost in feces, urine, and sweat and through sloughing of intestinal enterocytes and skin cells. Given this, the amount of iron in the body is determined primarily by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Biliary excretion of iron into the gut

choices.label: B
choices.text: Control of dietary iron absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Renal tubular reabsorption of filtered iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rate at which skin cells are shed

choices.label: E
choices.text: The rate of iron loss in sweat

explanation.summary: Because iron excretion is unregulated, total body iron is set by how much iron is absorbed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Only small, unregulated amounts of iron leave the body in feces, urine, sweat, and shed enterocytes and skin cells. Because of this, the amount of body iron is determined by controlling iron absorption, which is why hepcidin and ferroportin act at the enterocyte.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliary excretion is not described as a regulated route of iron elimination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The kidney does not regulate body iron; urinary iron loss is small and not controlled.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sloughing of skin cells is one of the small, unregulated losses, not the controlling factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sweat losses are likewise minor and unregulated.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman started ferrous sulfate 2 weeks ago for iron-deficiency anemia caused by heavy menses. She reports constipation, nausea, and black stools. A fecal occult blood test is negative and her hemoglobin has risen since starting therapy. Which of the following best explains her black stools?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An expected adverse effect of the oral iron preparation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic hookworm infection of the small intestine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure to absorb the tablet because of antacid use

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron overload deposited in the intestinal mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ongoing bleeding from an undiagnosed peptic ulcer

explanation.summary: Black stools on oral iron come from the drug itself, not from GI bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Common side effects of oral iron include GI upset, constipation, dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, flatulence, diarrhea, and black stools that come from the drug rather than from GI bleeding. Her negative occult blood test and rising hemoglobin confirm the benign explanation, though these effects may limit adherence.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hookworm causes chronic GI blood loss, which would make the occult blood test positive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antacids blunt absorption and would prevent the hemoglobin rise she has had; they do not blacken stool.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron overload is not a consequence of 2 weeks of replacement therapy for a documented deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Melena from a bleeding ulcer would give a positive fecal occult blood test and a falling hemoglobin.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man who recently immigrated from a rural tropical region and works barefoot in the fields has a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with a ferritin of 6 ng/mL and guaiac-positive stool. Colonoscopy and upper endoscopy show no lesions. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his gastrointestinal blood loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Celiac disease with villous atrophy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Colon cancer bleeding slowly from a small tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hookworm infection with Ancylostoma species

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peptic ulcer disease producing melena

explanation.summary: In tropical and subtropical areas, GI blood loss causing iron deficiency is often due to parasitic hookworm infection with Ancylostoma species.
explanation.whyCorrect: In tropical and subtropical areas, GI blood loss may be due to parasitic hookworm infections caused by Ancylostoma species. This fits a young man from a rural tropical region with occult GI bleeding and no endoscopic lesion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Celiac disease causes iron deficiency through impaired absorption rather than GI blood loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A bleeding colonic tumor is the classic concern in an older adult and would have been seen on colonoscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PNH causes chronic intravascular hemolysis with urinary iron loss, not guaiac-positive stool.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A bleeding ulcer producing melena would have been visualized on upper endoscopy.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease on maintenance hemodialysis is found to be iron deficient despite a diet rich in meat. He is receiving erythropoietin. Which of the following best explains the ongoing iron loss in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Filtration of transferrin-bound iron across the dialysis membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravascular hemolysis of red cells within the dialyzer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced duodenal expression of heme carrier protein 1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small amounts of blood lost with each dialysis treatment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of erythropoietin production by uremia

explanation.summary: Hemodialysis patients routinely lose small amounts of blood with every treatment, and ongoing inflammation plus erythropoietin-driven demand compounds the deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with end-stage kidney disease receiving hemodialysis routinely lose small amounts of blood during each treatment. Ongoing inflammation may keep their marrow from compensating, and the erythropoietin they receive raises RBC production and therefore iron demand, so these patients are often given intravenous iron during dialysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron loss in these patients comes from blood lost during the treatment, not from filtration of transferrin-bound iron.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intravascular hemolysis with urinary iron loss is an uncommon cause, classically from a malfunctioning heart valve or PNH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: His iron-rich diet and the absence of a malabsorption syndrome make impaired duodenal uptake an unlikely explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: He is already receiving exogenous erythropoietin, which raises iron demand rather than causing iron loss.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman with a mechanical aortic valve has a microcytic anemia with a ferritin of 9 ng/mL. Fecal occult blood testing is negative on three separate specimens, and colonoscopy is normal. Which of the following is the most likely route of her iron loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased iron demand from an adolescent growth spurt

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron lost in sweat and in sloughed intestinal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced iron absorption across the duodenal mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sequestration of iron within macrophages of the spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urinary hemoglobin loss from intravascular hemolysis

explanation.summary: A malfunctioning heart valve causes chronic intravascular hemolysis, and hemoglobin lost in the urine is a route of urinary iron loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Urinary iron loss is a relatively uncommon cause of iron deficiency. It can be due to chronic intravascular hemolysis in which hemoglobin is lost in the urine, as with a malfunctioning heart valve, and also to a genitourinary malignancy causing bleeding or to paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Growth spurts raise iron demand in children and adolescents, not in a 58-year-old woman.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Losses in sweat and shed skin cells are small and unregulated and do not cause deficiency on their own.
whyWrongByChoice.C: She has no malabsorption syndrome, chronic diarrhea, bariatric surgery, or offending medication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrophage sequestration is the mechanism of anemia of chronic disease, which shows normal or high ferritin.

questions.stem: A 13-month-old boy is found on routine screening to have a hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL with a low mean corpuscular volume. His diet consists almost entirely of cow's milk, and he has never received an iron supplement. Which of the following best explains his iron deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cow's milk accelerates urinary excretion of absorbed iron

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cow's milk binds iron irreversibly within the duodenal lumen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cow's milk iron is poorly absorbed and can irritate the gut

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cow's milk stimulates hepatocytes to secrete more hepcidin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cow's milk suppresses renal erythropoietin production

explanation.summary: An infant whose diet is heavily biased toward cow's milk without supplementation becomes iron deficient because that iron is poorly absorbed and can irritate and bleed the gut.
explanation.whyCorrect: An infant whose diet is heavily biased toward cow's milk and who is not given iron supplementation is a classic example of insufficient dietary iron intake. Iron from cow's milk is not as readily absorbed and can cause GI tract irritation and bleeding, adding a blood-loss component.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron excretion is minimal and unregulated and is not driven by diet.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The problem is poor absorption of the iron cow's milk contains, not irreversible binding in the lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepcidin rises with adequate plasma iron and inflammation, not with a milk-based diet.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erythropoietin rises appropriately in anemia; cow's milk does not suppress it.

questions.stem: A pediatrician routinely obtains a complete blood count on healthy patients at their 12-month visit to screen for anemia. Which of the following complications of untreated iron deficiency most strongly justifies screening at this age?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atrophic glossitis with esophageal web formation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lifelong impairment of neurologic development

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent ingestion of nonfood items such as dirt

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactive thrombocytosis on the blood count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spoon-shaped nails and cracking at the mouth corners

explanation.summary: In infants, iron deficiency can impair neurologic development, and the deficit may be lifelong if not corrected with iron replacement.
explanation.whyCorrect: In infants, iron deficiency can be associated with impaired neurologic development, which may remain lifelong if it is not corrected with iron replacement. That risk is the reason screening for anemia via CBC is routinely performed for children at their 12-month visit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atrophic glossitis with esophageal webs describes Plummer-Vinson syndrome, a concern in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pica is a symptom of iron deficiency, and it resolves with iron replacement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactive thrombocytosis is an incidental laboratory finding that causes no lasting harm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nail and lip changes are physical signs of chronic deficiency but are reversible and not the reason for infant screening.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation has taken no prenatal vitamin and is found to have iron-deficiency anemia. Fetal growth parameters and fetal hemoglobin are normal. Which of the following best explains the normal fetal findings despite the mother's deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal erythropoiesis does not require iron until after delivery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal hemoglobin is assembled without an iron-containing heme group

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fetal hepcidin is suppressed, which spares maternal iron stores

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal ferritin crosses the placenta intact and is stored by the fetus

choices.label: E
choices.text: The placenta strips iron from the mother even when she is deficient

explanation.summary: The placenta is very efficient at scavenging iron and will strip it from the mother to supply the fetus even when she is iron deficient.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pregnancy is a time of increased iron need, and most women cannot absorb enough iron for both the growing fetus and themselves without supplementation. The placenta is very efficient at scavenging iron and will ruthlessly strip iron from the mother to supply the fetus, even if the mother is iron deficient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The fetus makes red cells throughout gestation and needs iron to do so, which is why maternal demand rises.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heme, the iron-containing component of hemoglobin, is required for fetal hemoglobin as for any hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mechanism described is placental iron scavenging from the mother, not fetal sparing of maternal stores.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ferritin is an intracellular storage protein, not a placental transfer vehicle.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with newly diagnosed iron-deficiency anemia has a reticulocyte count of 0.3%. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythropoietin production has been suppressed by the anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron is being lost faster than red cells can be destroyed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reticulocytes are being lysed prematurely in the circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reticulocytes are being sequestered within the spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: The marrow lacks the iron needed to produce nascent red cells

explanation.summary: Anemias due to decreased red cell production, including iron deficiency, have low reticulocyte counts of less than 0.5%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reticulocyte count is decreased in iron-deficiency anemia because there is not enough iron for the bone marrow to produce enough nascent RBCs, so the number of immature red cells in the blood goes down. Anemias due to decreased RBC production have reticulocyte counts less than 0.5%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythropoietin rises when tissue oxygen delivery falls; it is not suppressed by anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron loss explains the deficiency itself but not the marrow's failure to release reticulocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency is a production problem, not a hemolytic process destroying young red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic sequestration is not part of the mechanism of iron-deficiency anemia.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with heavy menses has a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, a mean corpuscular volume of 71 fL, and a platelet count of 615,000/mm3. Coagulation studies are normal and she has not had a splenectomy. Which of the following best accounts for the platelet count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumption of transferrin-bound iron by megakaryocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marrow infiltration by a myeloproliferative process

choices.label: C
choices.text: Platelet release triggered directly by hepcidin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactive thrombocytosis accompanying iron deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spurious counting of fragmented microcytic red cells

explanation.summary: Reactive thrombocytosis, an abnormally high platelet count, may be observed in iron-deficiency anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reactive thrombocytosis, an abnormally high number of platelets, may be observed in iron-deficiency anemia along with the hypochromic microcytic red cells and anisocytosis. Her microcytic anemia from heavy menses makes this the expected explanation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Megakaryocytes do not raise the platelet count by consuming transferrin-bound iron.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is a clear cause for her anemia and no findings to suggest a primary marrow disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepcidin acts on ferroportin to control iron export and has no direct role in platelet release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron deficiency produces small, pale red cells and anisocytosis rather than fragments that would be miscounted.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with fatigue has a serum ferritin of 8 ng/mL (reference range, 20 to 200 ng/mL). She has no infection and no inflammatory disease. Which of the following best characterizes this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It excludes iron deficiency and points to thalassemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: It indicates iron overload with hepatic iron deposition

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is virtually diagnostic of iron-deficiency anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is within the expected range for premenopausal women

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reflects an acute-phase response to inflammation

explanation.summary: Ferritin is proportional to total body iron stores, and a level below 15 ng/mL is virtually diagnostic of iron-deficiency anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ferritin is an iron storage protein proportional to total body iron stores, with normal levels ranging from 20 ng/mL to 200 ng/mL. A low ferritin, particularly below 15 ng/mL, is virtually diagnostic of iron-deficiency anemia, and the absence of inflammation removes the main limitation of the test.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A low ferritin points toward iron deficiency; thalassemia is evaluated when the iron studies are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron overload would produce a markedly elevated, not a low, ferritin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stated normal range begins at 20 ng/mL, so 8 ng/mL is clearly below normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: As a positive acute-phase reactant, ferritin rises with inflammation; a low value is not an inflammatory effect.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman reports dysphagia, a chronic cough, and fatigue. Her tongue is shiny and smooth with flattened papillae, laboratory studies confirm iron-deficiency anemia, and barium swallow demonstrates esophageal webs. This patient is at increased risk for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adenocarcinoma of the gastric cardia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma from hepatic iron overload

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oropharyngeal candidiasis due to AIDS

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus

explanation.summary: Plummer-Vinson syndrome, the triad of atrophic glossitis, esophageal webs, and iron-deficiency anemia, carries a risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is characterized by atrophic glossitis, esophageal webs, and iron-deficiency anemia, with typical symptoms of dysphagia, chronic cough, and fatigue. Patients with this syndrome are at risk for developing squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colon cancer is a cause of iron deficiency through occult blood loss, not a consequence of this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric cardia adenocarcinoma is not the malignancy linked to this triad.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Her problem is iron deficiency, not iron overload, so hepatic iron deposition is not expected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AIDS is listed among other causes of glossitis, but her presentation is the Plummer-Vinson triad.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with known ischemic heart disease is admitted for evaluation of iron-deficiency anemia. He is not actively bleeding and is hemodynamically stable, but reports chest pain on exertion. His hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of his anemia at this time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythropoietin injections to raise the hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravenous iron, deferring transfusion until hemoglobin is below 7

choices.label: C
choices.text: Observation with a repeat hemoglobin in 48 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral ferrous sulfate alone, since he is not bleeding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

explanation.summary: Patients with ischemic heart disease are transfused at a hemoglobin threshold of 8, higher than the threshold of 7 used for noncritical inpatients who are not bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Indications for transfusion include patients with active bleeding and low hemoglobin, noncritical inpatients who are not bleeding with a hemoglobin less than 7, and patients with ischemic heart disease with a hemoglobin less than 8. Transfusions are also given to older patients with iron deficiency along with chest pain, which describes this man at 7.6 g/dL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythropoietin is used in dialysis patients to drive red cell production; it is not the acute treatment here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The threshold of 7 applies to noncritical inpatients who are not bleeding, not to ischemic heart disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Observation ignores an indication for transfusion that is already met in a patient with cardiac ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral iron corrects stores over weeks and does nothing for a hemoglobin already below his transfusion threshold.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents for her first prenatal visit at 10 weeks' gestation. She is not anemic and has no history of GI disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate iron supplementation for her?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 30 mg to 60 mg of oral elemental iron daily

choices.label: B
choices.text: 300 mg of oral elemental iron daily

choices.label: C
choices.text: An intravenous iron infusion during each trimester

choices.label: D
choices.text: No iron unless anemia develops later in the pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral iron beginning only in the third trimester

explanation.summary: Pregnant patients require 30 mg to 60 mg of oral elemental iron daily, typically supplied by a routine prenatal vitamin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients who are pregnant require iron supplementation to maintain adequate iron stores, and this may be provided as 30 mg to 60 mg of oral elemental iron daily in a routine prenatal vitamin. Most women cannot absorb enough iron for both the fetus and themselves without supplementation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This dose far exceeds the recommended daily elemental iron for routine prenatal supplementation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intravenous iron is reserved for patients who need rapid replacement or who cannot tolerate or absorb oral iron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pregnant patients are likely to develop iron deficiency without supplements, so waiting for anemia is inappropriate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron demand rises across the pregnancy, so supplementation is not delayed to the third trimester.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is found to have a hemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 68 fL on routine testing. She is asymptomatic. Her red blood cell count is elevated, her red cell distribution width is normal, and her serum ferritin is normal. Which of the following findings most reliably distinguishes her condition from iron-deficiency anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated red cell distribution width (RDW)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low hemoglobin concentration in whole blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low mean corpuscular volume (microcytosis)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal to increased red blood cell count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Presence of hypochromia on the peripheral smear

explanation.summary: In mild thalassemia the RBC count is normal or increased and the RDW is normal, unlike iron deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that although hemoglobin is low in mild thalassemia, the RBC count is usually normal or increased, whereas it is low in iron-deficiency anemia. This is a key distinguishing clue in the CBC, along with a normal RDW.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An elevated RDW favors iron deficiency; in thalassemia minor the RDW is typically normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low hemoglobin occurs in both conditions and does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both thalassemia trait and iron deficiency produce a low MCV (microcytosis), so this does not separate them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypochromia is seen in both microcytic anemias and is not discriminating.

questions.stem: A patient of Southeast Asian descent has moderate to severe microcytic anemia. Genetic testing shows a genotype in which three of the four alpha-globin genes are deleted, and hemoglobin analysis reveals an unstable tetramer composed of four beta chains. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-thalassemia trait

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-thalassemia major

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin H disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrops fetalis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silent carrier (alpha-thalassemia minima)

explanation.summary: Deletion of three alpha-globin genes produces HbH disease, with excess beta chains forming HbH (beta-4) tetramers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Per Table 1, deletion of three alpha genes (a-/--) causes HbH disease with moderate to severe anemia. The excess unpaired beta chains aggregate into HbH tetramers, which are insoluble, cannot carry oxygen, and shorten RBC lifespan.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-thalassemia trait involves two deleted alpha genes and causes only mild anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-thalassemia major is caused by beta-globin mutations, not alpha-gene deletions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrops fetalis results from deletion of all four alpha genes and is usually fatal in utero, forming Hb Barts (gamma-4), not HbH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The silent carrier has only one alpha gene deleted and is asymptomatic with no anemia.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has been chronically jaundiced and anemic since childhood and has required transfusions for repeated episodes of severe anemia. Examination shows splenomegaly, frontal bossing, and prominent malar eminences. The CBC shows a microcytic, hypochromic anemia, and hemoglobin electrophoresis shows elevated HbA2 and HbF with undetectable HbA. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-thalassemia trait with two gene deletions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-thalassemia major

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-thalassemia trait (thalassemia minor)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemoglobin Bart disease (hydrops fetalis)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemoglobin H disease (three gene deletions)

explanation.summary: Undetectable HbA with transfusion dependence and skeletal changes indicates beta-thalassemia major (beta-0/beta-0).
explanation.whyCorrect: The transfusion requirement, severe anemia, splenomegaly, and bossing from extramedullary hematopoiesis, combined with electrophoresis showing no HbA, point to transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia. With no beta chains produced, HbF and HbA2 rise to compensate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-thalassemia trait is usually asymptomatic with a normal hemoglobin electrophoresis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-thalassemia trait is asymptomatic and shows low-normal HbA with only mildly elevated HbA2 and HbF, not absent HbA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin Bart disease is incompatible with life and causes intrauterine fetal demise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin H disease shows elevated HbH with low HbA, HbA2, and HbF, not the pattern described.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with severe beta-thalassemia has received regular red blood cell transfusions for many years. He now develops a cardiomyopathy with heart failure and abnormal liver function tests. Which of the following is the most likely complication responsible for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Graft-versus-host disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatitis C infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased hemolysis from mismatched transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Iron overload (secondary hemochromatosis)

explanation.summary: Chronic transfusion causes iron overload, depositing iron in the heart, liver, and endocrine organs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that frequent transfusions increase the risk of iron overload, or secondary hemochromatosis, leading to iron deposition in the heart, liver, and endocrine organs, with complications such as heart failure, arrhythmias, and liver disease. Iron chelators like deferoxamine are given to prevent this.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Graft-versus-host disease is a complication of stem cell transplant, not routine transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transfusion-transmitted hepatitis C is rare in developed countries because of adequate blood screening.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transfusion-transmitted HIV is likewise rare due to blood screening and does not explain the iron-loading pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemolysis from a mismatched transfusion is very rare and would not cause chronic organ iron deposition.

questions.stem: A newborn with a genetically confirmed severe form of beta-thalassemia major appears healthy at birth and remains asymptomatic for the first several months of life, developing anemia only around 6 to 12 months of age. Which of the following best explains the delayed onset of symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta chain synthesis is maximal at birth and declines slowly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal hemoglobin contains alpha and gamma chains

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron stores from birth prevent anemia until they are depleted

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal HbA crosses the placenta and persists for the first year

choices.label: E
choices.text: Newborns compensate by producing excess HbA2 (alpha-2 delta-2)

explanation.summary: HbF (alpha-2 gamma-2) does not require beta chains and sustains oxygen delivery until it declines after birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that fetal hemoglobin (HbF) contains alpha and gamma globin and does not contain beta globin, so it is unaffected by beta-thalassemia. HbF persists for at least 6 months after birth and delivers oxygen adequately; children become symptomatic only as HbF levels fall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta chain synthesis is defective in beta-thalassemia and rises after birth as gamma falls, which is when symptoms appear.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron stores are not the protective factor; the anemia is due to defective globin production, not iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes protection to the newborn's own HbF, not to persistent maternal hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HbA2 is only a minor hemoglobin and is not the reason neonates are protected.

questions.stem: A fetus is found on prenatal evaluation to have severe, diffuse edema and profound anemia, and intrauterine demise occurs. Molecular studies show deletion of all four alpha-globin genes. Which abnormal hemoglobin is most likely responsible for this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin A (alpha-2 beta-2)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin A2 (alpha-2 delta-2)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin Barts (gamma-4 tetramer)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemoglobin H (beta-4 tetramer)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemoglobin S (sickle hemoglobin)

explanation.summary: With no alpha chains, fetal gamma chains form Hb Barts (gamma-4), causing hydrops fetalis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Deletion of all four alpha genes prevents alpha chain production. In the fetus, the unpaired gamma chains that normally partner with alpha chains clump into tetramers of four gamma chains called Hb Barts. This causes extremely severe anemia, diffuse edema, and usually intrauterine death (hydrops fetalis).

whyWrongByChoice.A: HbA requires alpha chains, which cannot be made when all four alpha genes are deleted.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HbA2 is a minor normal hemoglobin and requires alpha chains, which are absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HbH (beta-4) forms in adults with three-gene alpha deletion, not in the alpha-null fetus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin S is a structural beta-chain variant unrelated to alpha-gene deletions.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with untreated severe thalassemia has a depressed nasal bridge, maxillary hypertrophy, prominent malar eminences, exposed upper teeth, and frontal bossing. Hepatosplenomegaly is also present. These findings are best explained by which of the following processes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of erythroid precursors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic hypoxic injury to growth plates

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis and marrow expansion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deposition in bone and soft tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeated microvascular occlusion by sickled cells

explanation.summary: Ineffective erythropoiesis drives extramedullary hematopoiesis and marrow hyperplasia, expanding facial and skull bones and enlarging liver and spleen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because of ineffective erythropoiesis, patients with severe thalassemia make RBCs at extramedullary sites such as the spleen and liver (causing hepatosplenomegaly) and in the bones of the skull and face. Marrow hyperplasia produces the depressed nasal bridge, maxillary hypertrophy, prominent malar eminence, exposed upper teeth, and frontal bossing described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thalassemia is a genetic globin-production disorder, not an autoimmune anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The facial and skull changes result from marrow hyperplasia, not hypoxic growth-plate injury.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron overload harms the heart, liver, and endocrine organs but does not cause the described skeletal marrow expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaso-occlusion is a feature of sickle cell disease, not the marrow-expansion changes of thalassemia.

questions.stem: A hematologist explains that the two broad categories of beta-globin gene mutations in beta-thalassemia are designated beta-0 and beta-plus. Which of the following correctly describes the beta-0 mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deletion of one beta-globin gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deletion of two beta-globin genes

choices.label: C
choices.text: No beta chain production from the affected gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: Production of a structurally abnormal beta chain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced but present beta chain production

explanation.summary: Beta-0 mutations produce no beta chains, whereas beta-plus mutations produce some but not enough.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the two broad categories of mutations in beta-thalassemia are those that result in no beta chain production (designated beta-0) and those that result in some, but not enough, beta chain production (beta-plus). A beta-0/beta-0 genotype produces transfusion-dependent thalassemia major.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-thalassemia is caused by non-deletional mutations, not gene deletions; alpha-thalassemia is the deletional disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-thalassemia results from mutations, not deletions, of the two chromosome 11 beta genes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A structurally abnormal chain describes a structural hemoglobinopathy (e.g., HbS), not the quantitative beta-0 defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced but present production describes the beta-plus mutation, not beta-0.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old asymptomatic man has a mild microcytic anemia with a normal serum ferritin. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is ordered and shows an elevated HbA2 with a slightly increased HbF. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-thalassemia trait

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-thalassemia trait

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin H disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron-deficiency anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silent carrier alpha-thalassemia

explanation.summary: An elevated HbA2 on electrophoresis in a person with mild microcytic anemia indicates beta-thalassemia trait.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemoglobin electrophoresis is often adequate to diagnose beta-thalassemias. When beta chain output is reduced, other hemoglobins rise to compensate; in beta-thalassemia trait, HbA2 rises (up to about 5%) with mildly elevated HbF, producing mild anemia in an otherwise asymptomatic patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-thalassemia trait shows a normal hemoglobin electrophoresis, not elevated HbA2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HbH disease shows decreased HbA with detectable HbH and causes moderate to severe anemia, not this mild picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency does not raise HbA2, and this patient's ferritin is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The silent carrier state has no anemia and a normal electrophoresis.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia is started on a drug intended to reduce her transfusion requirement. The medication works by binding transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) ligands on erythroid precursor cells in the bone marrow, thereby enhancing erythroid maturation. Which of the following agents was most likely prescribed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deferoxamine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydroxyurea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Luspatercept

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prednisone

explanation.summary: Luspatercept binds TGF-beta ligands on erythroid precursors to enhance erythroid maturation and reduce transfusion need.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that transfusion needs can sometimes be reduced using luspatercept, which increases bone marrow RBC production by binding transforming growth factor-beta ligands on erythroid precursor cells, leading to enhanced erythroid maturation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deferoxamine is an iron chelator used to prevent iron overload, not to stimulate erythroid maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin stimulates precursor proliferation via the EPO receptor, not by binding TGF-beta ligands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxyurea raises HbF in some hemoglobinopathies but is not the TGF-beta ligand trap described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prednisone is a corticosteroid and is not the described mechanism of enhancing erythroid maturation in thalassemia.

questions.stem: A researcher explains why reduced alpha or beta chain synthesis leads to anemia in thalassemia. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathophysiology?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A membrane cytoskeletal defect causes spherocyte formation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A structurally abnormal globin chain polymerizes and deforms RBCs into a sickle shape

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antibodies coat RBCs and trigger their destruction in the spleen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired heme synthesis leads to iron accumulation in mitochondria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unbound globin chains precipitate within developing RBCs

explanation.summary: Chain imbalance leaves free globin chains that precipitate in RBCs, causing ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that reduced alpha or beta chain synthesis disrupts the tightly controlled 1.0 alpha-to-beta ratio, leaving free unbound chains that precipitate within the developing RBC and damage it. This causes reduced RBC development (ineffective erythropoiesis) and early RBC death, plus membrane changes that promote lysis in the circulation (hemolysis).

whyWrongByChoice.A: A cytoskeletal membrane defect causing spherocytes describes hereditary spherocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Polymerization of an abnormal chain into a sickle shape describes sickle cell disease, a structural hemoglobinopathy, not thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibody-mediated destruction describes autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron accumulation in mitochondria describes sideroblastic anemia, not thalassemia.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with severe beta-thalassemia develops worsening cytopenias, massive symptomatic splenomegaly, and a rising transfusion requirement. His physicians consider a procedure to reduce transfusion needs and improve the cytopenias. Which of the following interventions is most appropriate for these specific findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deferoxamine therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythropoietin injections

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron supplementation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Observation only

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy

explanation.summary: Splenectomy is appropriate for hypersplenism causing cytopenias and rising transfusion needs with symptomatic splenomegaly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that splenectomy may be appropriate for individuals with severe thalassemia who have findings such as a dramatic increase in transfusion requirements, hypersplenism leading to other cytopenias, and symptomatic splenomegaly. Removing the spleen reduces cell trapping and transfusion needs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deferoxamine treats iron overload but does not address the hypersplenism and splenomegaly driving these findings.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin is not the described intervention for hypersplenism and symptomatic splenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron supplementation is inappropriate and can worsen the iron overload common in these patients.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Observation is inadequate given the dramatic rise in transfusion requirement and symptomatic splenomegaly.

questions.stem: A medical student is comparing two groups of hemoglobin disorders. She notes that the thalassemias are classified as quantitative disorders, whereas sickle cell anemia is classified as a structural hemoglobinopathy. Which of the following best describes the defect in the thalassemias?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Globin chains are structurally abnormal but made in normal amounts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Globin chains are structurally normal but made in reduced amounts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Globin output is normal but the red cell membrane is defective

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heme synthesis is reduced while globin output remains normal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Iron incorporation into the heme ring is blocked

explanation.summary: Thalassemias are quantitative disorders: too little globin is made, but what is made is structurally normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the thalassemias are quantitative disorders, meaning the primary defect lies in the amount of globin produced. In contrast, the structural hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell anemia are characterized by a normal amount of structurally abnormal globin chains.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A normal amount of structurally abnormal globin describes the structural hemoglobinopathies, such as sickle cell anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A red cell membrane defect is not the abnormality in thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thalassemia is a defect of globin production, not of heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocked iron incorporation into heme is not the mechanism described for thalassemia.

questions.stem: A public health survey in a malaria-endemic region of Africa finds that about 10% of the population carries a beta-globin gene mutation. Which of the following best explains the persistence of such a high carrier rate in this population?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antimalarial drugs used regionally cause acquired globin mutations

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consanguineous marriage is required to inherit the mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endemic iron deficiency selects for microcytic red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeated malarial infection induces beta-globin gene mutations

choices.label: E
choices.text: The trait may be protective against the malaria parasite

explanation.summary: Thalassemia trait is thought to confer protection against malaria, which maintains a high carrier frequency in endemic regions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that beta-thalassemia has a high prevalence worldwide, including a 10% prevalence in malaria-endemic areas of Africa and Asia, where the trait might be protective against the malaria parasite, just as in sickle cell disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thalassemia is genetic and is not acquired from drug exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Consanguinity is not required; the alleles are inherited in the usual fashion and carriers are common.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency does not select for globin gene mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thalassemia mutations are inherited germline defects, not induced by infection.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor explains that the beta chain gene has two co-dominantly expressed alleles, one on each chromosome 11. Which of the following correctly describes the alpha-globin genes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four alleles, all on a single chromosome 16

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four alleles, two on each chromosome 11

choices.label: C
choices.text: Four alleles, two on each chromosome 16

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two alleles, both on chromosome 11

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two alleles, one on each chromosome 16

explanation.summary: The alpha-globin gene has four co-dominantly expressed alleles, two on each chromosome 16.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the alpha-globin gene has four alleles or copies, two on each chromosome 16, and that they are co-dominantly (equally) expressed and all needed to make the normal quantity of alpha chains. This is why alpha-thalassemia severity depends on the number of deleted alleles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The four alpha alleles are split evenly between the two copies of chromosome 16.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The beta genes are on chromosome 11; the alpha genes are on chromosome 16.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromosome 11 carries the beta-globin genes, not the alpha genes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There are four alpha alleles, not two; two alleles per chromosome pair describes the beta gene.

questions.stem: Family screening identifies a 28-year-old man who has a deletion of one of his four alpha-globin genes. He feels well and has no history of anemia. Which of the following is most likely to be found on his blood work?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mild anemia with an elevated HbA2 fraction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mild microcytosis without anemia or hypochromia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Moderate anemia with target cells on the smear

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal mean corpuscular volume with marked hypochromia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Severe anemia requiring intermittent transfusion

explanation.summary: Deletion of one alpha gene causes alpha-thalassemia minima, an asymptomatic carrier state with at most mild microcytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that deletion of one alpha chain gene produces the asymptomatic carrier state alpha-thalassemia minima. Because three working alpha genes remain, hemoglobin production is not significantly affected; asymptomatic mild microcytosis without anemia or hypochromia on the smear can sometimes be seen, and that is usually how it is diagnosed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An elevated HbA2 is the pattern of beta-thalassemia trait; alpha carriers have a normal hemoglobin analysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Moderate anemia with target cells reflects more severe thalassemia, not a single-gene deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The silent carrier shows mild microcytosis without hypochromia, not the reverse.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion requirement indicates severe disease, not the silent carrier state.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has always felt well, but after an abdominal operation she is noted to have a mild anemia that resolves over several weeks. Genetic testing shows deletion of two of her alpha-globin genes. Which of the following best describes the expected course of her disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mild anemia occurring mostly after surgery or infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Moderate anemia present continuously since early childhood

choices.label: C
choices.text: No anemia at any time, including during physiologic stress

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progressive anemia with hepatosplenomegaly by adolescence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Severe anemia requiring lifelong red blood cell transfusions

explanation.summary: Two-gene alpha deletion produces alpha-thalassemia trait, with mild anemia that tends to appear after stressors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Per the brick, deletion of two alpha chain genes results in alpha-thalassemia trait. The patient still has two working alpha chain genes, so the anemia is usually mild and occurs mostly after stressors like surgery or infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Continuous moderate anemia from childhood corresponds to a more severe genotype, such as HbH disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-thalassemia trait does cause mild anemia, particularly under stress; complete absence of anemia describes the silent carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progressive anemia with hepatosplenomegaly indicates severe disease with extramedullary hematopoiesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lifelong transfusion dependence is a feature of the most severe thalassemias, not the alpha trait.

questions.stem: A fetus with deletion of all four alpha chain genes is found on ultrasonography to have severe, diffuse edema before intrauterine demise. Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for the edema?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal liver failure lowers albumin and plasma oncotic pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron deposition in the fetal myocardium impairs contraction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and lyse fetal red cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Precipitated gamma chains obstruct the fetal capillary beds

choices.label: E
choices.text: The heart beats faster and more forcefully to compensate, then fails

explanation.summary: Profound fetal anemia drives compensatory cardiac overwork, and when the heart fails the fetus develops diffuse edema.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that fetuses who cannot produce alpha chains have extremely severe anemia, and the heart attempts to compensate by beating faster and more forcefully. However, it eventually fails, and the fetus develops severe, diffuse edema, which may lead to intrauterine demise.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatic failure with low oncotic pressure is not the mechanism the brick gives for hydrops in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myocardial iron deposition follows years of chronic transfusion and is not the fetal mechanism described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Maternal alloantibody hemolysis is a different disorder; here the anemia is from absent alpha chain production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Precipitated chains damage the developing red cell itself; they do not plug capillaries.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy has had a moderate microcytic anemia since childhood but has never required a blood transfusion. Genetic testing shows one beta-plus and one beta-0 mutation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-thalassemia trait

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-thalassemia trait (beta-thalassemia minor)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin H disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Non-transfusion dependent thalassemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion-dependent thalassemia

explanation.summary: Two mutated beta genes with at least some beta chain output gives non-transfusion dependent thalassemia (formerly thalassemia intermedia).
explanation.whyCorrect: Per the brick and Table 2, patients with two mutated beta chain genes of the beta-plus/beta-0 or beta-plus/beta-plus type have non-transfusion dependent thalassemia, previously called beta-thalassemia intermedia. They can make at least some beta chains and have moderate anemia, but transfusions are usually not needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-thalassemia trait is a two-gene alpha deletion and causes only mild anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-thalassemia trait involves only one mutated beta gene and causes mild, not moderate, anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin H disease results from deletion of three alpha genes, not beta gene mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion-dependent thalassemia is the beta-0/beta-0 genotype, in which no beta chains are made.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man of Southeast Asian descent has a moderate to severe microcytic anemia. Genetic testing confirms hemoglobin H disease. Which of the following hemoglobin analysis patterns is most consistent with this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HbA absent, HbA2 increased, HbF up to 95%, HbH 0%

choices.label: B
choices.text: HbA decreased, HbA2 decreased, HbF up to 95%, HbH 0%

choices.label: C
choices.text: HbA decreased, HbA2 increased, HbF up to 50%, HbH 0%

choices.label: D
choices.text: HbA decreased, HbA2 normal, HbF normal, HbH 0% to 30%

choices.label: E
choices.text: HbA normal, HbA2 normal, HbF normal, HbH 0%

explanation.summary: In HbH disease, HbA is decreased with normal HbA2 and HbF, and HbH makes up 0% to 30% of the hemoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 4 lists HbH disease (genotype alpha-/- -) as showing decreased HbA with normal HbA2 and normal HbF, plus an HbH fraction of 0% to 30%. Detectable HbH is what separates this from the other microcytic states.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absent HbA with increased HbA2 and HbF up to 95% is the transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HbA2 is normal rather than decreased in HbH disease, and no HbH would be reported in this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased HbA with increased HbA2 and HbF up to 50% is the pattern of non-transfusion dependent beta-thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An entirely normal analysis is seen in the alpha silent carrier and in alpha-thalassemia trait.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man has a mild to moderate anemia. Testing shows that one of his beta chain genes carries the HbS mutation and the other carries a beta-thalassemia mutation. Compared with a patient who has two HbS mutations, which of the following best describes his expected anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent, because the two different mutations cancel each other

choices.label: B
choices.text: Identical in severity to full sickle cell anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Milder, tending to be less severe than full sickle cell anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Severe and transfusion-dependent from the first months of life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uniformly more severe than full sickle cell anemia

explanation.summary: Sickle cell beta-thalassemia has variable presentations but tends to cause anemia that is milder than HbS/HbS disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation notes that thalassemias and sickle cell disease can coexist. Sickle cell beta-thalassemia patients have a single HbS mutation in one beta chain gene and a beta-thalassemia mutation in the other; presentations are variable but tend to feature anemia that is mild to moderate and less severe than full sickle cell anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inheriting two different beta gene mutations does not cancel the defect; anemia is still present.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Severity is variable but characteristically milder than full sickle cell anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transfusion dependence from infancy describes the beta-0/beta-0 genotype, not sickle cell beta-thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The combination is generally less severe, not more severe, than HbS/HbS disease.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with severe beta-thalassemia has a peripheral blood smear showing several red blood cell precursors that still contain nuclei. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of mature red cells spares the precursors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron chelation therapy mobilizes precursors out of the marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: The marrow works harder, so precursors slip into the blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfused donor red blood cells carry nuclei into the circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency blocks nuclear maturation in precursors

explanation.summary: Nucleated RBCs appear in moderate to severe thalassemia because the hard-driven marrow releases precursors into the circulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that nucleated RBCs may be seen in moderate to severe cases of thalassemia because the more severe the anemia, the harder the bone marrow works to get RBCs out into circulation, and the more likely it is for these precursor RBCs, normally seen only in the marrow, to slip into the blood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thalassemia is a genetic globin production defect, not an autoimmune hemolytic process.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron chelators prevent iron overload; they do not push precursors out of the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Donor red blood cells in a transfusion are mature and anucleate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anemia and is not the mechanism described here.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a hemoglobin of 11.0 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 63 fL. Which of the following relationships among her complete blood count indices most favors thalassemia minor over iron-deficiency anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The hematocrit is decreased proportionally more than the RBC count

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hemoglobin is decreased proportionally more than the MCV

choices.label: C
choices.text: The MCV and hemoglobin are decreased to a proportionally equal degree

choices.label: D
choices.text: The MCV is decreased proportionally more than the hemoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: The RDW is increased out of proportion to the MCV

explanation.summary: In thalassemia minor the MCV falls out of proportion to the hemoglobin; in iron deficiency the reverse is true.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 3 contrasts clues from the CBC: in thalassemia minor the MCV is proportionally more decreased than the hemoglobin, whereas in iron deficiency the hemoglobin is proportionally more decreased than the MCV. A hemoglobin of 11.0 g/dL with an MCV of 63 fL fits the thalassemic pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The hematocrit-to-RBC count relationship is not the discriminator the brick describes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin falling more than the MCV is the iron-deficiency pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Equal proportional decreases do not distinguish the two disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An increased RDW favors iron deficiency; the RDW is normal in thalassemia minor.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man of Asian descent is found to have mild microcytosis. His serum ferritin is normal, and hemoglobin electrophoresis shows normal HbA, HbA2, and HbF. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish a precise diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow biopsy with iron staining

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) testing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genetic testing for alpha-globin gene deletions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Measurement of the serum erythropoietin level

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat hemoglobin electrophoresis in six months

explanation.summary: Because alpha-thalassemias have a normal hemoglobin analysis, genetic testing is required to diagnose them precisely.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that although history, physical exam, and CBC may be suggestive, genetic testing is best for making a precise diagnosis in most cases, especially in the alpha-thalassemias. Table 4 shows that the alpha silent carrier and alpha-thalassemia trait both have normal HbA, HbA2, and HbF, so electrophoresis cannot make the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow biopsy is not the test the brick identifies for confirming thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A Coombs test evaluates immune hemolysis, which is not the mechanism in thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The erythropoietin level does not identify a globin gene abnormality.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Repeating electrophoresis will again be normal, since alpha-thalassemia does not alter the hemoglobin fractions.

questions.stem: A hemoglobin analysis performed during the evaluation of a microcytic anemia reports the percentages of HbA, HbA2, and HbF. Which of the following describes the globin chain composition of HbA2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four beta chains

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four gamma chains

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two alpha chains and two beta chains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two alpha chains and two delta chains

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two alpha chains and two gamma chains

explanation.summary: HbA2 consists of two alpha and two delta chains; HbF is two alpha and two gamma chains.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the other hemoglobin forms relevant to diagnosing thalassemias are HbA2, with two alpha and two delta chains, and HbF, with two alpha chains and two gamma chains. Normal adult hemoglobin (HbA) is two alpha and two beta chains.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A tetramer of four beta chains is HbH, formed from excess unpaired beta chains.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A tetramer of four gamma chains is Hb Barts, formed in the alpha-null fetus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Two alpha and two beta chains describes normal adult HbA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two alpha and two gamma chains describes fetal hemoglobin, HbF.
