questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with untreated severe beta-thalassemia has radiographs of the lower extremities showing expansion of the metaphyses, producing an Erlenmeyer flask appearance of the long bones. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic osteomyelitis acquired from transfused blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperplasia of the bone marrow causing modeling deformity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deposition within the metaphyseal growth plate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeated microinfarction of metaphyseal bone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secondary hyperparathyroidism from chronic kidney disease

explanation.summary: Marrow hyperplasia in severe thalassemia remodels bone, producing metaphyseal expansion (Erlenmeyer flask deformity).
explanation.whyCorrect: Under Radiology, the brick states that hyperplasia of the bone marrow may lead to modeling deformities of the bone, such as metaphyseal expansion described as Erlenmeyer flask deformities of the long bones.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transfusion-transmitted infection is rare with modern screening and does not cause this deformity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deposition affects the heart, liver, and endocrine organs, not the growth plate architecture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bone microinfarction is a feature of sickle cell disease rather than thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal osteodystrophy from hyperparathyroidism is not a described complication of thalassemia in this brick.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with non-transfusion dependent thalassemia undergoes chest CT for atypical chest pain. The scan shows bilateral paraspinal soft-tissue masses. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these masses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron deposition within the paraspinal musculature

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metastatic carcinoma of unknown primary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurofibromas arising from spinal nerve roots

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tuberculous paraspinal abscess

explanation.summary: Paraspinal masses on CT in thalassemia represent extramedullary hematopoiesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states directly that CT scan may show paraspinal masses due to extramedullary hematopoiesis. Ineffective erythropoiesis in the marrow drives red cell production at other sites, including paraspinal tissue as well as the liver, spleen, and bones of the skull and face.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron overload deposits in the heart, liver, and endocrine organs, not as paraspinal masses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metastatic disease is not a described feature of thalassemia and is not suggested by this history.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neurofibromas are unrelated to thalassemia and are not described in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A tuberculous abscess would be expected to cause systemic infectious findings not present here.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with non-transfusion dependent thalassemia has never received a blood transfusion. Surveillance testing shows a markedly elevated ferritin with iron deposition in the liver. Which of the following best explains his excess iron stores?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dietary iron supplements taken for microcytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased intestinal absorption of iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron chelation therapy with deferoxamine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red blood cell transfusions received during childhood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy performed for hypersplenism

explanation.summary: Excess iron in thalassemia comes from increased intestinal iron absorption as well as from transfusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the goals of treating anemia in thalassemia, the brick lists reducing excess iron stores associated with increased intestinal iron absorption and/or transfusion. In a patient who has never been transfused, the increased gastrointestinal absorption of iron accounts for the iron loading.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No iron supplementation is described, and iron therapy is inappropriate in thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deferoxamine is a chelator used to remove iron; it does not cause iron loading.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stem states he has never received a transfusion, so transfusional iron is not the source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is not described in this patient and does not by itself produce iron overload.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man has a routine complete blood count showing a low hemoglobin, low mean corpuscular volume, low mean cell hemoglobin concentration, and a high red blood cell count. He is asymptomatic and his physical examination is normal. Serum ferritin is normal, and hemoglobin electrophoresis confirms beta-thalassemia trait. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic red cell transfusions to normalize the hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deferoxamine chelation therapy for iron overload

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral iron supplementation to correct the microcytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reassurance and genetic counseling, with no treatment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy to reduce ongoing splenic hemolysis

explanation.summary: Mild thalassemia, including trait, requires no treatment; counseling about implications for offspring is what matters.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that mild cases of thalassemia, including trait, typically do not require treatment because anemia and symptoms are absent or mild. In the case discussion, the patient is asymptomatic with a hemoglobin level that is not extreme, so no further treatment is necessary once he understands the diagnosis and its implication for his children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic transfusion is reserved for severe disease and would expose him to iron overload.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chelation is indicated for iron overload, which he does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.C: His ferritin is normal, so he is not iron deficient; iron would not correct thalassemic microcytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is considered only in severe thalassemia with hypersplenism or symptomatic splenomegaly.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman is found to have a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with a high red blood cell count, and thalassemia trait is suspected. Which of the following laboratory tests should be obtained to exclude the principal alternative diagnosis before her hemoglobin analysis is interpreted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin test

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactate dehydrogenase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reticulocyte count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum ferritin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum haptoglobin

explanation.summary: A serum ferritin is needed to rule out coexisting iron deficiency, the main alternative cause of microcytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's case discussion, a check of serum ferritin is described as needed to rule out an underlying iron deficiency before the hemoglobin electrophoresis is used to confirm thalassemia trait. Iron-deficiency anemia is the more common microcytic anemia and must be excluded.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The direct antiglobulin test evaluates immune-mediated hemolysis, which is not the alternative here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactate dehydrogenase is a nonspecific marker of cell turnover and does not exclude iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A reticulocyte count does not distinguish iron deficiency from thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haptoglobin reflects hemolysis generally and does not identify iron deficiency.

questions.stem: The parents of a child with transfusion-dependent thalassemia ask about definitive treatment. They are told that stem cell transplant is reserved for the most severe cases because of risks such as immunosuppression and graft-versus-host disease. Which of the following is increasingly being used instead and is likely to become the best therapy option?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gene therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-dose erythropoietin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydroxyurea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Luspatercept infusions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy

explanation.summary: Gene therapy is increasingly used in place of stem cell transplant and is expected to become the best definitive option.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation states that very severe cases may be treated definitively with stem cell transplant, reserved for the most severe cases because the benefit outweighs risks such as immunosuppression and graft-versus-host disease, and that gene therapy is increasingly being used instead in these patients and is likely to become the best therapy option.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin is not the therapy the brick names as replacing transplant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxyurea is not among the definitive treatments described for thalassemia in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Luspatercept reduces transfusion requirements but is not presented as a definitive curative therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy addresses hypersplenism and transfusion burden; it does not correct the globin defect.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with severe beta-thalassemia is about to start a chronic transfusion program to keep his hemoglobin stable within an appropriate range. Which of the following medications must be given along with the transfusions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deferoxamine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral ferrous sulfate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prophylactic antibiotics

choices.label: E
choices.text: Systemic corticosteroids

explanation.summary: Patients on chronic transfusion must receive an iron chelator such as deferoxamine to prevent iron overload.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that more severe cases may require chronic transfusions to keep the hemoglobin stable, and that patients receiving chronic transfusions must receive iron-chelating agents like deferoxamine to prevent iron overload.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin is not the agent the brick pairs with chronic transfusion therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron supplementation would add to the iron burden these patients already accumulate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not described as part of a chronic transfusion program here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Corticosteroids are not indicated; the anemia is genetic rather than immune-mediated.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a mild microcytic anemia reports that her mother and an aunt were both told they had iron-deficiency anemia. Both took iron pills without improvement, and both had normal colonoscopies performed to look for bleeding. Which of the following best explains this family history?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inherited thalassemia repeatedly misdiagnosed as iron deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Familial autoimmune hemolytic anemia with antibody-coated red cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Familial occult gastrointestinal blood loss from small-bowel lesions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hereditary hemochromatosis presenting as a microcytic anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inherited vitamin B12 deficiency with a microcytic picture

explanation.summary: Relatives with thalassemia are often mislabeled as iron deficient and subjected to needless iron therapy and testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that many patients with thalassemia have a family history of some form of anemia, and that relatives may have been falsely diagnosed with iron-deficiency anemia and undergone unnecessary treatments such as taking iron pills or tests such as colonoscopies looking for bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoimmune hemolysis is not inherited and does not produce this pattern of failed iron therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Occult bleeding would have been sought and was not found on colonoscopy, and it does not cluster in families this way.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemochromatosis causes iron overload rather than a microcytic anemia unresponsive to iron.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency produces a macrocytic, not microcytic, anemia.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with thalassemia develops an influenza-like illness. Over the next few days she notices worsening fatigue and yellowing of her eyes. Which of the following best explains the yellow discoloration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Biliary obstruction by a pancreatic head mass

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct hepatitis caused by the influenza virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolysis of red blood cells during the acute infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deposition in the liver from prior transfusions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Marrow expansion compressing the intrahepatic bile ducts

explanation.summary: Stress such as infection worsens thalassemia symptoms, and jaundice appears as red blood cells hemolyze.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that during periods of stress, such as in an infection, symptoms may worsen, and patients may note jaundice as blood cells hemolyze. Her worsening fatigue and scleral icterus during an acute infection fit this pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pancreatic mass is not suggested by this history and would not fluctuate with an infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Influenza is not described as causing hepatitis in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transfusional iron overload causes liver disease over years, not acute jaundice with an infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marrow expansion affects the skull, face, and long bones; it does not compress bile ducts.

questions.stem: A hematologist explains that in the thalassemias the number of mutated or deleted alleles is directly proportional to the severity of disease. Which of the following properties of the globin chain genes best accounts for this relationship?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All copies of the genes contribute equally to total globin synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each additional mutation raises hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mutated alleles act in a dominant-negative fashion on normal alleles

choices.label: D
choices.text: One allele is imprinted and silenced in each generation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only the maternally inherited allele is expressed in erythroid cells

explanation.summary: Globin genes are co-dominantly expressed, so each lost allele removes a fixed share of globin output.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that because all the copies or alleles of globin chain genes contribute equally to the total amount of globin synthesized, the number of mutated alleles is proportional to the severity of the disease. This is why one abnormal allele is usually asymptomatic, half the alleles gives trait, and more losses give intermedia and major.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Severity reflects the quantity of globin made, not a change in oxygen affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mutated alleles reduce output from their own gene; they do not suppress the normal alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Globin genes are not imprinted; all copies are expressed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both parental alleles are expressed co-dominantly, not just the maternal copy.

questions.stem: In hemoglobin H disease, the anemia is more severe than would be predicted from the reduction in alpha chain output alone. Which of the following properties of hemoglobin H best accounts for this additional severity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates complement on the red blood cell surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds oxygen so tightly that it is not released to tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cannot carry oxygen and is insoluble, precipitating in the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: It consumes the intracellular iron needed for HbA synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: It polymerizes and deforms the red cell into a sickle shape

explanation.summary: HbH is both nonfunctional and insoluble, so it precipitates and shortens red cell survival on top of the reduced hemoglobin output.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that in HbH disease patients already have a hard time making hemoglobin with only one working alpha chain gene, and that to make matters worse, HbH is unable to carry oxygen and is insoluble, precipitating within the cell and causing the RBCs to be removed from the circulation earlier than their normal lifespan.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement activation describes immune hemolysis, not the behavior of HbH tetramers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The problem is that HbH cannot carry oxygen at all, not that it holds oxygen too tightly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HbH does not deplete intracellular iron; the defect is in alpha chain production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polymerization producing sickled cells is the mechanism of sickle cell disease, a structural hemoglobinopathy.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman with a 5-year history of rheumatoid arthritis reports 3 months of worsening fatigue and pallor. Her hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 88 fL (normal). Iron studies show a low serum iron, a low total iron-binding capacity, a normal transferrin saturation, and an elevated ferritin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia of chronic disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-thalassemia minor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron-deficiency anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sideroblastic anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency

explanation.summary: A normocytic anemia with low serum iron, low TIBC, and high ferritin in a patient with a chronic inflammatory disease is anemia of chronic disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: In anemia of chronic disease (ACD), inflammation raises hepcidin, trapping iron in macrophages and hepatocytes. This produces low serum iron with a paradoxically normal or high ferritin (a positive acute-phase reactant) and a low TIBC (transferrin is a negative acute-phase reactant). The link to rheumatoid arthritis and the normocytic indices fit ACD.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Thalassemia minor gives microcytosis with normal or high iron studies and a normal/high RBC count, not iron sequestration tied to inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron-deficiency anemia shows a LOW ferritin and a HIGH TIBC, the opposite of this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sideroblastic anemia typically shows high serum iron and high ferritin with ring sideroblasts, not a low serum iron.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic (high MCV) anemia, not a normocytic anemia with these iron studies.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with fatigue and mild shortness of breath when climbing stairs. Her complete blood count shows a hemoglobin of 10.0 g/dL. Increased synthesis of which of the following most likely led to this anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Haptoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepcidin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypoxia-inducible factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protoporphyrin

explanation.summary: Inflammatory cytokines drive hepcidin production, which sequesters iron and causes anemia of chronic disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic inflammatory disease such as lupus, high IL-6 increases hepcidin. Hepcidin degrades ferroportin-1, reducing iron release from macrophages and hepatocytes and iron transfer from enterocytes, so less iron reaches the marrow to make new RBCs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythropoietin rises in response to anemia; it is an effect, not the cause of ACD (and is not the driver except in chronic kidney disease).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin after intravascular hemolysis and falls in hemolytic anemia; it is normal in ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypoxia-inducible factor stimulates erythropoietin and RBC production in any anemia; it does not cause ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protoporphyrin is a heme component; an increase in it does not cause ACD.

questions.stem: In a patient with anemia of chronic disease/inflammation, an increased value in which of the following serum tests is most characteristic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ferritin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serum iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transferrin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferrin saturation

explanation.summary: Ferritin is a positive acute-phase reactant and is normal or high in ACD.
explanation.whyCorrect: During inflammation the liver makes more ferritin, so it is normal or increased in ACD. A high ferritin is the key value that distinguishes ACD from iron-deficiency anemia, in which ferritin is low.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum iron is LOW in ACD because iron is trapped in macrophages and hepatocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TIBC is LOW because transferrin is a negative acute-phase reactant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transferrin (measured as TIBC) is LOW, since the liver makes less of it during inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transferrin saturation is most often low, sometimes normal, but not increased.

questions.stem: Anemia of chronic disease is caused primarily by a decrease in which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excretion of iron in the urine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxidation of iron in hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Release of iron from macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Storage of iron in the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uptake of intestinal iron by enterocytes

explanation.summary: Increased hepcidin blocks iron release from macrophages and hepatocytes, limiting iron for RBC production.
explanation.whyCorrect: In ACD, hepcidin degrades ferroportin-1 so macrophages and hepatocytes cannot release stored iron. Less circulating iron reaches the marrow, limiting incorporation into RBC precursors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Urinary iron excretion does not play a role in the pathogenesis of ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxidation of iron within hemoglobin is not a mechanism of ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no increased marrow iron storage; iron cannot even reach the marrow because it is trapped in hepatocytes and macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enterocyte uptake of intestinal iron is normal; the problem is that iron cannot exit the enterocyte into plasma.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus, treated with several medications, presents for follow-up. Her complete blood count shows a hemoglobin of 10.0 g/dL (normal 12.0-16.0) with a mean corpuscular volume of 90 fL (normal 80-100). She has only mild symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythropoietin injections

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravenous iron supplementation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral iron supplementation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red blood cell transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treat the underlying disease

explanation.summary: Management of ACD focuses on treating the underlying disorder, not on directly treating the anemia in mild cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of ACD is aimed at the underlying disease; controlling the inflammation typically resolves the anemia. In mild, normocytic anemia without documented iron deficiency, no specific anemia-directed therapy is required.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythropoietin is generally reserved for severe cases, not mild ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IV iron is generally not required for mild ACD and is reserved for more severe cases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral iron is warranted only if a concurrent iron deficiency is documented with iron studies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transfusion is not indicated until anemia is profound, typically below 7 g/dL.

questions.stem: In chronic inflammation, hepcidin lowers plasma iron primarily through which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Causing internalization and degradation of ferroportin-1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Directly lysing red blood cell precursors in the marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhancing iron absorption across the duodenal brush border

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing transferrin synthesis by the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulating erythropoietin release from the kidney

explanation.summary: Hepcidin degrades the iron exporter ferroportin-1, trapping iron inside cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin triggers internalization and degradation of ferroportin-1. Decreased ferroportin blocks iron release from enterocytes into plasma and from macrophages and hepatocytes, lowering circulating iron.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepcidin controls iron handling; it does not directly lyse RBC precursors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepcidin inhibits, rather than enhances, iron transfer from the enterocyte into the plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transferrin (TIBC) actually falls in inflammation because it is a negative acute-phase reactant; hepcidin does not increase it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepcidin acts on iron transport, not on renal erythropoietin release.

questions.stem: A patient with a chronic inflammatory condition develops anemia of chronic disease. Which of the following inflammatory cytokines most directly increases hepcidin production by the liver?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interleukin-10 (IL-10)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interleukin-6 (IL-6)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intrinsic factor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta)

explanation.summary: IL-6 is the key inflammatory cytokine that drives hepcidin production.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic inflammation, high levels of IL-6 increase hepatic hepcidin production, which in turn sequesters iron and produces anemia of chronic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythropoietin is a hormone that stimulates RBC production; increased erythropoietic activity actually suppresses hepcidin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine and is not the driver of hepcidin in ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intrinsic factor is required for vitamin B12 absorption and has no role in hepcidin regulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is not described as the cytokine that raises hepcidin in this setting.

questions.stem: A patient with anemia of chronic disease has a low serum iron but an elevated ferritin. Which of the following best explains the elevated ferritin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ferritin is a positive acute-phase reactant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ongoing intravascular hemolysis is releasing iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: The kidney is failing to excrete ferritin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Total body iron stores are depleted

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferrin saturation is markedly elevated

explanation.summary: Ferritin rises in inflammation because it is a positive acute-phase reactant.
explanation.whyCorrect: The liver produces more ferritin during inflammation, so ferritin is normal or high in ACD even though usable circulating iron is low. This high ferritin distinguishes ACD from iron-deficiency anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolysis is not the mechanism of the high ferritin in ACD; the iron is sequestered, not released by RBC destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferritin is not elevated because of impaired renal excretion; it reflects increased synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Depleted iron stores would produce a LOW ferritin, as seen in iron-deficiency anemia, not a high one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transferrin saturation is typically low or normal in ACD, not elevated.

questions.stem: In addition to decreased erythrocyte production, which of the following additional mechanisms contributes to the anemia of chronic disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytokines causing macrophages to prematurely destroy RBCs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased renal erythropoietin output

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mechanical fragmentation of RBCs producing schistocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenic sequestration of RBCs from portal hypertension

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm autoantibodies coating the red cell membrane

explanation.summary: Inflammatory cytokines shorten the RBC lifespan by driving early macrophage-mediated destruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond reduced production, inflammation reduces RBC lifespan. Cytokines such as IL-1 and IL-6 cause macrophages to prematurely ingest and destroy RBCs, worsening the anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased erythropoietin would raise, not lower, RBC production and is a response to anemia, not a cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Schistocyte formation from mechanical fragmentation occurs in microangiopathic hemolysis, not ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic sequestration from portal hypertension is a separate cause of anemia unrelated to the ACD mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autoantibody-mediated (warm autoimmune) hemolysis is a distinct entity, not the mechanism taught for ACD.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has a hemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL. Which of the following is the most common finding on his complete blood count indices and peripheral smear?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated MCV with hypersegmented neutrophils on the smear

choices.label: B
choices.text: Markedly low MCV with prominent basophilic stippling of red cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal MCV (normocytic) with a largely unremarkable smear

choices.label: D
choices.text: Numerous schistocytes scattered throughout the peripheral smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: Numerous spherocytes with an elevated MCHC on the smear

explanation.summary: ACD is most often normocytic with a largely normal peripheral smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: In ACD the MCV is normal or decreased, with a normal value being most common. The peripheral blood smear usually shows few abnormalities, although RBCs may be hypochromic (pale) when hemoglobin-deficient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An elevated MCV with hypersegmented neutrophils indicates a megaloblastic anemia (B12/folate deficiency), not ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A markedly low MCV with basophilic stippling suggests thalassemia or lead poisoning, not typical ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Abundant schistocytes indicate microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, not ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spherocytes with a high MCHC point to hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolysis, not ACD.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease is found to have a hemoglobin of 9.5 g/dL. Which of the following best explains the mechanism and appropriate treatment of his anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepcidin deficiency causing iron overload, treated with phlebotomy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced renal erythropoietin production, treated with erythropoietin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Urinary iron loss causing iron deficiency, treated with oral iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B12 malabsorption, treated with parenteral B12

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm autoimmune hemolysis, treated with corticosteroids

explanation.summary: Anemia of chronic kidney disease results largely from deficient renal erythropoietin and is treated with synthetic erythropoietin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The kidney produces erythropoietin; in CKD, reduced erythropoietin leads to ineffective erythropoiesis and fewer RBCs (there is also shortened RBC lifespan from the uremic environment). This form of anemia is treated with synthetic erythropoietin injections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no hepcidin deficiency or iron overload here; phlebotomy is not the treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anemia of CKD is not primarily from urinary iron loss; the central problem is deficient erythropoietin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B12 malabsorption is unrelated to the erythropoietin-deficiency mechanism of CKD anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autoimmune hemolysis is a different entity; steroids are not the treatment for anemia of CKD.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with ulcerative colitis and chronic gastrointestinal blood loss has a hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL. Iron studies show a low serum iron AND a low ferritin. Which of the following is the best interpretation and next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coexisting iron-deficiency anemia is present, and iron repletion is indicated

choices.label: B
choices.text: This is anemia of chronic kidney disease requiring erythropoietin therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: This is classic anemia of chronic disease, in which the ferritin would be high

choices.label: D
choices.text: This is sideroblastic anemia with iron overload and a high ferritin

choices.label: E
choices.text: This represents beta-thalassemia trait with normal iron studies

explanation.summary: A low ferritin in a patient with chronic disease signals a coexisting iron deficiency, which should be treated with iron.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inflammatory GI diseases such as ulcerative colitis can cause anemia by both chronic blood loss (iron deficiency) and inflammation. Because ACD normally shows a high ferritin, a LOW ferritin here indicates a superimposed iron-deficiency anemia, so iron supplementation is warranted after ruling it in with serum studies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no indication of kidney disease; the picture is driven by GI blood loss and inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: In pure ACD the ferritin is normal or high; a low ferritin argues against pure ACD and points to iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sideroblastic anemia causes iron overload with high ferritin and serum iron, the opposite of this low-ferritin picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thalassemia trait shows microcytosis with normal or high iron studies, not a low ferritin from blood loss.

questions.stem: Anemia of chronic disease/inflammation is the second most common type of anemia. Which of the following is the most common type of anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aplastic anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron-deficiency anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Megaloblastic anemia from folate deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sickle cell anemia

explanation.summary: Iron-deficiency anemia is the most common anemia; anemia of chronic disease ranks second.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anemia of chronic disease (ACD) is described as the second most common type of anemia, after iron-deficiency anemia. This ranking matters clinically because the two are frequently confused: both show a low serum iron, and both can be microcytic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aplastic anemia is a rare marrow failure state, not the most common anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is an uncommon cause of anemia relative to iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folate-deficiency megaloblastic anemia is far less common than iron deficiency and is not the leading cause of anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sickle cell anemia is an inherited hemoglobinopathy limited to specific populations, not the most common anemia overall.

questions.stem: The incidence of anemia of chronic disease/inflammation is highest in which of the following groups?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adolescents during the pubertal growth spurt

choices.label: B
choices.text: Menstruating women of reproductive age

choices.label: C
choices.text: Newborn infants during the first weeks after delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Older adults with several coexisting chronic diseases

choices.label: E
choices.text: Young men recovering from an acute viral illness

explanation.summary: ACD incidence rises with age because older adults more often have chronic inflammatory diseases.
explanation.whyCorrect: The incidence of ACD increases with age. Older adults are more likely to have this type of anemia precisely because they are more likely to have one or more chronic diseases capable of generating sustained inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rapid adolescent growth outstrips iron supply and favors iron deficiency, not the inflammatory mechanism of ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Menstrual blood loss is the classic setting for iron-deficiency anemia rather than anemia of inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neonates are not the group in whom chronic inflammatory disease, and therefore ACD, accumulates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ACD arises from chronic, not brief self-limited, inflammatory illness.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed colon cancer has a hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL. His physician notes that his anemia has more than one cause. In addition to inflammation, which of the following mechanisms is most likely contributing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibody-mediated destruction of circulating red cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss with iron depletion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infiltration of the bone marrow by malignant cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mechanical fragmentation of red cells in small vessels

explanation.summary: Colon cancer causes anemia through chronic GI blood loss in addition to inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACD is often part of a syndrome in which anemia results from more than one mechanism. Cancer is a recognized cause of ACD, and colon cancer specifically also causes anemia through chronic gastrointestinal blood loss, which depletes iron stores.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoantibody-mediated hemolysis is a distinct entity and is not the second mechanism at work in colon cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ileal malabsorption of vitamin B12 is not among the mechanisms by which colon cancer produces anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow infiltration is the additional mechanism attributed to malignancies such as the leukemias, not to colon cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Red cell fragmentation occurs in microangiopathic processes, which are not the described mechanism here.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with acute leukemia is anemic. Her physician explains that the malignancy is contributing to the anemia by a mechanism separate from inflammation. Which of the following is that mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of circulating red blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss from mucosal ulceration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infiltration of the bone marrow by malignant cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of erythropoietin-producing tissue in the kidney

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration of red cells from portal hypertension

explanation.summary: Leukemias cause anemia by infiltrating and crowding the bone marrow, on top of the inflammatory mechanism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer can cause anemia by more than one route. In the leukemias, malignant cells infiltrate the bone marrow, and this marrow infiltration adds to the reduced erythrocyte production driven by chronic inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune red cell destruction is a distinct hemolytic process, not the mechanism attributed to leukemia here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GI blood loss is the second mechanism listed for tumors such as colon cancer, not for leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of renal erythropoietin production is the mechanism of anemia in chronic kidney disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Portal hypertension with splenic sequestration is a separate cause of anemia unrelated to the leukemic mechanism.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis feels well and has no complaints. A routine complete blood count shows a hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL with a normal mean corpuscular volume; iron studies show low iron, low TIBC, and high ferritin. Which of the following best characterizes the clinical presentation of this type of anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fever and drenching night sweats are characteristic

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jaundice and dark urine are typically present

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients may have no symptoms whatsoever

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral neurologic deficits usually accompany it

choices.label: E
choices.text: Symptoms are always severe enough to limit activity

explanation.summary: Patients with anemia of chronic disease may be entirely asymptomatic.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACD patients may be asymptomatic, or they may have the common symptoms of anemia such as fatigue, weakness, dizziness, shortness of breath, headache, pallor, feeling cold, and tachycardia. Detection on a routine CBC in a well-feeling patient is therefore expected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fever and night sweats belong to the underlying disease if at all; they are not features of the anemia itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Jaundice and dark urine reflect hemolysis, which is not a feature of the presentation described for ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neurologic deficits accompany vitamin B12 deficiency, not anemia of inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Severity varies widely, and many patients have no limitation at all.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic osteomyelitis has fatigue and pallor from anemia of chronic disease. In addition to the symptoms of anemia, which of the following is most likely also present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dark-colored urine occurring after exertion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypersegmented neutrophils on the peripheral smear

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marked splenomegaly with early satiety

choices.label: D
choices.text: Signs and symptoms of the underlying chronic disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spoon-shaped nails and a craving for ice

explanation.summary: ACD patients generally show features of the chronic illness driving the inflammation, alongside anemia symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to anemia symptoms, patients with ACD generally have one or more symptoms associated with the underlying chronic disease. A patient with rheumatoid arthritis, for instance, has joint pain and swelling; the underlying illness is part of the clinical picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dark urine after exertion suggests hemoglobinuria from hemolysis, not ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypersegmented neutrophils indicate a megaloblastic anemia, not anemia of inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Massive splenomegaly is not a described feature of anemia of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Koilonychia and pica are associated with iron-deficiency anemia rather than ACD.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions is most likely to produce anemia of chronic disease/inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute hemorrhage following blunt trauma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha-thalassemia trait

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Systemic sclerosis

explanation.summary: Systemic sclerosis is one of the chronic inflammatory conditions that causes ACD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inflammatory conditions associated with ACD include rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus, systemic sclerosis, chronic infections, and cancer. The unifying feature is sustained inflammation that suppresses RBC formation and shortens RBC lifespan.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute traumatic bleeding causes anemia by volume and red cell loss, not by chronic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-thalassemia trait is an inherited globin disorder, unrelated to chronic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidative hemolysis and is not among the inflammatory causes of ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited membrane defect causing hemolysis, not an inflammatory disease.

questions.stem: In a patient with chronic inflammation, the body iron that fails to reach the bone marrow is stored chiefly in which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circulating erythrocytes and reticulocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Duodenal enterocytes and gastric parietal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macrophages and liver cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal tubular cells and the adrenal cortex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic lymphocytes and plasma cells

explanation.summary: A large share of body iron is stored in macrophages and hepatocytes, and inflammation locks it there.
explanation.whyCorrect: A large amount of the body's iron is stored in macrophages and liver cells. In chronic inflammation, hepcidin prevents these cells from releasing that stored iron, so reduced iron delivery to the bone marrow becomes an important reason for decreased RBC production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron in circulating red cells is committed to hemoglobin and is not the sequestered storage pool.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The enterocyte handles newly absorbed dietary iron in transit; it is not the major body storage site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal tubular and adrenal cells are not described as iron storage compartments in this process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lymphocytes and plasma cells do not serve as the body's iron reservoir; macrophages do.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes decreases hepcidin production?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rise in the plasma iron concentration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Active joint inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis

choices.label: C
choices.text: High circulating levels of interleukin-6

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased erythropoietic activity in the marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased hepatic synthesis of ferritin

explanation.summary: Hepcidin is stimulated by inflammatory cytokines and plasma iron, but suppressed by increased erythropoietic activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin production is pushed up by increased plasma iron and by inflammatory cytokines, and pushed down by increased erythropoietic activity. A marrow working hard to make red cells therefore signals for more available iron by lowering hepcidin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased plasma iron is a positive stimulus that raises hepcidin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inflammatory arthritis supplies the cytokines that drive hepcidin up, not down.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-6 is the inflammatory cytokine that increases hepcidin production, the opposite direction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferritin synthesis rises with inflammation alongside hepcidin; it does not suppress hepcidin.

questions.stem: Apart from inflammatory cytokines, which of the following stimuli increases hepcidin production?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fall in the plasma iron concentration

choices.label: B
choices.text: A rise in the plasma iron concentration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degradation of ferroportin-1 on macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Expansion of erythroid precursors in the marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced hepatic synthesis of transferrin

explanation.summary: Increased plasma iron, like inflammatory cytokines, is a positive stimulus for hepcidin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin has two positive inputs: increased plasma iron and inflammatory cytokines. Raising plasma iron increases hepcidin, which then limits further iron entry into the circulation, a negative feedback loop on plasma iron.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A low plasma iron does not stimulate hepcidin; high plasma iron does.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of ferroportin-1 is the downstream consequence of hepcidin, not an upstream stimulus for it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased erythropoietic activity is a negative input that lowers hepcidin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced transferrin synthesis is a separate effect of inflammation and does not itself drive hepcidin.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis and anemia of chronic disease is given oral ferrous sulfate, but her serum iron does not rise. Which of the following steps in iron handling is most directly blocked?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of plasma iron to circulating transferrin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incorporation of iron into heme in erythroid precursors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron transport across the basal membrane of the enterocyte

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron uptake at the duodenal brush border surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduction of dietary ferric iron within the gastric lumen

explanation.summary: Hepcidin blocks iron transfer out of the enterocyte into the plasma, so oral iron does not raise serum iron.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin inhibits iron transport across the basal membrane of intestinal cells, blocking transfer of iron from the duodenal enterocyte into the plasma. Iron entering the enterocyte therefore never reaches the circulation, and oral supplementation fails to correct the low serum iron.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transferrin still binds whatever iron reaches the plasma; the problem is that too little iron gets there.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythroid precursors can use iron normally; they simply are not supplied with enough of it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Uptake of intestinal iron by enterocytes is normal; the defect is the exit step out of the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gastric handling of dietary iron is not the step hepcidin acts on.

questions.stem: In anemia of chronic disease, less iron in the circulation means less iron delivered to the bone marrow, which limits production of new red blood cells. This limited production is best termed which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow infiltration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ineffective erythropoiesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intravascular hemolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration

explanation.summary: Limited RBC production from inadequate iron delivery to the marrow is called ineffective erythropoiesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because iron is trapped in hepatocytes and macrophages or is not delivered from the intestine, circulating iron falls, less iron reaches the marrow, and production of new RBCs is limited. This limited production is termed ineffective erythropoiesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow infiltration refers to malignant cells crowding the marrow, as in leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Extramedullary hematopoiesis is blood cell production outside the marrow, not the term for limited marrow output.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intravascular hemolysis is destruction of circulating red cells, a different process entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration is trapping of red cells in the spleen, not impaired production.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with stage 5 chronic kidney disease has a hemoglobin of 9.0 g/dL. Besides a lack of erythropoietin, which of the following additional mechanisms is contributing to his anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against red cell membrane antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased hepcidin generated by inflamed joints

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replacement of the marrow space by fibrous tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shortened red cell lifespan caused by the uremic environment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urinary loss of transferrin-bound circulating iron

explanation.summary: Anemia of chronic kidney disease combines erythropoietin deficiency with a shortened RBC lifespan from uremia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The anemia of chronic kidney disease is usually considered a separate form of anemia from ACD but shares features with it. RBC lifespan is shortened by the uremic environment as toxins build up in the blood from poorly filtering kidneys, and ineffective erythropoiesis results from lack of renally produced erythropoietin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody-mediated hemolysis is a separate disorder and is not the described mechanism in uremia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepcidin-driven iron sequestration from joint inflammation is the ACD mechanism, not what is described for kidney disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow fibrosis is not the mechanism attributed to chronic kidney disease here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary iron loss is not a described contributor to the anemia of chronic kidney disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why anemia of chronic disease/inflammation is often a diagnosis of exclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bone marrow biopsy is required in every case to confirm it

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can be identified only after a therapeutic trial of iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is secondary to another disorder and lacks a specific test

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its iron studies are identical to those of thalassemia trait

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its symptoms appear only once hemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL

explanation.summary: ACD is secondary to an underlying disorder and lacks tests as specific as those available for other anemias.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because ACD is secondary to an underlying disorder and does not have tests as specific as those for other anemias, it is often diagnosed by exclusion. The workup combines laboratory testing with the history and physical exam, which may reveal signs and symptoms of the underlying disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow biopsy is not a required part of diagnosing ACD; CBC and iron studies are typically used.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diagnosis rests on serum studies rather than on an empiric iron trial.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thalassemia trait does not share the ACD iron profile; the diagnostic overlap emphasized is with iron-deficiency anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Symptoms do not require a hemoglobin below 7 g/dL, and symptom threshold is not why the diagnosis is one of exclusion.

questions.stem: A physician suspects anemia of chronic disease and wants nonspecific laboratory evidence that inflammation is present. Which of the following pairs of tests is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum haptoglobin and serum lactate dehydrogenase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum iron and total iron-binding capacity

explanation.summary: ESR and CRP are the nonspecific tests used to document inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nonspecific tests for inflammation include the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and the C-reactive protein (CRP). They do not identify a particular disease but confirm that an inflammatory process is active.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ANA and rheumatoid factor are disease-specific tests aimed at particular autoimmune conditions, not nonspecific inflammatory markers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coagulation times assess clotting function and are not used to document inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Haptoglobin and LDH are markers of hemolysis rather than general inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum iron and TIBC are iron studies used to characterize the anemia, not inflammation markers.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has a malar rash, arthralgias, and a normocytic anemia with a low serum iron, low TIBC, and high ferritin. Which of the following tests is most likely to identify the underlying disease responsible for her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antinuclear antibody test

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow biopsy with iron staining

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum vitamin B12 level

explanation.summary: Testing for the suspected inflammatory disease, here lupus with an ANA, identifies the cause of the ACD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because ACD is secondary, the workup includes testing for the suspected inflammatory disease with appropriate tests, such as the antinuclear antibody (ANA) test for lupus. Her iron studies already fit ACD; the ANA targets the underlying disorder driving it.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Marrow biopsy is not needed when the CBC and iron studies already indicate ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A Coombs test screens for antibody-mediated hemolysis, not for the inflammatory cause of ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin electrophoresis evaluates hemoglobinopathies, which her iron studies do not suggest.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A B12 level addresses macrocytic anemia, which her normal MCV makes unlikely.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of complete blood count results is expected in a patient with anemia of chronic disease/inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High hemoglobin, low hematocrit, low RBC count

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low hemoglobin, high hematocrit, high RBC count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low hemoglobin, low hematocrit, low RBC count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low hemoglobin, normal hematocrit, high RBC count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal hemoglobin, low hematocrit, normal RBC count

explanation.summary: As in any anemia, ACD lowers hemoglobin, hematocrit, and the RBC count together.
explanation.whyCorrect: As in any anemia, the CBC in ACD shows low blood hemoglobin, low hematocrit, and a low RBC count. The distinguishing CBC feature is the index: the MCV is normal or decreased, with a normal value most common.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high hemoglobin contradicts the presence of anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A high hematocrit and RBC count are incompatible with anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An elevated RBC count with anemia suggests thalassemia trait, not ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A normal hemoglobin would not define an anemia at all.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with Crohn disease has a hemoglobin of 10.1 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 76 fL. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the low MCV?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The low MCV also occurs in ACD, so serum studies decide

choices.label: B
choices.text: The low MCV confirms iron-deficiency anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: The low MCV excludes anemia of chronic disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: The low MCV indicates a coexisting thalassemia trait

choices.label: E
choices.text: The low MCV points to an underlying megaloblastic process

explanation.summary: ACD can be microcytic, so a low MCV cannot separate it from iron deficiency; serum iron studies must decide.
explanation.whyCorrect: CBC indices in ACD show a normal or decreased MCV. A low MCV may lead to confusing ACD with iron-deficiency anemia, which is exactly why the serum iron studies, especially ferritin, are important for the distinction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A low MCV alone does not confirm iron deficiency, since ACD can produce the same index.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Microcytosis does not exclude ACD, because the anemia can be microcytic as well as normocytic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thalassemia is not established by a low MCV in a patient with an inflammatory bowel disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Megaloblastic processes raise, rather than lower, the MCV.

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a patient with anemia of chronic disease shows red blood cells that appear pale. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The red cells are coated with immunoglobulin

choices.label: B
choices.text: The red cells are deficient in hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: The red cells contain precipitated globin chains

choices.label: D
choices.text: The red cells have been fragmented by fibrin strands

choices.label: E
choices.text: The red cells have lost membrane surface area

explanation.summary: Hypochromia in ACD reflects red cells that are deficient in hemoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The peripheral smear in ACD typically shows few abnormalities, but RBCs may sometimes be hypochromic (pale) because they are deficient in hemoglobin. With less iron reaching the marrow, precursors cannot fill each cell with a normal amount of hemoglobin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immunoglobulin coating indicates autoimmune hemolysis, which is not the mechanism in ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Precipitated globin chains occur in thalassemias, not in anemia of inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrin-strand fragmentation produces schistocytes, a feature of microangiopathic hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of membrane surface area produces spherocytes, which appear densely staining rather than pale.

questions.stem: Which of the following serum values is LEAST useful for distinguishing anemia of chronic disease from iron-deficiency anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serum ferritin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum transferrin concentration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Total iron-binding capacity

explanation.summary: Serum iron is low in both ACD and iron deficiency, so it cannot separate them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serum iron is low in ACD because iron is trapped in macrophages and hepatocytes. This is the same as in iron-deficiency anemia, so serum iron is not helpful in distinguishing the two types.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An elevated ESR supports an active inflammatory process underlying ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferritin is the key discriminator: normal or high in ACD and low in iron-deficiency anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transferrin, measured as TIBC, falls in inflammation and therefore carries discriminating information.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TIBC is low in ACD, in contrast to the high TIBC of iron deficiency, so it does help distinguish them.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has a low serum iron, a low TIBC, a high ferritin, and a transferrin saturation within the normal range. Which of the following best explains the normal transferrin saturation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both serum iron and transferrin are reduced together

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her hepcidin level has returned to the normal range

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her liver is producing more transferrin than usual

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her total body iron stores have been completely depleted

choices.label: E
choices.text: She has a coexisting iron-deficiency anemia

explanation.summary: Transferrin saturation is a ratio, so it can look normal when both iron and transferrin fall.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because of the low circulating iron, the transferrin saturation percentage is most often low, but it can be normal since both transferrin and iron are reduced. The saturation is a ratio of iron to available binding capacity, and proportional falls in each leave the ratio unchanged.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A normalized hepcidin would restore the serum iron and TIBC, which remain abnormal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transferrin synthesis falls during inflammation, which is why the TIBC is low.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Depleted stores would give a low ferritin; hers is high, indicating iron is present but sequestered.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Coexisting iron deficiency is signaled by a low ferritin, not the high ferritin seen here.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the low total iron-binding capacity seen in anemia of chronic disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The liver produces less transferrin during inflammation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transferrin binding sites are saturated by excess plasma iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transferrin is consumed by iron-laden macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transferrin is degraded by hepcidin along with ferroportin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferrin is lost in the urine during inflammation

explanation.summary: Transferrin is a negative acute-phase reactant, so the liver makes less of it and the TIBC falls.
explanation.whyCorrect: The serum transferrin, measured as the total iron-binding capacity, is low because transferrin is a negative acute-phase reactant: the liver makes less of it when inflammation is present. This contrasts with ferritin, a positive acute-phase reactant that rises.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma iron is low in ACD, so saturation of binding sites by excess iron cannot be the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrophages sequester iron but do not consume circulating transferrin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepcidin degrades ferroportin-1, not transferrin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary transferrin loss is not a described mechanism in ACD.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic osteomyelitis and known anemia of chronic disease is now dyspneic at rest. His hemoglobin has fallen to 6.4 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for his anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin a course of oral corticosteroids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Begin vitamin B12 injections

choices.label: C
choices.text: Observe and repeat the CBC in 3 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start oral iron supplementation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfuse red blood cells

explanation.summary: Transfusion in ACD is reserved for profound anemia, typically a hemoglobin below 7 g/dL.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood transfusions are generally not needed in ACD as long as the underlying cause can be treated, and transfusion is not indicated until the patient has a more profound anemia, typically not until the hemoglobin is below 7 g/dL. This symptomatic patient at 6.4 g/dL has crossed that threshold.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corticosteroids are not the described treatment for the anemia itself in ACD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin B12 addresses a megaloblastic anemia, which is not the process described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Watchful waiting is unsafe in a patient who is dyspneic at rest with a hemoglobin of 6.4 g/dL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral iron is appropriate only when a coexisting iron deficiency has been documented with serum studies.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman has severe anemia of chronic disease despite ongoing treatment of her underlying inflammatory disease, and iron deficiency has been excluded. Which of the following therapies may be used in severe cases of this anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythropoietin injections

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folic acid supplementation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term corticosteroid therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenectomy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Therapeutic phlebotomy

explanation.summary: Erythropoietin is reserved for severe anemia of chronic disease, not mild cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of ACD is directed at the underlying disorder, and erythropoietin is generally not required for mild cases. Erythropoietin can, however, be used in severe cases such as this one, where the anemia persists despite treatment of the inflammatory disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Folic acid addresses megaloblastic anemia and does not correct iron-restricted erythropoiesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corticosteroids may treat some underlying diseases but are not a described therapy for the anemia itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenectomy is not among the treatments for anemia of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phlebotomy removes iron and would worsen an anemia in which iron availability is already limited.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for anemia. A bone marrow aspirate stained with Prussian blue reveals erythroid precursors with a ring of blue granules encircling the nucleus. The iron responsible for these granules has accumulated within which of the following structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Golgi apparatus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lysosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleolus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rough endoplasmic reticulum

explanation.summary: Ringed sideroblasts form because unchelated iron accumulates in the mitochondria of erythroblasts.
explanation.whyCorrect: In sideroblastic anemia, impaired heme synthesis leaves iron unchelated, and this iron builds up within the mitochondria. Because mitochondria are arranged around the nucleus of erythroid progenitor cells, the trapped iron creates the characteristic perinuclear ring seen as ringed sideroblasts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Golgi apparatus packages and modifies proteins and is not the site of iron accumulation in ringed sideroblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysosomes degrade cellular material; the perinuclear iron ring reflects mitochondrial, not lysosomal, iron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nucleolus is a site of ribosome assembly; the iron ring surrounds the nucleus within mitochondria rather than being inside the nucleolus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is involved in protein synthesis, not in trapping the excess iron of sideroblastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use is found to have a microcytic anemia. His physician suspects sideroblastic anemia. Which of the following is the most common finding on his peripheral blood smear?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heinz bodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pappenheimer bodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ringed sideroblasts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schistocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sickle cells

explanation.summary: Pappenheimer bodies are the most common peripheral smear finding in sideroblastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing inclusions that appear as clusters of blue granules, usually at the periphery of circulating red blood cells, and reflect the abnormal iron incorporation of sideroblastic anemia. They are the most common peripheral smear finding across the various causes of the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heinz bodies represent denatured hemoglobin and are characteristic of G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ringed sideroblasts are nucleated erythroid progenitors confined to the bone marrow and are not seen on the peripheral blood smear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schistocytes are fragmented red cells seen in microangiopathic hemolysis, not in sideroblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sickle cells are found in sickle cell disease, not in sideroblastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with fatigue over several weeks. He was recently started on isoniazid after exposure to tuberculosis. CBC shows decreased hemoglobin and decreased mean corpuscular volume. Iron studies show increased ferritin and decreased total iron-binding capacity, and the smear shows red cells with blue inclusions. Which of the following treatments would be most effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deferoxamine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folic acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phlebotomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B12

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B6

explanation.summary: Isoniazid-induced sideroblastic anemia results from vitamin B6 depletion and is treated with vitamin B6 supplementation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Isoniazid reduces vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) levels, and B6 is the coenzyme required for ALAS, the first enzyme of heme synthesis. Replacing vitamin B6 restores heme production and is the most effective treatment for this acquired sideroblastic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deferoxamine is an iron chelator used for iron overload, which is uncommon in acquired sideroblastic anemia and does not correct the underlying B6 deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate deficiency also causes megaloblastic anemia and would not correct impaired heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phlebotomy treats iron overload but would worsen this patient's anemia and does not address the cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia, not this microcytic picture.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old male is brought to the physician for failure to thrive that began shortly after birth. Workup confirms sideroblastic anemia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased ALAS activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased ferrochelatase activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dysplastic cells in the bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal iron deficiency during pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B6 deficiency

explanation.summary: Congenital sideroblastic anemia is most often due to an X-linked mutation that decreases ALAS activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The patient's age and onset shortly after birth indicate a hereditary form. The most common inherited cause is an X-linked gene mutation that decreases delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS) activity, the enzyme catalyzing the first step of heme synthesis; this predominance in males reflects X-linked inheritance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased ferrochelatase activity is characteristic of lead toxicity rather than hereditary sideroblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dysplastic marrow cells occur in myelodysplastic syndrome, an acquired disorder of adults, not a congenital cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maternal iron deficiency during pregnancy is not a recognized cause of sideroblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B6 deficiency is an acquired cause from malnutrition, alcohol, or isoniazid, not a congenital disorder in a neonate.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl living in a house built in 1940 with peeling paint is evaluated for irritability, abdominal pain, and anemia. Her blood smear shows microcytic red cells with basophilic stippling. The suspected exposure causes sideroblastic anemia by inhibiting which of the following pairs of enzymes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ALA synthase and ALA dehydratase

choices.label: B
choices.text: ALA synthase and ferrochelatase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Porphobilinogen deaminase and ALA synthase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase and ferrochelatase

explanation.summary: Lead poisoning causes sideroblastic anemia by inhibiting ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vignette describes lead poisoning from old lead-based paint. Lead inhibits ferrochelatase (the final step inserting iron into protoporphyrin IX) and ALA dehydratase (which converts delta-ALA to porphobilinogen), impairing heme synthesis and producing sideroblastic anemia with basophilic stippling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although ALA dehydratase is inhibited by lead, ALA synthase is not; the correct second enzyme is ferrochelatase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ALA synthase is not inhibited by lead; it is deficient in the hereditary X-linked form. Ferrochelatase alone does not describe the lead-inhibited pair.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither porphobilinogen deaminase nor ALA synthase is the target of lead in this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase is not the enzyme inhibited by lead in sideroblastic anemia.

questions.stem: The first and rate-limiting step of heme synthesis converts glycine and succinyl-CoA to delta-aminolevulinic acid. The enzyme catalyzing this reaction requires which of the following as a coenzyme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vitamin B1 (thiamine)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)

explanation.summary: ALA synthase requires vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) as a coenzyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS) catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step of heme synthesis and requires vitamin B6 to function. This dependence explains why B6 deficiency causes sideroblastic anemia and why hereditary forms often respond to B6 supplementation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate participates in one-carbon transfer for nucleotide synthesis, not as the ALAS coenzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thiamine is a coenzyme for reactions such as pyruvate dehydrogenase, not ALAS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin B12 is required for methylmalonyl-CoA and methionine metabolism, not for ALAS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Riboflavin contributes to FAD/FMN-dependent reactions and is not the ALAS coenzyme.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis has a low hemoglobin, low mean corpuscular volume, and rare Pappenheimer bodies on his smear. To distinguish his anemia from iron deficiency anemia, which of the following iron study patterns is most expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased ferritin with decreased serum iron

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased ferritin with increased total iron-binding capacity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased serum iron with increased total iron-binding capacity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased ferritin with decreased total iron-binding capacity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal ferritin with increased transferrin saturation only during hemolysis

explanation.summary: Sideroblastic anemia shows increased iron stores (high ferritin) with low TIBC, opposite to iron deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because iron cannot be incorporated into heme, iron accumulates and marrow iron stores rise, producing an increased ferritin and a decreased total iron-binding capacity. This contrasts sharply with iron deficiency anemia, in which ferritin is low and TIBC is high.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased ferritin and low serum iron indicate depleted iron stores, which is not seen in sideroblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low ferritin with high TIBC is the classic pattern of iron deficiency anemia, the opposite of sideroblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Low serum iron with high TIBC again reflects iron deficiency, not the iron-replete state of sideroblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sideroblastic anemia has persistently elevated iron stores rather than transient changes limited to hemolytic episodes.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing sideroblastic anemia is being monitored for secondary hemochromatosis. Which of the following findings is LEAST suggestive of the development of iron overload?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bilateral peripheral pitting edema

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conjunctival pallor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated liver enzymes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excess thirst and urination

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hyperpigmented skin

explanation.summary: Conjunctival pallor reflects the anemia itself, not the iron overload of secondary hemochromatosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary hemochromatosis results from excess iron depositing in the heart, liver, pancreas, and skin. Conjunctival pallor is a sign of low hemoglobin from the anemia and does not indicate iron overload, making it the least suggestive finding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiac iron deposition causes heart failure, which presents with bilateral peripheral pitting edema, a sign of iron overload.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatic iron deposition causes inflammation and elevated liver enzymes, consistent with iron overload.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pancreatic iron injury produces diabetes mellitus with excess thirst and urination.
