whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron deposition in the skin stimulates melanocytes, producing hyperpigmentation.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has fatigue and pancytopenia. Bone marrow examination shows dysplastic erythroid precursors, and about a third of the erythroblasts are ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain. Which of the following is the most likely underlying disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia of chronic disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-thalassemia minor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hereditary X-linked ALAS mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Myelodysplastic syndrome

explanation.summary: Ringed sideroblasts with marrow dysplasia in an older adult point to myelodysplastic syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myelodysplastic syndrome is a clonal hematologic neoplasm that disrupts marrow blood cell formation; approximately 30-35% of patients have ringed sideroblasts. The patient's age, pancytopenia, and dysplastic precursors make MDS the most likely acquired cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anemia of chronic disease results from impaired iron utilization due to inflammation but does not characteristically produce ringed sideroblasts with marrow dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-thalassemia minor causes microcytosis from reduced globin chain synthesis, not ringed sideroblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The X-linked ALAS mutation is a hereditary disorder diagnosed in infancy and predominantly affects males.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency anemia has depleted iron stores and would not produce iron-laden ringed sideroblasts.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who has been taking high-dose zinc supplements develops a microcytic anemia with ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow examination. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of his anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excess zinc decreases gut copper absorption, causing copper deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Zinc accelerates hemolysis of mature erythrocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zinc chelates circulating iron and prevents its delivery to the marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Zinc directly inhibits ferrochelatase in erythroblasts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zinc induces an X-linked mutation in the ALAS gene

explanation.summary: Excess zinc lowers gut copper absorption, and the resulting copper deficiency causes sideroblastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Copper deficiency is an unusual cause of sideroblastic anemia and is most often due to excess zinc taken as a supplement, because zinc decreases copper absorption in the gut. The copper deficiency then impairs normal erythropoiesis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sideroblastic anemia is an anemia of ineffective erythropoiesis, and zinc does not act by accelerating hemolysis of mature red cells here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The problem is copper deficiency from reduced absorption, not zinc chelation of iron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ferrochelatase inhibition is the mechanism of lead poisoning, not of zinc-related copper deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acquired zinc excess does not induce the hereditary X-linked ALAS mutation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with hereditary sideroblastic anemia has received frequent transfusions and now has evidence of iron overload with cardiac and hepatic involvement. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy to remove the excess iron?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Additional packed red cell transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corticosteroids

choices.label: C
choices.text: High-dose folic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron chelation with deferasirox

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral ferrous sulfate

explanation.summary: Iron overload in sideroblastic anemia is treated with iron chelation therapy such as deferasirox.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with iron overload should receive chelation therapy (for example, deferasirox) to remove excess iron. Iron overload is common in hereditary forms and is worsened by frequent transfusions, so chelation directly addresses the accumulated iron.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Additional transfusions would add more iron and worsen the overload.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids are not a treatment for the iron overload of sideroblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folic acid supports erythropoiesis but does not remove excess iron.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oral iron supplementation would increase the iron burden in a patient who is already iron overloaded.

questions.stem: A hematology student notes that although bone marrow examination in sideroblastic anemia reveals ringed sideroblasts, these cells are never reported on the peripheral blood smear. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circulating red cells have too many mitochondria to display the ring

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prussian blue stain cannot be applied to peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ringed sideroblasts are nucleated erythroid progenitors found only in the bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ringed sideroblasts are rapidly destroyed by the spleen before entering circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ringed sideroblasts lose their iron ring once hemoglobin synthesis is complete

explanation.summary: Ringed sideroblasts are nucleated erythroid precursors, so they remain in the marrow and are not seen peripherally.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ringed sideroblasts are nucleated erythroid progenitor cells. Because these precursors reside in the bone marrow and do not circulate, they are present only in the marrow and are absent from the peripheral blood smear; peripheral smears instead show Pappenheimer bodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mature circulating erythrocytes lack mitochondria entirely, which is why they cannot synthesize heme; this does not explain a ring being obscured.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prussian blue stain is in fact used on peripheral smears to demonstrate Pappenheimer bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The reason is their location as marrow precursors, not splenic destruction of circulating ringed sideroblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The absence is due to the cells being non-circulating precursors, not loss of the iron ring at maturity.

questions.stem: In the bone marrow, macrophages transfer iron to erythroblasts, where it combines with protoporphyrin IX to form heme. A mature erythrocyte in the peripheral circulation is unable to carry out this reaction. Which of the following best explains this inability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of a cell nucleus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absence of cytoplasmic ferritin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Absence of mitochondria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Absence of ribosomes for globin synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Absence of transferrin receptors

explanation.summary: Heme synthesis occurs in mitochondria, which mature circulating erythrocytes lack.
explanation.whyCorrect: The protoporphyrin synthesis pathway takes place within erythroblasts, and iron delivered by macrophages enters the mitochondria to combine with protoporphyrin IX. Peripherally circulating mature erythrocytes cannot synthesize heme because they do not have mitochondria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of the nucleus accompanies red cell maturation, but the stated reason heme cannot be made in circulating cells is the loss of mitochondria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferritin serves as an iron storage protein and is not the structure in which protoporphyrin IX and iron are joined.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Globin synthesis is a separate process; the limiting factor for heme production in a mature red cell is the missing mitochondrial compartment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron delivery is not the barrier described; heme cannot be assembled because the organelle that houses the pathway is gone.

questions.stem: Iron deficiency anemia and anemia of chronic disease both produce ineffective erythropoiesis. Which of the following best characterizes the iron abnormality specific to anemia of chronic disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Available iron cannot be utilized by the body

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss depletes iron stores

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron becomes trapped inside erythroblast mitochondria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron is lost in the urine as hemosiderin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Total body iron levels are severely reduced

explanation.summary: Anemia of chronic disease reflects an inability to utilize available iron, whereas iron deficiency anemia reflects low iron levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both anemias limit the formation of new red blood cells by the bone marrow, which is what ineffective erythropoiesis means. The distinction is that iron deficiency anemia is defined by low iron levels while anemia of chronic disease is defined by the inability to utilize iron that is actually present.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blood loss is a route to depleted iron stores and therefore describes iron deficiency rather than impaired iron utilization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron accumulating within erythroblast mitochondria is the defect of sideroblastic anemia, not anemia of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urinary hemosiderin loss is not the mechanism given for anemia of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Severely reduced total body iron corresponds to iron deficiency anemia; in anemia of chronic disease the iron is present but unusable.

questions.stem: A hematologist reviews United States data on infants who present with anemia. Approximately what percentage of these infants have ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow?

explanation.summary: Roughly 8% of infants with anemia in the United States have ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hereditary sideroblastic anemia is uncommon and is usually diagnosed in infants and young children, which makes it worth considering in an anemic infant. In the United States the prevalence of ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow is approximately 8% among infants with anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This underestimates the reported prevalence among anemic infants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is below the cited figure for ringed sideroblasts in anemic infants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overstates the prevalence in this population.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Approximately 30-35% is the proportion of patients with myelodysplastic syndromes who have ringed sideroblasts, not the figure for anemic infants.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old boy is evaluated for failure to thrive that began shortly after birth. He also has developmental delay, recurrent fevers with immunodeficiency, myopathy, and lactic acidosis. Bone marrow examination confirms sideroblastic anemia. Which of the following best explains this constellation of findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The anemia is an adverse effect of isoniazid therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: The anemia is caused by dietary copper deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: The anemia is one component of a larger metabolic disorder

choices.label: D
choices.text: The anemia is the result of chronic lead ingestion

choices.label: E
choices.text: The anemia reflects an underlying myelodysplastic syndrome

explanation.summary: In hereditary sideroblastic anemia of infancy, the anemia is often one feature of a broader metabolic disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infants and children with the rare hereditary forms of sideroblastic anemia may show failure to thrive, developmental delay, immunodeficiency, fevers, myopathy, and lactic acidosis. In these cases the anemia is part of a larger metabolic disorder rather than an isolated hematologic problem.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Isoniazid-related sideroblastic anemia occurs in treated patients through vitamin B6 depletion, which does not apply to this untreated infant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Copper deficiency is an unusual acquired cause, most often from excess zinc intake, and does not cause this multisystem congenital picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lead poisoning classically presents in a toddler exposed to chipped paint and does not produce this metabolic syndrome from birth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myelodysplastic syndrome is an acquired disorder seen mostly in adults and would not explain congenital myopathy and lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with a known myeloproliferative neoplasm is found to have sideroblastic anemia. In addition to the anemia, which of the following findings should be specifically looked for on examination and laboratory testing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure to thrive with lactic acidosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperpigmented skin with elevated liver enzymes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jaundice with an elevated unconjugated bilirubin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrocytic red cells from vitamin B12 deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenomegaly with petechiae from reduced platelets

explanation.summary: In sideroblastic anemia with a concurrent myeloproliferative or myelodysplastic disorder, look for splenomegaly and platelet abnormalities.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients whose sideroblastic anemia accompanies a myeloproliferative or myelodysplastic disorder should be assessed for signs such as splenomegaly and for reduced platelet number or decreased platelet function, which manifest as bleeding and petechiae.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failure to thrive with lactic acidosis characterizes hereditary disease in infants, not an adult with a myeloproliferative neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperpigmentation and elevated liver enzymes indicate established iron overload rather than the marrow neoplasm itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Despite a component of marrow hemolysis, patients with sideroblastic anemia do not typically show jaundice or elevated unconjugated bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency produces a macrocytic megaloblastic anemia and is not a feature sought in this setting.

questions.stem: A pediatrician counsels a family about reducing their toddler's risk of lead exposure. Apart from lead paint in older housing, which of the following is a recognized source of lead exposure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chlorinated swimming pool water

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluoridated toothpaste

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lead water service lines

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stainless steel cookware

choices.label: E
choices.text: Well water high in nitrates

explanation.summary: Lead water service lines are one of the persisting sources of lead exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although lead-based paint has decreased in use, areas of lead exposure remain, including industrial emissions, lead paint in older housing, lead-contaminated soil, water service lines, and consumer products. Water service lines are therefore a genuine ongoing source.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chlorinated pool water is not listed among the residual sources of environmental lead exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluoride in toothpaste is unrelated to lead exposure or to impaired heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stainless steel cookware is not among the consumer products identified as causing lead exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nitrate contamination of well water is a separate water quality concern and is not a lead source.

questions.stem: A public health nurse screens young children living in older rental units for lead exposure. Housing units built before which of the following years most often used lead-based paint?

explanation.summary: Housing built prior to 1960 used lead-based paint, which young children may ingest.
explanation.whyCorrect: The classic vignette of childhood lead poisoning is an anemic child with neurologic symptoms living in an old house with chipped paint, because older housing units built prior to 1960 used lead-based paint that gets ingested by young children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Restricting concern to homes built before 1920 would miss the large group of at-risk homes built in the following decades.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Homes built in the 1940s and 1950s also used lead-based paint, so this cutoff is too early.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This cutoff is later than the year given for lead-based paint use in housing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lead-based paint use in housing had already declined well before this date.

questions.stem: The first step of the heme synthesis pathway generates delta-aminolevulinic acid. Which of the following pairs of substrates is used in this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alanine and succinyl-CoA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutamate and acetyl-CoA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycine and acetoacetyl-CoA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycine and succinyl-CoA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serine and acetyl-CoA

explanation.summary: ALA synthase condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA to form delta-aminolevulinic acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: The eight-step heme synthesis pathway begins with glycine and succinyl-CoA, which are converted by delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS) into delta-aminolevulinic acid. This first step is the one impaired in hereditary sideroblastic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Succinyl-CoA is correct, but the amino acid used in the reaction is glycine rather than alanine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamate is not the amino acid substrate of the first step of this pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycine is correct, but the second substrate in the pathway is succinyl-CoA rather than acetoacetyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serine does not enter the pathway that forms delta-aminolevulinic acid.

questions.stem: In the heme synthesis pathway, porphobilinogen is converted to hydroxymethylbilane. Which of the following enzymes catalyzes this conversion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ALA dehydratase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coproporphyrinogen III oxidase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Porphobilinogen deaminase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase

explanation.summary: Porphobilinogen deaminase converts porphobilinogen to hydroxymethylbilane.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the heme synthesis pathway, delta-aminolevulinic acid is converted to porphobilinogen by ALA dehydratase, and porphobilinogen is then converted to hydroxymethylbilane by porphobilinogen deaminase before further processing to uroporphyrinogen III.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ALA dehydratase acts one step earlier, converting delta-aminolevulinic acid to porphobilinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coproporphyrinogen III oxidase converts coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX later in the pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase converts protoporphyrinogen IX to protoporphyrin IX near the end of the pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase acts on hydroxymethylbilane to form uroporphyrinogen III, the following step.

questions.stem: A researcher examines the final enzymatic step of heme synthesis inside erythroblast mitochondria. Which of the following describes that step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ALA dehydratase converts delta-aminolevulinic acid to porphobilinogen

choices.label: B
choices.text: ALA synthase condenses glycine with succinyl-CoA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ferrochelatase combines protoporphyrin IX with iron to form heme

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase converts protoporphyrinogen IX to protoporphyrin IX

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uroporphyrinogen III decarboxylase forms coproporphyrinogen III

explanation.summary: Ferrochelatase catalyzes the last step, inserting iron into protoporphyrin IX to make heme.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first and last steps of the eight-step pathway are catalyzed by ALA synthase and ferrochelatase respectively. Ferrochelatase adds iron to protoporphyrin IX to yield heme, which is why its inhibition by lead leaves iron unchelated in the mitochondria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is the second step of the pathway and is also inhibited by lead, but it is not the final reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is the first, rate-limiting step of the pathway rather than the final one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reaction produces protoporphyrin IX and immediately precedes the ferrochelatase step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This step occurs in the middle of the pathway, converting uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with sideroblastic anemia has progressively rising total body iron despite never having been transfused. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of this iron accumulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocked intestinal iron absorption shunts stored iron into the plasma pool

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess marrow iron generates free radicals that cause hemolysis within the marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Falling transferrin saturation diverts circulating iron into hepatocyte storage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepcidin blocks the release of iron from splenic macrophages into the plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration of circulating red cells liberates iron into the circulation

explanation.summary: Ineffective iron incorporation raises marrow iron, generating free radicals and intramedullary hemolysis that increase total iron.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because iron is not incorporated into heme, iron stores in the bone marrow increase. With so much excess iron, free radical production rises and red blood cells undergo hemolysis within the bone marrow, leading to an increase in total iron and potential iron overload.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking intestinal absorption would reduce rather than increase total body iron.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Total iron-binding capacity is decreased in this disorder, and hepatic storage is a consequence of the overload rather than its mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The accumulation described arises in the marrow from failed heme synthesis, not from a block in macrophage iron export.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysis in this disorder occurs within the bone marrow rather than through splenic sequestration.

questions.stem: Sideroblastic anemia can include a component of red cell destruction within the bone marrow. Despite this, which of the following findings is typically absent in affected patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythroid hyperplasia in the bone marrow aspirate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased iron stores within the bone marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jaundice with increased unconjugated bilirubin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microcytic red blood cells with a low MCV

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pappenheimer bodies on the peripheral blood smear

explanation.summary: Although sideroblastic anemia may have a hemolytic component, the usual hemolytic findings of jaundice and high unconjugated bilirubin are absent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Excess marrow iron leads to free radical formation and hemolysis within the bone marrow, so sideroblastic anemia is largely an anemia of ineffective erythropoiesis with a partial hemolytic component. Even so, these patients do not typically show jaundice or an increased serum unconjugated bilirubin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow examination shows erythroid hyperplasia as precursors attempt to compensate for ineffective erythropoiesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Marrow iron stores are increased because iron is not incorporated into heme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The complete blood count usually shows a microcytic anemia with a low mean corpuscular volume.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pappenheimer bodies are the most common peripheral smear finding in this disorder.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man completes a prolonged course of an oral antibiotic for a resistant gram-positive skin and soft tissue infection. He then develops fatigue, and a complete blood count shows a microcytic anemia with Pappenheimer bodies on the smear. Which of the following drugs most likely caused his anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deferasirox

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ferrous sulfate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydroxyurea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isoniazid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linezolid

explanation.summary: Linezolid is an antibiotic that can inhibit heme synthesis and cause sideroblastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among toxins and drugs that cause sideroblastic anemia, the antibiotics linezolid and chloramphenicol can inhibit heme synthesis. Linezolid fits this patient because it is used for resistant gram-positive infections and produced a microcytic anemia with Pappenheimer bodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deferasirox is an iron chelator given for iron overload and does not inhibit heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferrous sulfate supplies iron and is not a cause of impaired protoporphyrin synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxyurea is used to treat myeloproliferative and myelodysplastic disorders, not gram-positive infections.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isoniazid does cause sideroblastic anemia by lowering vitamin B6, but it is an antituberculosis drug rather than a treatment for gram-positive skin infection.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is found to have ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow examination. His hematologist attributes the finding to an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm. Which of the following disorders is that neoplasm most likely to be?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hairy cell leukemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hodgkin lymphoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multiple myeloma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polycythemia vera

explanation.summary: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm that can cause acquired sideroblastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hematologic neoplasms disrupt red blood cell and other blood cell formation in the bone marrow and are an important acquired cause of sideroblastic anemia. The myeloproliferative neoplasms named in this setting are polycythemia vera and chronic myeloid leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a lymphoid leukemia, not a myeloproliferative neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hairy cell leukemia is a lymphoid disorder and is not one of the myeloproliferative neoplasms cited.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hodgkin lymphoma is a lymphoid malignancy and is not among the neoplasms associated with sideroblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy and is not the myeloproliferative neoplasm linked to ringed sideroblasts here.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has sideroblastic anemia attributed to a myelodysplastic syndrome. His iron studies show no evidence of overload. Which of the following is the most appropriate management approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chemotherapy such as hydroxyurea for the underlying neoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Copper replacement with oral supplements

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lifelong oral iron supplementation therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strict avoidance of zinc-containing supplements

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B6 supplementation as the sole therapy

explanation.summary: Sideroblastic anemia from a marrow neoplasm is managed by treating the underlying disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of non-hereditary sideroblastic anemia is directed at the underlying cause. Myelodysplastic syndromes and myeloproliferative neoplasms should be treated with hydroxyurea or other chemotherapy drugs and/or bone marrow transplantation, with supportive anemia care as needed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Copper replacement is appropriate when copper deficiency is the cause, which is not the case here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron supplementation would add to iron stores that are already elevated because iron is not being incorporated into heme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Avoiding zinc applies to zinc-induced copper deficiency, not to anemia driven by a myelodysplastic syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B6 benefits hereditary disease and B6-deficient states; it does not treat a clonal marrow neoplasm.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with hereditary sideroblastic anemia remains transfusion dependent despite adequate vitamin B6 supplementation. Which of the following interventions offers the possibility of cure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allogenic stem cell transplantation

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-dose folic acid therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term deferasirox chelation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral copper supplementation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serial therapeutic phlebotomy

explanation.summary: Allogenic stem cell transplantation can occasionally cure hereditary sideroblastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many cases of hereditary sideroblastic anemia respond to vitamin B6, but when they do not, a cure can occasionally be achieved using allogenic stem cell transplantation, which replaces the defective erythroid progenitors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Folic acid supports erythropoiesis generally but cannot cure a hereditary defect in heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chelation removes accumulated iron and controls overload but does not correct the underlying enzyme defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Copper replacement treats copper deficiency, which is an acquired cause unrelated to this boy's inherited defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phlebotomy addresses iron overload and would worsen anemia in a transfusion-dependent child.

questions.stem: Four patients are followed in a hematology clinic for sideroblastic anemia. Which of the following patients is at greatest risk of developing iron overload?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 22-year-old with hereditary disease and years of transfusions

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 30-year-old with copper deficiency from zinc supplements

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 45-year-old who took isoniazid for 3 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 60-year-old with a 6-month history of alcohol-related disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: A 70-year-old with newly diagnosed myelodysplastic syndrome

explanation.summary: Iron overload is most common in hereditary sideroblastic anemia, is related to disease duration, and is worsened by frequent transfusions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because ineffective erythropoiesis leads to a buildup of unused iron, iron overload can develop with findings similar to congenital hemochromatosis. It is most common in the rare hereditary forms and is related to disease duration, and frequent transfusions given for the anemia make it worse.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Copper deficiency from zinc excess is an acquired and correctable cause without a long transfusion history.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A brief course of isoniazid produces a reversible B6-related anemia without time for significant iron accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This acquired case is of short duration and lacks the transfusion burden that drives overload.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A newly diagnosed acquired disorder has neither the long disease duration nor the transfusion history that raise risk.

questions.stem: The parents of an infant boy with hereditary sideroblastic anemia due to an ALAS mutation ask why this condition affects boys far more often than girls. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estrogen increases ALAS activity in females

choices.label: B
choices.text: Males absorb more dietary iron than females

choices.label: C
choices.text: Males carry only one X chromosome copy of the gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mutation arises only during spermatogenesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: The responsible gene is located on the Y chromosome

explanation.summary: The common hereditary form follows X-linked inheritance, so males are predominantly affected.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common hereditary cause of sideroblastic anemia is a gene mutation that decreases ALAS activity and is usually X-linked. Because males have only one X chromosome, a single mutated copy is fully expressed, which is why the disorder is most common in males.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin B6 is the cofactor that supports ALAS activity; hormonal upregulation is not the stated reason for the sex difference.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Differences in dietary iron absorption do not account for the inheritance pattern of this enzyme defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The male predominance reflects the X-linked pattern of the mutation rather than where the mutation originates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mutation involves the ALAS gene on the X chromosome, not a gene on the Y chromosome.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old boy with a microcytic anemia has ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow aspirate. His physician suspects a hereditary cause. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Empiric iron chelation therapy with deferoxamine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genetic testing to identify the causative mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Measurement of serum ceruloplasmin and copper

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat bone marrow biopsy and aspirate in six months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Therapeutic phlebotomy to remove excess iron

explanation.summary: Genetic testing is performed in infants and children with suspected hereditary sideroblastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genetic testing is done for infants and children with suspected hereditary causes in order to identify the specific gene mutation. Knowing the mutation guides both prognosis and therapy in these patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chelation is reserved for documented iron overload, which has not been demonstrated here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Copper deficiency is an unusual acquired cause tied to excess zinc intake and is not the suspected mechanism in this infant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The diagnosis has already been established by marrow findings, so repeating the biopsy adds nothing at this point.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phlebotomy removes iron at the cost of worsening anemia and is not the next diagnostic step.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with heavy alcohol use has a microcytic anemia, and her peripheral smear shows red cells with clusters of blue granules. Which of the following studies is required to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow aspirate showing ringed sideroblasts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis with quantitative HbA2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prussian blue staining of the peripheral blood smear

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reticulocyte count and absolute reticulocyte index

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum ferritin with total iron-binding capacity

explanation.summary: Confirmation of sideroblastic anemia requires ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow aspirate or biopsy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Confirmation of the diagnosis requires the presence of ringed sideroblasts on microscopic examination of a bone marrow aspirate or biopsy sample. Marrow examination also shows compensatory hyperplasia of erythroid progenitor cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin electrophoresis evaluates hemoglobin variants and thalassemias, not iron-laden erythroid precursors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prussian blue staining of the smear demonstrates Pappenheimer bodies, which are suggestive but not confirmatory because ringed sideroblasts never appear peripherally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The reticulocyte count reflects marrow output in general and cannot establish this specific diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron studies support the diagnosis by showing iron-replete stores but do not confirm it.

questions.stem: A bone marrow biopsy from a patient with sideroblastic anemia is stained with Prussian blue and shows ringed sideroblasts. Which of the following additional marrow findings is most likely to be present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hypocellular marrow with fatty replacement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absent stainable iron stores

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erythroid hyperplasia with increased normoblasts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marrow fibrosis with teardrop-shaped red cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Myeloblasts making up more than 20% of cells

explanation.summary: Marrow in sideroblastic anemia shows erythroid hyperplasia as precursors futilely compensate for ineffective erythropoiesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to Prussian blue-stained ringed sideroblasts, bone marrow samples display erythroid hyperplasia, described as compensatory hyperplasia of erythroid progenitor cells (normoblasts) as they try futilely to make up for the ineffective erythropoiesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The marrow is hyperplastic rather than hypocellular, because erythroid precursors proliferate in compensation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron stores in the marrow are increased, not absent, because iron is not incorporated into heme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow fibrosis with teardrop cells is not among the described findings of sideroblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A marked myeloblast excess is not a feature described for sideroblastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man being evaluated for anemia has a complete blood count showing both normocytic and microcytic red cell populations. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this dimorphic red cell finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can also occur when two different anemias coexist

choices.label: B
choices.text: It confirms a diagnosis of sideroblastic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: It excludes a diagnosis of sideroblastic anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: It indicates ongoing hemolysis within the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is diagnostic of lead poisoning

explanation.summary: Dimorphic red cells occur in some cases of sideroblastic anemia but are not pathognomonic, since two coexisting anemias can produce them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some cases of sideroblastic anemia show dimorphic red cells, meaning both normocytic and microcytic cells on the complete blood count. This finding is not pathognomonic, because it can also be seen in patients who have two different types of anemia simultaneously.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The finding is suggestive but explicitly not pathognomonic, so it cannot confirm the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dimorphic cells are compatible with sideroblastic anemia and therefore do not exclude it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intramedullary hemolysis relates to excess iron and free radicals and is not what a dimorphic population indicates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lead poisoning is suggested by basophilic stippling in the right exposure history, not by dimorphic red cells alone.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman has sideroblastic anemia confirmed on bone marrow biopsy, yet her mean corpuscular volume is within the normal reference range. Which of the following best explains this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A normal MCV indicates concurrent iron deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: A normal MCV rules out an underlying myelodysplastic syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: A normal MCV signals resolution of the underlying cause

choices.label: D
choices.text: A normal or even high MCV can occur in this disorder

choices.label: E
choices.text: The confirmed diagnosis should be reconsidered and rejected

explanation.summary: Sideroblastic anemia usually causes microcytosis, but the MCV may sometimes be normal or even high.
explanation.whyCorrect: The complete blood count in sideroblastic anemia usually shows a microcytic anemia with decreased hemoglobin and hematocrit and a low mean corpuscular volume. However, the MCV may sometimes be normal or high, so a normal value does not contradict a marrow-confirmed diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron deficiency causes microcytosis and would not be inferred from a normal MCV in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myelodysplastic syndrome is diagnosed by marrow findings, not excluded by a normal red cell volume.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cell size does not track resolution of the causative disorder in this way.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The diagnosis rests on ringed sideroblasts in the marrow, which a normal MCV does not overturn.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with heavy daily alcohol use is diagnosed with sideroblastic anemia. He is hemodynamically stable, his hemoglobin is mildly reduced, and he has no evidence of iron overload. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol cessation plus vitamin B6

choices.label: B
choices.text: Allogenic stem cell transplantation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydroxyurea therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immediate red blood cell transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Therapeutic phlebotomy

explanation.summary: Adult sideroblastic anemia from alcohol is managed by removing the offending exposure and replacing vitamin B6.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of non-hereditary sideroblastic anemia is targeted to the underlying cause, which here means avoidance of alcohol along with vitamin B6 replacement, since B6 deficiency can itself cause the anemia. Transfusion is reserved for patients who need supportive treatment for the anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Stem cell transplantation is an occasional curative option in hereditary disease, not in an acquired alcohol-related case.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxyurea is used when a myelodysplastic or myeloproliferative disorder underlies the anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transfusion is supportive care given as needed; a stable patient with mild anemia does not require it now, and transfusions can worsen iron accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phlebotomy is directed at iron overload, which this patient does not have, and it would lower his hemoglobin further.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old premenopausal woman presents with 2 months of fatigue, dizziness, and weakness. She reports 4 months of heavy menstrual bleeding with clots. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 10.1 g/dL (normal for females 12.0-15.5 g/dL) and a low serum ferritin, consistent with iron-deficiency anemia. Which of the following additional findings would most likely be present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased hematocrit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased mean platelet volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hyperchromic red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased mean cell volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased red blood cell count

explanation.summary: Anemia is characterized by low hemoglobin, hematocrit, and RBC count, and iron deficiency produces microcytic red cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hemoglobin, hematocrit, and RBC count all move together and are used to diagnose anemia; a patient with anemia typically has a low hemoglobin along with a low hematocrit. Because the hematocrit tracks with hemoglobin, this patient's hematocrit would also be decreased.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mean platelet volume is a platelet index and is not part of the RBC picture of iron-deficiency anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Most anemias are normochromic and iron deficiency is hypochromic; red cells would not be hyperchromic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron-deficiency anemia is a microcytic anemia, so the MCV is decreased rather than increased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Patients with anemia have a low RBC count, not an increased one.

questions.stem: A newborn delivered to a 24-year-old mother who had no prenatal care is stillborn with hydrops fetalis. Genetic testing reveals deletion of all four alpha-globin genes, causing production of gamma-globin chain tetramers (hemoglobin Barts) and a diagnosis of alpha-thalassemia. Which of the following laboratory tests would most directly demonstrate this abnormal hemoglobin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin test

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmotic fragility test

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reticulocyte count

choices.label: E
choices.text: White blood cell differential

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin electrophoresis identifies the types and amounts of hemoglobin and can reveal abnormal species such as hemoglobin Barts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates and identifies the different hemoglobin types in the blood and is used to diagnose conditions such as thalassemia. In this form of alpha-thalassemia it would show the presence of hemoglobin Barts, the gamma-chain tetramer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The direct antiglobulin test detects antibody or complement coating RBCs and is positive in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osmotic fragility measures how easily RBCs lyse and is typically abnormal in hereditary spherocytosis, not alpha-thalassemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A reticulocyte count reflects marrow output but does not identify hemoglobin types.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A white blood cell differential evaluates leukocytes and would not identify an abnormal hemoglobin.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with worsening chronic anemia is being evaluated, and her physician wants to assess her reticulocytes. Which of the following stains is most appropriate to visualize the ribosomal RNA inside reticulocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Periodic acid-Schiff stain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prussian blue stain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sudan black B stain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supravital staining

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wright-Giemsa stain

explanation.summary: Supravital stains applied to fresh blood reveal the ribosomal RNA network of reticulocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Supravital stains such as new methylene blue and brilliant cresyl blue are performed on fresh (living) blood and highlight structures not seen on dried smears, including the ribosomal RNA that defines reticulocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Periodic acid-Schiff stains carbohydrates, not reticulocyte RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prussian blue stains iron (for example, siderotic granules), not the RNA of reticulocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sudan black B stains lipids and is not used to visualize ribosomal RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wright-Giemsa is the gold-standard differential stain for blood, but RNA is not directly visible on it (reticulocytes only appear as slightly lilac polychromatophilic cells).

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has a cold agglutinin causing red cell agglutination in her blood sample. When the complete blood count is run on the automated analyzer, which of the following parameters is most likely to remain accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin (MCH)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mean cell hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean cell volume (MCV)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cell count

explanation.summary: With red cell clumping, hemoglobin stays accurate because it is measured after the red cells are lysed.
explanation.whyCorrect: When red cells clump (by agglutination or rouleaux), the analyzer counts the clumps as single large cells: the RBC count is falsely decreased and the MCV falsely increased. Hemoglobin is measured after the cells are lysed, so it usually remains accurate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MCH is a calculated index that becomes falsely increased when the RBC count is falsely low.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MCHC is likewise falsely increased when red cell clumping distorts the RBC count and volume measurements.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Because clumps are read as single large particles, the MCV is falsely increased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Clumped cells are counted as one, so the RBC count is falsely decreased.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with primary myelofibrosis has a peripheral blood smear examined. Which of the following red blood cell morphologies is most characteristically seen in this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bite cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Schistocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sickle cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Target cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teardrop cells

explanation.summary: Dacryocytes (teardrop cells) are associated with chronic myelofibrosis and other marrow-infiltrating processes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Teardrop cells (dacryocytes) are the classic red cell shape abnormality of chronic myelofibrosis and other space-occupying lesions of the marrow, where cells are deformed as they are squeezed out of a fibrotic marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bite cells are associated with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Schistocytes are seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sickle cells are seen in sickle cell anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Target cells (codocytes) are seen in thalassemia, liver disease, and iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man with a family history of hemolytic anemia has splenomegaly and jaundice, and his peripheral smear shows numerous round red cells lacking central pallor. Osmotic fragility testing is performed. Which of the following results would most likely be found?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete resistance to lysis across the full range of NaCl concentrations

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased osmotic fragility, with lysis only in strongly hypotonic saline solutions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased osmotic fragility, with lysis at higher-than-normal NaCl concentrations

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysis only in hypertonic saline solutions above physiologic tonicity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal osmotic fragility identical to that of healthy control cells

explanation.summary: Hereditary spherocytosis increases osmotic fragility because spherocytes rupture at higher-than-normal salt concentrations.
explanation.whyCorrect: The smear findings indicate hereditary spherocytosis. Spherocytes are less flexible than normal RBCs because of cytoskeleton mutations, making them prone to rupture; they are so sensitive to tonicity that they lyse even at higher-than-normal NaCl concentrations, meaning increased osmotic fragility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spherocytes lyse more easily, not less; they do not resist lysis at all concentrations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased osmotic fragility (resistance to lysis) is seen in sickle cell anemia and thalassemia, not hereditary spherocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemolysis in this test occurs in hypotonic solutions as water enters the cell, not in hypertonic solutions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osmotic fragility is abnormal, not normal, in hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman develops fatigue and jaundice, and laboratory studies show anemia with an elevated reticulocyte count and spherocytes on the smear. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is suspected. Which of the following tests best confirms that her red cells are coated with antibody or complement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin test

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmotic fragility test

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red cell distribution width

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reticulocyte count

explanation.summary: The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test detects antibody or complement bound to the patient's red cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the direct antiglobulin test, anti-immunoglobulin (Coombs) reagent is added to the patient's RBCs; if they are coated with immunoglobulin or complement, they agglutinate and the test is positive. A positive DAT is seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin electrophoresis identifies hemoglobin types and does not detect antibody coating of red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osmotic fragility measures how easily RBCs lyse and does not detect surface antibody or complement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RDW reflects variability in red cell size and gives no information about antibody coating.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A reticulocyte count shows the marrow is responding to hemolysis but does not identify the immune cause.

questions.stem: During hemoglobin electrophoresis, an electrical charge is applied to a gel and the different hemoglobin types migrate away from the negatively charged electrode, traveling various distances. Which of the following correctly lists the hemoglobins in their order of travel from farthest to closest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A, F, S, C

choices.label: B
choices.text: A, S, F, C

choices.label: C
choices.text: C, S, F, A

choices.label: D
choices.text: F, A, C, S

choices.label: E
choices.text: S, C, A, F

explanation.summary: On hemoglobin electrophoresis the order of travel from farthest to closest is A, F, S, C ("A Fat Santa Claus").
explanation.whyCorrect: As the hemoglobins migrate away from the negatively charged electrode, they land at different distances; the order from farthest to closest is hemoglobin A, then F, then S, then C, captured by the mnemonic 'A Fat Santa Claus.'

whyWrongByChoice.B: F, not S, is the second-farthest hemoglobin, so this ordering is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the order; C travels the least, not the most.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin A migrates farthest and must come first, not F.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S and C do not lead the sequence; hemoglobin A migrates farthest.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with anemia has a reticulocyte count that, after correction for her degree of anemia, is below 2%. Which of the following best describes what this corrected reticulocyte value indicates about her bone marrow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The marrow is hypoproliferative and not responding appropriately

choices.label: B
choices.text: The marrow is releasing an excess of reticulocytes into the blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: The marrow is responding briskly to ongoing hemolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: The marrow is responding briskly to recent hemorrhage

choices.label: E
choices.text: The marrow response is normal and no anemia is present

explanation.summary: A corrected reticulocyte count below 2% indicates a hypoproliferative marrow that is not responding to the anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reticulocyte count should be corrected for the degree of anemia to judge whether the marrow is responding. A corrected value under 2% means the marrow is hypoproliferative and not mounting an adequate response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An excess of reticulocytes would give a high, not low, corrected reticulocyte count.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A brisk response to hemolysis would raise the corrected reticulocyte count above 2%, not below.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recent hemorrhage with a responsive marrow also drives the corrected count above 2%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patient is anemic, and a low corrected count reflects an inadequate marrow response, not a normal one.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man develops acute hemolysis after taking an oxidant medication. His peripheral smear shows red cells that appear to have had a semicircular piece removed from their edge. This bite cell morphology is most characteristic of which of the following conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advanced chronic liver disease with cirrhosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis of the marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hereditary spherocytosis from a spectrin defect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia from DIC

explanation.summary: Bite cells are the classic red cell abnormality of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bite cells are associated with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, in which oxidant stress damages hemoglobin and the spleen removes the denatured portion, leaving a bite-like defect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Liver disease is classically associated with acanthocytes (spur cells), not bite cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myelofibrosis is associated with teardrop cells (dacryocytes).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hereditary spherocytosis produces spherocytes, round cells without central pallor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia produces schistocytes, not bite cells.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child with a history of pica and living in an old home is found to have anemia. The peripheral smear shows red cells containing coarse blue granules dispersed throughout the cytoplasm (basophilic stippling). Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lead poisoning

choices.label: B
choices.text: Malaria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prior splenectomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sideroblastic anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

explanation.summary: Basophilic stippling is the red cell inclusion classically associated with lead poisoning.
explanation.whyCorrect: Basophilic stippling appears as blue granules throughout the red cell and is a recognized inclusion of lead poisoning; the clinical picture of pica and old-home exposure supports lead as the cause.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Malaria is identified by intracellular Plasmodium organisms, not basophilic stippling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prior splenectomy is associated with Howell-Jolly bodies, single round nuclear remnants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sideroblastic anemia is associated with Pappenheimer (iron-containing) bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia produces spherocytes and a positive direct antiglobulin test, not basophilic stippling.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a hemoglobinopathy has red blood cells that are resistant to lysis during automated hematology analysis. Which of the following results is most likely to occur on his complete blood count as a consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Falsely decreased mean cell volume with a normal hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Falsely decreased platelet count with a normal hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Falsely elevated hemoglobin with a falsely low white blood cell count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Falsely elevated red blood cell count with an unchanged hemoglobin level

choices.label: E
choices.text: Falsely low hemoglobin with a possibly elevated white blood cell count

explanation.summary: Red cells resistant to lysis cause a falsely low hemoglobin and can be miscounted as white cells, raising the WBC count.
explanation.whyCorrect: Analyzers measure hemoglobin after lysing the red cells; when RBCs resist lysis (as in some hemoglobinopathies or in infants), less hemoglobin is released and the value is falsely low, and the intact red cells may be counted as white cells, falsely raising the WBC count.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MCV is not falsely lowered by lysis-resistant cells; this scenario primarily distorts hemoglobin and the WBC count.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A falsely decreased platelet count is not the expected effect; small RBC or WBC fragments would instead falsely raise the platelet count.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure to lyse red cells lowers, rather than raises, the measured hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysis resistance does not falsely elevate the RBC count; that pattern is more typical of counting artifacts unrelated to this scenario.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred for purplish spots on her skin. She reports 2 weeks of easy bruising, recurrent nosebleeds, and fatigue. She takes carbamazepine for a seizure disorder. On examination she is pale with diffuse ecchymoses and petechiae. A complete blood count shows low white blood cells, low hemoglobin, and low platelets with no abnormal cells. Which of the following best describes the underlying process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Immune destruction of circulating mature red blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired hemoglobin synthesis from iron deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infiltration of the marrow by neoplastic cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of myeloid hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration of blood cells in an enlarged spleen

explanation.summary: Aplastic anemia is pancytopenia caused by loss of myeloid hematopoietic stem cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The combination of low red cells, white cells, and platelets (pancytopenia) with no abnormal cells, in a patient on carbamazepine (a recognized idiosyncratic cause), points to aplastic anemia. The ultimate mechanism regardless of etiology is loss of myeloid HSCs in the bone marrow, reducing all myeloid-derived lines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immune destruction of mature RBCs (hemolysis) causes anemia with reticulocytosis, not pancytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deficiency limits hemoglobin production causing microcytic anemia confined to red cells, not pancytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow infiltration by leukemia or metastatic carcinoma can cause pancytopenia, but abnormal cells would typically be seen; here none are present.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypersplenism causes pancytopenia through sequestration but would present with splenomegaly, not drug-triggered marrow failure, and is not suggested here.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with newly diagnosed aplastic anemia has pancytopenia on his complete blood count. Which of the following cell types is most likely to remain within the normal range?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythrocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophils

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelets

explanation.summary: Lymphocytes derive from lymphoid, not myeloid, progenitors and are relatively spared in aplastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aplastic anemia primarily destroys myeloid stem cells. Lymphocytes arise from the lymphoid line, so a CBC with differential shows low levels of all blood cells except lymphocytes, which remain near normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythrocytes come from erythroblasts (myeloid line) and are decreased, causing normocytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocytes come from monoblasts (myeloid line) and are decreased in aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils come from myeloblasts (myeloid line) and are decreased, raising infection risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets come from megakaryoblasts (myeloid line) and are decreased, causing bleeding.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man with suspected aplastic anemia undergoes a bone marrow biopsy. Which of the following findings would most strongly support the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extensive fibrous replacement of the marrow space

choices.label: B
choices.text: Large lymphoid aggregates scattered through the marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marked proliferation of erythroid precursor cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Near-complete replacement of marrow by adipose tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sheets of blast cells replacing normal marrow

explanation.summary: Aplastic anemia shows a hypocellular marrow in which stem cells are replaced by fat.
explanation.whyCorrect: In aplastic anemia the number of hematopoietic stem cells is markedly decreased, so the marrow becomes hypocellular and the empty spaces fill with abundant adipocytes. A biopsy confirming near-complete replacement of HSCs with adipose tissue supports the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Extensive fibrosis suggests primary myelofibrosis, a different cause of marrow failure that must be ruled out.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphoid aggregates are not characteristic of aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proliferation of erythroid precursors indicates active production, the opposite of the hypocellular marrow of aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sheets of blasts indicate acute leukemia infiltrating the marrow, not aplasia.

questions.stem: A researcher studies how ionizing radiation used in radiotherapy damages the bone marrow. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which radiation injures hematopoietic stem cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding to stem cell antigens as a hapten

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct activation of cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Generation of free radicals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of ribosomal protein synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration of stem cells in the spleen

explanation.summary: Radiation causes dose-dependent marrow toxicity by generating free radicals.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ionizing radiation used for radiotherapy causes dose-dependent toxicity on the bone marrow by generating free radicals, which damage hematopoietic stem cells. The larger the initial and cumulative dose, the greater the risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hapten binding to stem cell antigens is the mechanism of idiosyncratic drug reactions, not radiation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Drugs and viruses lead to T-cell mediated cytotoxicity indirectly by altering antigens; radiation acts through free radicals.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ribosomal protein dysfunction underlies Diamond-Blackfan syndrome, not radiation injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration is a mechanism of hypersplenism, unrelated to radiation.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman returns from a camping trip and develops fever, myalgia, headache, and a rash on her wrists and ankles. She is diagnosed with Rocky Mountain spotted fever and treated with chloramphenicol because of a tetracycline allergy. One week later she develops worsening fatigue and mucosal bleeding, and a complete blood count shows marked decreases in red cells, white cells, and platelets. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer granulocyte colony-stimulating factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Administer N-acetylcysteine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decrease the dose of chloramphenicol

choices.label: D
choices.text: Discontinue chloramphenicol

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perform allogeneic stem cell transplantation

explanation.summary: When a causative drug is identified in aplastic anemia, the first step is to withdraw it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The patient developed pancytopenia after starting chloramphenicol, a known cause of aplastic anemia. Management of aplastic anemia is initially aimed at eliminating potential secondary causes, so the causative drug should be discontinued immediately.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor is typically used for neutropenic fever after chemotherapy, not as first-line here; withdrawing the drug comes first.
whyWrongByChoice.B: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose, not aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Merely decreasing the dose is insufficient given the life-threatening nature of aplastic anemia; the drug must be stopped.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Allogeneic transplantation carries high mortality and is reserved for severe idiopathic disease after conservative measures fail.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with easy bruising, and his parents are concerned about poor growth. Examination shows short stature, petechiae, and several cafe-au-lait spots, and one thumb has three phalanges. Laboratory testing reveals pancytopenia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow biopsy and aspirate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromosomal breakage test

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatitis B and C serology

choices.label: D
choices.text: HIV antibody and RNA testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parvovirus B19 IgM serology

explanation.summary: Fanconi anemia is diagnosed by demonstrating increased chromosomal breaks with DNA cross-linking agents.
explanation.whyCorrect: The childhood onset, short stature, cafe-au-lait spots, thumb/radial abnormality (triphalangeal thumb), and pancytopenia strongly suggest Fanconi anemia. Diagnostic testing demonstrates increased chromosomal breaks in lymphocyte culture with agents that cause DNA cross-links, such as diepoxybutane (DEB) or mitomycin C.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A bone marrow biopsy would show aplasia but would not specifically establish Fanconi anemia as the cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatitis testing is useful when evaluating acquired aplastic anemia, but the constitutional features here point to Fanconi anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV testing is part of the workup for acquired aplastic anemia, but does not confirm the suspected hereditary syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Parvovirus B19 serology is useful in pure red cell aplasia, which causes isolated anemia rather than pancytopenia.

questions.stem: A hematologist starts a patient with idiopathic aplastic anemia on eltrombopag. Which of the following best describes how this medication improves the patient's blood counts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acts as a thrombopoietin receptor agonist

choices.label: B
choices.text: It increases only the platelet count

choices.label: C
choices.text: It removes iron accumulated from transfusions

choices.label: D
choices.text: It replaces the patient's stem cells with donor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It suppresses cytotoxic T cells attacking stem cells

explanation.summary: Eltrombopag is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist that boosts all cell lines in aplastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Eltrombopag (EPAG) is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist acting on stem cells that increases production of all cell lines, not just platelets, making it useful in aplastic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Although it is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist, eltrombopag stimulates all cell lines rather than platelets alone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chelation removes excess transfusional iron and is unrelated to eltrombopag's mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Replacing stem cells with donor cells describes allogeneic stem cell transplantation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immunosuppression of T cells describes cyclosporine or antithymocyte globulin, not eltrombopag.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with severe idiopathic aplastic anemia has failed medical therapy and undergoes allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Which of the following is a recognized complication of this procedure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Graft-versus-host disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isolated reticulocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microcytic red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reversal of cancer predisposition

explanation.summary: Allogeneic transplantation risks graft-versus-host disease, where donor cells attack the recipient.
explanation.whyCorrect: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation can be curative but carries a high mortality rate, so it is only considered after other treatments fail. Complications include increased infections and graft-versus-host disease, in which the transplanted cells attack the recipient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deficiency is not a characteristic complication of transplantation for aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reticulocytosis reflects active red cell production and is not a complication of transplantation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aplastic anemia is normocytic; microcytosis points to other anemias and is not a transplant complication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: In Fanconi anemia, transplant reverses the hematologic abnormalities but not the predisposition to malignancy; it does not reverse cancer risk.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman is being evaluated for isolated anemia. Her complete blood count shows low hemoglobin and a low reticulocyte count, but normal platelet and white blood cell counts. Bone marrow shows decreased erythroid precursors with normal granulocytes and megakaryocytes. Which of the following infections is most likely associated with this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatitis B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: HIV

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parvovirus B19

explanation.summary: Pure red cell aplasia selectively affects erythroid precursors and is associated with parvovirus B19.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is anemia with decreased erythroid precursors, while granulocytes and megakaryocytes/platelets are unaffected. Acquired causes include infection with parvovirus B19, along with thymoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, autoimmune disorders, medications, or idiopathic cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with aplastic anemia (pancytopenia), not isolated pure red cell aplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatitis B is listed among viral causes of aplastic anemia affecting all myeloid lines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Herpes is associated with aplastic anemia, which would show pancytopenia, not selective erythroid loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV is a cause of aplastic anemia, which produces pancytopenia rather than isolated anemia.

questions.stem: A pediatrician evaluates a 6-month-old infant with pallor and fatigue during feeding. Workup reveals macrocytic anemia with reticulocytopenia, and genetic testing identifies a mutation in a gene encoding a ribosomal protein. Which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diamond-Blackfan syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fanconi anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Idiopathic aplastic anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

explanation.summary: Diamond-Blackfan syndrome is a congenital pure red cell aplasia caused by ribosomal protein gene mutations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diamond-Blackfan syndrome is the most important congenital form of pure red cell aplasia. It is a rare inherited bone marrow failure syndrome associated with mutations in genes that encode ribosomal proteins, characterized by macrocytic anemia, reticulocytopenia, and cancer predisposition, usually presenting before the first birthday.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fanconi anemia causes pancytopenia from defective DNA repair, not isolated macrocytic anemia from ribosomal protein mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Idiopathic aplastic anemia produces pancytopenia and is normocytic, not an isolated congenital red cell disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia, not macrocytic anemia with ribosomal protein mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is an acquired clonal disorder causing hemolysis and thrombosis, not congenital pure red cell aplasia.

questions.stem: A student is asked which patient group has the worst prognosis when aplastic anemia is left untreated. Which of the following patients is at greatest risk of death within one year?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A middle-aged patient after successful treatment

choices.label: B
choices.text: A young patient after stem cell transplantation

choices.label: C
choices.text: A young patient with mild disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: A young patient with moderate disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: An elderly patient with severe disease

explanation.summary: Untreated aplastic anemia has high one-year mortality, concentrated in elderly patients with severe disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: As high as 7 out of 10 untreated patients will die within 1 year, with the majority being elderly patients and those with severe disease. Treated patients, by contrast, have a 5- to 10-year survival rate greater than 80%, especially the young with mild-to-moderate disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Successful treatment yields a survival rate above 80%, so this patient is not at greatest risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A young transplanted patient has been treated and does not carry the highest untreated-mortality risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Young patients with mild disease have the best prognosis, especially when treated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Young patients with moderate disease fare relatively well, particularly with treatment.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with aplastic anemia is counseled about her expected complications. Which of the following is the least likely complication of her disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dyspnea

choices.label: B
choices.text: Menorrhagia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pharyngitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Syncope

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombosis

explanation.summary: Aplastic anemia causes cytopenias, so bleeding and infection dominate; thrombosis is not expected.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased clot formation occurs in hypercoagulable states or malignancy. Patients with aplastic anemia have low platelets and are therefore less likely to form clots, making thrombosis the least likely complication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dyspnea is a manifestation of severe anemia or pulmonary infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Menorrhagia reflects the low platelet count causing bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pharyngitis and other infections may increase due to neutropenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Syncope results from low cerebral oxygen delivery seen in severe anemia.

questions.stem: A public health researcher compares the incidence of aplastic anemia across populations. The incidence is higher in Asian countries than in the United States, but the incidence among Asian people living in the United States matches the general US rate. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A higher carrier rate for defective DNA repair genes

choices.label: B
choices.text: An inherited predisposition among people of Asian ancestry

choices.label: C
choices.text: Greater exposure to toxic environmental factors

choices.label: D
choices.text: More frequent use of radiotherapy for cancer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Underdiagnosis of pancytopenia in the United States

explanation.summary: The higher incidence of aplastic anemia in Asian countries reflects environmental exposure rather than genetic predisposition.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aplastic anemia is rare, with about 2 new cases per million people diagnosed annually in the United States, and its incidence is higher in Asian countries. Because the higher incidence is not seen in Asian people living in the United States, the difference is most likely due to increased exposure to toxic environmental factors rather than inherited risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Defective DNA repair explains hereditary Fanconi anemia, which is rare and would not disappear with a change in country of residence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A genetic predisposition would travel with the population, yet the elevated rate disappears among Asian people living in the United States.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radiotherapy causes dose-dependent marrow toxicity in individual patients but does not explain a population-level difference that resolves with migration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nothing about the comparison points to differences in how often pancytopenia is recognized.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with long-standing chronic kidney disease is evaluated for fatigue. His hemoglobin is low with a normal mean corpuscular volume, and his white blood cell and platelet counts are normal. A bone marrow biopsy shows normal cellularity with normal numbers of erythroid precursors. Which of the following best explains his anemia?

choices.label: A
