choices.text: Blocked red blood cell production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Limited hemoglobin production from low iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of erythroid precursors in the marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of myeloid hematopoietic stem cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shortened red blood cell lifespan

explanation.summary: Most anemias are confined to the red cell line; chronic kidney disease blocks red blood cell production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anemias differ by mechanism: limited hemoglobin production in iron deficiency, blocked RBC production in chronic kidney disease, and shortened RBC lifespan in hemolytic anemias. This patient's isolated normocytic anemia with a normocellular marrow in the setting of kidney disease reflects blocked red blood cell production.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deficiency limits hemoglobin synthesis and produces a microcytic anemia, but this patient's mean corpuscular volume is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of erythroid precursors describes pure red cell aplasia, but the biopsy shows normal numbers of erythroid precursors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of myeloid stem cells is the mechanism of aplastic anemia and would produce pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow, not isolated anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A shortened RBC lifespan describes hemolytic anemia, which is not suggested by these findings.

questions.stem: A medical student reviews myeloid development in the bone marrow. Which of the following cells arises from the myeloblast?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eosinophil

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythrocyte

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocyte

choices.label: D
choices.text: Natural killer cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet

explanation.summary: Myeloblasts give rise to neutrophils, basophils, eosinophils, and mast cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myeloid stem cells give rise to several blast populations. Myeloblasts mature into neutrophils, basophils, eosinophils, and mast cells, so the eosinophil is the cell derived from the myeloblast.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythrocytes arise from erythroblasts by way of reticulocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocytes (and the macrophages they become) arise from monoblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Natural killer cells arise from the lymphoid line by way of lymphoblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets arise from megakaryoblasts by way of megakaryocytes.

questions.stem: A hematologist reviews a series of patients with aplastic anemia in whom an underlying cause was identified. Which of the following categories accounts for the largest share of these cases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired gene mutations in stem cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune diseases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drugs and viral infections

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hereditary conditions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ionizing radiation from radiotherapy

explanation.summary: Among identifiable causes of aplastic anemia, drugs and viral infections are the most common.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although most cases of aplastic anemia are idiopathic, several conditions and substances damage hematopoietic stem cells. Of the known causes, drugs and viral infections are the most common, followed by autoimmune, genetic, and hereditary diseases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acquired stem cell gene mutations, as in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, cause aplastic anemia only rarely.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoimmune conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus and graft versus host disease follow drugs and viruses in frequency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hereditary causes such as Fanconi anemia are explicitly rare.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Radiotherapy damages the marrow in a dose-dependent way but accounts for fewer cases than drugs and viral infections.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man who has worked for 20 years in a plant with heavy benzene, solvent, and insecticide exposure is found to have pancytopenia and a hypocellular bone marrow. Which of the following best describes how these substances injure hematopoietic stem cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of marrow fibroblasts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding to stem cell antigens as a hapten

choices.label: C
choices.text: DNA breaks that induce apoptosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Generation of free radicals by ionizing energy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration of stem cells in the spleen

explanation.summary: Benzene, solvents, and insecticides cause DNA breaks in hematopoietic stem cells that trigger apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Toxins such as benzene, solvents, and insecticides cause DNA breaks in hematopoietic stem cells, which induce apoptosis. Benzene acts as an alkylating agent that cross-links and breaks DNA rather than acting on fibroblasts or immune cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Benzene does not act by activating fibroblasts; marrow fibrosis is a separate cause of marrow failure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hapten binding to stem cell antigens describes idiosyncratic drug reactions, not chemical toxins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Free radical generation is how ionizing radiation used in radiotherapy damages stem cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration is a mechanism of hypersplenism and does not involve stem cell injury.

questions.stem: An oncologist counsels a patient that the risk of marrow suppression rises with both the initial and the cumulative dose of her treatment. Which of the following classes of drugs most commonly causes this dose-dependent damage to hematopoietic stem cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-epileptic drugs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcium channel blockers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chemotherapy drugs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sulfonamide antibiotics

explanation.summary: Chemotherapy drugs are the most common cause of dose-dependent marrow damage in aplastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The severity of stem cell damage from drugs, toxins, and radiation is usually dose dependent, and the larger the initial and cumulative dose the greater the risk. The most common drugs in this category are chemotherapy drugs, which are designed to kill rapidly dividing cells and can kill normal stem cells at the same time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbamazepine, valproic acid, and phenytoin cause aplastic anemia through idiosyncratic, not dose-dependent, reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nifedipine is an idiosyncratic cause and is not the most common dose-dependent offender.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NSAIDs are also idiosyncratic causes rather than predictable dose-dependent marrow toxins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sulfonamides are listed among the idiosyncratic causes of aplastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with hyperthyroidism is started on methimazole. Six weeks later she develops fever and mucosal bleeding, and a complete blood count shows pancytopenia. Which of the following best explains the marrow failure in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alkylation and cross-linking of stem cell DNA by a chemical toxin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibody-mediated destruction of mature circulating granulocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct marrow cytotoxicity proportional to the cumulative drug dose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug binding to stem cell antigens, making them T cell targets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Free radical generation within hematopoietic stem cells

explanation.summary: Idiosyncratic drug reactions cause aplastic anemia when the drug binds stem cell antigens and provokes T cell-mediated cytotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methimazole is one of the drugs listed as an idiosyncratic cause of aplastic anemia. In idiosyncratic reactions the drug or its metabolites bind to antigens on stem cells, making them immunogenic and susceptible to T cell-mediated cytotoxicity, independent of dose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alkylation and DNA cross-linking describe benzene and similar chemical toxins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The target in aplastic anemia is the hematopoietic stem cell in the marrow, not mature circulating granulocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dose-dependent cytotoxicity characterizes chemotherapy drugs, azathioprine, and chloramphenicol rather than idiosyncratic reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Free radical generation is the mechanism by which ionizing radiation damages stem cells.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man requires a new antihypertensive. He previously developed pancytopenia on a medication and his physician wants to avoid drugs implicated in aplastic anemia. Which of the following medications carries this recognized risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atorvastatin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lisinopril

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metformin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nifedipine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Omeprazole

explanation.summary: Nifedipine is among the drugs recognized as idiosyncratic causes of aplastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The drugs listed as idiosyncratic causes of aplastic anemia include the antibiotics sulfonamides and chloramphenicol, the anti-epileptics carbamazepine, valproic acid, and phenytoin, the antithyroid drug methimazole, nifedipine, and NSAIDs. Nifedipine is the only agent among these choices on that list.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atorvastatin is not among the medications identified as a cause of aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lisinopril is not among the medications identified as a cause of aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metformin is not among the medications identified as a cause of aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Omeprazole is not among the medications identified as a cause of aplastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with Epstein-Barr virus infection develops progressive pancytopenia, and a bone marrow biopsy shows a hypocellular marrow. Which of the following best describes how the virus produced this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Altered stem cell antigens attacked by cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clonal expansion of virus-infected myeloblasts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct viral lysis of mature red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sequestration of myeloid cells in an enlarged spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral suppression of erythropoietin production

explanation.summary: Viruses cause aplastic anemia by altering stem cell antigens or activating T cells, which then destroy hematopoietic stem cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viruses such as Epstein-Barr, HIV, hepatitis B and C, and herpes induce hematopoietic stem cell destruction either by altering the antigens on blast cells or by activating T cells. Activated cytotoxic T cells become self-reactive against the altered antigens and destroy the stem cells, producing a hypocellular marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Proliferation of blast cells describes leukemic marrow infiltration, the opposite of the hypocellular marrow described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Destruction of mature circulating red cells would cause hemolysis with reticulocytosis, not a hypocellular marrow with pancytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic sequestration is the mechanism of hypersplenism, which is a separate cause of pancytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocked red cell production from reduced erythropoietin is the mechanism of anemia in chronic kidney disease and affects only the red cell line.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops pancytopenia. She takes no marrow-suppressing medications, and a bone marrow biopsy shows a hypocellular marrow with abundant adipose tissue and no abnormal cells. Which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chemical cross-linking of stem cell DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inherited defects in DNA repair mechanisms

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replacement of the marrow by fibrous tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration of blood cells in an enlarged spleen

explanation.summary: Systemic lupus erythematosus and graft versus host disease cause aplastic anemia through autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune diseases are a recognized cause of aplastic anemia. Systemic lupus erythematosus and graft versus host disease after bone marrow transplantation of stem cells induce autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells, producing pancytopenia and a hypocellular marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chemical cross-linking of DNA describes toxins such as benzene, and this patient has no such exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defective DNA repair underlies Fanconi anemia, a hereditary disease that presents in childhood with constitutional features.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow replaced by fibrous tissue describes primary myelofibrosis, but this biopsy shows adipose tissue instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypersplenism causes pancytopenia by sequestration and would not empty the marrow of stem cells.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man is found to have pancytopenia. He also reports episodes of dark brown urine on waking, and he was recently treated for a deep vein thrombosis. Laboratory studies show evidence of ongoing hemolysis. Which of the following conditions best accounts for this combination of findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired pure red cell aplasia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diamond-Blackfan syndrome of infancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inherited Fanconi anemia of childhood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low-risk myelodysplastic syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

explanation.summary: Aplastic anemia from an acquired stem cell mutation may accompany paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, which causes hemolysis, thrombosis, and hemoglobinuria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rarely, patients develop aplastic anemia as part of an acquired gene mutation in the hematopoietic stem cells, often accompanied by another disorder. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is one such disorder and is characterized by autoimmune hemolytic anemia, thrombosis, and hemoglobinuria, matching this patient's dark urine, clot, and hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pure red cell aplasia affects only the erythroid line and would not cause pancytopenia, thrombosis, or hemoglobinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diamond-Blackfan syndrome is a congenital pure red cell aplasia presenting in infancy with macrocytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fanconi anemia is a hereditary condition presenting in childhood with constitutional features, not adult-onset hemolysis and thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myelodysplastic syndrome is the other acquired-mutation disorder associated with marrow failure, but it does not produce hemoglobinuria and thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is diagnosed with Fanconi anemia. His parents and an older sister are healthy, and there is no known family history of a blood disorder. Which of the following is the inheritance pattern of this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired somatic mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive

explanation.summary: Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive condition of defective DNA repair.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fanconi anemia, the most common form of the rare hereditary aplastic anemias, is an autosomal recessive genetic condition in which DNA repair mechanisms are defective. Unaffected carrier parents with an affected child fit this pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acquired somatic mutations underlie paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and myelodysplastic syndromes, not the hereditary aplastic anemias.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A dominant pattern would typically produce affected individuals in each generation, which is not the case here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitochondrial transmission is maternal and is not the pattern described for Fanconi anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fanconi anemia is not transmitted on the X chromosome.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with short stature and dysmorphic facies has been diagnosed with Fanconi anemia, and her blood counts are being monitored as the disease progresses. Which of the following abnormalities is usually the first to appear?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphopenia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutropenia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombocytopenia

explanation.summary: Fanconi anemia causes gradually progressive pancytopenia, and thrombocytopenia is usually the first abnormality.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fanconi anemia usually presents during childhood, with a median age of about 7 years, with gradually progressive pancytopenia. Thrombocytopenia is usually the first abnormality to appear, which is why easy bruising and petechiae are often the presenting complaint.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anemia develops as the pancytopenia progresses but is not typically the earliest change.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocytes derive from the lymphoid line and are relatively spared in marrow failure of this type.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocyte counts fall rather than rise when myeloid stem cells are lost.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutropenia appears as part of the progressive pancytopenia rather than first.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old girl with pallor and fatigue during feeding is found to have macrocytic anemia with a low reticulocyte count, and Diamond-Blackfan syndrome is diagnosed. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromosomal breakage testing with diepoxybutane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Corticosteroids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eltrombopag

choices.label: E
choices.text: Horse antithymocyte globulin

explanation.summary: The majority of cases of Diamond-Blackfan syndrome respond to corticosteroids.
explanation.whyCorrect: The majority of cases of Diamond-Blackfan syndrome respond to corticosteroids, with transfusions and stem cell transplant as the other options. Corticosteroids are therefore the appropriate initial therapy in a newly diagnosed infant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stem cell transplant is the only curative option but is reserved rather than used first.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chromosomal breakage testing is a diagnostic study for Fanconi anemia, not a treatment, and the diagnosis here is already established.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eltrombopag is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist used in aplastic anemia to raise all cell lines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Horse antithymocyte globulin is an immunosuppressive used in severe aplastic anemia, not as initial therapy for this syndrome.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy with Fanconi anemia has worsening counts but is not currently a candidate for transplantation. Which of the following medications may improve his blood counts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Androgens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deferoxamine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydroxyurea

choices.label: E
choices.text: Methotrexate

explanation.summary: Some patients with Fanconi anemia respond to androgens or corticosteroids, while allogeneic transplant is the treatment of choice for severe cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some patients with Fanconi anemia may respond to androgens or corticosteroids. Allogeneic stem cell transplant is the treatment of choice for severe cases; it reverses the hematologic abnormalities but not the predisposition to malignancies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron chelation addresses transfusional iron overload but does not improve stem cell production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythropoietin drives red cell production and would not correct a global loss of stem cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxyurea suppresses marrow output and is not a treatment for a marrow failure syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methotrexate is an antimetabolite that suppresses rapidly dividing cells, worsening cytopenias.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue and a bone marrow biopsy is performed. The pathologist reports a bone marrow cellularity of 30% with normal maturation of all cell lines. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this biopsy finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A normal finding for his age

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diagnostic of aplastic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diagnostic of primary myelofibrosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indicates a myeloproliferative disorder

choices.label: E
choices.text: Indicates metastatic carcinoma in the marrow

explanation.summary: Marrow cellularity declines normally with age, so 30% cellularity is expected in an elderly patient.
explanation.whyCorrect: A bone marrow cellularity of 30% would be a normal finding in a 78-year-old patient because of the normal age-related decline in cellularity. Aplastic anemia instead shows near-complete replacement of hematopoietic stem cells with adipose tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Aplastic anemia shows a markedly hypocellular marrow with near-complete loss of stem cells, not age-appropriate cellularity with normal maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary myelofibrosis is identified by extensive marrow fibrosis, which is not reported here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myeloproliferative disorders are marked by findings such as large lymphoid aggregates or marked proliferation of erythroid precursors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metastatic carcinoma would be recognized by infiltrating neoplastic cells in the marrow.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with pancytopenia and a suspected diagnosis of aplastic anemia is scheduled for a bone marrow biopsy. Apart from assessing marrow morphology, which of the following is the main purpose of the biopsy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To confirm sequestration of blood cells in the spleen

choices.label: B
choices.text: To demonstrate parvovirus B19 within erythroid precursors

choices.label: C
choices.text: To document chromosomal breaks after exposure to cross-linking agents

choices.label: D
choices.text: To exclude primary myelofibrosis or metastatic carcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: To measure the reticulocyte response to her anemia

explanation.summary: Bone marrow biopsy in suspected aplastic anemia rules out other potentially treatable causes of marrow failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: A bone marrow biopsy must be performed to evaluate marrow morphology and to rule out other potentially treatable causes of bone marrow failure such as primary myelofibrosis or metastatic carcinoma. Aplastic anemia itself shows near-complete replacement of stem cells with adipose tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Splenic sequestration is assessed clinically by finding splenomegaly, not by marrow biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Parvovirus B19 is evaluated by serology and is relevant to pure red cell aplasia rather than pancytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chromosomal breakage testing is performed in lymphocyte culture and is used when Fanconi anemia is suspected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reticulocyte count is obtained from peripheral blood, not from a marrow biopsy.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with newly diagnosed aplastic anemia reports bleeding gums, recurrent epistaxis, and unusually heavy menstrual periods. Which of the following laboratory findings best explains these complaints?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low neutrophil count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low platelet count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low reticulocyte count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal lymphocyte count

explanation.summary: Epistaxis, bleeding gums, and menorrhagia are the signs of thrombocytopenia in aplastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: On physical examination, signs of thrombocytopenia in aplastic anemia include epistaxis, menorrhagia, and bleeding gums. These follow directly from the loss of megakaryoblast-derived platelets.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Low hemoglobin causes pallor, fatigue, dizziness, and shortness of breath rather than bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutropenia produces fever and sepsis with hypotension and tachycardia, not mucosal bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A low reticulocyte count reflects reduced marrow red cell production and does not itself cause bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lymphocytes remain normal in aplastic anemia and are unrelated to bleeding.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man with pancytopenia is being evaluated for aplastic anemia. Which of the following sets of red blood cell findings is most consistent with this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fragmented cells with a low reticulocyte count

choices.label: B
choices.text: Macrocytic cells with an elevated reticulocyte count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Microcytic cells with an elevated reticulocyte count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normocytic cells with a low reticulocyte count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normocytic cells with an elevated reticulocyte count

explanation.summary: The anemia of aplastic anemia is normocytic with a low reticulocyte count and normal red cell morphology.
explanation.whyCorrect: In aplastic anemia the anemia is normocytic, meaning the mean corpuscular volume is normal. Reticulocytes, which are markers of bone marrow red cell synthesis, are low, and red cells are decreased in number but normal in morphology on the peripheral smear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fragmented red cells suggest a microangiopathic process rather than a hypocellular marrow with normal red cell morphology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrocytosis with reticulocytosis is not the picture of aplastic anemia; macrocytic anemia with reticulocytopenia instead suggests Diamond-Blackfan syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Microcytosis points to impaired hemoglobin synthesis such as iron deficiency, and a high reticulocyte count indicates a productive marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An elevated reticulocyte count would indicate preserved or increased marrow production, the opposite of marrow failure.

questions.stem: The parents of a 2-year-old girl with Diamond-Blackfan syndrome ask about her long-term risks. In addition to leukemia and myelodysplastic neoplasms, this syndrome carries an increased risk of which of the following malignancies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatoblastoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neuroblastoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osteosarcoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retinoblastoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wilms tumor

explanation.summary: Diamond-Blackfan syndrome predisposes to leukemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, and osteosarcoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diamond-Blackfan syndrome is an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by macrocytic anemia, reticulocytopenia, and cancer predisposition, specifically leukemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, and osteosarcoma. Other congenital abnormalities such as skeletal and cardiac defects may also be present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatoblastoma is not among the malignancies associated with this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neuroblastoma is not among the malignancies associated with this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retinoblastoma is not among the malignancies associated with this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wilms tumor is not among the malignancies associated with this syndrome.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has pancytopenia attributed to a thrombotic microangiopathy. Which of the following mechanisms best explains her low blood counts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excessive destruction of circulating blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired cell production from nutritional deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infiltration of the marrow by fibrous tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of myeloid stem cells in the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration of blood cells in an enlarged spleen

explanation.summary: Thrombotic microangiopathies cause pancytopenia by destroying blood cells in the circulation rather than by marrow failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pancytopenia has several causes besides aplastic anemia. In the thrombotic microangiopathies, a subset of cases of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, the low counts result from excessive destruction of blood cells in the circulation, with the marrow itself intact.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Deficiencies of vitamin B12 or folate impair production of blood cells in the marrow rather than destroying them in the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow fibrosis causes pancytopenia in primary myelofibrosis and other marrow-infiltrating disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of myeloid stem cells is the mechanism of aplastic anemia, which produces a hypocellular marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sequestration in an enlarged spleen is the mechanism in hypersplenism, such as that due to cirrhosis.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is newly diagnosed with aplastic anemia. He has a hemoglobin of 6.2 g/dL, a platelet count of 8,000/mm3 with active gum bleeding, and a fever with a productive cough. No causative exposure can be identified. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation from a matched donor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Long-term corticosteroids with iron chelation therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasma exchange to remove circulating autoantibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenectomy to reduce sequestration of blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion of blood products with antibiotics for infection

explanation.summary: Initial treatment of aplastic anemia is supportive: transfusions and antibiotics for infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: After eliminating or limiting exposure to potential secondary causes, initial treatment of aplastic anemia is supportive, including transfusions of red blood cells or platelets and appropriate antibiotics for infections. This patient needs both for symptomatic anemia, active bleeding, and infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allogeneic transplantation carries a high mortality rate and is considered only after other treatments fail.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids with chelation is not the supportive regimen used at presentation in aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma exchange is not part of the management of aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenectomy addresses sequestration in hypersplenism, which is not the mechanism of aplastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with severe idiopathic aplastic anemia remains transfusion dependent after all potential exposures have been removed and supportive care has been optimized. Which of the following medications is most appropriate to add?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deferasirox

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Horse antithymocyte globulin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hydroxyurea

explanation.summary: Severe aplastic anemia is treated with immunosuppressive drugs such as cyclosporine A or horse antithymocyte globulin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Idiopathic cases of aplastic anemia are treated with medications or stem cell transplantation in the setting of severe transfusion dependence or life-threatening infections. The immunosuppressive drugs cyclosporine A or horse antithymocyte globulin are used in severe cases such as this one.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron chelation manages transfusional iron overload but does not treat the marrow failure itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin stimulates only the red cell line and does not address the global loss of stem cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor is typically used for neutropenic fever after chemotherapy rather than for severe aplastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hydroxyurea suppresses marrow production and would worsen the cytopenias.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has fatigue and a low hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count. Her white blood cell count and differential and her platelet count are normal. Bone marrow biopsy shows decreased erythroid precursors with normal granulocytes and megakaryocytes. CT of the chest shows a mass arising from the thymus. Which of the following is most likely associated with her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fanconi anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatitis B infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myelodysplastic syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymoma

explanation.summary: Acquired pure red cell aplasia is associated with malignancies such as thymoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pure red cell aplasia is anemia with decreased erythroid precursors while granulocytes and megakaryocytes/platelets are unaffected, exactly as described here. Acquired causes include malignancies such as thymoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and the thymic mass identifies thymoma in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is also associated with pure red cell aplasia, but her white blood cell count and differential are normal and a thymic mass is present instead.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fanconi anemia is a hereditary cause of pancytopenia presenting in childhood with constitutional features.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatitis B is listed among the viral causes of aplastic anemia, which produces pancytopenia rather than isolated red cell aplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myelodysplastic syndrome is a cause of bone marrow failure affecting multiple lines, not selective loss of erythroid precursors.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man of northern European descent presents with intermittent jaundice, fatigue, and left upper quadrant discomfort. His father was diagnosed with a hemolytic anemia. On examination he is icteric with splenomegaly. A peripheral smear shows round red blood cells lacking central pallor, and an eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test is reduced. Which of the following defects most likely underlies this patient's condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of red blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defect in ankyrin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Defect in CD55 and CD59

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defect in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defect in the beta-chain of hemoglobin

explanation.summary: Hereditary spherocytosis results from defects in RBC membrane/cytoskeletal proteins, most commonly ankyrin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The family history, spherocytes on smear, splenomegaly, and reduced EMA binding are classic for hereditary spherocytosis. HS is caused by mutations in cytoskeletal proteins such as spectrin and ankyrin, or anchoring proteins (band 3, 4.1, 4.2), and a defect in ankyrin is the most common.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune destruction can produce spherocytes, but it would give a positive direct antiglobulin test rather than reduced EMA binding, and the strong family history points to an inherited defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A defect in CD55 and CD59 causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, which does not produce spherocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase defect causes oxidative hemolysis, not spherocytes or reduced EMA binding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A defect in the beta-chain of hemoglobin causes sickle cell disease, characterized by sickled cells, not spherocytes.

questions.stem: Which of the following laboratory values is most characteristic of and helps distinguish hereditary spherocytosis from other anemias?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased conjugated (direct) bilirubin concentration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV) with frank macrocytosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal red blood cell distribution width (RDW) value

explanation.summary: An increased MCHC, from mild intracellular dehydration, is the distinctive lab feature of hereditary spherocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: HS is the only type of anemia in which the MCHC is routinely increased, reflecting the smaller, more concentrated red cells that result from membrane loss and mild intracellular dehydration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: LDH is increased, not decreased, because it leaks out of destroyed red blood cells during hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolysis raises unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin, since the pigment has not yet been conjugated by the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MCV is normal in HS, which is a normocytic anemia; the cells do not become larger.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RDW is increased, because some cells become smaller while others remain larger.

questions.stem: A hematologist wants a test that would be abnormal in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis but normal in a patient with anemia of chronic disease. Which of the following tests best meets this criterion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmotic fragility test

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum folate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum iron

explanation.summary: The osmotic fragility test is abnormal in spherocytosis but normal in anemia of chronic disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: In HS and other forms of spherocytosis, red cells lack excess membrane and cannot accommodate the water that enters in a hypotonic solution, so they lyse readily (increased fragility). Anemia of chronic disease does not cause spherocytes, so osmotic fragility remains normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemoglobin is low in both hereditary spherocytosis and anemia of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MCV is normal in both conditions and would not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serum folate is usually normal in both conditions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum iron is usually normal in HS and would not reliably separate it from anemia of chronic disease in this framing.

questions.stem: A newborn is found to have moderate-to-severe hemolytic anemia. The peripheral smear shows red blood cells with marked variation in size and shape that resemble the cells seen in patients with extensive burns. Genetic testing reveals two spectrin gene mutations. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hereditary elliptocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sickle cell anemia

explanation.summary: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis is an autosomal recessive disorder with two spectrin mutations and burn-like RBC morphology.
explanation.whyCorrect: HPP is a rare autosomal recessive condition in which two hereditary elliptocytosis mutations (spectrin gene mutations) are inherited, producing moderate-to-severe hemolysis and red cells that resemble those seen after extensive burns.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia produces round spherocytes and a positive direct antiglobulin test, not burn-like poikilocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hereditary elliptocytosis is due to a single spectrin defect and shows elliptocytes with little hemolysis at baseline.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hereditary spherocytosis produces round spherocytes from an ankyrin (or related protein) defect, not burn-like cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sickle cell anemia is caused by a beta-globin chain defect and shows sickled cells, not burn-like poikilocytes.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with hereditary spherocytosis has a mild normocytic anemia and is otherwise asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: No treatment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral prednisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red blood cell transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy

explanation.summary: Most adults with mild, asymptomatic hereditary spherocytosis require no treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mild HS in an asymptomatic adult does not require therapy; observation is appropriate. Interventions are reserved for more severe or symptomatic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folic acid is used in moderate-to-severe HS and in pregnancy, where metabolic demand for making red cells is high.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral prednisone is used for autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not hereditary spherocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transfusion is not needed here because the anemia is mild and the patient is asymptomatic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is reserved for patients with chronic, severe, symptomatic anemia.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has mild anemia, splenomegaly, and spherocytes on a blood smear, but the diagnosis remains uncertain. Which of the following is the best confirmatory test for hereditary spherocytosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow biopsy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral blood smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum haptoglobin level

explanation.summary: EMA binding measured by flow cytometry is the main confirmatory test for hereditary spherocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: EMA is a fluorescent dye that binds band 3 and Rh-related proteins in the RBC membrane; reduced binding measured by flow cytometry indicates deficiency of band 3 or other proteins such as ankyrin or spectrin, confirming HS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone marrow biopsy is not required to diagnose HS and does not confirm the membrane protein defect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A direct antiglobulin test is used to exclude immune-mediated hemolysis and is negative in HS, but it does not confirm HS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The smear may already show spherocytes but is nonspecific; it does not confirm HS when the diagnosis is uncertain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A low haptoglobin only reflects that hemolysis is occurring and is not specific for HS.

questions.stem: A patient with hereditary spherocytosis has chronic anemia and an enlarged spleen. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism of red blood cell destruction in this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complement-mediated intravascular lysis in the circulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extravascular hemolysis by macrophages in the spleen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ineffective erythropoiesis within the bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mechanical shearing of cells passing through damaged vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidative destruction of red blood cells in the bloodstream

explanation.summary: Anemia in HS results primarily from extravascular hemolysis, meaning splenic macrophages destroy trapped spherocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spherocytes lack the excess membrane needed to squeeze through the splenic sinusoids, so they are damaged by the tight fit and destroyed by splenic macrophages at a much higher rate than normal, causing extravascular hemolysis and splenomegaly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement-mediated intravascular lysis in the circulation characterizes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, not HS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The defect in HS is a membrane protein problem, not ineffective erythropoiesis in the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mechanical shearing in damaged vasculature causes microangiopathic (fragmentation) hemolysis, not the splenic destruction of HS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidative destruction in the bloodstream describes G6PD deficiency, not hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has anemia, jaundice, and spherocytes on her peripheral smear. To distinguish hereditary spherocytosis from autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which of the following results would be expected in hereditary spherocytosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased reticulocyte count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated serum haptoglobin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Negative direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test

choices.label: E
choices.text: Positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test

explanation.summary: The direct antiglobulin test is negative in hereditary spherocytosis, distinguishing it from immune hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because HS is caused by an inherited membrane protein defect rather than antibodies coating the red cells, the direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative, whereas it is positive in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which can also show spherocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MCHC is increased in HS, not decreased.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The reticulocyte count is increased as the marrow compensates for hemolysis, not decreased.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Haptoglobin is low, not elevated, because it is consumed while binding free hemoglobin released during hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A positive direct antiglobulin test is expected in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not in HS.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with known hereditary spherocytosis develops a viral illness and becomes markedly more pale and fatigued. Laboratory studies show a sharp drop in hemoglobin with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count. Which of the following complications and causative agents best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aplastic crisis caused by iron deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aplastic crisis caused by parvovirus B19

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolytic crisis caused by G6PD deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenic sequestration caused by Bartonella

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaso-occlusive crisis caused by dehydration

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 can trigger an aplastic crisis in patients with chronic hemolytic anemia such as HS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aplastic crisis is a temporary shutdown of red blood cell formation in the bone marrow, most often during infection with parvovirus B19. In a chronic hemolytic anemia like HS, where RBC lifespan is already reduced, this marrow suppression produces a sharp fall in hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron deficiency causes a gradual microcytic anemia, not an abrupt aplastic crisis with low reticulocytes during a viral illness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G6PD deficiency causes oxidative hemolysis and is not the underlying disorder in this patient with HS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bartonella is listed as a cause of spherocytosis on a smear, not of splenic sequestration, and would not explain a low reticulocyte count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaso-occlusive crisis is a feature of sickle cell disease, not hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman with moderate hereditary spherocytosis is started on folic acid supplementation. Which of the following best explains the rationale for this therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folate directly stabilizes the defective red blood cell membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate reduces the elevated mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate suppresses the autoantibodies responsible for the hemolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ongoing hemolysis increases demand for producing new red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: She has a documented dietary folate deficiency on testing

explanation.summary: Folic acid supports the increased red cell production required by the constant low-grade hemolysis of HS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Folate is a necessary ingredient for making red blood cells. Because patients with HS undergo constant low-grade hemolysis and must produce many new RBCs, supplementation is helpful, especially with the added metabolic demands of pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate does not repair or stabilize the defective membrane cytoskeleton in HS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate does not lower the MCHC, which remains increased in HS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HS is not antibody-mediated, so there are no autoantibodies for folate to suppress.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum folate levels are usually normal in HS; supplementation is given for the high production demand, not a documented deficiency.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man of African descent is noted to have a mild anemia. His peripheral smear shows a large number of elliptical (cigar-shaped) red blood cells with little hemolysis at baseline. The disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and is caused by a defect in a cytoskeletal protein. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hereditary elliptocytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sickle cell disease

explanation.summary: Hereditary elliptocytosis is an autosomal dominant spectrin defect causing elliptocytes with usually mild disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: HE is the most common congenital RBC membrane abnormality, especially in patients of African descent. It is autosomal dominant, caused by a spectrin defect, and most patients are asymptomatic or have mild anemia with numerous elliptocytes on smear.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis has two spectrin mutations, is autosomal recessive, and causes moderate-to-severe hemolysis with burn-like cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hereditary spherocytosis produces round spherocytes, not elliptocytes, and is usually seen in people of northern European descent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency anemia is microcytic and hypochromic and does not produce elliptocytes from a spectrin defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sickle cell disease is caused by a beta-globin defect and shows sickled cells, not elliptocytes.

questions.stem: A blood smear from a patient with hereditary spherocytosis is reviewed. Which of the following morphologic descriptions best characterizes the abnormal red blood cells in this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cells with a central dense area surrounded by a pale ring (target cells)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cells with basophilic stippling and normal shape

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elliptical cells with pointed ends

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fragmented cells (schistocytes)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Overly round cells lacking central pallor with smaller diameter

explanation.summary: Spherocytes appear overly round, lack central pallor, and have a smaller diameter with less surface area.
explanation.whyCorrect: On microscopy, spherocytes are seen as overly round cells lacking the normal central pallor, with a smaller diameter and less surface area than normal biconcave red blood cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Target cells are a different morphology and are not characteristic of hereditary spherocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Basophilic stippling with normal shape is not the defining feature of spherocytes, which are distinctly round and lack central pallor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elliptical cells with pointed ends describe sickled cells, not spherocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fragmented schistocytes are seen in microangiopathic hemolysis, not HS.

questions.stem: A hematology fellow is preparing a teaching session comparing inherited hemolytic anemias and notes that sickle cell disease affects roughly 1 in 600 individuals. Which of the following best approximates the estimated prevalence of hereditary spherocytosis in the United States and northern Europe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 in 100 to 1 in 200 individuals

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1 in 100,000 to 1 in 200,000 individuals

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 5,000 individuals

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1 in 20,000 to 1 in 50,000 individuals

choices.label: E
choices.text: 1 in 500,000 to 1 in 1,000,000 individuals

explanation.summary: Hereditary spherocytosis is a very uncommon genetic hemolytic anemia, with an estimated prevalence of about 1 in 5,000 to 1 in 2,000 in the United States and northern Europe.
explanation.whyCorrect: HS is rare compared with sickle cell disease, which affects approximately 1 in 600 individuals. Its estimated prevalence ranges between 1 in 5,000 and 1 in 2,000 people in the United States and northern Europe, where it is most concentrated. It is rarer still elsewhere, for example 0.2 to 1.5 cases per 100,000 individuals in China.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This would make HS more common than sickle cell disease, which is the opposite of the actual relationship.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Figures in this range approximate the rarity of HS in populations outside northern Europe, not within them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This underestimates the prevalence in northern European populations by roughly an order of magnitude.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HS is uncommon but not this rare in any population described.

questions.stem: The parents of an 8-year-old boy newly diagnosed with hereditary spherocytosis ask how likely it is that other family members carry the same condition. Which of the following best describes the inheritance of hereditary spherocytosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant in about 25% of cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal dominant in about 75% of cases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autosomal recessive in about 75% of cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitochondrial in essentially all cases

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive in essentially all cases

explanation.summary: Hereditary spherocytosis is autosomal dominant in roughly three-quarters of cases and autosomal recessive in the remaining quarter.
explanation.whyCorrect: HS is caused by mutations in several different red blood cell membrane- or cytoskeleton-related genes. Depending on which gene and mutation is involved, the disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern in 75% of cases and an autosomal recessive pattern in the remaining 25%. A dominant pattern is consistent with the frequent family history of anemia across generations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the proportions; 25% is the share of autosomal recessive cases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The autosomal recessive form accounts for about 25% of cases, not 75%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HS results from nuclear genes encoding membrane and cytoskeletal proteins, not mitochondrial DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HS is not X-linked; affected fathers can transmit the disease to sons, as in the classic family histories described.

questions.stem: Hereditary spherocytosis results from improper formation of one of five proteins: some of these form the red blood cell cytoskeleton itself, while others anchor that cytoskeleton to the overlying membrane. Which of the following proteins serves the anchoring function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ankyrin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Band 3

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD59

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spectrin

explanation.summary: Band 3, band 4.1, and band 4.2 anchor the red cell cytoskeleton to the membrane, whereas spectrin and ankyrin make up the cytoskeleton itself.
explanation.whyCorrect: In HS the genetic defect causes improper formation of one of five proteins. Spectrin and ankyrin are cytoskeletal proteins, while band 3, band 4.1, and band 4.2 anchor the cytoskeleton to the red blood cell membrane. Loss of either category destabilizes the membrane so that portions bleb off the cell surface.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ankyrin is also a cytoskeletal protein; a defect in it is the most common cause of HS but it is not the anchor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD59 is a complement regulatory protein whose deficiency underlies paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, not HS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase is a red cell enzyme, not a structural membrane or cytoskeletal protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spectrin is a component of the red cell cytoskeleton rather than an anchoring protein.

questions.stem: In hereditary spherocytosis, the abnormal red blood cell membrane also produces defective glycolysis, accumulation of lactic acid, and a reduction in intracellular ATP. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this fall in ATP?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cross-linking of spectrin into rigid polymers that stiffen the cytoskeleton

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased binding of eosin-5-maleimide to band 3 at the cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of the membrane sodium-potassium pump, with sodium and water entering the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of complement regulatory proteins from the outer surface of the membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidation of hemoglobin with precipitation of Heinz bodies inside the cell

explanation.summary: Reduced ATP in spherocytes inhibits the membrane sodium-potassium pump, so sodium and water accumulate intracellularly and further deform the cell into a sphere.
explanation.whyCorrect: The membrane abnormalities of HS lead to defective glycolysis, accumulation of lactic acid, and reduction of intracellular ATP. Because the sodium-potassium pump is ATP dependent, it is inhibited, and sodium and water accumulate within the cell. This osmotic swelling contributes to the spherical deformation that occurs alongside the loss of membrane through blebbing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The spectrin abnormality in HS is a formation defect from mutation, not ATP-dependent polymer cross-linking.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosin-5-maleimide binding is reduced, not increased, when band 3 and related proteins are deficient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complement regulatory proteins are lost in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and are not affected by intracellular ATP depletion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heinz body formation reflects oxidative injury to hemoglobin, a mechanism of hemolysis distinct from the membrane defect of HS.

questions.stem: A physiologist explains why normal red blood cells can squeeze through capillaries and the sinusoids of the spleen without bursting, whereas spherocytes cannot. Which property of the normal red blood cell best accounts for this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A biconcave disc shape that provides a relative excess of membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: A full complement of regulatory proteins on its outer surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: A greater oxygen-carrying capacity than a spherocyte

choices.label: D
choices.text: A higher intracellular hemoglobin concentration than a spherocyte

choices.label: E
choices.text: A smaller diameter and less surface area than a spherocyte

explanation.summary: The biconcave disc shape gives normal red blood cells a relative excess of membrane, which is the deformability reserve that spherocytes lack.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normal red blood cells have an unusual biconcave disc shape that gives them a relative excess of membrane for their volume. That excess is what allows them to deform and pass through tiny spaces such as capillaries and splenic sinusoids without bursting. Spherocytes have no such wiggle room, so they are damaged by the tight fit in the spleen and destroyed by macrophages at a much higher rate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Surface regulatory proteins govern complement-mediated lysis and have nothing to do with passage through splenic sinusoids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spherocytes have normal oxygen-carrying capacity, so this is not the distinguishing property.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intracellular hemoglobin concentration is higher in spherocytes, which is why the mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration rises in HS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It is the spherocyte, not the normal cell, that has a smaller diameter and less surface area.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with long-standing hereditary spherocytosis has had progressive splenomegaly since childhood. His hematologist counsels him that over time the enlarged spleen tends to become less functional. Which of the following consequences is he most likely to face as a result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A progressively positive direct antiglobulin test

choices.label: B
choices.text: A reduced ability to fight off infections

choices.label: C
choices.text: A shift of hemolysis from the spleen into the bloodstream

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversion of his anemia from normocytic to macrocytic

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normalization of his mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration

explanation.summary: Chronic extravascular hemolysis enlarges the spleen, and the spleen may become functionally asplenic over time, impairing defense against infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Extravascular hemolysis in HS leads to splenomegaly. The spleen can become less functional over time, a state termed functional asplenia, and is therefore less able to assist in fighting off infections. This is a recognized consequence of the chronic splenic workload in HS rather than of the membrane defect itself.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The direct antiglobulin test is negative in HS, which is what distinguishes it from immune-mediated hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemolysis in HS is extravascular; a decline in splenic function does not convert it to an intravascular process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HS is a normocytic anemia; the mean corpuscular volume remains normal rather than rising.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The increased mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration reflects intracellular dehydration of spherocytes and is not corrected by splenic dysfunction.

questions.stem: A student asks whether the spherocytes circulating in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis are functionally abnormal apart from being fragile. Which of the following best describes the function of a spherocyte other than its propensity to be damaged?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds complement more readily than a normal red blood cell does

choices.label: B
choices.text: It contains less hemoglobin per unit volume than a normal red blood cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: It releases lactate dehydrogenase continuously while in the circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its oxygen-carrying capacity and other red cell functions are normal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its oxygen-carrying capacity falls in proportion to the membrane it has lost

explanation.summary: Apart from their propensity to be damaged in the spleen, spherocytes have normal oxygen-carrying capacity and other red cell functions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The problem in HS is mechanical rather than functional: the sphere shape leaves no deformability reserve, so the cells are damaged by the tight fit in the spleen and cleared by macrophages. Other than that propensity to be damaged, spherocytes carry oxygen and perform other red blood cell functions normally. The anemia therefore reflects shortened red cell survival, not defective cells in circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased complement binding characterizes disorders such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, not HS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Spherocytes are mildly dehydrated and contain more hemoglobin per unit volume, giving the characteristic increased mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactate dehydrogenase rises because the enzyme leaks out when cells are destroyed, not because intact spherocytes release it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxygen-carrying capacity is preserved despite the loss of membrane surface area.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with no personal or family history of anemia is found to have numerous spherocytes on a peripheral smear two days after receiving a unit of packed red blood cells. His hemoglobin has fallen and his bilirubin is elevated. Which of the following best explains the spherocytes on his smear?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A transfusion reaction

choices.label: B
choices.text: An aplastic crisis

choices.label: C
choices.text: An inherited defect in ankyrin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hereditary elliptocytosis

explanation.summary: Spherocytes are not specific to hereditary spherocytosis; more common causes include autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hyposplenism, transfusion reactions, and some infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although HS is the classic teaching association, it is rare, and acquired causes of spherocytosis are encountered far more often. A falling hemoglobin with rising bilirubin and new spherocytes appearing within days of a transfusion points to a transfusion reaction. The absence of any prior anemia or family history argues against a lifelong inherited membrane disorder.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An aplastic crisis is a temporary shutdown of marrow red cell production and does not generate spherocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An ankyrin defect causes HS, which presents as a lifelong hemolytic anemia rather than appearing abruptly after a transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causes oxidative hemolysis and is not a described cause of spherocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hereditary elliptocytosis produces elliptocytes on the smear, not spherocytes, and causes little hemolysis at baseline.

questions.stem: A neonate whose mother has hereditary spherocytosis develops worsening jaundice on the second day of life, with a rising unconjugated bilirubin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folic acid supplementation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Observation alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral prednisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phototherapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy

explanation.summary: Neonates with hereditary spherocytosis and jaundice may need therapy to decrease bilirubin, such as phototherapy, because jaundice can impede neurologic development.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because HS is a congenital condition, some neonates present at or shortly after birth with worsening jaundice. Unlike the mild adult case that needs no therapy, the neonate requires treatment to lower bilirubin, and phototherapy is the standard measure. The rationale is that jaundice in the newborn period can impede neurologic development.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folic acid is used for moderate to severe HS to support ongoing red cell production; it does not lower an acutely rising bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Observation is appropriate for mild disease in adults but risks neurologic injury when a neonate's bilirubin is climbing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral prednisone is a treatment for autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not for HS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is reserved for the unusual patient with chronic, severe, symptomatic anemia, not for neonatal jaundice.

questions.stem: A term neonate with hereditary spherocytosis has severe jaundice that continues to worsen despite initial measures to lower the bilirubin. Which of the following is most appropriate at this point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exchange transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folic acid supplementation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral prednisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osmotic fragility testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy

explanation.summary: Exchange transfusion is sometimes used in neonates with hereditary spherocytosis and severe jaundice.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transfusion of red blood cells may be needed in HS when there is a hemolytic or aplastic crisis, and exchange transfusion is specifically described for neonates with severe jaundice. It removes bilirubin and the hemolysis-prone red cells at the same time, which is what is required when the bilirubin continues to rise despite first-line measures.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Folic acid supports erythropoiesis over time and has no role in the acute control of a rising bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prednisone treats autoimmune hemolytic anemia; the hemolysis in HS is not immune mediated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Testing does not treat the neonate, and the diagnosis is already established in this scenario.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is an option only for the unusual patient with chronic, severe, symptomatic anemia, not for acute neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with hereditary spherocytosis has chronic, severe anemia with fatigue and exertional dyspnea despite folic acid supplementation, and has required repeated transfusions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exchange transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oral prednisone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phototherapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat eosin-5-maleimide binding testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy

explanation.summary: Splenectomy is performed for the unusual patient with chronic, severe, symptomatic hereditary spherocytosis because most of the hemolysis occurs in the spleen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most adults with mild HS need no therapy, and folic acid suffices for moderate to severe disease. For the unusual patient with chronic severe anemia and symptoms, splenectomy can be performed, since most of the hemolysis occurs in the spleen. Removing the site of destruction addresses the cause of her ongoing transfusion requirement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Exchange transfusion is described for neonates with severe jaundice rather than for chronic anemia in an adult.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prednisone is a treatment for autoimmune hemolytic anemia; the hemolysis in HS is mechanical, not immune.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phototherapy lowers bilirubin in jaundiced neonates and does nothing for chronic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Repeating a confirmatory test adds nothing when the diagnosis is established and the problem is symptomatic anemia.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old pregnant woman with moderate hereditary spherocytosis has been taking folic acid. A serum folate level is drawn and returns within the reference range. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folate malabsorption is present and parenteral therapy is needed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate stores are adequate and the supplement can be stopped

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her hemolysis has resolved and she no longer needs monitoring

choices.label: D
choices.text: She is nonadherent to the supplement and should be counseled

choices.label: E
choices.text: The finding is expected and supplementation should continue

explanation.summary: Serum folate levels are usually normal in hereditary spherocytosis; folic acid is given to meet the demand of continuous red cell production, not to correct a measured deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Folate is a necessary ingredient for making red blood cells, and patients with HS undergo constant low-grade hemolysis and so must produce large numbers of new red cells. Folic acid supplementation is used for moderate to severe HS, including most patients who are pregnant because of their high metabolic needs. Serum folate levels in these patients are usually normal, so a normal value is expected and is not a reason to change therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nothing in this picture suggests malabsorption; the level is normal, which is the usual finding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The supplement is given for ongoing erythropoietic demand, particularly in pregnancy, rather than to replete a deficient store.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HS causes constant low-grade hemolysis, and a folate level says nothing about whether hemolysis has stopped.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A normal serum folate is the expected result in HS whether or not a supplement is taken, so it cannot be used to judge adherence.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman with hereditary spherocytosis has a hemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL. Which of the following mean corpuscular volume findings is most characteristic of her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Markedly decreased, indicating a microcytic anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Markedly increased, indicating a macrocytic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mildly decreased, in proportion to the membrane that has been lost

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mildly increased, reflecting the reticulocyte response

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal, indicating a normocytic anemia

explanation.summary: The complete blood count in hereditary spherocytosis shows a low hemoglobin with a normal mean corpuscular volume, making it a normocytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The CBC in HS is typical of a chronic hemolytic anemia: low hemoglobin, normal MCV, and increased red blood cell distribution width. The red cells do not become larger in HS, so the anemia is normocytic. What does change is the mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, which is increased.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A markedly low MCV points toward a microcytic process, which is not the pattern in HS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A macrocytic picture is not seen in HS; it suggests a different category of anemia entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Although spherocytes have a smaller diameter and less surface area, the measured cell volume remains in the normal range.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The MCV stays normal in HS even though reticulocytes are increased.

questions.stem: The complete blood count of a 25-year-old man with hereditary spherocytosis shows an increased red blood cell distribution width. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin is distributed unevenly within each individual cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemolysis leaves some cells smaller while others remain larger

choices.label: C
choices.text: Membrane blebs are counted by the analyzer as separate cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mean corpuscular volume is increased in the majority of cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reticulocyte response is suppressed by the chronic hemolysis

explanation.summary: In hereditary spherocytosis the hemolytic process makes some red cells smaller while others remain larger, widening the red blood cell distribution width.
explanation.whyCorrect: RDW measures the variability in red blood cell size within a sample. In HS, hemolysis causes some cells to become smaller while others remain larger, so the population is more heterogeneous and the RDW rises. This sits alongside a low hemoglobin and a normal MCV in the characteristic CBC pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RDW reports variation in cell size across the population, not the distribution of hemoglobin within a single cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Membrane blebs shed from the cell surface do not account for the measured size variation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The MCV is normal in HS, so an elevated average volume cannot explain the widened distribution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reticulocytes are increased in HS, not suppressed, except transiently during an aplastic crisis.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man with hereditary spherocytosis is evaluated during an episode of increased hemolysis. Which of the following serum findings is most consistent with this episode?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A positive direct antiglobulin test

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased haptoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased lactate dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated conjugated bilirubin with a normal unconjugated fraction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Elevated haptoglobin

explanation.summary: Serum studies during hemolysis in hereditary spherocytosis show a low haptoglobin, a high lactate dehydrogenase, an indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and a negative direct antiglobulin test.
explanation.whyCorrect: A low serum haptoglobin reflects the hemolytic anemia and is part of the expected serum panel in HS when hemolysis is active. It accompanies a high lactate dehydrogenase and an indirect, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The direct antiglobulin test stays negative, which separates HS from immune-related hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A positive direct antiglobulin test indicates immune-mediated hemolysis, and in HS this test is negative.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactate dehydrogenase leaks out of destroyed red cells, so it is high during hemolysis, not low.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The hyperbilirubinemia of HS is indirect and unconjugated because the pigment has not yet been metabolized by the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haptoglobin is consumed during hemolysis and therefore falls rather than rises.

questions.stem: A patient with hereditary spherocytosis has a markedly elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase during a hemolytic episode. Which of the following best explains the elevation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Splenic macrophages secrete the enzyme as they ingest damaged cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: The bone marrow releases the enzyme during the reticulocyte response

choices.label: C
choices.text: The enzyme accumulates in serum because red cell glycolysis is defective

choices.label: D
choices.text: The enzyme leaks out of red blood cells as they are destroyed

choices.label: E
choices.text: The liver increases production of the enzyme in response to the bilirubin load

explanation.summary: Lactate dehydrogenase is an intracellular red cell enzyme that leaks out when red blood cells are destroyed, so it rises during hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: LDH is an enzyme contained within red blood cells. When hemolysis occurs, the enzyme leads out of the destroyed cells into the serum, and the measured level climbs. Together with an indirect hyperbilirubinemia and a low haptoglobin, a high LDH is one of the serum signatures that hemolysis is occurring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Macrophages clear the damaged spherocytes, but the measured enzyme comes from the red cells themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reticulocytosis reflects increased marrow output and does not release the enzyme into serum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defective glycolysis in HS reduces intracellular ATP; it does not push the enzyme into the circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The liver conjugates bilirubin; it does not manufacture additional lactate dehydrogenase in response to a pigment load.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with hereditary spherocytosis is jaundiced, and a liver function panel is obtained. Which of the following patterns is most likely, and what accounts for it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased total bilirubin, because haptoglobin binds the released pigment

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased conjugated bilirubin, because the enlarged spleen obstructs biliary drainage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased conjugated bilirubin, because the liver rapidly processes the heme load

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased unconjugated bilirubin, because it has not yet been metabolized by the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal total bilirubin, because hemolysis occurs outside the vasculature
