explanation.summary: Hemolysis in hereditary spherocytosis produces an indirect, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia because the pigment has not yet been conjugated by the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: A liver function panel in a patient with active hemolysis indicates an indirect, or unconjugated, hyperbilirubinemia. The bilirubin released from destroyed red cells has not yet been metabolized by the liver, so it is the unconjugated fraction that rises. This is the pattern that produces the yellow skin and icteric sclerae seen in symptomatic HS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and is consumed during hemolysis; it does not lower the bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Splenomegaly in HS does not obstruct the biliary tree, so a conjugated pattern is not produced this way.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The conjugated fraction would rise only after hepatic processing, which is precisely what has not yet occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Extravascular hemolysis still liberates a large pigment load, and total bilirubin rises.

questions.stem: In an osmotic fragility test, a patient's red blood cells are placed in a hypotonic solution so that water flows into the cells by osmosis. Which of the following best explains why spherocytes lyse under these conditions while normal red blood cells do not?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spherocytes actively pump water inward using the sodium-potassium pump

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spherocytes cannot extrude sodium because band 3 is entirely absent

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spherocytes have a higher intracellular osmolarity that draws in extra water

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spherocytes lack the membrane excess needed to accommodate an influx of water

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spherocytes present a greater surface area across which water can enter

explanation.summary: Spherocytes have no membrane excess, so when water enters them in a hypotonic solution they have no room to swell and they burst.
explanation.whyCorrect: In an isotonic solution the water transported into a cell equals the water transported out. In a hypotonic solution more water flows in by osmosis. The biconcave-disk shape of a normal red blood cell, with its membrane excess, leaves plenty of room for that influx, whereas spherocytes have no membrane excess and therefore tend to burst.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Water movement in this test is passive osmosis; the sodium-potassium pump does not transport water.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Band 3 is deficient rather than absent in HS, and the test's result depends on membrane reserve rather than sodium handling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The driving force is the hypotonicity of the external solution, not an unusually high internal osmolarity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spherocytes have less surface area than normal red cells, not more.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a newly detected anemia and equivocal red cell morphology on smear has an abnormal osmotic fragility test. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It confirms spherocytes without identifying their cause

choices.label: B
choices.text: It establishes a diagnosis of hereditary elliptocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It establishes a diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It excludes autoimmune hemolytic anemia as the cause

choices.label: E
choices.text: It shows her red cells carry excess surface membrane

explanation.summary: The osmotic fragility test confirms that spherocytes are present but is positive in any type of spherocytosis, so it does not establish the cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: When spherocytes are equivocal on the blood smear, the osmotic fragility test can confirm that they are present. However, the test is positive for any type of spherocytosis, including autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hyposplenism, transfusion reactions, and some infections, not just HS. Confirming HS specifically requires eosin-5-maleimide binding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hereditary elliptocytosis is diagnosed by finding elliptocytes on the peripheral smear, and it does not produce spherocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HS is confirmed with eosin-5-maleimide binding; osmotic fragility alone cannot distinguish it from acquired spherocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia also produces spherocytes and an abnormal test, so it is not excluded.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An abnormal result indicates a deficit of membrane reserve, which is the opposite of excess surface membrane.

questions.stem: A blood sample is incubated with eosin-5-maleimide, a fluorescent dye, and the extent of binding is then measured by flow cytometry. To which of the following does this dye bind?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Band 3 and Rh-related proteins within the red cell membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD55 and CD59 on the red cell outer surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin tetramers within the red cell cytoplasm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immunoglobulin already bound to the red cell surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spectrin tetramers within the red cell cytoskeleton

explanation.summary: Eosin-5-maleimide binds band 3 and Rh-related proteins in the red cell membrane, and reduced binding indicates deficiency of band 3 or other membrane proteins such as ankyrin or spectrin.
explanation.whyCorrect: EMA is a fluorescent dye able to bind band 3 and Rh-related proteins within the red blood cell membrane. After the dye is added, the extent of binding is measured by flow cytometry. Reduced levels of EMA binding indicate deficiencies in band 3 or other proteins such as ankyrin or spectrin, which is how the test confirms HS.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD55 and CD59 are assessed by flow cytometry in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, a different assay and a different disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The dye is a membrane probe and does not report on intracellular hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Detecting antibody on the red cell surface is the purpose of the direct antiglobulin test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spectrin deficiency is detected indirectly through reduced dye binding at the membrane, not by direct binding to spectrin.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man of African descent has a mild anemia and a family history of anemia in an autosomal dominant pattern. Hereditary elliptocytosis is suspected. Which of the following is the basic diagnostic test for this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin testing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eosin-5-maleimide binding by flow cytometry

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmotic fragility testing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral blood smear evaluation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum haptoglobin measurement

explanation.summary: Hereditary elliptocytosis is diagnosed by peripheral smear evaluation, on which a large number of elliptocytes are observed.
explanation.whyCorrect: HE is the most common congenital red blood cell membrane abnormality in patients of African descent, is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, and is caused by a defect in spectrin. Most patients are asymptomatic or have mild anemia with little hemolysis at baseline. The basic diagnostic test is peripheral smear evaluation, in which large numbers of elliptocytes are seen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A direct antiglobulin test looks for immune-mediated hemolysis and would not identify elliptocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosin-5-maleimide binding is the confirmatory test for hereditary spherocytosis, not for hereditary elliptocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osmotic fragility testing detects spherocytes and is not the diagnostic approach for elliptocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haptoglobin reflects whether hemolysis is occurring and cannot identify the shape abnormality; baseline hemolysis in HE is minimal.

questions.stem: Two related patients are evaluated. One has hereditary elliptocytosis with little hemolysis at baseline; the other has hereditary pyropoikilocytosis with moderate to severe baseline hemolysis. Which of the following best describes the genetic difference between the two disorders?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first has a spectrin mutation and the second a hemoglobin mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first has an ankyrin mutation and the second a band 3 mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first has one spectrin mutation and the second has two

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first is autosomal recessive and the second autosomal dominant

choices.label: E
choices.text: The first is X-linked recessive and the second autosomal dominant

explanation.summary: Hereditary elliptocytosis is autosomal dominant with a single spectrin defect, whereas hereditary pyropoikilocytosis is autosomal recessive with two hereditary elliptocytosis mutations and far more severe hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: HE is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and causes a defect in the spectrin protein, with most patients asymptomatic or mildly anemic. HPP is rare and inherited as an autosomal recessive condition in which two HE mutations are present, and these patients have moderate to severe baseline hemolysis. The doubled spectrin defect accounts for the much greater severity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neither disorder involves a hemoglobin mutation; a beta-chain hemoglobin defect causes sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ankyrin and band 3 defects underlie hereditary spherocytosis; both HE and HPP involve spectrin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The inheritance patterns are reversed: HE is autosomal dominant and HPP is autosomal recessive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neither disorder is X-linked; HE is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man of African descent has a chronic hemolytic anemia. His peripheral smear shows elongated cells with pointed ends rather than round or oval cells, and evaluation reveals no red blood cell membrane protein defect. Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Defect in ankyrin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defect in CD55 and CD59

choices.label: C
choices.text: Defect in glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defect in spectrin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defect in the beta-chain of hemoglobin

explanation.summary: Sickled cells are elliptical with pointed ends and arise from a beta-chain hemoglobin defect rather than from a membrane protein defect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The red blood cells in sickle cell anemia are sickled in shape, elliptical with pointed ends, and they do not arise from a membrane protein defect. That disorder is caused by a defect in the beta-chain of hemoglobin. The absence of any membrane protein abnormality in this patient points away from the inherited membrane disorders.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An ankyrin defect causes hereditary spherocytosis, whose cells are round and lack central pallor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of CD55 and CD59 is seen in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and does not produce sickled cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causes oxidative hemolysis without this characteristic cell shape.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A spectrin defect causes hereditary elliptocytosis, whose cells are elliptical but lack the pointed ends of sickled cells.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated for a chronic hemolytic anemia. Her peripheral smear shows no spherocytes, and flow cytometry demonstrates a deficiency of CD55 and CD59 on her red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Classic hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hereditary elliptocytosis (ovalocytosis)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Severe hereditary pyropoikilocytosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

explanation.summary: A defect in CD55 and CD59 is seen in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, and spherocytes are not part of that picture.
explanation.whyCorrect: A defect in CD55 and CD59 is the hallmark of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. Spherocytes are not seen in this disorder, which fits the absence of spherocytes on her smear. This is one of the entities that must be separated from hereditary spherocytosis when a young adult presents with chronic hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hereditary spherocytosis produces round spherocytes on the smear and is confirmed by reduced eosin-5-maleimide binding, not by CD55 and CD59 loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hereditary elliptocytosis is identified by large numbers of elliptocytes on the peripheral smear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis produces red cells with marked variation in size and shape resembling those seen after extensive burns.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia produces round spherocytes similar to those of hereditary spherocytosis and a positive direct antiglobulin test.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy of West African descent develops painful swelling of his hands and feet. Hemoglobin electrophoresis confirms homozygous HbSS. His disease results from which of the following types of mutation in the beta-globin gene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Frameshift mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nonsense mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Point mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splice-site mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trinucleotide repeat expansion

explanation.summary: Sickle cell disease is caused by a single point mutation in the beta-globin gene.
explanation.whyCorrect: SCD results from a single point mutation at the sixth codon of the beta-globin gene, in which the GAG codon is changed to GTG. This single-nucleotide substitution changes one amino acid and is the defining lesion of this hemoglobinopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Frameshift mutations shift the reading frame and are not the mechanism in sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon and is not seen in SCD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splice-site mutations occur in several diseases but not in the hemoglobinopathies such as SCD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trinucleotide repeat expansions cause diseases such as Huntington disease, not sickle cell disease.

questions.stem: Sequencing of the beta-globin gene in a patient with sickle cell disease reveals a single nucleotide change (GAG to GTG) at the sixth codon. Which of the following amino acid substitutions does this produce?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glutamate replaced by lysine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutamate replaced by valine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glutamine replaced by valine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysine replaced by glutamate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Valine replaced by glutamate

explanation.summary: The sickle mutation swaps hydrophilic glutamate for hydrophobic valine at position 6 of the beta chain.
explanation.whyCorrect: At the sixth codon of the beta-globin gene, the GAG codon that normally codes for glutamate (a hydrophilic amino acid) is mutated to GTG, which codes for valine (a hydrophobic amino acid). The exposed hydrophobic valine drives HbS polymerization when deoxygenated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glutamate replaced by lysine at position 6 defines hemoglobin C disease, not sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The normal residue at position 6 is glutamate, not glutamine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This is neither the sickle nor the Hb C substitution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the direction of the change; the normal residue is glutamate and it is replaced by valine.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with sickle cell disease is being counseled about triggers of painful crises. Which of the following conditions most promotes red blood cell sickling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acidosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alkalosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased body temperature

choices.label: E
choices.text: High fetal hemoglobin levels

explanation.summary: Conditions that shift the oxygen dissociation curve to the right favor deoxygenated HbS and promote sickling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acidosis decreases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen and shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, favoring the deoxygenated (taut) state of HbS in which the valine residue is exposed. Fever, hypoxia, hypercapnia, and increased 2,3-BPG act similarly to promote sickling.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alkalosis shifts the curve to the left, increasing oxygen affinity and reducing sickling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased 2,3-BPG shifts the curve to the left and decreases sickling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lower temperature shifts the curve to the left; it is elevated temperature (fever) that promotes sickling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fetal hemoglobin resists sickling and inhibits HbS polymerization, decreasing crises.

questions.stem: A researcher studies why sickle hemoglobin (HbS) forms rigid intracellular strands under low-oxygen conditions. Which of the following best explains the polymerization of HbS in the deoxygenated state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hydrophobic valine residue is exposed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disulfide bridges form between adjacent beta chains

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heme iron is oxidized from the ferrous to the ferric state

choices.label: D
choices.text: The alpha-globin chains misfold and aggregate

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mutated glutamate residue becomes phosphorylated

explanation.summary: In the taut deoxygenated state, exposed hydrophobic valine causes HbS molecules to polymerize.
explanation.whyCorrect: When HbS is deoxygenated (taut state), the valine at position 6 of the beta chain is exposed. Because valine is hydrophobic, the HbS molecules line up (polymerize) with the valine residues facing inward to shield them from the polar environment, forming long inflexible strands that distort the red cell into a sickle shape.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sickling reflects hydrophobic polymerization, not covalent disulfide bond formation between beta chains.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferric iron (methemoglobin) formation is a separate process and is not what drives HbS polymerization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The defect is in the beta chain, not misfolding of the alpha chains.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphorylation of glutamate is not the mechanism; the mutation replaces glutamate with valine.

questions.stem: A couple, both of whom have sickle cell trait, seek genetic counseling before starting a family. What is the probability that any given child of theirs will have sickle cell disease?

explanation.summary: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive, so two carrier parents have a 25% chance of an affected child.
explanation.whyCorrect: SCD is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, requiring two mutated beta-globin genes. When both parents carry one sickle gene (sickle cell trait), each child has a 25% chance of inheriting both sickle genes and having disease, a 50% chance of being a carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two carriers can have an affected child, so the risk is not zero.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 50% represents the chance of an unaffected carrier child, not an affected child.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 75% is the chance of a child having at least one normal gene, not the chance of disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 100% would apply only if both parents had disease (HbSS), not trait.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with sickle cell disease has repeated splenic infarctions resulting in functional asplenia. She is at greatest risk of overwhelming, life-threatening infection from which of the following organisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disseminated Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enteric Escherichia coli

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: Functional asplenia in SCD predisposes to sepsis from encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococcus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vaso-occlusion in the spleen causes ischemia, infarction, fibrosis, and eventual functional asplenia. Without splenic macrophages to clear encapsulated organisms, patients are at high risk of bacteremia and sepsis from Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria meningitidis, which is why these children receive vaccines and prophylactic penicillin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida is a fungus and is not the encapsulated bacterial threat posed by asplenia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E coli infections are not the hallmark risk from functional asplenia in SCD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pseudomonas is not the encapsulated organism typically associated with asplenic sepsis in these patients.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Staphylococcus aureus is not an encapsulated organism cleared preferentially by the spleen and is not the classic asplenia risk.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presents with shortness of breath, mild fever, and chest pain he rates as 10/10. There is no cough. His oxygen saturation is 88%. His chart shows one to two admissions per year for infection or bone pain, and a blood smear shows sickled red blood cells. The chest x-ray is normal. Which of the following treatments would most quickly correct his low oxygen saturation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daily oral folic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily oral hydroxyurea

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exchange transfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intravenous antibiotics

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scheduled oral ibuprofen

explanation.summary: Acute chest syndrome with hypoxemia is treated with exchange transfusion to remove sickled cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient with sickle cell disease is having acute chest syndrome, marked by chest pain, fever, shortness of breath, and hypoxemia. Exchange transfusion removes sickled cells and replaces them with normal donor RBCs, most rapidly correcting the hypoxia in this severe acute complication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate supports chronic red cell production and does not correct acute hypoxia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydroxyurea reduces the frequency of future episodes but is not an acute treatment for hypoxemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibiotics are needed only with concurrent infection; the normal chest x-ray and absent cough argue against pneumonia here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ibuprofen treats pain but does not correct the low oxygen saturation.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has frequent painful crises and two prior episodes of acute chest syndrome. Her hematologist starts hydroxyurea to reduce these events. This drug decreases episodes primarily through which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking splenic clearance of sickled cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chelating excess iron from transfusions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Directly dissolving existing HbS polymers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increasing production of adult hemoglobin (HbA)

explanation.summary: Hydroxyurea reduces sickle crises by raising fetal hemoglobin, which resists sickling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hydroxyurea increases the amount of fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which has two gamma subunits instead of beta subunits and is therefore not subject to the sickle mutation. This raises the number of normally shaped red cells, and high HbF also inhibits the polymerization of HbS, decreasing pain and acute chest syndrome episodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydroxyurea does not work by blocking splenic clearance of cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron chelation is used to manage transfusional iron overload and is not the mechanism of hydroxyurea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxyurea prevents polymerization by raising HbF rather than dissolving polymers that already exist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The benefit comes from increasing HbF, not adult HbA, which still carries the mutated beta chain in these patients.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease develops sudden severe fatigue and pallor after several days of a viral illness with a facial rash. His hemoglobin has fallen sharply and, unlike his usual baseline, his reticulocyte count is now very low. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his profound anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parvovirus B19 infection

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 causes an aplastic crisis by transiently halting marrow red cell production.
explanation.whyCorrect: In SCD, RBCs have a shortened lifespan, so the marrow must make many more cells daily, reflected by a high baseline reticulocyte count. Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursors and causes the bone marrow to temporarily stop making red cells for a few days, producing a profound anemia with a drop in reticulocytes, an acute aplastic crisis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CMV does not typically cause the transient red cell aplasia seen with parvovirus B19.
whyWrongByChoice.B: EBV is not the classic cause of aplastic crisis in patients with hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G6PD deficiency causes episodic hemolysis, which would raise reticulocytes rather than suppress them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency causes a gradual microcytic anemia, not a sudden aplastic crisis with low reticulocytes.

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a 15-year-old with sickle cell disease shows several red blood cells containing small, deeply basophilic, spherical nuclear remnants. The presence of these inclusions most directly indicates which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active intravascular hemolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron overload from transfusions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lead poisoning

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of normal splenic function

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency

explanation.summary: Howell-Jolly bodies persist when the spleen cannot remove nuclear remnants, indicating functional asplenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Howell-Jolly bodies are small remnants of DNA that are normally removed by the spleen. In the absence of splenic function (functional asplenia, common in SCD due to repeated splenic infarction), they remain in red cells and appear as deeply basophilic spherical inclusions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemolysis raises bilirubin and reticulocytes; Howell-Jolly bodies specifically reflect absent splenic filtering.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron overload is assessed with ferritin and does not produce Howell-Jolly bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lead poisoning classically causes basophilic stippling, a different finding, not Howell-Jolly bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils, not these inclusions specifically.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman of African descent has a lifelong mild hemolytic anemia with splenomegaly and jaundice. Her peripheral smear shows numerous target cells. Hemoglobin electrophoresis confirms homozygous hemoglobin C disease. Which of the following smear findings is the hallmark of this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hb C crystals

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sickle cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spherocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Target cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teardrop cells

explanation.summary: Intracellular Hb C crystals are the hallmark peripheral smear finding of hemoglobin C disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Homozygous hemoglobin C disease (arising from substitution of lysine for glutamate at the sixth position of the beta chain) presents with mild hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, and jaundice. Its hallmark peripheral smear finding is the presence of Hb C crystals, along with target cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sickle cells are the hallmark of sickle cell disease, not hemoglobin C disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spherocytes are seen in hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Target cells are seen in Hb C disease but are not specific, also appearing in iron deficiency, thalassemia, and liver disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Teardrop cells are seen with myelofibrosis or other marrow space-occupying lesions.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is admitted with a severe vaso-occlusive crisis causing 9/10 pain in his back and extremities. Which of the following is the most useful to manage the symptoms of his acute pain episode?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Analgesic drugs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folic acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydroxyurea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stem cell transplantation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion with whole blood

explanation.summary: Prompt analgesia is the first-line treatment of an acute vaso-occlusive pain crisis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vaso-occlusive crises are extremely painful, and the first line of treatment is analgesia, with prompt appropriate dosing of pain medication such as morphine. Hydration is a secondary treatment. Effective pain control directly manages the symptoms of the acute episode.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Folic acid supports baseline red cell production but does not act fast enough to help an acute crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxyurea reduces the frequency of future episodes but is not particularly helpful during an ongoing pain crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stem cell transplantation is a carefully planned, long-term option for severe complications, not acute pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Whole blood transfusion is reserved for acute bleeding, not routine management of a pain crisis.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the burden of inherited blood disorders in the United States. Approximately what proportion of the overall US population has sickle cell disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 in 30

explanation.summary: Sickle cell disease occurs in about 1:3000 in the US and is the most common inherited blood disorder in the country.
explanation.whyCorrect: SCD affects millions of people worldwide and is found in 1:3000 in the US population overall, which makes it by far the most common inherited blood disorder in the United States. Prevalence is highest among people of Sub-Saharan African, South Asian, Middle Eastern, and Mediterranean ancestry.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1 in 30 would approach the carrier frequency in some populations, not the frequency of the disease itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 1 in 30,000 is far too rare for the most common inherited blood disorder in the US.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 1 in 300 overstates the overall US disease prevalence by an order of magnitude.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 1 in 300,000 would describe an orphan disease, not SCD.

questions.stem: A researcher observes that the geographic distribution of the sickle mutation within Africa closely parallels the distribution of malaria, and that people with sickle cell trait have some protection against malaria infection. Which of the following best explains this protection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carriers maintain high fetal hemoglobin levels that block parasite entry into the red cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infected red cells of carriers lyse in the circulation before the parasite can mature

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sickle hemoglobin cannot be catabolized by the parasite, starving it of amino acids

choices.label: D
choices.text: The parasite lowers oxygen within the infected cell, causing it to sickle and be cleared by the spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: The valine substitution alters the surface receptor the parasite uses to attach to the red cell

explanation.summary: Parasite-induced deoxygenation makes trait red cells sickle, and the spleen then removes them along with the parasite.
explanation.whyCorrect: One theory for the malaria protection seen in sickle cell trait is that the parasite causing malaria decreases oxygenation within the red cell it infects. In a person with SCT, this drop in oxygen causes that cell to sickle, and the sickled cell is then cleared by the spleen, limiting the parasite's ability to reproduce and infect the host.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sickle cell trait does not maintain high fetal hemoglobin levels; the proposed protection involves deoxygenation-induced sickling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The proposed mechanism is splenic clearance of sickled infected cells, not lysis of cells within the vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protection is attributed to sickling and splenic clearance of infected cells, not to resistance of HbS to parasite digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mutation changes an internal residue of the beta chain that becomes exposed when deoxygenated; a surface receptor change is not the proposed mechanism.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college athlete known to have sickle cell trait spends a week training at high altitude and becomes dehydrated. He then notices painless blood in his urine. Which of the following processes is most likely responsible for his hematuria?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial invasion of the bladder mucosa with mucosal ulceration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immune complex deposition along the glomerular basement membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infarction of the outer renal cortex from arterial thrombosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Necrosis of the renal tubular cells in the innermost part of the nephron

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage of a calcium oxalate stone through the ureter

explanation.summary: People with sickle cell trait can develop hematuria and renal papillary necrosis under extreme conditions such as high altitude or dehydration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with sickle cell trait do not express the full range of SCD symptoms, but they may become symptomatic when exposed to extreme conditions such as high altitude or dehydration. The symptoms described include blood in the urine (hematuria) and renal papillary necrosis, which is necrosis of the renal tubular cells in the innermost part of the nephron.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cystitis would be expected to cause dysuria and frequency and is unrelated to altitude and dehydration in a trait carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glomerular immune complex disease is not the mechanism linked to sickle cell trait under these conditions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The sickling-related renal lesion described in this setting involves the papilla (innermost nephron), not the outer cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stone passage typically produces colicky flank pain rather than the painless hematuria described here.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old asymptomatic woman is found to carry one mutated beta-globin gene during family screening. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on her peripheral blood smear?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Howell-Jolly bodies in many red cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intracellular hemoglobin C crystals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Numerous sickle-shaped red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Numerous spherocytes with absent central pallor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red cells that are essentially normal in shape

explanation.summary: Patients with sickle cell trait typically do not have sickle cells on the peripheral smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: A person who inherits only one mutated beta chain gene is a carrier and is described as having sickle cell trait rather than sickle cell disease. Patients with sickle cell trait typically will not have sickle cells on their peripheral smear, which is one way their smear differs from that of a patient with homozygous SCD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Howell-Jolly bodies reflect absent splenic function, which is a consequence of repeated splenic infarction in SCD rather than trait.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin C crystals are the hallmark of hemoglobin C disease, a different beta-chain hemoglobinopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sickled red cells on the smear characterize sickle cell disease, not sickle cell trait.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spherocytes are characteristic of hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

questions.stem: A newborn with two mutated beta-globin genes is well at birth, but at 10 months of age he develops anemia and his first painful episode. Which of the following best explains why sickle cell disease tends to present in late infancy or early childhood rather than at birth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal hemoglobin levels fall and are replaced by HbS instead of normal adult hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal antibodies protect the infant's red cells during the first months of life

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neonatal alkalosis keeps hemoglobin in the relaxed state and prevents polymerization

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenic clearance of abnormal red cells does not begin until the second year of life

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mutated beta-globin gene is not transcribed until the spleen matures

explanation.summary: Symptoms begin when protective fetal hemoglobin declines and is replaced by HbS.
explanation.whyCorrect: SCD tends to present in late infancy or early childhood, which is when fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels drop. Normally HbF is replaced by normal adult hemoglobin (HbA), but in SCD it is instead replaced by abnormal sickled hemoglobin (HbS), and the anemia then persists through adulthood with acute worsening during sickle crises.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Maternal antibody does not protect red cells from an intrinsic hemoglobin defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sickling depends on the deoxygenated (taut) state of HbS; an acid-base explanation does not account for the age of onset.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic function is present in infancy; the timing of symptoms follows the decline in HbF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mutated beta chain gene is expressed as beta-globin production ramps up; splenic maturation does not control its transcription.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with sickle cell disease asks what he can do to reduce how often he has painful episodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exercise to the point of exhaustion several times each week

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have a nightly alcoholic drink to promote peripheral vasodilation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Limit fluid intake in the evening to reduce circulating blood volume

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stay well hydrated and avoid high altitude and overly strenuous exercise

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take a daily oral iron supplement to raise the hemoglobin level

explanation.summary: Preventing pain crises relies on hydration and avoidance of smoking, excess alcohol, high altitude, and strenuous exercise.
explanation.whyCorrect: To prevent pain crises, patients should be advised to cease smoking, avoid excess alcohol, stay well hydrated, and avoid high altitude and overly strenuous exercise. These measures reduce exposure to the hypoxic, dehydrated, and low-flow conditions that promote sickling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Overly strenuous exercise is specifically to be avoided in patients with SCD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess alcohol is to be avoided, and alcohol is itself identified as a trigger of painful episodes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dehydration is a recognized trigger of painful episodes; fluid restriction would make crises more likely.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron supplementation is not part of preventing crises; it is folic acid that is supplemented in SCD.

questions.stem: In sickle cell disease, fragile sickled red cells are removed from the circulation at a faster rate by splenic macrophages. This process is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune hemolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extravascular hemolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ineffective erythropoiesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intravascular hemolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidative hemolysis

explanation.summary: Macrophage removal of red cells in the spleen is extravascular hemolysis; damage within vessels is intravascular hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sickle cells are more fragile than normal red blood cells and are removed from circulation at a faster rate by splenic macrophages, which is extravascular hemolysis. They are also damaged in the peripheral circulation, which is intravascular hemolysis, and both mechanisms shorten the red cell lifespan.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immune destruction of red cells is a separate general cause of hemolysis and is not the mechanism in SCD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ineffective erythropoiesis describes failure of red cell production in the marrow; in SCD the marrow is hyperactive with a high reticulocyte count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intravascular hemolysis refers to red cells damaged within the peripheral circulation, not cells taken up by splenic macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidative stress is another general cause of hemolysis, but here the cells are cleared because they are rigid and fragile.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with sickle cell disease develops right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. Ultrasound shows multiple gallstones. Which of the following best explains the formation of her stones?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic bacterial infection of the biliary tree

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of iron within the wall of the gallbladder

choices.label: C
choices.text: High concentrations of unconjugated bilirubin from ongoing hemolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stasis of bile caused by compression from an enlarged spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supersaturation of bile with cholesterol from a high-fat diet

explanation.summary: Chronic hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, which can precipitate as bilirubin gallstones.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemoglobin released by hemolysis is catabolized to bilirubin, leading to high concentrations of unconjugated bilirubin. This is the same process that produces the jaundice and scleral icterus seen in these patients, and it can sometimes cause bilirubin gallstones.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliary infection is not the explanation for stones arising from chronic hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron overload is a consequence of repeated transfusion but does not form gallstones.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic enlargement does not obstruct the biliary tree or cause stone formation in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cholesterol supersaturation produces cholesterol stones and is not the mechanism tied to chronic hemolysis.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man with sickle cell disease reports several months of right groin pain that is worse when he bears weight on that leg. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute bleeding into the hip joint space

choices.label: B
choices.text: Avascular necrosis of the head of the femur

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compression of a lumbar nerve root by a disc

choices.label: D
choices.text: Salmonella osteomyelitis of the iliac crest

choices.label: E
choices.text: Septic arthritis of the hip joint with effusion

explanation.summary: Bone infarction in SCD commonly causes avascular necrosis of the hip and femoral head, with groin pain on weight bearing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vaso-occlusion produces bone infarctions in larger bones that cause avascular necrosis, particularly of the hip and head of the femur. This causes pain that is often felt in the groin and is brought out by bearing weight, exactly as described here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemarthrosis is a bleeding-disorder complication; SCD causes ischemia and infarction rather than joint bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Radicular compression would produce radiating leg pain and neurologic signs, not infarction-related groin pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The characteristic site of avascular necrosis in SCD is the femoral head and hip, not the iliac crest.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Septic arthritis would be expected to produce an acutely hot, swollen joint with fever rather than months of weight-bearing pain.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy with sickle cell disease presents with a painful erection that has lasted four hours. Which of the following best explains this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An adverse drug effect of hydroxyurea therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autonomic neuropathy caused by chronic tissue hypoxia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess circulating androgens from marrow hyperplasia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infection of the corpora with encapsulated bacteria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Occlusion of the penile venules by rigid sickled cells

explanation.summary: Priapism in SCD results from vaso-occlusion of the penile venules by rigid sickled cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Priapism, a painful and prolonged erection, is listed among the specific vaso-occlusive complications of SCD and is due to occlusion of the penile venules. Rigid sickled cells lose their flexibility and become trapped in small vessels, blocking outflow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydroxyurea's described adverse effects are leukopenia and an increased risk of skin cancer and leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Priapism here is an occlusive vascular event, not a neuropathic one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow hyperplasia in SCD reflects compensatory erythropoiesis and does not produce excess androgens.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Encapsulated organisms cause bacteremia and sepsis in functionally asplenic patients, not priapism.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with sickle cell disease develops sudden right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. Which of the following best accounts for her neurologic deficit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Occlusion of cerebral arteries by rigid sickled cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Profound hypoglycemia resulting from poor oral intake

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rupture of a congenital berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Septic embolus arising from bacterial endocarditis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombosis of the cerebral venous sinuses and veins

explanation.summary: Stroke in SCD is a vaso-occlusive complication caused by occlusion of cerebral arteries.
explanation.whyCorrect: Strokes are listed among the specific vaso-occlusive complications of SCD and are due to occlusion of cerebral arteries. When RBCs sickle they lose their flexibility and become trapped in vessels, blocking flow and producing downstream ischemia and infarction. Stroke is also one of the situations in which RBC transfusion is used.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypoglycemia produces global rather than focal deficits and is unrelated to vaso-occlusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aneurysmal rupture causes hemorrhage and is not the mechanism of stroke attributed to sickling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endocarditis with septic emboli is not a described complication of SCD in this context.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The described cerebrovascular complication is arterial occlusion, not venous sinus thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old with sickle cell disease is being evaluated for possible acute chest syndrome. Which of the following findings best establishes this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A new radiodensity on chest imaging with fever and/or respiratory symptoms

choices.label: B
choices.text: A positive blood culture drawn during an episode of fever and chills

choices.label: C
choices.text: An elevated cardiac troponin level with chest pain occurring at rest

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bilateral wheezing that improves promptly with an inhaled bronchodilator

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chest pain and dyspnea in the absence of fever or new radiographic changes

explanation.summary: Acute chest syndrome is defined as a new radiodensity on chest imaging with fever and/or respiratory symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute chest syndrome is defined as a new radiodensity on chest imaging accompanied by fever and/or respiratory symptoms. It results from clogging of the blood vessels of the lungs, can be triggered by infection, is a significant cause of hospitalization and one of the most common causes of mortality, and requires immediate intervention regardless of the patient's age.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A positive blood culture indicates bacteremia, a separate risk in these functionally asplenic patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Troponin elevation reflects myocardial injury and is not part of the definition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reversible wheezing points toward airway disease rather than the imaging-defined syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Symptoms alone do not define the syndrome; the definition requires a new radiodensity on imaging.

questions.stem: A hematologist explains that patients other than those with sickle cell disease can also develop an aplastic crisis when infected with parvovirus B19. Which of the following conditions carries this same risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia of chronic disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polycythemia vera

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency

explanation.summary: Any condition that prematurely destroys red cells can produce an aplastic crisis when parvovirus B19 halts erythropoiesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Other conditions that prematurely destroy RBCs can lead to an aplastic crisis with parvovirus B19 infection; these include hereditary spherocytosis, hemoglobin C disease, thalassemia, G6PD deficiency, and pyruvate kinase deficiency. Because these patients depend on a high rate of red cell production, even a few days of marrow shutdown causes a profound fall in hemoglobin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anemia of chronic disease is not one of the hemolytic conditions that predispose to aplastic crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency reduces red cell production but does not prematurely destroy circulating red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polycythemia vera is a disorder of red cell overproduction, not premature red cell destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: B12 deficiency impairs red cell maturation rather than shortening red cell survival by hemolysis.

questions.stem: The peripheral smear of a patient with sickle cell disease shows a fraction of red cells with a dense central zone of hemoglobin surrounded by a pale ring. Which of the following best explains how these cells form in this disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of excess cholesterol in the membrane from liver dysfunction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cellular dehydration from abnormal loss of intracellular potassium chloride

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of membrane surface area during repeated passage through the spleen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Precipitation of denatured hemoglobin against the inner cell membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retention of DNA remnants that are normally removed by the spleen

explanation.summary: Target cells in SCD arise from cellular dehydration caused by abnormal loss of intracellular potassium chloride.
explanation.whyCorrect: A fraction of RBCs in SCD appear as target cells. These cells arise due to cellular dehydration caused by abnormal loss of intracellular potassium chloride (KCl). Target cells are not specific to SCD and are also seen in liver disease, the thalassemias, iron deficiency, and after splenectomy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Membrane cholesterol excess is the mechanism in liver disease; in SCD the described cause is dehydration from KCl loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of membrane surface area produces spherocytes, which are seen in hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Precipitated denatured hemoglobin forms inclusions associated with oxidative injury, not the targetoid appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retained nuclear DNA remnants are Howell-Jolly bodies, which indicate absent splenic function.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with known sickle cell disease has a complete blood count drawn at a routine clinic visit while he is at his baseline. Which of the following combinations of findings is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Macrocytic anemia with a low reticulocyte count

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microcytic anemia with a low reticulocyte count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Microcytic anemia with an elevated reticulocyte count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normocytic anemia with a low reticulocyte count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normocytic anemia with an elevated reticulocyte count

explanation.summary: The CBC in SCD shows a normocytic anemia with a compensatory reticulocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The complete blood count in SCD shows a normocytic anemia, with decreased hemoglobin and hematocrit but a normal mean corpuscular volume. The reticulocyte count is typically increased, signifying the bone marrow's attempt to compensate for the increased destruction of red blood cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SCD does not produce macrocytosis, and reticulocytes are elevated at baseline.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The MCV is normal in SCD, and the marrow response raises rather than lowers the reticulocyte count.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Microcytosis suggests iron deficiency or thalassemia rather than SCD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The cell size is right, but a low reticulocyte count would suggest an aplastic crisis rather than the baseline state.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man with sickle cell disease has laboratory studies drawn during evaluation of his anemia. Which of the following additional findings is most expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased haptoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased indirect bilirubin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased reticulocyte count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated mean corpuscular volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased haptoglobin

explanation.summary: As in other hemolytic anemias, SCD shows increased indirect bilirubin and decreased haptoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: As in other hemolytic anemias, laboratory testing in SCD may show increased indirect bilirubin and decreased haptoglobin. Haptoglobin is consumed as it binds hemoglobin released from destroyed red cells, so its level falls.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin is increased by hemolysis, which is why these patients develop jaundice and scleral icterus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The reticulocyte count is increased at baseline as the marrow compensates for shortened red cell survival.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The anemia of SCD is normocytic, so the mean corpuscular volume is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haptoglobin falls rather than rises when red cells are being destroyed.

questions.stem: On cellulose acetate gel electrophoresis, sickle hemoglobin migrates a shorter distance away from the cathode than normal adult hemoglobin. Which of the following best explains this difference in migration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sickle hemoglobin binds the cellulose acetate matrix more avidly than HbA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sickle hemoglobin gains a positively charged lysine residue at position 6

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sickle hemoglobin has a substantially higher molecular weight than HbA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sickle hemoglobin polymerizes within the gel and is retarded by its size

choices.label: E
choices.text: Valine carries less negative charge than the glutamate it replaces

explanation.summary: HbS migrates less far because valine is less negatively charged than the glutamate it replaced.
explanation.whyCorrect: In electrophoresis, proteins move through the gel based on their size and charge. Normal adult hemoglobin (two normal alpha and two normal beta chains) migrates relatively far from the cathode, while sickle hemoglobin migrates to a lesser degree and finishes closer to the cathode. This is due to the lesser negative charge on valine, which is part of the SCD mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Differential binding to the matrix is not the basis of separation in this test.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lysine substitution at position 6 defines hemoglobin C; in HbS the substituted residue is valine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single amino acid substitution does not meaningfully change the molecular weight of the hemoglobin tetramer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polymerization occurs in deoxygenated red cells; the migration difference is explained by charge.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old asymptomatic man undergoes hemoglobin electrophoresis. The gel shows two bands: one at the position of normal adult hemoglobin and a second, smaller band at the position of sickle hemoglobin. Which of the following is the most likely interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin SC disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homozygous hemoglobin C disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygous sickle cell disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal adult hemoglobin pattern

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sickle cell trait

explanation.summary: Bands at both the A and S positions indicate a heterozygote, which is sickle cell trait.
explanation.whyCorrect: Electrophoresis tells us not only whether HbS is present but also whether the patient is heterozygous with sickle cell trait (one normal beta chain gene and one sickle beta chain gene) or homozygous with SCD (two sickle beta chain genes). Bands at both the A and S positions indicate the heterozygous AS pattern of sickle cell trait, consistent with this asymptomatic man.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemoglobin SC disease arises from inheriting genes for both HbS and HbC and would not show a normal HbA band.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Homozygous hemoglobin C disease would show hemoglobin C rather than a normal A band plus an S band.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homozygous SCD produces a band at the S position without a normal HbA band.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A normal adult would show only the HbA band, with no band at the S position.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl with sickle cell disease is seen for health maintenance. Which of the following regimens is most appropriate to reduce her risk of serious infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions plus rotavirus and hepatitis A vaccination

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prophylactic oral acyclovir plus varicella, measles, and hepatitis A vaccination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prophylactic oral fluconazole plus hepatitis B and inactivated polio vaccination

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prophylactic penicillin plus meningococcal, pneumococcal, and H influenzae type B vaccination

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus annual inactivated influenza vaccination alone

explanation.summary: Infection prevention in SCD combines the MPH vaccines with prophylactic penicillin in childhood.
explanation.whyCorrect: It is very important to vaccinate patients with the meningococcal, pneumococcal, and H influenza type B (MPH) vaccines. Patients will often also receive prophylactic penicillin during childhood to help protect against pneumococcal pneumonia, which is a particular threat because vaso-occlusion in the spleen leads to functional asplenia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immunoglobulin replacement is used for antibody deficiencies, not for the asplenia of SCD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antiviral prophylaxis does not address the bacteremia and sepsis risk from encapsulated bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antifungal prophylaxis is not indicated; the organisms of concern are encapsulated bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This regimen does not cover the encapsulated organisms that threaten functionally asplenic patients.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has been taking hydroxyurea for two years. Which of the following adverse effects is she at increased risk of developing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A decreased leukocyte count and a higher risk of leukemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemorrhagic cystitis with painful gross hematuria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron overload requiring long-term chelation therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral sensory neuropathy of the hands and feet

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progressive nephrotoxicity with a steadily rising creatinine

explanation.summary: Hydroxyurea reduces circulating leukocytes and is associated with increased risk of skin cancer and leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hydroxyurea has an adverse effect of reducing the number of circulating white blood cells (leukocytes). It is also associated with an increased risk of skin cancer and leukemia, which must be weighed against its benefit of decreasing the number of pain and acute chest syndrome episodes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemorrhagic cystitis is not among the described adverse effects of this drug.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron overload comes from repeated RBC transfusion rather than from hydroxyurea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peripheral neuropathy is not a described complication of hydroxyurea therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal injury in these patients relates to renal papillary necrosis from vaso-occlusion, not to hydroxyurea.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with sickle cell disease is prescribed daily folic acid. Which of the following best explains why this supplement is given?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folate binds the free iron that is released during hemolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate directly inhibits the polymerization of sickle hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolysis causes large amounts of folate to be lost in the urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydroxyurea blocks folate absorption in the small intestine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased red cell production consumes high levels of folate

explanation.summary: Accelerated hematopoiesis in SCD consumes folate, so patients are supplemented with folic acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: In SCD, increased hematopoiesis will consume high levels of folate, which is an important substrate for red cell production. Patients are therefore supplemented with folic acid alongside the other measures used to treat their anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate has no iron-binding role; transfusional iron overload is managed with chelation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It is high levels of fetal hemoglobin, not folate, that inhibit HbS polymerization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate is consumed by accelerated erythropoiesis rather than lost in the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxyurea acts by increasing fetal hemoglobin; it does not impair folate absorption.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is admitted with a vaso-occlusive crisis. He receives prompt analgesia, and the team then orders intravenous fluids. Which of the following is the most important consideration regarding his hydration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluids should be restricted to prevent transfusion-related iron overload

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluids should be withheld entirely until his pain has fully resolved

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydration is the first-line therapy and takes priority over analgesia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intravenous fluids should be replaced by whole blood transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Large fluid boluses risk hypernatremia and should be avoided

explanation.summary: Hydration is a secondary treatment in a pain crisis, and large boluses must be avoided because of the risk of hypernatremia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first line of treatment in an acute pain episode is analgesia, with prompt appropriate dosing of pain medication such as morphine. Hydration is a secondary treatment, and care must be taken to avoid hypernatremia from large boluses. Intravenous hydration helps by decreasing blood viscosity and improving blood flow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron overload is a consequence of repeated transfusion and has no bearing on fluid orders.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydration is a recognized secondary treatment during the crisis and is not withheld until the pain resolves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Analgesia, not hydration, is the first line of treatment for an acute pain episode.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Whole blood transfusion is reserved for acute bleeding and does not replace hydration in a pain crisis.

questions.stem: The parents of a child with severe sickle cell disease complications ask whether any treatment can cure the disease. Which of the following options is potentially curative but reserved for patients with severe complications?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow (stem cell) transplantation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic exchange transfusion every month

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daily folic acid supplementation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Long-term oral hydroxyurea therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prophylactic oral penicillin therapy

explanation.summary: Bone marrow or stem cell transplantation can be curative but is considered only for severe SCD complications.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bone marrow or stem cell transplants can potentially be curative in sickle cell disease, but they are considered only for patients with severe SCD complications because the process is long, carefully planned, and requires extensive investigations.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Exchange transfusion removes sickled cells and replaces them with donor RBCs for acute severe events; it is not curative.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folic acid supports red cell production but has no curative potential.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxyurea reduces the frequency of pain and acute chest syndrome episodes but does not cure the disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillin prophylaxis prevents pneumococcal infection in childhood and does not alter the underlying defect.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman of African descent has occasional mild painful episodes, and her course has been considerably milder than that of her cousin with homozygous sickle cell disease. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows sickle hemoglobin and hemoglobin C with no normal adult hemoglobin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemoglobin SC disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heterozygous hemoglobin C (Hb A/Hb C)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygous hemoglobin C disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homozygous sickle cell disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sickle cell trait

explanation.summary: Inheriting one HbS gene and one HbC gene produces hemoglobin SC disease, a milder sickling disorder than HbSS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some patients inherit genes for both Hb S and Hb C, which is called hemoglobin SC. In these patients the sickling disease is generally milder than in homozygous Hb SS, which fits this woman's milder course and her electrophoresis showing both HbS and HbC without normal HbA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The heterozygous Hb A/Hb C state is clinically silent and would show a normal HbA band alongside hemoglobin C.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homozygous Hb C disease would show hemoglobin C alone, with mild hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, jaundice, and Hb C crystals.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Homozygous SCD would show sickle hemoglobin without hemoglobin C and typically follows a more severe course.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sickle cell trait is one normal beta gene plus one sickle gene, and the electrophoresis would include a normal HbA band.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops lower back pain and dark urine one day after eating a meal of fava beans. He recalls that his grandfather avoided fava beans because they made him "feel ill." On examination he is jaundiced with icteric sclerae. A complete blood count shows anemia with normal leukocytes and platelets, and the mean corpuscular volume is normal. Which of the following is the most likely type of anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aplastic anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Macrocytic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Megaloblastic anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microcytic hypochromic anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normocytic anemia

explanation.summary: Hemolysis after an oxidant exposure in G6PD deficiency produces a normocytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The oxidant exposure (fava beans), family history, jaundice, and back pain point to a G6PD-deficiency hemolytic crisis. Hemolytic anemias characteristically have a normal mean corpuscular volume (normocytic), with normal leukocytes and platelets.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aplastic anemia decreases all cell lineages from marrow failure; the normal leukocyte and platelet counts make this unlikely.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mean corpuscular volume is not increased in G6PD hemolysis, so it is not macrocytic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Megaloblastic anemia is caused by vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, not consistent with this acute oxidant-triggered picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Microcytic hypochromic anemia is seen in iron deficiency, which does not fit this presentation.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is found to have G6PD deficiency on genetic testing. He is otherwise healthy with no anemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allogeneic bone marrow transplant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Avoidance of oxidant triggers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daily oral corticosteroids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Daily vitamin E supplementation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scheduled weekly blood transfusions

explanation.summary: The easiest, most practical treatment for G6PD deficiency is avoiding oxidant triggers.
explanation.whyCorrect: A healthy patient with G6PD deficiency stays asymptomatic as long as oxidizing agents such as fava beans and certain drugs are avoided. Trigger avoidance prevents hemolytic episodes and is the mainstay of management.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone marrow transplant is a last resort for very severe anemias and is unnecessary in G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corticosteroids help autoimmune hemolytic anemia but are not effective in G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin E is not involved in the mechanism of G6PD deficiency and does not relieve it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusions are unnecessary because the patient will not be anemic unless exposed to an oxidant.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: Which of the following substances is most likely to be decreased in the red blood cells of a patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucokinase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphatase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidized glutathione (GS-SG)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyruvate kinase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced glutathione

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency reduces NADPH and therefore the level of reduced glutathione.
explanation.whyCorrect: G6PD generates NADPH, which is needed to keep glutathione in its reduced state. Without adequate G6PD, the cell cannot replenish reduced glutathione, lowering its level and leaving red cells vulnerable to free-radical damage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucokinase is a glycolytic enzyme unrelated to G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causes von Gierke disease, a glycogen storage disorder, not G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxidized glutathione (GS-SG) increases, not decreases, because reduced glutathione cannot be regenerated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyruvate kinase is not affected in G6PD deficiency; it is a separate enzyme deficiency.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 1-month-old boy presents with fatigue, irritability, jaundice, and elevated bilirubin. His CBC shows a marked normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL) with an increased reticulocyte count. The team suspects pyruvate kinase deficiency. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate at this time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High-dose corticosteroids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Observation without treatment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral iron supplementation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red blood cell transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urgent total splenectomy

explanation.summary: Severe symptomatic anemia in pyruvate kinase deficiency is corrected with red cell transfusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: In this infant with pyruvate kinase deficiency and severe anemia, correcting the anemia with red blood cell transfusion is the priority in this initial phase, and he may require chronic transfusions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corticosteroids are not a documented treatment for pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Withholding treatment would not address his severe symptomatic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron supplementation is not needed because the patient does not have iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy can help severe cases but is generally not recommended until after age 3.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man of Mediterranean descent is admitted during a hemolytic crisis. A vital (supravital) stain of his peripheral blood reveals red cell inclusions composed of denatured, clumped globin attached to the inner cell membrane. Which of the following best describes these inclusions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basophilic stippling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heinz bodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Howell-Jolly bodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pappenheimer bodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Target cells

explanation.summary: Denatured globin clumped on the RBC membrane, seen with vital stains, defines Heinz bodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: In G6PD deficiency, oxidation causes hemoglobin to dissociate into heme and globin; the denatured globin forms a clump that attaches to the inner red cell membrane. These inclusions are Heinz bodies, visualized with vital stains.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophilic stippling is aggregated ribosomal material, not clumped globin on the membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants, not denatured globin, and are typical after splenectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing granules, not denatured globin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Target cells are a red cell shape abnormality, not an intracellular globin inclusion.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A hematologist explains that the characteristic "bite cells" seen in G6PD deficiency form through a specific process. Which of the following best describes how bite cells are produced?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies coat the red cell membrane and fix complement along its surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mechanical shearing by fibrin strands within small blood vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmotic swelling produced by an inherited membrane skeleton defect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Precipitation of excess iron granules within the cell cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic macrophages remove the membrane to which a Heinz body is attached

explanation.summary: Bite cells form when splenic macrophages remove the Heinz-body-laden membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: As red cells with Heinz bodies pass through the spleen, macrophages recognize them as abnormal and, rather than destroying the whole cell, engulf and remove the portion of membrane holding the Heinz body. This produces the characteristic bite cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody and complement coating describes autoimmune hemolysis, not the mechanism of bite cell formation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrin-strand shearing produces schistocytes in microangiopathic hemolysis, not bite cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osmotic swelling from a membrane protein defect describes hereditary spherocytosis, not bite cell formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intracellular iron precipitation forms Pappenheimer bodies, not bite cells.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man recovers from a G6PD-related hemolytic crisis. His physician wants to confirm the diagnosis with an enzyme activity assay. Which of the following is the most appropriate timing for this test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least 3 months after the crisis

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the acute hemolytic crisis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enzyme assays cannot diagnose G6PD deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immediately after the crisis resolves

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only when the patient is re-exposed to an oxidant

explanation.summary: Confirmatory G6PD enzyme assays should wait at least 3 months after a hemolytic crisis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Newly made red cells and reticulocytes have relatively higher G6PD activity, which can mask the reduced activity of the disorder. Because the red cell lifespan is about 120 days, waiting at least 3 months allows a new batch of red cells so the assay reflects the true deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: During a crisis, the surviving and newly produced cells give falsely higher enzyme readings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The diagnosis is in fact confirmed by an enzymatic study measuring G6PD activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immediately after a crisis, young reticulocytes still mask the reduced enzyme activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Re-exposing the patient to an oxidant would provoke another dangerous crisis and is not how the assay is timed.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is diagnosed with G6PD deficiency. His mother is an asymptomatic carrier. Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multifactorial with no clear pattern

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency is inherited in an X-linked pattern.
explanation.whyCorrect: G6PD deficiency is passed in an X-linked pattern, so males with a single affected X chromosome usually manifest the disorder while females are typically heterozygous carriers. Females may be symptomatic only if homozygous or if their normal X is inactivated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The disorder is not autosomal dominant; carrier females are usually asymptomatic rather than affected.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal recessive describes pyruvate kinase deficiency, not G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It is not mitochondrial; inheritance is tied to the X chromosome, not maternal cytoplasmic DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The disorder follows a clear X-linked pattern, not a vague multifactorial one.
