questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman is treated for a urinary tract infection with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Four days later she becomes jaundiced and fatigued, with dark urine and back pain. Which of the following mechanisms best explains her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inherited defect in the red cell membrane skeleton protein spectrin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Crowding of the marrow space by infiltrating malignant cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired heme synthesis from lead inhibition of ferrochelatase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidative damage overwhelming a G6PD-deficient antioxidant defense

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm-reactive IgG autoantibodies directed against red cell surface antigens

explanation.summary: A sulfonamide antibiotic triggered oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sulfonamides such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are oxidizing agents. In a G6PD-deficient patient, the reduced-glutathione defense is inadequate, so oxidative membrane damage causes intravascular hemolysis hours to days later, producing hemoglobinuria (dark urine), jaundice, and back pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A spectrin membrane defect describes hereditary spherocytosis, not an oxidant-triggered crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Marrow infiltration causes cytopenias from crowding, not an acute drug-triggered hemolytic episode.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lead poisoning impairs heme synthesis and causes basophilic stippling, not acute oxidant hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgG autoantibodies cause autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is not triggered by an oxidant drug in this way.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: During a G6PD hemolytic crisis, a patient develops rising serum creatinine and flank pain. Which of the following best explains the acute kidney injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct autoimmune attack on renal glomeruli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron deposition from chronic transfusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Obstruction of ureters by gallstones

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prerenal azotemia from dehydration alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxic effect of filtered hemoglobin

explanation.summary: Filtered free hemoglobin is toxic to renal tubular cells, causing acute kidney injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intravascular hemolysis releases free hemoglobin that is filtered into the urine. This filtered hemoglobin has a toxic effect on the renal tubular cells, elevating serum creatinine (acute kidney injury) and causing back or flank pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The kidney injury is from filtered hemoglobin toxicity, not autoimmune glomerular attack.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deposition from chronic transfusion is a long-term issue, not the cause of acute injury during a first crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gallstones are a complication of chronic hemolysis and do not obstruct the ureters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes the injury specifically to the toxic effect of hemoglobin, not dehydration alone.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child of Northern European descent has had chronic anemia since birth. Pyruvate kinase deficiency is diagnosed. Which of the following best explains why the red cells hemolyze in this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abnormal spectrin in the membrane skeleton

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibody-mediated red cell destruction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inability to generate NADPH for glutathione

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidation of hemoglobin by ingested oxidants

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced ATP production making red cells rigid

explanation.summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency lowers ATP, making red cells rigid and prone to hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the final step of glycolysis, transferring phosphate to ADP to make ATP. Its deficiency lowers ATP, making red cells more rigid and more likely to hemolyze, mainly extravascularly as macrophages in the spleen phagocytize them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abnormal spectrin describes hereditary spherocytosis, a membrane skeleton disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody-mediated destruction describes autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not an enzyme deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inability to generate NADPH describes G6PD deficiency, not pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidant-triggered hemoglobin oxidation is the mechanism of G6PD deficiency, not pyruvate kinase deficiency.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A student notes that G6PD deficiency and pyruvate kinase deficiency differ in where red cell destruction predominantly occurs. Which of the following correctly pairs each disorder with its main site of hemolysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both predominantly extravascular

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both predominantly intravascular

choices.label: C
choices.text: G6PD extravascular; pyruvate kinase intravascular

choices.label: D
choices.text: G6PD in bone marrow; pyruvate kinase in liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: G6PD intravascular; pyruvate kinase extravascular

explanation.summary: G6PD hemolysis is mainly intravascular, whereas pyruvate kinase hemolysis is mainly extravascular.
explanation.whyCorrect: In G6PD deficiency, oxidative membrane damage can be severe enough that red cells burst within blood vessels, so hemolysis is mainly intravascular. In pyruvate kinase deficiency, rigid ATP-depleted cells are phagocytized by splenic macrophages, so hemolysis is mainly extravascular.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only pyruvate kinase deficiency is predominantly extravascular; G6PD is not.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only G6PD deficiency is predominantly intravascular; pyruvate kinase is not.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the two disorders; G6PD is intravascular and pyruvate kinase is extravascular.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither disorder localizes its hemolysis primarily to the bone marrow or liver as described.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: The worldwide prevalence of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is less than 1% in most regions. In people with genetic roots in which of the following areas is this deficiency most common?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Andean South America, including Peru and Bolivia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arctic regions, including Greenland and northern Canada

choices.label: C
choices.text: Central Asia, including Mongolia and Kazakhstan

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mediterranean countries such as Greece, Spain, and Turkey

choices.label: E
choices.text: Northern European countries such as Sweden and Norway

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency clusters in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and some tropical populations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although prevalence is under 1% in most of the world, G6PD deficiency is most common in individuals with genetic roots in the Mediterranean (Greece, Spain, Italy, Turkey, the Middle East) and in some tropical regions such as Nigeria and Thailand. Approximately 10% of Black people in the United States are deficient, depending on their region of genetic origin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Andean South America is not among the regions of high G6PD deficiency prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Arctic populations are not among the regions of high G6PD deficiency prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Central Asia is not among the regions of high G6PD deficiency prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Northern European descent is the background associated with pyruvate kinase deficiency, not with G6PD deficiency.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man who grew up in a malaria-endemic region has G6PD deficiency and has never contracted malaria. Which of the following best explains the relative resistance to malaria seen in G6PD deficiency, sickle cell disease, pyruvate kinase deficiency, and hemoglobin C?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies against the parasite are produced at higher titers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatocytes fail to support the liver stage of the parasite

choices.label: C
choices.text: Red blood cells are inhospitable and lyse before the parasite reproduces

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenic macrophages clear the parasite directly from the plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: The parasite cannot attach to the altered red cell surface antigens

explanation.summary: These red cell disorders make the erythrocyte an inhospitable home for the malaria parasite.
explanation.whyCorrect: Malaria is a blood-borne intracellular pathogen that must reproduce inside red blood cells. In G6PD deficiency, sickle cell disease and trait, pyruvate kinase deficiency, and hemoglobin C, the red cell environment is inhospitable and the cell lyses before the parasite can reproduce, conferring relative resistance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The resistance is a property of the red cell itself, not of a heightened antibody response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The protection operates in the red blood cell, not by blocking a liver stage of infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Malaria is an intracellular pathogen of red cells; plasma clearance by macrophages is not the explanation given.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Resistance is attributed to early lysis of an inhospitable red cell, not to altered surface antigen attachment.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: Free radicals are produced steadily inside red blood cells. Which of the following best describes a free radical?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A denatured globin clump bound to the cell membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: A molecule that exists in reduced and oxidized states

choices.label: C
choices.text: A molecule with an unpaired electron that readily reacts

choices.label: D
choices.text: A reduced cofactor that regenerates an antioxidant

choices.label: E
choices.text: An enzyme that transfers a phosphate group to ADP

explanation.summary: A free radical is a molecule carrying an unpaired electron that is ready to react.
explanation.whyCorrect: A free radical has an unpaired electron that is ready to react with other substances. Whatever it reacts with is said to be oxidized, and that oxidation damages the body, including red blood cells. If unchecked, this oxidative damage would cause rapid hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This describes a Heinz body, an inclusion formed from denatured globin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This describes glutathione, which exists as reduced 2 GSH and oxidized GS-SG.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes NADPH, which keeps glutathione in its reduced state.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This describes pyruvate kinase, the enzyme that generates ATP in the final step of glycolysis.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: Reduced glutathione (2 GSH) is the antioxidant molecule that protects red blood cells from oxidative damage. Which of the following actions accounts for this protective effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It converts glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconate

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detoxifies hydrogen peroxide by turning it into water

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reduces NADP+ to NADPH inside the red cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: It strips denatured globin clumps from the cell membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: It transfers phosphate from phosphoenolpyruvate to ADP

explanation.summary: Reduced glutathione protects red cells by detoxifying hydrogen peroxide into water.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reduced state of glutathione protects red blood cells from oxidative damage by hydrogen peroxide, detoxifying it and turning it into water. Maintaining an adequate pool of reduced glutathione therefore requires NADPH, which G6PD supplies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This conversion is catalyzed by G6PD, not by glutathione.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The relationship runs the other way: NADPH keeps glutathione reduced, not the reverse.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Removal of membrane bearing denatured globin is done by splenic macrophages, producing bite cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is the reaction catalyzed by pyruvate kinase, the final step of glycolysis.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: In the red blood cell, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase couples a substrate conversion to the generation of the reducing equivalent needed to keep glutathione reduced. Which of the following conversions does this enzyme catalyze?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucose to glucose-6-phosphate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate

explanation.summary: G6PD converts glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconate while reducing NADP+ to NADPH.
explanation.whyCorrect: G6PD catalyzes the conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconate. This reaction is coupled to the reduction of NADP+ to NADPH, and NADPH is what keeps glutathione in its reduced, protective state.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phosphorylation of glucose is carried out by glucokinase, a glycolytic enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Releasing free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate is the role of glucose-6-phosphatase, deficient in von Gierke disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Regenerating reduced glutathione consumes the NADPH that G6PD produces; G6PD does not perform this step itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This final glycolytic step is catalyzed by pyruvate kinase, a separate enzyme.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with G6PD deficiency has a hemolytic episode after starting nitrofurantoin. The drug is stopped, and over the next several days his hemoglobin stabilizes and then rises without any transfusion. Which of the following best explains why most hemolytic events in this disorder are self-limiting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies formed against the drug are cleared within a few days

choices.label: B
choices.text: Newly made red blood cells have relatively more G6PD than older cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Older red blood cells have relatively more G6PD and replace the destroyed cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced glutathione is regenerated by pyruvate kinase once the drug stops

choices.label: E
choices.text: The liver conjugates the remaining free hemoglobin in the circulation

explanation.summary: Rapidly produced young red cells carry more G6PD, so most hemolytic events are self-limited.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most hemolytic events do not progress to severe anemia because newer red blood cells can be made rapidly and they contain relatively more G6PD than the older cells being destroyed. Because G6PD activity falls as a red cell ages, the older cells are the vulnerable ones, and treatment is usually unnecessary.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The hemolysis is from direct oxidative damage, not from drug-directed antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the relationship: enzyme activity declines with red cell age, so older cells have less G6PD and are more susceptible.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyruvate kinase generates ATP in glycolysis and has no role in regenerating reduced glutathione.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recovery reflects production of new, enzyme-replete red cells, not hepatic handling of free hemoglobin.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with G6PD deficiency develops fever and a rash followed by pallor and fatigue. Hemoglobin is 5.8 g/dL. Unlike his previous drug-triggered episodes, the reticulocyte count is low. Parvovirus B19 infection is confirmed. Which of the following best explains the low reticulocyte count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low reduced glutathione suppresses release of reticulocytes from marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reticulocytes contain less G6PD and are therefore destroyed preferentially

choices.label: C
choices.text: The virus consumes the iron required for new red cell production

choices.label: D
choices.text: The virus impairs the bone marrow's ability to produce red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus limits hemolysis to the spleen, so no reticulocytosis occurs

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 both oxidizes red cells and impairs the marrow's compensatory production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infections, particularly parvovirus B19, can have an oxidizing effect that causes hemolysis, and they also impair the bone marrow's ability to produce red blood cells to compensate for those destroyed. The blunted marrow response explains a low reticulocyte count despite ongoing hemolysis and severe anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Depletion of reduced glutathione leaves cells vulnerable to oxidation; it does not block reticulocyte release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Newly produced cells and reticulocytes have relatively higher G6PD activity, not lower.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The problem is impaired marrow production from the infection itself, not depletion of iron stores.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is mainly intravascular, and site of destruction does not explain an absent marrow response.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with G6PD deficiency is starting several new prescriptions, including treatment for a parasitic infection. Which of the following medications is an oxidizing agent that should be avoided in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetaminophen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amoxicillin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metformin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Omeprazole

choices.label: E
choices.text: Primaquine

explanation.summary: Primaquine is among the oxidizing drugs that trigger hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oxidizing drugs that trigger hemolysis in G6PD deficiency include sulfonamides, dapsone, cotrimoxazole, aspirin, primaquine, nitrofurantoin, chloramphenicol, and rasburicase. Primaquine, an antimalarial, is on that list and should be avoided.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetaminophen is not among the oxidizing agents identified as hemolytic triggers; aspirin is the analgesic on that list.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Amoxicillin is not among the oxidizing agents identified as hemolytic triggers in this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metformin is not among the oxidizing agents identified as hemolytic triggers in this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Omeprazole is not among the oxidizing agents identified as hemolytic triggers in this disorder.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with G6PD deficiency presents during a hemolytic crisis with dark urine and flank pain. The offending drug has been stopped. Her hemoglobin is 10.5 g/dL, which the team does not consider dangerously low. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin corticosteroid therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Give oral or intravenous volume repletion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perform an urgent splenectomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start iron chelation therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfuse two units of packed red blood cells

explanation.summary: Volume repletion prevents the nephrotoxic effects of hemoglobinuria during a hemolytic crisis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients in a hemolytic crisis should receive oral or intravenous volume repletion to prevent the nephrotoxic effects of hemoglobinuria. Filtered hemoglobin is toxic to the renal tubular cells, so maintaining volume protects the kidneys while the self-limited episode resolves.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corticosteroids are used in autoimmune hemolytic anemia and are not effective in G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Splenectomy is not part of the management of a G6PD hemolytic crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron chelation addresses iron overload from chronic transfusion, which is not the issue here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Red cell transfusion is reserved for hemoglobin levels that are dangerously low, which is not the case.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is in an acute hemolytic crisis from G6PD deficiency. Which of the following sets of results is most likely on his liver function panel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased indirect bilirubin, decreased haptoglobin, increased LDH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased direct bilirubin, decreased haptoglobin, decreased LDH

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased direct bilirubin, increased haptoglobin, decreased LDH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased indirect bilirubin, decreased haptoglobin, increased LDH

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased indirect bilirubin, increased haptoglobin, increased LDH

explanation.summary: Hemolysis produces increased indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and elevated LDH.
explanation.whyCorrect: As in other hemolytic anemias, a liver function panel during a G6PD crisis shows evidence of hemolysis: increased indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Indirect bilirubin rises rather than falls when red cells are destroyed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The bilirubin rise is in the indirect fraction, and LDH is elevated, not decreased.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemolysis raises indirect, not direct, bilirubin, and it lowers haptoglobin while raising LDH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haptoglobin is consumed and therefore falls in hemolysis rather than rising.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with known G6PD deficiency is seen for a routine health visit. He has had no recent illness and has avoided oxidizing agents for the past year. Which of the following is most likely on his complete blood count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low hemoglobin and hematocrit with a high mean corpuscular volume

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low hemoglobin and hematocrit with a normal mean corpuscular volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low hemoglobin with a markedly low leukocyte count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal hemoglobin with a markedly low platelet count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal hemoglobin, hematocrit, and mean corpuscular volume

explanation.summary: Between crises, the complete blood count in G6PD deficiency is generally normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with G6PD deficiency are often asymptomatic and are not anemic when triggers are successfully avoided. The low hemoglobin and hematocrit with a normal mean corpuscular volume are findings of an acute hemolytic episode; these values are generally normal when a crisis is not occurring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The mean corpuscular volume is normal in this hemolytic anemia, and he is not anemic at baseline.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is the pattern seen during an acute hemolytic crisis, not between episodes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukocyte counts are normal in G6PD deficiency; all lineages are not affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet counts are normal in G6PD deficiency; the defect is confined to red blood cells.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A smear from a patient recovering from a G6PD-related hemolytic episode shows rounded red cells with reduced membrane surface area and decreased flexibility. Which of the following best explains how these cells arose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inherited spectrin defect reduced the membrane surface area

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bite cells lost deformability and took on a spherical shape while circulating

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrin strands sheared the cells as they crossed small vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatic macrophages engulfed a portion of the cell cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxidized hemoglobin precipitated and compacted the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: Circulating bite cells round up into spherocytes, which are then cleared extravascularly.
explanation.whyCorrect: After splenic macrophages remove the membrane bearing a Heinz body, the resulting bite cells continue to circulate and their shape becomes less deformed and more rounded, producing spherocytes. These have reduced membrane surface and less flexibility, so they are often destroyed in the spleen by extravascular hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An inherited spectrin defect describes hereditary spherocytosis, a different cause of spherocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrin-strand shearing produces red cell fragments in a damaged vascular system, not spherocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The membrane removal that begins this sequence is performed by macrophages in the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Denatured globin clumping on the membrane forms Heinz bodies; it does not compact the whole cell.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a normocytic anemia and numerous spherocytes on her peripheral blood smear. Her physician notes that spherocytes are not specific to any single disorder. Which of the following conditions also characteristically produces spherocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic lead poisoning

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red cell pyruvate kinase deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Von Gierke glycogen storage disease

explanation.summary: Spherocytes occur in autoimmune hemolytic anemia and hereditary spherocytosis as well as in G6PD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spherocytes are also seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia and hereditary spherocytosis. Their presence therefore does not by itself establish an oxidant-induced hemolytic process and must be interpreted alongside the clinical history and other smear findings.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deficiency produces a microcytic hypochromic anemia rather than spherocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lead poisoning is not among the disorders that characteristically produce spherocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyruvate kinase deficiency has no characteristic red cell morphology; nonspecific echinocytes may be present instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Von Gierke disease is a glycogen storage disorder caused by glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, not a spherocytic anemia.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A Wright-Giemsa-stained smear drawn during a hemolytic episode in a patient with G6PD deficiency shows spherocytes, bite cells, and red cell fragments, but the characteristic intracellular inclusions of this disorder are not visible. Which of the following is required to visualize those inclusions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gram stain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Periodic acid-Schiff stain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prussian blue stain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Silver stain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vital stain

explanation.summary: Heinz bodies are demonstrated with vital stains, not with routine Wright-Giemsa staining.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heinz bodies, the clumps of denatured globin attached to the inner red cell membrane, are visualized with vital stains. A Wright-Giemsa-stained smear during a hemolytic episode can show spherocytes, bite cells, and red cell fragments, but it does not display the Heinz bodies themselves.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gram stain is used for bacteria and has no role in demonstrating red cell inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Periodic acid-Schiff is not the stain used to demonstrate these globin inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prussian blue demonstrates iron, whereas Heinz bodies are composed of denatured globin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Silver stain is not the stain used to demonstrate these globin inclusions.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman develops jaundice and dark urine several days after starting dapsone. Genetic testing shows that one of her X chromosomes carries a G6PD mutation and the other carries a normal G6PD allele. Which of the following best explains why she became symptomatic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heterozygous female carriers of this mutation are usually symptomatic

choices.label: B
choices.text: She inherited two mutant alleles, one from each parent

choices.label: C
choices.text: The disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern in females

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mutation was transmitted through maternal mitochondrial DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: X inactivation silenced her normal allele in most of her red cells

explanation.summary: A heterozygous female becomes symptomatic when her normal X chromosome is inactivated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Female carriers are almost always heterozygous, carrying one X with the mutation and one without, and are unlikely to show symptoms. A female may be symptomatic if she is homozygous or if inactivation of her normal X chromosome occurs, leaving red cells that express only the mutant allele.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heterozygous carriers are usually asymptomatic, which is why her presentation requires a further explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Her testing shows one mutant and one normal allele, so she is heterozygous rather than homozygous.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G6PD deficiency is passed in an X-linked pattern; autosomal recessive inheritance describes pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inheritance is tied to the X chromosome, not to maternal mitochondrial DNA.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: Two unrelated men both have G6PD deficiency confirmed by enzyme assay. One has never had symptoms despite occasional oxidant exposure, while the other has had several prominent hemolytic crises. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Older red cells in the asymptomatic man retain full enzyme activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Penetrance is variable, and partial deficiency causes few symptoms

choices.label: C
choices.text: The asymptomatic man hemolyzes only extravascularly, so it is silent

choices.label: D
choices.text: The symptomatic man also has an inherited pyruvate kinase deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: The symptomatic man's spleen removes Heinz bodies more efficiently

explanation.summary: Penetrance of G6PD deficiency is variable, so symptom severity tracks the degree of enzyme absence.
explanation.whyCorrect: In G6PD deficiency there is a complete or partial absence of the enzyme, and penetrance of the disease is variable. Patients with a partial deficiency may have few or no symptoms, whereas those with a more complete deficiency present with more prominent symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: G6PD activity declines as red cells age in everyone, making older cells more susceptible rather than fully protected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is mainly intravascular, and the severity difference is explained by residual enzyme activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is a separate autosomal recessive disorder and is not what distinguishes these two men.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic removal of Heinz-body-laden membrane produces bite cells; it is not the source of differing severity.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl with pyruvate kinase deficiency has a chronically low hemoglobin, yet she tolerates exertion better than expected for her degree of anemia. Which of the following red cell changes best accounts for this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased 2,3-BPG, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased 2,3-BPG, decreasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased ATP, increasing red blood cell deformability

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased fetal hemoglobin, increasing affinity for oxygen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased NADPH, increasing the level of reduced glutathione

explanation.summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency raises 2,3-BPG, which lowers hemoglobin's oxygen affinity and improves tissue delivery.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to lowering ATP, pyruvate kinase deficiency causes an increased level of 2,3-BPG. This decreases the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, so oxygen is released more readily to the tissues despite the anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2,3-BPG is increased rather than decreased in pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ATP is decreased in this disorder, which is what makes the red cells rigid and prone to hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The described change is an increase in 2,3-BPG with lower oxygen affinity, not a shift to fetal hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The NADPH and glutathione pathway is the one disrupted in G6PD deficiency, not pyruvate kinase deficiency.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A newborn of Northern European descent has a hemolytic anemia and is found to have pyruvate kinase deficiency. Both parents are healthy and have no history of anemia. Which of the following describes the inheritance of this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multifactorial

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked

explanation.summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive condition of Northern European populations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive condition occurring most commonly in patients of Northern European descent. Unaffected parents can each carry one mutant allele and pass the disorder to a child.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An autosomal dominant pattern would be expected to affect one of the parents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial inheritance would come through the mother, who is unaffected here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This disorder follows a defined single-gene recessive pattern rather than a multifactorial one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked inheritance describes G6PD deficiency, in which males usually manifest and females are carriers.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with severe pyruvate kinase deficiency and lifelong hemolysis develops episodic right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. Which of the following complications of chronic hemolysis is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gallstones

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gouty arthritis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatic adenoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nephrolithiasis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peptic ulcer disease

explanation.summary: Gallstones are a recognized complication of the chronic hemolysis in pyruvate kinase deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with severe hemolysis from pyruvate kinase deficiency may develop the complications of chronic hemolytic states, which include extramedullary hematopoiesis, gallstones, and iron overload. Postprandial right upper quadrant pain fits biliary colic from gallstones.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gouty arthritis is not among the complications attributed to chronic hemolysis in this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatic adenoma is not among the complications attributed to chronic hemolysis in this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nephrolithiasis is not among the complications attributed to chronic hemolysis in this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peptic ulcer disease is not among the complications attributed to chronic hemolysis in this disorder.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: An 8-year-old with pyruvate kinase deficiency has required red blood cell transfusions every few weeks for several years. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his long-term care?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daily oral iron supplementation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily vitamin E supplementation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron monitoring with chelation if needed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Routine corticosteroid therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weekly red cell enzyme activity assays

explanation.summary: Chronically transfused patients need iron monitoring and chelation because of iron overload risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because of the risk of iron overload in patients receiving chronic red cell transfusions, iron status is monitored regularly, with the addition of iron chelation therapy if necessary. Iron overload is one of the recognized complications of chronic hemolytic states managed by transfusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding iron would worsen the iron overload that chronic transfusion already causes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin E is not part of the management of this enzyme deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Corticosteroids are not a documented treatment for pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The enzyme deficiency is already established; repeated assays do not guide ongoing care.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear is reviewed in a patient with genetically confirmed pyruvate kinase deficiency. Which of the following findings is most likely to be present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bite cells (degmacytes)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Echinocytes (burr cells)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heinz bodies (denatured globin)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Red cell fragments (schistocytes)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Target cells (codocytes)

explanation.summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency has no characteristic morphology; nonspecific echinocytes may appear.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are no characteristic red blood cell morphologic findings in pyruvate kinase deficiency. Nonspecific changes such as echinocytes, also called burr cells, may be present, which is why diagnosis rests on enzyme assay or genetic testing rather than on the smear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bite cells are the characteristic finding of G6PD deficiency, formed when splenic macrophages remove Heinz-body-laden membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heinz bodies are denatured globin inclusions of oxidative injury, seen in G6PD deficiency rather than this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Red cell fragments are seen on the smear during a G6PD hemolytic episode, not as a feature of this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Target cells are not a described feature of pyruvate kinase deficiency.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 2-week-old infant has a hemolytic anemia with jaundice. The peripheral smear shows no characteristic morphologic abnormality. Which of the following will establish a diagnosis of pyruvate kinase deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Measurement of red cell G6PD activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Red cell enzyme assay or genetic testing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serial reticulocyte counts over several weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum haptoglobin and lactate dehydrogenase levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vital staining of the peripheral blood smear

explanation.summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is diagnosed by enzyme assay or genetic testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because there are no characteristic morphologic findings, the diagnosis of pyruvate kinase deficiency is typically made by either enzyme assay or genetic testing. This disorder is an important consideration whenever hemolytic anemia presents in a newborn.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Measuring G6PD activity tests for a different enzyme deficiency and would not identify this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reticulocyte counts reflect the marrow response to hemolysis and are not diagnostic of the enzyme defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Haptoglobin and lactate dehydrogenase confirm that hemolysis is occurring but do not identify its cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vital stains demonstrate Heinz bodies, an oxidative finding of G6PD deficiency, not this enzyme defect.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has had a mildly elevated indirect bilirubin and reticulocytosis on every blood test since childhood, but his hemoglobin has always been normal and he has never needed a transfusion. An older sibling with the same enzyme defect has required transfusions since birth. Which of the following best describes his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He has an oxidant-triggered hemolytic disorder that is now quiescent

choices.label: B
choices.text: He has fully compensated chronic hemolysis at the mild end of the spectrum

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is an unaffected carrier and does not have the enzyme defect

choices.label: D
choices.text: His enzyme activity is normal and the findings are unrelated to hemolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: His marrow has failed to respond, producing a compensated aplastic state

explanation.summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency spans mild compensated hemolysis to transfusion-dependent disease from birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical presentation of pyruvate kinase deficiency is highly variable, ranging from a mild, fully compensated chronic hemolysis without anemia to life-threatening transfusion-dependent hemolysis present at birth. Lifelong reticulocytosis and indirect hyperbilirubinemia with a normal hemoglobin fit the compensated end of that range, while his sibling sits at the severe end.

whyWrongByChoice.A: His hemolysis is chronic and continuous rather than episodic and oxidant-triggered.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ongoing reticulocytosis and indirect hyperbilirubinemia indicate real hemolysis, not a silent carrier state.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The indirect hyperbilirubinemia and reticulocytosis are direct evidence that red cells are being destroyed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reticulocytosis shows a vigorous marrow response, which is the opposite of marrow failure.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines hemolytic anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fall in hemoglobin caused by inadequate body iron stores

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anemia from blood loss exceeding the marrow's replacement rate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anemia from impaired DNA synthesis in red cell precursors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of the bone marrow to produce all three cell lineages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cells destroyed faster than new cells can be produced

explanation.summary: Hemolytic anemia occurs when red cell destruction outpaces red cell production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemolytic anemia occurs when red blood cells are being destroyed faster than new red blood cells can be produced. Hemolysis may result from metabolic changes within the red cell, increased red cell fragility, genetic abnormalities of the red cell membrane, immune destruction, oxidative stress in the blood, or physical damage as cells circulate through a damaged vascular system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inadequate iron stores produce a microcytic hypochromic anemia rather than hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blood loss removes red cells from the circulation; it does not destroy them within the body.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Impaired DNA synthesis in precursors describes megaloblastic anemia from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes aplastic anemia, in which marrow production of all lineages falls.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman develops fatigue, shortness of breath, and yellowing of the eyes. Laboratory studies show a low hemoglobin, a normal mean corpuscular volume, an elevated reticulocyte count, and an elevated indirect bilirubin. A peripheral blood smear shows numerous spherocytes, and a direct antiglobulin test is positive. Binding of which of the following antibodies to her red blood cells is the most likely cause of her anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-CD20 antibodies against B lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibodies against the C5 complement component

choices.label: C
choices.text: Biphasic IgG antibodies directed against the P antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG antibodies that bind most avidly at 37 C

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgM antibodies that bind most avidly below 30 C

explanation.summary: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is caused by IgG autoantibodies most active at body temperature.
explanation.whyCorrect: In warm AHA, IgG autoantibodies bind red blood cells most avidly at normal body temperature (37 C). IgG-coated RBCs are partially phagocytosed by splenic macrophages, losing membrane and rounding into fragile spherocytes, which explains the spherocytes on the smear and the positive direct antiglobulin test.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-CD20 describes rituximab, a treatment for AHA, not an autoantibody that causes the disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-C5 antibody describes eculizumab, a drug used for PNH, not a cause of warm AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Biphasic anti-P (Donath-Landsteiner) IgG causes paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, a self-limited disorder of children after viral infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgM cold agglutinins active below 30 C cause cold AHA, which produces RBC agglutinates rather than the spherocytes seen here.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man develops fatigue and jaundice one week after starting a cephalosporin antibiotic for pneumonia. A complete blood count reveals a low hemoglobin with a normal mean corpuscular volume, and a peripheral blood smear shows spherocytes. Which of the following test results would most specifically distinguish an autoimmune hemolytic anemia from other causes of hemolysis in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated indirect bilirubin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low blood hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal mean corpuscular volume

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive direct antiglobulin test

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spherocytes on the blood smear

explanation.summary: The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is what specifically identifies an autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The direct antiglobulin test detects antibody or complement coating the patient's red blood cells. It is positive in autoimmune hemolytic anemia but negative in nonimmune hemolytic anemias, so it specifically separates AHA from other causes of hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevated indirect bilirubin reflects any hemolysis and does not indicate an immune mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A low hemoglobin is present in essentially every anemia and is not specific for an immune cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A normal MCV occurs in many anemias, including numerous hemolytic anemias, so it is not specific.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spherocytes are also seen in hereditary spherocytosis and some infections, so they are not specific for AHA.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man recovering from Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection develops painful bluish discoloration of his fingers when outdoors in cold weather, along with fatigue. Laboratory studies show anemia with an elevated reticulocyte count, and a blood smear performed on cold blood shows clumping of red blood cells. Which of the following best describes the antibody responsible for his hemolysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibody against the GPI-anchored protein CD55

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgG monomer that binds most avidly at 37 C

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgM pentamer that agglutinates RBCs in the cold

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monoclonal antibody against complement component C5

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretory IgA dimer released onto mucosal surfaces

explanation.summary: Cold AHA is caused by IgM cold agglutinins that clump RBCs at cool temperatures.
explanation.whyCorrect: The autoantibodies in cold AHA are IgM 'cold agglutinins,' secreted as pentamers. A single IgM pentamer can bind up to 10 antigens, so it agglutinates several RBCs at once in cooler body regions, producing the clumping seen on a cold smear and the acrocyanosis. Cold AHA is classically triggered by Mycoplasma or EBV infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of the CD55 GPI anchor is the defect in PNH, not an autoantibody causing cold AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgG active at 37 C causes warm AHA, which produces spherocytes rather than cold-dependent agglutination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-C5 describes eculizumab, a PNH therapy, not the cold agglutinin responsible here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgA is not the mediator of autoimmune hemolytic anemia described in this brick.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is diagnosed with primary (idiopathic) warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eculizumab

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucocorticoids such as prednisone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydroxyurea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immediate splenectomy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Strict avoidance of cold temperatures

explanation.summary: Glucocorticoids are first-line therapy for warm AHA.
explanation.whyCorrect: For primary warm AHA, anti-inflammatory glucocorticoids such as prednisone are effective and are the first-line therapy. Rituximab is another option that reduces autoantibody production by depleting B cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eculizumab, an anti-C5 antibody, is used for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, not warm AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxyurea is a treatment for sickle cell disease and has no role in warm AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenectomy is reserved for warm AHA that is refractory to other therapies because of its infection risk, not as first-line treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Avoiding cold is a management strategy for cold AHA, not warm AHA.

questions.stem: A patient is evaluated for cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Which of the following laboratory findings would be LEAST likely in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased haptoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased mean corpuscular volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased reticulocyte count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive direct antiglobulin test

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red blood cell agglutination on the smear

explanation.summary: AHA is a normocytic anemia, so a decreased MCV is not expected.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm and cold) is normocytic, meaning the mean corpuscular volume is normal, not decreased. A decreased MCV would therefore be the least likely finding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Haptoglobin is decreased because it is consumed clearing free hemoglobin released by hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reticulocytes are increased as the bone marrow compensates for destroyed RBCs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A positive direct antiglobulin test is expected and is diagnostic of AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RBC agglutination may be seen on the peripheral smear in cold AHA.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with no significant past history presents with fatigue. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 6.4 g/dL, an MCV of 101 fL, mildly decreased white blood cell and platelet counts, and no morphologic abnormalities on the smear. Flow cytometry reveals a red blood cell population lacking CD55 and CD59 surface proteins. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Avoidance of cold temperatures

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corticosteroids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eculizumab

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydroxyurea

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy

explanation.summary: Absent CD55/CD59 by flow cytometry identifies PNH, treated with eculizumab.
explanation.whyCorrect: The absence of the GPI-anchored complement inhibitors CD55 and CD59, combined with pancytopenia and hemolysis, indicates paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. Eculizumab, a recombinant antibody against complement C5, decreases hemolysis and thrombosis risk and is the appropriate treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Avoiding cold treats cold AHA, not the complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis of PNH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corticosteroids are used for warm AHA and are not the treatment for PNH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxyurea is used for sickle cell disease, not PNH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy targets extravascular splenic hemolysis; PNH hemolysis is intravascular, so it would not help.

questions.stem: In warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, spherocytes appear on the peripheral blood smear. Which of the following best explains how these spherocytes are formed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A splenic macrophage removes a portion of the antibody-coated RBC membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: An inherited mutation in the RBC membrane cytoskeleton produces the spheres from birth

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgM pentamers cross-link and physically clump red blood cells together

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of CD55 and CD59 anchors makes cells prone to complement lysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: The membrane attack complex lyses cells directly within the vasculature

explanation.summary: Spherocytes form when a splenic macrophage removes part of the antibody-coated RBC membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: In warm AHA, a splenic macrophage sometimes removes only a chunk of the IgG-coated RBC membrane rather than the whole cell. The remaining RBC seals the hole and, having lost membrane, loses its biconcave shape and rounds up into a fragile spherocyte that continues to circulate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An inherited cytoskeletal defect describes hereditary spherocytosis, not the acquired spherocytes of warm AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgM cross-linking causes RBC agglutination in cold AHA, not the individual spherocytes of warm AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of CD55/CD59 is the mechanism of PNH, unrelated to spherocyte formation in warm AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Membrane attack complex lysis is intravascular hemolysis and does not create surviving spherocytes.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia has persistent severe hemolysis despite glucocorticoids and rituximab. Splenectomy is being considered. Which feature of warm AHA best explains why removing the spleen would be expected to reduce his hemolysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most hemolysis in warm AHA occurs extravascularly in the spleen

choices.label: B
choices.text: The spleen is the primary source of the IgM cold agglutinins

choices.label: C
choices.text: The spleen manufactures haptoglobin that drives hemolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: The spleen produces the CD55 and CD59 complement inhibitors

choices.label: E
choices.text: The spleen synthesizes the C5b-9 membrane attack complex

explanation.summary: Warm AHA hemolysis is predominantly extravascular in the spleen, so splenectomy can reduce it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bulk of hemolysis in warm AHA is extravascular, occurring when splenic macrophages phagocytose IgG-coated RBCs. Removing the spleen eliminates this main site of destruction and mostly cures the hemolysis, though it is reserved for refractory cases because of infection risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Warm AHA is mediated by IgG, not IgM cold agglutinins, and the spleen is not their source.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Haptoglobin is a plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin and does not drive hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD55 and CD59 are GPI-anchored proteins on blood cells; their loss defines PNH and is unrelated to the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The membrane attack complex is a complement product, not something synthesized by the spleen.

questions.stem: A patient with cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia has symptoms that persist despite avoiding cold exposure. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate if therapy is needed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic RBC transfusion alone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrocortisone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prednisone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rituximab

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy

explanation.summary: Rituximab may be useful in cold AHA, whereas glucocorticoids and splenectomy are not.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cold AHA is harder to treat than warm AHA, but rituximab may be useful. Glucocorticoids and splenectomy have not been found to be clinically useful in cold AHA, so rituximab is the best listed option when pharmacologic therapy is required.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transfusion offers only temporary support and does not remove the autoantibodies; it is not definitive therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydrocortisone is also a glucocorticoid, which is not effective in cold AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prednisone, a glucocorticoid, has not been found clinically useful in cold AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is not useful in cold AHA because its hemolysis is not predominantly splenic extravascular destruction.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops sudden fatigue and passes dark red urine two weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. Testing reveals a peculiar antibody that binds red blood cells at cold temperatures and fixes complement, then causes intravascular hemolysis as the blood rewarms. The disorder is self-limited. Which of the following antibodies is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-CD20 antibody against B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibody against the C5 complement component

choices.label: C
choices.text: Biphasic IgG anti-P antibody

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgM cold agglutinin against the I antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm-reactive IgG against Rh antigens

explanation.summary: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria is caused by the biphasic Donath-Landsteiner IgG anti-P antibody.
explanation.whyCorrect: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria commonly occurs in children after a viral infection or vaccination. It is caused by a biphasic IgG antibody against the P antigen (the Donath-Landsteiner antibody) that fixes complement at cool temperatures and completes hemolysis at warmer temperatures, causing intravascular hemolysis. It is usually self-limited.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-CD20 describes rituximab, a therapy, not an autoantibody causing this disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-C5 describes eculizumab, used in PNH, not the antibody responsible for PCH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgM cold agglutinins cause cold AHA with agglutination, not the biphasic IgG mechanism of PCH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warm-reactive IgG causes warm AHA, which is extravascular and not the biphasic, cold-triggered process described.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has chronic intravascular hemolysis, mild pancytopenia, and a recent portal vein thrombosis. Hemolytic workup shows elevated LDH and reticulocytes with low haptoglobin, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which of the following is the key diagnostic test for his suspected condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indirect antiglobulin test

choices.label: E
choices.text: Osmotic fragility test

explanation.summary: The PNH triad with a negative DAT points to PNH, diagnosed by flow cytometry for CD55/CD59.
explanation.whyCorrect: The triad of DAT-negative hemolytic anemia, pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis (here, portal vein) is characteristic of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. The key diagnostic test is flow cytometry on peripheral blood demonstrating the absence of the CD55 and CD59 GPI anchors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The direct antiglobulin test is negative in PNH and is used to diagnose autoimmune hemolytic anemia instead.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin electrophoresis detects hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease, not PNH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The indirect antiglobulin test detects circulating antibodies (pretransfusion/pregnancy screening) and does not diagnose PNH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osmotic fragility testing evaluates hereditary spherocytosis, not PNH.

questions.stem: In the direct antiglobulin test used to diagnose autoimmune hemolytic anemia, the patient's red blood cells are mixed with antihuman immunoglobulin (Coombs reagent). Which of the following best explains why this test can detect both warm and cold AHA?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reagent binds the GPI-anchored proteins CD55 and CD59 on RBCs

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reagent contains both anti-IgG and anticomplement antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reagent detects the P blood group antigen on the RBC surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reagent directly lyses only spherocytes already coated with IgG

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reagent measures the level of free haptoglobin in the serum

explanation.summary: Antihuman immunoglobulin (AHG) combines anti-IgG and anticomplement, detecting both AHA types.
explanation.whyCorrect: AHG (Coombs reagent) is a combination of anti-IgG and anticomplement antibodies. It agglutinates RBCs coated with IgG (warm AHA) or with complement and IgM (cold AHA), so a positive DAT detects both types while remaining negative in nonimmune hemolytic anemias.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD55 and CD59 are tested by flow cytometry for PNH, not by the Coombs reagent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The P antigen relates to the Donath-Landsteiner antibody in PCH and is not what AHG detects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The DAT works by agglutination of coated RBCs, not by lysing spherocytes, and it is not limited to IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haptoglobin is measured by a separate serum study, not by antihuman immunoglobulin.

questions.stem: A hematology fellow is preparing a brief teaching session on autoimmune hemolytic anemia for a group of medical students. Which of the following best describes the epidemiology of this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 to 3 cases per 1,000 people per year, more often in females

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1 to 3 cases per 100,000 people per year, more often in females

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1 to 3 cases per 100,000 people per year, more often in males

choices.label: D
choices.text: 30 to 50 cases per 1,000 people per year, more often in males

choices.label: E
choices.text: 30 to 50 cases per 100,000 people per year, mostly in children

explanation.summary: AHA is rare, with an estimated 1 to 3 cases per 100,000 individuals per year and a female predominance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is a relatively rare condition with an estimated incidence of 1 to 3 cases in 100,000 individuals per year. More cases occur in females and in older individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A rate of 1 to 3 per 1,000 would make AHA roughly a hundred times more common than it actually is.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The incidence figure is right, but AHA is more common in females, not males.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both the rate and the sex predominance are wrong for AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This rate is far too high, and AHA occurs more often in older individuals than in children.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia reports a vague sense of abdominal fullness that has developed over several months. On examination, the spleen is palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Which of the following best explains her abdominal symptom?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capsular stretching from a subcapsular splenic hematoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis replacing splenic white pulp

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deposition in splenic macrophages from prior transfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Portal vein thrombosis obstructing splenic venous outflow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration of abnormal red blood cells

explanation.summary: Splenomegaly in AHA reflects splenic sequestration of abnormal red blood cells and can be felt as abdominal fullness.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with AHA may note a sense of abdominal fullness caused by splenomegaly. The spleen enlarges because it sequesters the abnormal, antibody-coated red blood cells and its macrophages phagocytose them, which is also the site of the extravascular hemolysis in warm AHA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A subcapsular hematoma implies trauma and would cause acute pain rather than months of gradual fullness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Extramedullary hematopoiesis is not the mechanism of splenic enlargement described in autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transfusional iron loading is not what produces the splenomegaly of AHA, and this patient's enlargement developed with her hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Venous thrombosis of the portal vein is a feature of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, not a mechanism of splenomegaly in warm AHA.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man develops fatigue and jaundice. Laboratory studies show a normocytic anemia with an elevated reticulocyte count and a positive direct antiglobulin test, and his physician suspects a drug-induced warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Which of the following medications on his list is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atorvastatin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Levothyroxine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lisinopril

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metformin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quinidine

explanation.summary: Quinidine is among the medications classically implicated as a cause of warm AHA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Medications are a major cause of warm AHA. The drugs implicated include quinidine, chemotherapy agents, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories, and some antibiotics, especially beta lactams such as penicillins and cephalosporins. Of the listed medications, only quinidine belongs to this group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atorvastatin is not listed among the medications that trigger warm AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Levothyroxine is hormone replacement and is not associated with drug-induced AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lisinopril is not among the drug classes implicated in warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metformin is not a recognized cause of autoimmune hemolysis.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is newly diagnosed with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. He takes no medications and has had no recent infection, so his physician evaluates him for an underlying condition. Which of the following findings would most likely be identified as the cause of his AHA?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gastroesophageal reflux disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osteoarthritis of both knees

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subclinical hypothyroidism

explanation.summary: Leukemias, lymphomas, and other lymphoproliferative disorders are recognized underlying causes of secondary AHA.
explanation.whyCorrect: When AHA is not idiopathic, it is associated with underlying conditions including acute infections, chronic inflammatory diseases, other autoimmune disorders, leukemias, lymphomas, and lymphoproliferative disorders, and solid cancers. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia falls squarely within that group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is not a malignancy and is not an associated cause of AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reflux disease has no described association with autoimmune destruction of red blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease, not one of the chronic inflammatory or autoimmune disorders linked to AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypothyroidism is not among the conditions associated with autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

questions.stem: In warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, IgG-coated red blood cells are removed from the circulation as they travel through the spleen. Which of the following properties of splenic macrophages best explains their ability to recognize these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Receptors for the Fc portion of antibodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Secretion of the membrane attack complex onto coated cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surface CD20 that binds immunoglobulin light chains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surface CD55 that binds complement regulatory proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toll-like receptors that recognize bacterial lipopolysaccharide

explanation.summary: Splenic macrophages carry Fc receptors that bind the constant portion of IgG coating red blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: As IgG-coated RBCs pass through the spleen they encounter macrophages that have receptors for the Fc portion of antibodies. When a splenic macrophage engages an IgG-coated RBC it often phagocytoses the entire cell, which is why extravascular hemolysis predominates in warm AHA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The membrane attack complex is a complement product assembled on target membranes, not a macrophage secretion used for recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD20 is a B-lymphocyte marker and the target of rituximab, not a macrophage receptor for IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD55 is a GPI-anchored complement inhibitor on blood cells; its loss defines PNH and it is not the macrophage recognition receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toll-like receptors sense microbial products and are not what identifies antibody-coated red cells.

questions.stem: A patient with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia has numerous spherocytes on the peripheral blood smear, and these cells lyse as they pass through small capillaries throughout the body. Which of the following best explains why spherocytes are more fragile than normal red blood cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are cross-linked by IgM pentamers into rigid clusters of cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: They carry a mutated spectrin cytoskeleton inherited from a parent

choices.label: C
choices.text: They contain polymerized hemoglobin that stiffens the interior of the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: They have lost the CD59 anchor that blocks the membrane attack complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: They lack the extra membrane that allows normal RBCs to contort and regain shape

explanation.summary: Spherocytes have lost surface membrane, so they cannot deform to squeeze through capillaries and burst instead.
explanation.whyCorrect: A spherocyte forms after a splenic macrophage removes a chunk of membrane from an antibody-coated RBC. Spherocytes lack the extra membrane that lets a normal biconcave RBC contort while passing through tiny holes and then regain its shape, so they burst as they try to pass through tiny capillaries. This lysis can happen anywhere in the body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgM cross-linking produces the red cell agglutinates of cold AHA, not the fragility of individual spherocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An inherited cytoskeletal mutation describes hereditary spherocytosis, not the acquired membrane loss of warm AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Polymerized hemoglobin stiffening the cell describes sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of CD59 is the defect of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and is unrelated to spherocyte fragility.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is evaluated for a lifelong normocytic anemia with jaundice. A peripheral blood smear shows numerous spherocytes, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

explanation.summary: Spherocytes with a negative direct antiglobulin test point away from AHA and toward hereditary spherocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: AHA is not the sole cause of spherocytes; they are also seen in hereditary spherocytosis, hyposplenism, transfusion reactions, and some infections. The direct antiglobulin test is positive in AHA but negative in nonimmune hemolytic anemias such as hereditary spherocytosis, so a negative DAT with lifelong spherocytosis identifies the inherited membrane disorder.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cold AHA gives a positive DAT and shows red cell agglutinates rather than spherocytes on the smear.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria occurs in children after viral illness with episodic hemoglobinuria, not lifelong spherocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PNH also has a negative DAT, but its smear shows no morphologic abnormalities and it presents with intravascular hemolysis, pancytopenia, and thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warm AHA produces spherocytes but would give a positive direct antiglobulin test.

questions.stem: The autoantibodies of cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia are secreted as pentamers, which are clusters of five antibody molecules. How many antigens can a single one of these pentamers bind?

explanation.summary: A single IgM pentamer has 10 antigen-binding sites, which is why it can clump several red cells at once.
explanation.whyCorrect: IgM antibodies are secreted as pentamers, clusters of five antibody molecules, and a single IgM pentamer can bind 10 antigens. This high valency lets one pentamer attach to several red blood cells simultaneously, forming the big clumps (agglutinates) characteristic of cold AHA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two binding sites is the valency of a single monomeric antibody such as IgG, not of an IgM pentamer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Five is the number of antibody molecules in the pentamer, not the number of antigens it binds.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Twenty would require ten antibody molecules rather than the five in a pentamer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fifty greatly overstates the binding capacity of an IgM pentamer.

questions.stem: IgM cold agglutinins activate the complement system more efficiently than IgG antibodies do, yet most of the hemolysis in cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia still takes place outside the blood vessels. Which of the following best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C3b is more readily formed and more potent than the C5b-9 complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgM activates complement less efficiently than the IgG of warm AHA

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgM pentamers detach from RBCs before terminal complement can be assembled

choices.label: D
choices.text: The membrane attack complex forms only at temperatures below 30 C

choices.label: E
choices.text: The spleen strips complement fragments from RBCs faster than the MAC assembles

explanation.summary: C3b-mediated splenic phagocytosis outweighs C5b-9 lysis, so extravascular hemolysis predominates even in cold AHA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemolysis in cold AHA occurs either through C3b-mediated phagocytosis in the spleen or through membrane attack complex (C5b-9)-mediated intravascular hemolysis. Because C3b is more readily formed and more potent than the C5b-9 complex, extravascular hemolysis is the predominant mechanism, although intravascular hemolysis is more common in cold AHA than in warm AHA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IgM actually activates complement more efficiently than IgG, which is the premise of the question.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cold agglutinins do fall off in warmer regions, but that explains the distribution of symptoms, not why C3b-driven phagocytosis dominates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The membrane attack complex is not temperature restricted in this way; it is the antibody binding that is cold dependent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic macrophages phagocytose C3b-coated cells rather than stripping complement fragments off them.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia develops pain and bluish discoloration of her fingertips while outdoors in winter, but she has no symptoms referable to her trunk. Which of the following best explains why her symptoms are confined to the extremities?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cold agglutinins detach from RBCs as blood circulates through warmer regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement proteins are absent from the central circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgM pentamers are too large to enter the capillaries of the trunk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenic macrophages clear coated cells before they reach the extremities

choices.label: E
choices.text: The target red cell antigen is expressed only on cells in the digits

explanation.summary: Cold agglutinins bind in the cool extremities and fall off again once the blood reaches warmer central regions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Symptoms in cold AHA are most often in the body extremities, which are usually the coldest parts of the body. Cold antibodies tend to bind red blood cells in cooler regions such as the fingertips, but the antibodies fall off the RBCs when the blood circulates through warmer regions such as the trunk, which confines the acrocyanosis and pain to the digits.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement proteins circulate throughout the body and are not absent centrally.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgM size does not restrict its access to the central circulation; the temperature dependence of binding is what matters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic macrophages clear antibody-coated cells but do not create a regional distribution of cold symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Red cells carry the same surface antigens regardless of where in the circulation they happen to be.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection is found to have cold agglutinin-mediated hemolysis. He has been hospitalized in a warm room and has had no cold exposure, yet his hemolysis continues. Which of the following best explains his ongoing hemolysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cold agglutinins generated by infection are IgG rather than IgM

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement activation raises the binding threshold above 37 C

choices.label: C
choices.text: His antibody is a biphasic antibody directed against the P antigen

choices.label: D
