choices.text: Infection-associated cold agglutinins can act at normal body temperature

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm and cold AHA always coexist in patients with pneumonia

explanation.summary: Cold AHA generally requires temperatures under 30 C but can occur at normal body temperature, especially when infection-related.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cold AHA usually occurs in cold weather and generally requires a temperature of under 30 C (86 F), but it can sometimes also occur at normal body temperature, especially when it is caused by infections such as Mycoplasma. That is why this patient continues to hemolyze without cold exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The autoantibodies in cold AHA are IgM cold agglutinins; infection does not convert them to IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement is activated after the antibody binds; it does not change the temperature at which binding occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A biphasic IgG antibody against the P antigen describes paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, a different disorder that follows viral illness in children.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warm and cold AHA are distinct entities and do not routinely coexist.

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a patient with autoimmune hemolytic anemia is reviewed. In addition to spherocytes, which of the following findings is most likely to be seen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basophilic stippling and ringed sideroblasts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypersegmented neutrophils and macro-ovalocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reticulocytes and red blood cell fragments

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rouleaux formation and circulating plasma cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Target cells and Howell-Jolly bodies

explanation.summary: Besides spherocytes, the AHA smear may show reticulocytes and red blood cell fragments.
explanation.whyCorrect: The peripheral blood smear in warm AHA typically shows spherocytes, and it may also show reticulocytes and red blood cell fragments, as is seen in many types of hemolytic anemia. The reticulocytes reflect the marrow's compensatory production of new red cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophilic stippling and ringed sideroblasts point to sideroblastic anemia or lead exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypersegmented neutrophils and macro-ovalocytes indicate a megaloblastic anemia, not hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rouleaux and circulating plasma cells suggest a plasma cell dyscrasia rather than autoimmune hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Howell-Jolly bodies indicate absent splenic function, the opposite of the active splenic clearance in warm AHA.

questions.stem: A patient is being evaluated for suspected cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia. A peripheral smear prepared from blood held at 37 C shows no clumping of red blood cells, while a smear prepared from the same patient's chilled blood shows prominent clumping. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cold agglutinins bind red blood cells avidly only at cooler temperatures

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement proteins are irreversibly inactivated at body temperature

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgM pentamers are enzymatically degraded by plasma proteases when warmed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spherocytes replace the red cell agglutinates as the blood sample warms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warming converts the bound IgM antibodies into warm-reactive IgG

explanation.summary: Agglutinates appear on a cold AHA smear only when the blood is cold, because the IgM binds avidly only at cool temperatures.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood smears from patients with cold AHA may show RBC agglutinates if the smear is performed on cold blood. The IgM cold agglutinins bind most avidly at cooler temperatures, usually under 30 C, and detach as the blood warms, so a smear made from warm blood will not show the clumps.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement is not inactivated at body temperature, and agglutination here is produced by antibody cross-linking rather than complement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The antibodies release the red cells when warmed; they are not enzymatically destroyed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spherocytes are the hallmark of warm AHA and do not form from agglutinates on warming.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An antibody's class is fixed when it is secreted and does not convert with temperature.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia has an elevated reticulocyte count and indirect hyperbilirubinemia, but his free haptoglobin level is only minimally reduced. Which of the following best explains this laboratory pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Haptoglobin rises as an acute phase reactant, masking its consumption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemolysis is mostly extravascular, so little free hemoglobin enters the plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Indirect bilirubin blocks hepatic clearance of haptoglobin complexes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reticulocytes synthesize haptoglobin to replace what hemolysis consumes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spherocytes bind haptoglobin and return it to the circulation

explanation.summary: Haptoglobin falls when hemoglobin is released into plasma, so extravascular hemolysis spares it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Haptoglobin is consumed binding the free hemoglobin that lysing red cells release into the blood. In warm AHA the hemolysis is mostly extravascular, taking place inside splenic macrophages, so relatively little free hemoglobin reaches the plasma and the free haptoglobin level does not change much even though bilirubin and reticulocytes are clearly abnormal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The near-normal level here reflects the site of hemolysis, not an acute phase rise in production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Indirect bilirubin is a product of heme breakdown and does not interfere with clearance of haptoglobin complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reticulocytes are immature red cells; haptoglobin is a plasma protein they do not produce.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin, not intact spherocytes, and is not recycled back to the plasma.

questions.stem: A physician orders an indirect antiglobulin test, in which a patient's serum is mixed with test red blood cells and antihuman immunoglobulin is added. Which of the following is the most common current indication for this test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confirming autoimmune hemolytic anemia when the direct test is positive

choices.label: B
choices.text: Detecting the absence of CD55 and CD59 on red blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monitoring the response to rituximab in warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Screening for antibodies before a blood transfusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Screening newborns for hereditary spherocytosis

explanation.summary: The indirect antiglobulin test is used mainly for pretransfusion antibody screening and in early pregnancy, not for diagnosing AHA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The indirect antiglobulin test detects circulating antibodies in the patient's serum, and agglutination of the test red cells after AHG is added indicates such an antibody. It is not routinely used to diagnose most cases of AHA; it is done mostly to test for antibodies prior to blood transfusion to avoid hemolysis, and in pregnant patients in the first trimester to look for antibodies incompatible with the fetus's red blood cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AHA is diagnosed with the direct antiglobulin test, which examines the patient's own red cells rather than the serum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Absent CD55 and CD59 are detected by flow cytometry on peripheral blood, the key test for PNH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The indirect test is not used to follow treatment response in warm AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hereditary spherocytosis is a nonimmune disorder and gives negative antiglobulin testing.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man with known sickle cell disease is admitted with an episode of hemolysis. A direct antiglobulin test is performed as part of the workup. Which of the following results is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Negative, because his red cells are not coated with antibody or complement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Negative, because his spleen has undergone autoinfarction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Positive, because circulating reticulocytes bind antihuman immunoglobulin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive, because hemolysis releases free hemoglobin into the plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Positive, because sickled cells activate the alternative complement pathway

explanation.summary: The direct antiglobulin test is positive only when red cells are coated with antibody or complement, so it is negative in nonimmune hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The DAT mixes the patient's red blood cells with antihuman immunoglobulin, which agglutinates cells coated with IgG or complement. It is positive in both warm and cold AHA but negative in other forms of hemolytic anemia such as sickle cell disease and hereditary spherocytosis, where the red cells carry no antibody coating.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The test would be negative because his cells are uncoated; splenic status does not determine the DAT result.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reticulocytes are not coated with immunoglobulin and do not produce a positive DAT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Free plasma hemoglobin lowers haptoglobin but has no effect on the direct antiglobulin test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sickle cell disease causes hemolysis through polymerized hemoglobin and vaso-occlusion, not antibody or complement coating of red cells.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with severe warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and a hemoglobin of 5.8 g/dL receives two units of packed red blood cells. Her hemoglobin rises only briefly and hemolysis continues. Which of the following best explains this outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Donor plasma supplies complement that lyses her own red blood cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her autoantibodies remain in circulation and coat the transfused cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stored blood is infused at a temperature below 30 C

choices.label: D
choices.text: The transfused red blood cells lack the CD55 and CD59 anchors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion suppresses release of reticulocytes from the marrow

explanation.summary: Transfusion does not remove autoantibodies, so the newly transfused cells are attacked as well.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with anemia can be temporarily managed with RBC transfusion, but transfusion must be used with caution in AHA because it does not remove the autoantibodies. The circulating antibodies coat the donor red cells just as they coated the patient's own, so hemolysis continues and the benefit is short-lived.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The problem is the recipient's own autoantibody, not complement supplied in donor plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The temperature of the infused unit is not the reason transfusion fails in warm AHA, where the antibody is active at 37 C.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Missing CD55 and CD59 is the acquired defect of PNH in the patient's own stem cell clone, not a property of donor units.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marrow suppression would lower reticulocytes but would not produce continued hemolysis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man started quinidine for an arrhythmia 10 days ago and now has fatigue, jaundice, and a normocytic anemia with a positive direct antiglobulin test. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin a chronic transfusion program

choices.label: B
choices.text: Begin eculizumab

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perform splenectomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start hydroxyurea

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop the offending drug

explanation.summary: For secondary AHA, removing the inciting cause is the best treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Removing the underlying cause, such as stopping the offending medication or treating an underlying cancer or infection, is the best treatment for suspected secondary AHA. Quinidine is a recognized trigger of warm AHA, so stopping it is the first step.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic transfusion does not remove the autoantibody and would not address the drug trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eculizumab, an anti-C5 antibody, is a therapy for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Splenectomy is reserved for warm AHA refractory to other therapies because of its infection risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxyurea is a treatment for sickle cell disease and has no role here.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman has warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia refractory to glucocorticoids and rituximab, and splenectomy is planned. Which of the following long-term risks should be emphasized in counseling her before surgery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aplastic anemia from marrow failure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infection with encapsulated bacteria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deficiency anemia from blood loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Portal vein thrombosis from chronic hemolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secondary myelodysplastic syndrome

explanation.summary: Splenectomy can largely cure warm AHA but leaves the patient vulnerable to encapsulated organisms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the bulk of hemolysis in warm AHA is extravascular and occurs in the spleen, splenectomy mostly cures the hemolysis. However, removing the spleen carries risks such as increased infections due to encapsulated bacteria, which is why the operation is reserved for cases refractory to other therapies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aplastic anemia is associated with PNH, not with removal of the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency is not a described consequence of splenectomy in warm AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Venous thrombosis, including portal vein thrombosis, is a feature of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria rather than a consequence of splenectomy for AHA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myelodysplastic syndrome is not among the risks attributed to splenectomy here.

questions.stem: A patient with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia who has not responded adequately to prednisone is started on rituximab. Which of the following best describes how this medication reduces hemolysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks C5, preventing assembly of the membrane attack complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: It destroys CD20-bearing B cells, preventing autoantibody production

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases marrow reticulocyte output to offset the hemolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It replaces the missing CD55 and CD59 GPI anchors on red cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It suppresses Fc receptor expression on splenic macrophages

explanation.summary: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 biologic that depletes B cells and thereby reduces autoantibody production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 biologic medication that stimulates destruction of B cells. Because CD20 is present on B lymphocytes, rituximab is useful in preventing the creation of the autoantibodies that drive hemolysis in AHA, and it is an option in both warm and cold disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking C5 describes eculizumab, which is used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rituximab does not work by stimulating red cell production in the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nothing replaces the missing GPI anchors of PNH, and warm AHA does not involve that defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rituximab acts on B lymphocytes, not on macrophage Fc receptors.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with chronic intravascular hemolysis has flow cytometry showing red blood cells that lack CD55 and CD59. Which of the following genetic abnormalities underlies his disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired mutation of the JAK2 gene in a myeloid clone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acquired mutation of the PIGA gene on the X chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acquired translocation producing a BCR-ABL fusion gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inherited mutation of a red blood cell membrane cytoskeleton gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inherited point mutation in the beta-globin gene

explanation.summary: PNH arises from an acquired PIGA mutation that prevents formation of GPI anchors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is a clonal, non-malignant disorder of hematopoietic stem cells caused by an acquired mutation of the PIGA gene on the X chromosome. The defect prevents formation of glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors for complement inhibitors such as CD55 and CD59, leaving red cells, white cells, and platelets susceptible to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: JAK2 mutations drive myeloproliferative neoplasms and do not cause loss of CD55 and CD59.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A BCR-ABL fusion defines chronic myeloid leukemia, a malignant myeloproliferative disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An inherited membrane cytoskeleton defect describes hereditary spherocytosis, which gives spherocytes and a negative DAT rather than absent GPI anchors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A beta-globin point mutation produces sickle cell disease, in which GPI anchors are intact.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with newly diagnosed paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria reports that on several occasions he has passed unexpectedly red or pink urine on first waking. Which of the following statements about this symptom is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It indicates that portal vein thrombosis has already occurred

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is produced by myoglobin released from muscle overnight

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the presenting symptom in nearly all patients with the disorder

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurs in about one quarter of patients with the disorder

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reflects extravascular destruction of red cells within the spleen

explanation.summary: The morning hemoglobinuria that names PNH is uncommon, occurring in roughly 25% of patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: PNH takes its name from a unique but uncommon symptom, present in about 25% of patients, in which patients pass unexpected red or pink urine first thing in the morning. Most patients instead present with chronic intravascular hemolysis rather than these dramatic episodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Venous thrombosis is a separate complication of PNH and is not signaled by morning hemoglobinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The discoloration comes from hemoglobin released by lysed red cells, not from muscle myoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Far from universal, this presentation occurs in only about a quarter of patients.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PNH hemolysis is complement-mediated and intravascular; the pigment in the urine comes from hemoglobin released into the plasma.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is about to begin eculizumab. Which of the following is the most important step to take before starting this medication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron chelation to prevent iron overload

choices.label: B
choices.text: Splenectomy to reduce extravascular hemolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Starting lifelong anticoagulation with warfarin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Testing family members for the causative mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaccination against Neisseria species

explanation.summary: Blocking C5 with eculizumab raises the risk of Neisseria infection, so patients must be vaccinated first.
explanation.whyCorrect: Eculizumab decreases hemolysis and the risk of thrombosis and improves quality of life in PNH, but because it blocks the terminal complement pathway it increases the risk of Neisseria infections. Patients therefore have to be vaccinated prior to its use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron chelation is not a prerequisite for starting eculizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Splenectomy would not help in PNH, where the hemolysis is complement-mediated and intravascular.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eculizumab itself reduces thrombotic risk, and lifelong warfarin is not the required step before starting it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The PIGA mutation of PNH is acquired in a hematopoietic stem cell clone, so family testing is not indicated.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria asks which of his treatment options could actually cure the disease rather than control it. Which of the following should he be told is potentially curative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic red blood cell transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eculizumab

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate supplementation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hematopoietic stem cell transplant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenectomy

explanation.summary: Stem cell transplant is the one curative therapy for PNH, though it is used less often now.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment strategies for PNH include supportive care, such as folate supplementation and transfusion when needed, and eculizumab. Stem cell transplant is a curative therapy because it replaces the abnormal hematopoietic stem cell clone, but it is not tolerated by all patients and has become less common with the effective use of eculizumab.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transfusion is temporary supportive care and does not correct the underlying defect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eculizumab controls hemolysis and thrombosis risk but does not eliminate the abnormal stem cell clone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate supplementation is supportive care that helps sustain red cell production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy does not help in PNH because the hemolysis is intravascular rather than splenic.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman is evaluated for fatigue and a burning sensation in her upper abdomen. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL and an MCV of 112 fL. Serum vitamin B12 is low. Endoscopy reveals chronic atrophic gastritis, and serum antibodies against gastric parietal cells and intrinsic factor are detected. Which of the following best explains the impaired vitamin B12 absorption in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tapeworm competes for B12 in the terminal ileum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoantibodies destroy parietal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dietary intake of B12 is inadequate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methotrexate blocks conversion of B12 to its active form

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pancreatic enzymes fail to free B12 from transcobalamin

explanation.summary: Pernicious anemia is caused by autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells and loss of intrinsic factor.
explanation.whyCorrect: In pernicious anemia, autoantibodies against parietal cells or intrinsic factor destroy the gastric parietal cells. This leads to decreased gastric acidity and loss of the intrinsic factor needed for intestinal absorption of vitamin B12, and it is typically seen in patients with chronic gastritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The fish tapeworm Diphyllobothrium latum competes for B12 in the terminal ileum, but this patient has autoantibodies and gastritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dietary deficiency of B12 (e.g., strict vegan diet) is not associated with antiparietal cell or anti-intrinsic factor antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate impairs folate, not B12, and it inhibits conversion of folate to its active form rather than causing gastritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failure to free B12 from its transcobalamin protector describes pancreatic insufficiency, not the autoimmune gastritis seen here.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man reports 3 months of progressive numbness and unsteady gait. Neurologic examination shows decreased vibration and position sense in the lower extremities with hyperreflexia. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL and MCV is 108 fL. Which of the following serum metabolites is most likely to be elevated as a direct result of this patient's deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Methionine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methylmalonic acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Succinyl-CoA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tetrahydrofolate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12

explanation.summary: In vitamin B12 deficiency, impaired methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity causes methylmalonic acid to accumulate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B12 is required for the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, a step toward myelin synthesis. When B12 is deficient, this step is blocked, methylmalonyl-CoA accumulates, and methylmalonic acid rises. This explains both the neurologic findings (subacute combined degeneration) and the elevated MMA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Methionine is produced by the B12-dependent methionine synthase reaction, so it falls, not rises, in B12 deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Succinyl-CoA is the product downstream of the blocked mutase reaction, so it would decrease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tetrahydrofolate levels drop in B12 deficiency because folate is trapped as methyl-THF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 itself is low, since deficiency is the underlying problem.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is found to have a hemoglobin of 9.0 g/dL, an MCV of 110 fL, glossitis, and decreased vibration sense with an unsteady gait. Two weeks ago he was empirically started on oral folic acid. If his true underlying deficiency is vitamin B12, which of the following outcomes is most likely at follow-up?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Improvement of both the anemia and neurologic symptoms

choices.label: B
choices.text: Improvement of the anemia but unchanged neurologic symptoms

choices.label: C
choices.text: No change in the anemia or neurologic symptoms

choices.label: D
choices.text: Worsening anemia with improvement of neurologic symptoms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Worsening of both the anemia and neurologic symptoms

explanation.summary: Folic acid can reverse the hematologic abnormalities of B12 deficiency but not the neurologic ones.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that folic acid supplementation alone may reverse the hematologic abnormalities of vitamin B12 deficiency, but it will often not reverse the neurologic symptoms. Therefore the anemia improves while the neurologic deficits persist.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Improvement of both would be expected only if the patient received vitamin B12, which corrects the neurologic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The anemia responds to folate, so at least the hematologic picture improves.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folate improves rather than worsens the anemia, and it does not fix the neurologic deficits.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Folate does not worsen the anemia; it improves it.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with fatigue has a hemoglobin of 8.8 g/dL and an MCV of 114 fL. Which of the following peripheral blood smear findings is most specific for megaloblastic anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microcytic, hypochromic red cells with central pallor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Schistocytes (red cell fragments) with thrombocytopenia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spherocytes with an increased reticulocyte count

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teardrop cells and nucleated red blood cells

explanation.summary: Macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes) are the smear hallmarks of megaloblastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: While simple macrocytes can be seen in other anemias (e.g., heavy alcohol use), oval macrocytes (macro-ovalocytes) and hypersegmented neutrophils with more than five lobes are characteristic of megaloblastic anemia and are not seen in other causes of macrocytosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Microcytic, hypochromic cells point to iron deficiency, the opposite of macrocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Schistocytes indicate microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spherocytes with reticulocytosis suggest hereditary spherocytosis or hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Teardrop cells are seen in myelofibrosis and marrow-infiltrating processes.

questions.stem: A patient with severe vitamin B12 deficiency has a low tetrahydrofolate (THF) level despite adequate dietary folate intake. Which of the following best explains why folate becomes functionally deficient in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excess methionine synthase converts all folate to purines

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate absorption in the duodenum is blocked by antiparietal cell antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate is destroyed by increased gastric acid production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Folate is trapped as methyl-THF because B12 cannot accept its methyl group

choices.label: E
choices.text: Folate stores are depleted within days of B12 deficiency

explanation.summary: The methylfolate trap: without B12, folate is stuck as methyl-THF and cannot be regenerated to usable forms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methyl-THF normally donates its methyl group to vitamin B12, which reactivates the folate. If B12 is deficient, folate is trapped as methyl-THF, so levels of THF and methylene-THF drop and DNA synthesis is impaired even when dietary folate is sufficient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Methionine synthase is impaired, not overactive, when B12 is low.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antiparietal cell antibodies impair B12 (via intrinsic factor), not folate absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B12 deficiency from gastritis decreases gastric acidity; acid does not destroy folate here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Folate stores deplete over 4 to 5 months, not days, and dietary intake here is adequate.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who frequently eats undercooked freshwater fish develops fatigue and paresthesias. Laboratory studies show a macrocytic anemia and a low serum vitamin B12 level. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of his deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ancylostoma duodenale

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diphyllobothrium latum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enterobius vermicularis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Giardia lamblia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Helicobacter pylori

explanation.summary: The fish tapeworm Diphyllobothrium latum competes for vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick specifically lists infection with the fish tapeworm Diphyllobothrium latum, which colonizes the terminal ileum and competes for vitamin B12 uptake, as a cause of B12 deficiency. It is acquired from undercooked fish.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm) classically causes iron deficiency from blood loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) causes perianal itching, not B12 deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Giardia lamblia causes malabsorptive diarrhea, not competitive B12 uptake by a tapeworm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Helicobacter pylori is linked to gastritis and peptic ulcers but is not the B12-competing organism named here.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 8 weeks pregnant is counseled about vitamin supplementation. Adequate intake of which vitamin is most important to reduce the risk of neural tube defects in her infant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vitamin B12

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin C

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin D

explanation.summary: Folate deficiency in early pregnancy raises the risk of neural tube defects, so folate supplementation is essential.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that folate deficiency in women in early pregnancy is associated with a higher risk of neural tube defects, prompting FDA-mandated folate fortification of grain products and prenatal vitamins rich in folate. Pregnancy also increases folate demand due to high cell proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron prevents iron deficiency anemia but does not prevent neural tube defects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes neurologic disease and macrocytic anemia but is not the vitamin tied to neural tube defect prevention here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin C is not implicated in neural tube defects in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin D relates to bone metabolism, not neural tube defects.

questions.stem: A patient with folate deficiency has a bone marrow biopsy showing large erythroid progenitor cells with immature nuclear chromatin despite a mature-appearing cytoplasm. Which of the following best describes the mechanism producing these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clonal proliferation of a single malignant precursor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defective hemoglobin synthesis with normal nuclear maturation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired DNA synthesis with preserved RNA and protein synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron sequestration limiting heme production

choices.label: E
choices.text: Membrane skeletal protein defect causing premature cell lysis

explanation.summary: Megaloblastic changes result from impaired DNA synthesis while RNA/protein synthesis continues, causing nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony and ineffective erythropoiesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Deficiency of B12 or folate disrupts DNA synthesis and impedes cell division, but the cytoplasm keeps growing because RNA and protein (hemoglobin) synthesis remain normal. This nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony leads to ineffective erythropoiesis and the large precursors with immature chromatin seen on marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonal malignant proliferation describes leukemia, not vitamin-deficiency megaloblastosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Megaloblastic anemia is a defect of DNA synthesis (nucleus), not primarily of hemoglobin synthesis; cytoplasmic hemoglobin synthesis is actually preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron sequestration describes anemia of chronic disease, not megaloblastic changes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A membrane protein defect describes hereditary spherocytosis, not megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman has a macrocytic anemia. Serum studies show an elevated homocysteine level but a normal methylmalonic acid (MMA) level. Which of the following deficiencies best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combined B12 and folate deficiency with neurologic disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Copper deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency

explanation.summary: Folate deficiency elevates homocysteine but leaves methylmalonic acid normal; B12 deficiency raises both.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both homocysteine and MMA are high in vitamin B12 deficiency because B12 is needed for both the methionine synthase reaction and the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reaction. Folate participates only in the homocysteine-to-methionine pathway, so folate deficiency raises homocysteine while MMA stays normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Combined deficiency with neurologic disease implies B12 involvement, which would raise MMA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Copper deficiency can cause macrocytosis but is not characterized by isolated homocysteine elevation with normal MMA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency causes a microcytic anemia and does not elevate homocysteine or MMA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency would elevate both homocysteine and MMA, but this patient has a normal MMA.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and a proton pump inhibitor is found to have a hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL and an MCV of 104 fL. Serum vitamin B12 is low. Which of the following best explains how his medications contributed to the deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They destroy gastric parietal cells through autoantibodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: They increase renal excretion of vitamin B12

choices.label: C
choices.text: They inhibit conversion of folate to its active form

choices.label: D
choices.text: They inhibit folate absorption in the duodenum

choices.label: E
choices.text: They interfere with intestinal absorption of vitamin B12

explanation.summary: Metformin, H2 blockers, and proton pump inhibitors interfere with intestinal absorption of vitamin B12.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists metformin, H2 blockers, and proton pump inhibitors as drugs that interfere with vitamin B12 absorption, which can lead to deficiency over time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoantibody destruction of parietal cells is the mechanism of pernicious anemia, not of these drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These drugs impair absorption rather than increase renal excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting conversion of folate to its active form describes methotrexate and trimethoprim, which affect folate, not B12.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting duodenal folate absorption describes phenytoin and affects folate, not B12.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with heavy alcohol use has an MCV of 104 fL but normal serum vitamin B12 and folate levels, a normal MMA, and no hypersegmented neutrophils on smear. Which of the following best characterizes his macrocytosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemolytic anemia with schistocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Macrocytic anemia that is not megaloblastic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Megaloblastic anemia due to occult B12 deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microcytic anemia from chronic blood loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pure red cell aplasia

explanation.summary: A high MCV is not diagnostic alone; macrocytic anemia can occur without megaloblastic changes, as with heavy alcohol use.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that a high MCV is not diagnostic by itself because macrocytic anemia can occur without megaloblastic anemia, with causes including heavy alcohol use, copper deficiency, hypothyroidism, and myelodysplastic neoplasms. Normal B12, folate, and MMA plus absence of hypersegmented neutrophils argue against a megaloblastic process. Note that severe macrocytosis (MCV >115 fL) is what is commonly seen only in megaloblastic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There are no schistocytes or hemolytic features described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Occult B12 deficiency would typically show a low B12 or elevated MMA and hypersegmented neutrophils, none of which are present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic blood loss causes microcytosis, not the macrocytosis seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pure red cell aplasia (e.g., Diamond-Blackfan) is a congenital erythroid aplasia, not alcohol-related macrocytosis in an adult.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with pernicious anemia is started on vitamin B12 replacement. Which of the following is the most appropriate route and duration of therapy given the cause of her deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single high-dose oral course of folic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intramuscular folic acid until the MCV returns to normal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intramuscular vitamin B12, often required for life

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral ferrous sulfate supplementation for 3 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral vitamin B12 for 2 weeks, then discontinuation

explanation.summary: When B12 deficiency is due to impaired GI absorption such as pernicious anemia, the intramuscular route is required, often lifelong.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that B12 replacement can be oral or intramuscular, but if the deficiency is due to impaired GI absorption (e.g., pernicious anemia), the intramuscular route is required and patients may need supplemental B12 for life because they cannot absorb it enterally.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folic acid does not correct B12 deficiency and can mask it while neurologic disease progresses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folic acid, by any route, does not replace vitamin B12 in pernicious anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron does not treat a B12 deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oral B12 is ineffective when GI absorption is impaired, and short-term therapy would not maintain levels.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has followed a strict vegan diet for 8 years, avoiding meat, fish, eggs, cheese, and dairy. He eats generous amounts of grains, fruits, and green vegetables. He reports 4 months of fatigue and tingling in his feet. Hemoglobin is 10.6 g/dL, MCV is 109 fL, and the smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Deficiency of which of the following is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copper

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B12

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin C

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12 comes from animal products, so a strict vegan diet can produce B12 deficiency while folate intake remains adequate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Common dietary sources of vitamin B12 are animal liver, meat, fish, cheese, dairy, and eggs, and strict vegan or fad diets lacking these can cause or worsen deficiency. The macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils plus paresthesias fits vitamin B12 deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Copper deficiency can cause macrocytosis, but it is not produced by avoiding animal products and does not cause hypersegmented neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate is supplied by grains, fruits, and vegetables, all of which this patient eats in abundance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency produces a microcytic anemia rather than the macrocytosis seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin C deficiency does not impair DNA synthesis or cause megaloblastic changes.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman who underwent gastric bypass surgery 2 years ago reports fatigue and painful sores inside her mouth. She has no numbness, tingling, or gait disturbance. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL and MCV is 106 fL. Deficiency of which of the following is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copper

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B12

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin D

explanation.summary: Gastric bypass surgery is a specific cause of folate deficiency, which produces megaloblastic anemia and oral ulcers without neurologic findings.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastric bypass surgery is listed among the specific causes of folate deficiency. Folate deficiency causes oral ulcers because the rapidly dividing oral mucosa cannot renew itself when DNA synthesis drops, and folate deficiency is usually not associated with neurologic symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Copper deficiency is a cause of macrocytosis without megaloblastic change and is not linked to gastric bypass or oral ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency causes microcytosis, not the macrocytic anemia described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency characteristically adds neurologic deficits such as numbness and gait disturbance, which are absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin D deficiency affects bone metabolism and does not cause megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has a macrocytic anemia and reports several weeks of a painful, swollen, tender tongue. Which of the following conclusions about his deficiency is best supported by the tongue finding alone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It does not distinguish vitamin B12 from folate deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: It indicates a drug cause rather than a vitamin deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: It indicates folate deficiency rather than vitamin B12 deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: It indicates pernicious anemia rather than another cause

choices.label: E
choices.text: It indicates vitamin B12 deficiency rather than folate deficiency

explanation.summary: Glossitis occurs in both vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, so it does not separate the two.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glossitis, described as tongue pain, swelling, and tenderness, can be seen in both vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies. Distinguishing the two requires serum vitamin levels, and in vitamin B12 deficiency the presence of neurologic deficits.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glossitis is a manifestation of the vitamin deficiency itself, not a marker of a drug cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glossitis is not specific to folate deficiency; it occurs with vitamin B12 deficiency as well.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pernicious anemia is one cause of vitamin B12 deficiency, but glossitis does not identify the underlying cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glossitis is not specific to vitamin B12 deficiency; it occurs with folate deficiency as well.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the epidemiology of megaloblastic anemia caused by vitamin B12 and folate deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It accounts for about 20% of all anemia cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is more common in patients older than 40 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is most common in children younger than 10 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurs with equal frequency at every age

choices.label: E
choices.text: The number of new cases per year is rising

explanation.summary: Megaloblastic anemia is more common after age 40 because the prevalence of vitamin B12 and folate deficiency rises with age.
explanation.whyCorrect: The prevalence of these vitamin deficiencies increases with age, so megaloblastic anemia is more common in patients older than 40 years. Together, vitamin B12 and folate deficiency account for about 2% of all anemia cases, and the deficiencies are rare in children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The two deficiencies together account for roughly 2% of anemia cases, not 20%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These deficiencies are rare in children rather than most common in them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Frequency is not uniform across ages; it climbs with increasing age.
whyWrongByChoice.E: New cases per year are decreasing because of vitamin supplementation in pregnant and older patients.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL and MCV is 112 fL. The peripheral smear shows macro-ovalocytes and neutrophils with six-lobed nuclei, confirming megaloblastic anemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine the cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin empiric intramuscular vitamin B12

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measure serum ferritin and iron-binding capacity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Measure serum vitamin B12 and folate levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obtain hemoglobin electrophoresis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perform a bone marrow biopsy

explanation.summary: Once megaloblastic anemia is established, the next step is measuring serum vitamin B12 and folate levels; a low level of either or both makes the diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the diagnosis of megaloblastic anemia is made on the CBC and smear, serum studies of vitamin B12 and folate identify which deficiency is responsible. A low level of either or both establishes the cause and directs replacement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Treating before measuring levels would obscure whether the deficiency is vitamin B12 or folate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron studies evaluate microcytic anemia and would not identify the vitamin deficiency causing macrocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin electrophoresis evaluates hemoglobinopathies, not vitamin deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bone marrow biopsy is not routinely done to diagnose megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman is found to have megaloblastic anemia with a hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL. Which of the following groups of symptoms is she most likely to report?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fever, night sweats, and enlarged lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Joint swelling, morning stiffness, and skin rash

choices.label: C
choices.text: No symptoms, because anemia of any severity is silent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polyuria, polydipsia, and unintentional weight loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shortness of breath, weakness, dizziness, and tachycardia

explanation.summary: Moderate-to-severe anemia of any type causes shortness of breath, fatigue, weakness, dizziness or lightheadedness, and tachycardia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most patients with mild anemia are asymptomatic, but patients with moderate-to-severe anemia may experience shortness of breath, fatigue, weakness, dizziness or lightheadedness, and tachycardia. Her hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL places her in that range.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fever, night sweats, and lymphadenopathy suggest infection or lymphoma, not vitamin deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Joint swelling and morning stiffness point to inflammatory arthritis rather than anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only mild anemia is usually asymptomatic; moderate-to-severe anemia produces symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These are symptoms of hyperglycemia and are unrelated to megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: In contrast to vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency most often results from which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the gastric parietal cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competition for the vitamin by an intestinal tapeworm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deficient pancreatic enzymes needed to free the vitamin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of intrinsic factor-mediated intestinal absorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inadequate dietary intake, frequently combined with ethanol use

explanation.summary: Folate deficiency is mainly a problem of dietary deficiency and ethanol, whereas vitamin B12 deficiency is mainly a problem of malabsorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: For folate, the main cause of deficiency is dietary deficiency and ethanol, and malabsorption is rare. For vitamin B12 the situation is reversed: malabsorption is the main cause and dietary deficiency is rare.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antiparietal cell autoimmunity is the mechanism of pernicious anemia, a vitamin B12 disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphyllobothrium latum competes for vitamin B12 uptake in the terminal ileum, not for folate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pancreatic enzymes are required to free vitamin B12 from transcobalamin, not to absorb folate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of intrinsic factor impairs vitamin B12 absorption, not folate absorption.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with epilepsy has taken phenytoin for 2 years. She now has a hemoglobin of 10.4 g/dL and an MCV of 105 fL. Serum folate is low and serum vitamin B12 is normal. Which of the following best explains the effect of her medication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It accelerates renal clearance of circulating folate

choices.label: B
choices.text: It destroys gastric parietal cells over time

choices.label: C
choices.text: It displaces folate from hepatic storage sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits conversion of folate to its active form

choices.label: E
choices.text: It inhibits folate absorption in the duodenum

explanation.summary: Anti-epileptic drugs such as phenytoin cause folate deficiency by inhibiting folate absorption in the duodenum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenytoin is listed among the medications that cause folate deficiency, and its mechanism is inhibition of folate absorption in the duodenum. The result is a folate-deficient megaloblastic anemia with a normal vitamin B12 level.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased renal clearance is not the described mechanism for any of the drugs that cause folate deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Destruction of parietal cells is the autoimmune mechanism of pernicious anemia, which affects vitamin B12.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Displacement from hepatic stores is not a described mechanism of drug-induced folate deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking conversion of folate to its active form is the mechanism of the antimetabolites methotrexate and trimethoprim.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease has been taking hydroxyurea for 1 year. His MCV is 108 fL. Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels are both normal. Which of the following best explains the megaloblastic changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydroxyurea blocks folate absorption in the duodenum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydroxyurea blocks intestinal absorption of vitamin B12

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydroxyurea destroys gastric parietal cells directly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydroxyurea increases urinary excretion of folate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hydroxyurea inhibits DNA synthesis in marrow precursors

explanation.summary: Several drugs, including hydroxyurea, chemotherapy, and antiretroviral agents, cause megaloblastic anemia by directly inhibiting DNA synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Apart from vitamin deficiencies, several drugs inhibit DNA synthesis and cause megaloblastic anemia; these most commonly include chemotherapy and antiretroviral drugs and hydroxyurea, which is used for sickle cell disease. Because the block is at DNA synthesis itself, vitamin levels are normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhibition of duodenal folate absorption is the mechanism of phenytoin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metformin, H2 blockers, and proton pump inhibitors interfere with vitamin B12 absorption; hydroxyurea does not.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parietal cell destruction is the autoimmune mechanism of pernicious anemia, not a drug effect of hydroxyurea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased urinary folate loss is not a described mechanism of drug-induced megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with a chronic hemolytic anemia and a persistently high rate of red blood cell destruction develops fatigue. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL and MCV is 107 fL, and her serum folate is low. Her diet has not changed and is reported as adequate. Which of the following best explains her folate deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatic vitamin B12 stores are consumed within weeks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased red cell production raises folate demand

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intrinsic factor secretion falls as hemolysis progresses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ongoing hemolysis directly destroys circulating folate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration removes folate from the plasma

explanation.summary: Conditions that increase cell proliferation, such as chronic hemolytic anemia, can cause folate deficiency even when intake is sufficient.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because body folate reserves are not large, conditions that increase cell proliferation and require rapid use of folate for DNA synthesis can cause deficiency even when folate intake is adequate. Chronic hemolytic anemias qualify because red cell synthesis must increase to meet the demand of ongoing red cell loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatic vitamin B12 stores take years to deplete, and her deficiency is of folate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intrinsic factor relates to vitamin B12 absorption and is not affected by hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemolysis creates demand through accelerated erythropoiesis; it does not destroy folate in the circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration removes blood cells, not the vitamin itself.

questions.stem: Vitamin B12 serves as a cofactor for which of the following reactions that is required for DNA synthesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of adenosine to guanosine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of branched-chain amino acids to myelin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conversion of homocysteine to methionine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conversion of thymidine to methylene-THF

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12 is the cofactor for methionine synthase, which converts homocysteine to methionine, and methionine is required for DNA synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for the conversion of homocysteine to methionine by methionine synthase, and methionine is required for DNA synthesis. In donating its methyl group, vitamin B12 becomes inactive and must be reactivated by methyl-THF.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenosine and guanosine are purines synthesized with folate; vitamin B12 does not interconvert them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Branched-chain amino acids feed into methylmalonyl-CoA; they are not converted directly to myelin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This vitamin B12-dependent step, catalyzed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, leads toward myelin synthesis rather than DNA synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymidine is a product of the folate pathway, synthesized using methylene-THF, not a substrate that regenerates it.

questions.stem: Folate is required in which of the following forms to synthesize thymidine, one of the building blocks of DNA?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folate bound to intrinsic factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folate bound to transcobalamin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate complexed with methylmalonyl-CoA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methyl-tetrahydrofolate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Methylene-tetrahydrofolate

explanation.summary: Methylene-THF is the folate form used to make thymidine; folate is also needed to synthesize the purines adenosine and guanosine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Folate is needed in the form of methylene-THF to synthesize thymidine, one of the building blocks of DNA, and it is also needed to synthesize the purines adenosine and guanosine. In vitamin B12 deficiency, folate is trapped as methyl-THF and levels of methylene-THF fall, impairing DNA synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intrinsic factor is required for intestinal absorption of vitamin B12, not for folate function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transcobalamin is the protector protein for vitamin B12, not a carrier for folate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methylmalonyl-CoA is a substrate in the vitamin B12-dependent mutase reaction and does not complex with folate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methyl-THF is the form that donates its methyl group to vitamin B12; it is not the form used for thymidine synthesis.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with untreated vitamin B12 deficiency has decreased sensation in his legs, an ataxic gait, and brisk deep-tendon reflexes. Damage to which of the following groups of structures best accounts for this combination of findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anterior horn cells, ventral roots, and neuromuscular junctions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Basal ganglia, subthalamic nuclei, and thalamic relay nuclei

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cerebellar vermis, dentate nuclei, and middle cerebellar peduncles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal and spinocerebellar tracts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Optic nerves, optic chiasm, and lateral geniculate nuclei

explanation.summary: Subacute combined degeneration damages the dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts, producing sensory deficits, ataxia, and hyperreflexia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord is seen in vitamin B12 deficiency, in which the spinal cord dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts are damaged. This produces exactly the described triad of sensory deficits, ataxia, and hyperreflexia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lower motor unit involvement would cause weakness with decreased rather than increased reflexes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Basal ganglia and thalamic lesions are not the substrate of subacute combined degeneration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isolated cerebellar damage would cause ataxia without the sensory loss and hyperreflexia described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Visual disturbances have been described in vitamin B12 deficiency, but the visual pathway does not produce ataxia or hyperreflexia.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with a hemoglobin of 9.5 g/dL and an MCV of 108 fL has several painful ulcers of the buccal mucosa. Her serum folate is low. Which of the following best explains the oral ulcers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against oral squamous epithelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial overgrowth from decreased gastric acidity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the oral mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired renewal of rapidly dividing oral mucosal cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Microvascular thrombosis of submucosal oral capillaries

explanation.summary: Folate deficiency causes oral ulcers because the rapidly dividing oral mucosa cannot keep up when DNA synthesis is impaired.
explanation.whyCorrect: Folate deficiency can cause oral ulcers because of the rapid division of the oral mucosa, which drops with decreased DNA synthesis. The same impaired DNA synthesis accounts for the macrocytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoantibodies in this disease are directed against parietal cells and intrinsic factor, not oral epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased gastric acidity occurs in pernicious anemia and affects vitamin B12 absorption, not the oral mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unconjugated bilirubin may rise from ineffective erythropoiesis, but it is not deposited as mucosal ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microvascular thrombosis is a feature of microangiopathic processes, which produce schistocytes rather than ulcers.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is evaluated for anemia and has an MCV of 121 fL. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of this degree of macrocytosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It effectively rules out a vitamin deficiency as the cause

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is seen almost only in megaloblastic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the pattern typically produced by copper deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the pattern typically produced by heavy alcohol use

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the pattern typically produced by hypothyroidism

explanation.summary: Severe macrocytosis with an MCV above 115 fL is commonly seen only in megaloblastic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: A high MCV alone is not diagnostic, because macrocytic anemia can occur without megaloblastic anemia. However, severe macrocytosis, defined as an MCV greater than 115 fL, is commonly seen only in megaloblastic anemia, so this value strongly points to a vitamin B12 or folate problem.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin deficiency becomes more likely, not less, at this MCV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Copper deficiency is among the non-megaloblastic causes of macrocytosis and does not typically reach this level.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heavy alcohol use causes macrocytosis, but not typically an MCV above 115 fL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypothyroidism causes macrocytosis, but not typically this severe a degree.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with megaloblastic anemia has a white blood cell count of 3,100/mm3 and a platelet count of 95,000/mm3 in addition to a hemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL. Which of the following best explains these additional cytopenias?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against leukocytes and platelets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumption of platelets and leukocytes in microvascular thrombi

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dilution of all cell lines by an expanded plasma volume

choices.label: D
choices.text: Poor bone marrow production of white cell and platelet precursors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration of circulating white cells and platelets

explanation.summary: Low white blood cell and platelet counts in megaloblastic anemia reflect poor bone marrow precursor production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Impaired DNA synthesis affects all rapidly dividing marrow lineages, not just erythroid cells. Other CBC findings in megaloblastic anemia therefore include low white blood cell or platelet counts due to poor bone marrow precursor production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The autoantibodies relevant here target parietal cells and intrinsic factor, not blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Microvascular consumption occurs in microangiopathic disease, which shows schistocytes on smear.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma volume expansion does not explain a marrow process that also produces macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration is not a described mechanism of the cytopenias in megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with megaloblastic anemia has additional laboratory studies suggesting accelerated red blood cell turnover. Which of the following patterns is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased LDH, increased haptoglobin, increased conjugated bilirubin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased haptoglobin, decreased LDH, decreased unconjugated bilirubin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased LDH, decreased unconjugated bilirubin, increased haptoglobin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased LDH, increased unconjugated bilirubin, decreased haptoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal LDH, normal haptoglobin, increased conjugated bilirubin

explanation.summary: Megaloblastic anemia can produce laboratory evidence of hemolysis: increased LDH and unconjugated bilirubin with decreased haptoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with megaloblastic anemia may also have laboratory studies suggestive of hemolysis, specifically increased LDH and unconjugated bilirubin with a decreased haptoglobin. This reflects destruction of the defective cells produced by ineffective hematopoiesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemolysis raises unconjugated rather than conjugated bilirubin and lowers haptoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Each value moves in the direction opposite to that expected with hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Haptoglobin falls rather than rises, and bilirubin rises rather than falls, with hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An entirely normal LDH and haptoglobin would argue against the hemolytic pattern described.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with megaloblastic anemia undergoes bone marrow biopsy as part of an evaluation for another indication. Which of the following findings is most likely on the specimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fibrotic marrow with clustered, abnormally shaped megakaryocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypercellular marrow with enlarged erythroid and myeloid precursors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypocellular marrow with fatty replacement and few precursors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marrow replaced by sheets of clonal, malignant-appearing blasts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normocellular marrow with absent erythroid precursors only

explanation.summary: The marrow in megaloblastic anemia is hypercellular with increased enlarged erythroid and myeloid precursors, increased megakaryocytes, and dysplastic erythroblasts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although bone marrow biopsy is not routinely done, the marrow in megaloblastic anemia is hypercellular in appearance, with increased numbers of enlarged erythroid and myeloid precursors and megakaryocytes. Dysplastic erythroblasts with abnormally shaped nuclei can also be seen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow fibrosis is a feature of myelofibrosis, which produces teardrop cells on smear.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A hypocellular, fatty marrow describes aplastic anemia rather than megaloblastic change.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sheets of clonal blasts indicate leukemia, not a vitamin-deficiency state.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absence of erythroid precursors alone describes pure red cell aplasia, as in Diamond-Blackfan anemia.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has eaten a diet essentially devoid of both animal products and green vegetables for the past 5 months after a job loss. He was previously well nourished. He now has a hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL and an MCV of 104 fL. Which of the following is most likely on serum testing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low folate with a normal vitamin B12 level

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low folate with an elevated methylmalonic acid level

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low vitamin B12 and low folate levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low vitamin B12 with a normal folate level

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal vitamin B12 and normal folate levels

explanation.summary: Folate deficiency can appear after only 4 to 5 months of a folate-depleted diet, whereas hepatic vitamin B12 stores take years to deplete.
explanation.whyCorrect: The liver has a large store of vitamin B12, which typically takes years of poor intake or absorption to deplete. Folate deficiency, by contrast, may present with only 4 to 5 months of a folate-depleted diet, so at 5 months this patient should be folate deficient with a still-normal vitamin B12.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Methylmalonic acid rises in vitamin B12 deficiency and remains normal in isolated folate deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate would be low, but vitamin B12 would still be supported by hepatic stores.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin B12 stores would not be exhausted after only 5 months of poor intake.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Five months of a folate-depleted diet is enough to produce folate deficiency and macrocytosis.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with Crohn disease is found to have a folate-deficient megaloblastic anemia and is prescribed oral folic acid. Eight weeks later her hemoglobin and MCV are unchanged, and she confirms she has taken every dose. Which of the following best explains the treatment failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crohn disease is malabsorptive, so parenteral therapy is needed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Crohn disease markedly increases renal excretion of folate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folic acid must be freed by pancreatic enzymes before uptake

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gastric acid inactivates oral folic acid before it is absorbed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral folic acid requires intrinsic factor for its uptake

explanation.summary: In malabsorptive disease such as Crohn disease, oral vitamin supplements are ineffective and parenteral supplementation must be used.
explanation.whyCorrect: Crohn disease is one of the gastrointestinal malabsorption syndromes that impair intestinal vitamin absorption. Because oral vitamin supplements are not effective when the absorptive surface is diseased, parenteral supplementation is used instead.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased renal folate loss is not a described feature of Crohn disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pancreatic enzymes free vitamin B12 from transcobalamin; this is unrelated to folic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastric acid inactivation is not a described cause of folate replacement failure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intrinsic factor is required for vitamin B12 absorption, not for folate absorption.

questions.stem: In the vitamin B12-dependent reaction catalyzed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, the substrate methylmalonyl-CoA is generated by the metabolism of which of the following, and the pathway ultimately supports production of which product?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fatty acids and branched-chain amino acids; myelin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose and glycogen; hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heme and unconjugated bilirubin; haptoglobin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homocysteine and methionine; tetrahydrofolate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Purine and pyrimidine nucleotides; thymidine

explanation.summary: Fatty acids and branched-chain amino acids yield methylmalonyl-CoA, which vitamin B12 and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase convert to succinyl-CoA on the path to myelin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fatty acids and branched-chain amino acids are metabolized to methylmalonyl-CoA. Vitamin B12 is required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase to convert it to succinyl-CoA, a step toward myelin synthesis, which is why deficiency produces neurologic deficits and accumulation of methylmalonic acid.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbohydrate metabolism does not generate methylmalonyl-CoA, and hemoglobin is not the product of this pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heme breakdown products relate to hemolysis labs, not to the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Homocysteine and methionine belong to the methionine synthase reaction, which regenerates tetrahydrofolate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide synthesis, including thymidine, depends on folate rather than on the mutase pathway.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man has 4 months of progressive numbness in his feet and an unsteady gait. Hemoglobin is 13.8 g/dL, MCV is 91 fL, and the peripheral smear is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folate deficiency better explains isolated neurologic findings

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematologic and neurologic severity correlate closely in this disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neurologic disease from vitamin B12 deficiency follows severe anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal indices exclude vitamin B12 deficiency as the cause

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause neurologic disease without anemia

explanation.summary: The absence of anemia or macrocytosis does not exclude neurologic disease due to vitamin B12 deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: There is a poor correlation between neurologic and hematologic changes in vitamin B12 deficiency. Neurologic manifestations may be present without macrocytosis or anemia, so a normal CBC and smear do not rule out vitamin B12 deficiency in a patient with compatible neurologic findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate deficiency is usually not associated with neurologic symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The correlation between the hematologic and neurologic manifestations is poor, not close.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neurologic disease can precede or occur without any hematologic abnormality.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Normal indices specifically do not exclude vitamin B12-related neurologic disease.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old infant has a progressive macrocytic anemia with a low reticulocyte count. The white blood cell and platelet counts are normal. Examination shows craniofacial abnormalities, triphalangeal thumbs, and growth failure. Which of the following best distinguishes this disorder from aplastic anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It affects only the red cell line rather than all cell lines

choices.label: B
choices.text: It carries no increased predisposition to later malignancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is acquired in infancy rather than congenital in origin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It produces microcytic rather than macrocytic red cell indices

choices.label: E
choices.text: It responds fully to intramuscular vitamin B12 replacement

explanation.summary: Diamond-Blackfan anemia is a pure red cell aplasia, whereas aplastic anemia decreases all cell lines and causes pancytopenia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diamond-Blackfan anemia presents in infancy as a congenital erythroid aplasia with progressive macrocytic anemia, reticulocytopenia, and congenital abnormalities such as craniofacial abnormalities, triphalangeal thumbs, growth failure, and developmental delays. In contrast to aplastic anemia, which decreases all cell lines and leads to pancytopenia, it causes a pure red cell aplasia affecting only the red cell line.

whyWrongByChoice.B: It is associated with cancer predisposition, including leukemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, and osteosarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diamond-Blackfan anemia is a congenital disorder presenting in infancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The anemia is progressively macrocytic, which is why it appears on the macrocytic differential.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It is an erythroid aplasia, not a vitamin deficiency, so vitamin B12 replacement does not correct it.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant and has well-controlled HIV infection is found to have a serum vitamin B12 level slightly below the reference range on routine screening. She is asymptomatic. Hemoglobin, MCV, and peripheral smear are normal, and serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are both normal. Which of the following best explains her laboratory results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antiparietal cell antibodies are interfering with the assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatic vitamin B12 stores have been depleted by the pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Multiple myeloma is falsely raising her vitamin B12 level

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pregnancy and HIV infection can falsely lower measured vitamin B12

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal disease is falsely raising her methylmalonic acid level

explanation.summary: Pregnancy, multiple myeloma, and HIV infection can falsely lower serum vitamin B12 levels, which is why low values are confirmed with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pregnancy, multiple myeloma, and HIV infection can falsely lower vitamin B12 levels, while renal or liver disease and some malignancies can falsely raise them. Because of these accuracy concerns, low vitamin B12 levels are confirmed with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, both of which should be high in true deficiency; here both are normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antiparietal cell antibodies cause real vitamin B12 deficiency through parietal cell destruction rather than assay interference.
whyWrongByChoice.B: True depletion of the large hepatic vitamin B12 store takes years and would raise methylmalonic acid and homocysteine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multiple myeloma is among the conditions that falsely lower vitamin B12, and she has no evidence of myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal disease falsely raises vitamin B12 rather than methylmalonic acid, and her methylmalonic acid is normal.
